\section[{Source 18: Results, scope, and their relation to the source}]{Source 18. Results, scope, and their relation to the source}\label{gsr:fm:18:sec:d1}
\srcnote{18}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Higher-Order Cube Expansions and Sharp Degeneracy Bounds in Gowers' Szemer\'edi Framework / Simultaneous polynomial partitions, exact constants, and quantitative obstructions / Research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; the same in the PDF author field. Archive \file{gowers\_cubes\_degeneracy\_partitions.zip} (arrival \texttt{82bc38a30}), manuscript \file{gowers\_cubes\_degeneracy\_partitions.tex} (2,672 lines, 35 pages), pin \texttt{dca9f0638} (its \file{provenance.json}, shipped as \file{data/18-arrangement-degeneracy-provenance.json}). Printed below: the abstract, its keywords and Section~1; Section~2 is in Part~II (with source~19, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sections1516}), Section~3 in Part~III, Sections~4--5 in Part~I, Sections~6--9 and Appendix~A in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash T} ($\R/\Z$) is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash Tcirc} (the report's $\T$ is the same circle written $\mathbb T$).}
\begin{partabstract}{18}
We develop three explicit refinements of the local machinery in Gowers'
\emph{A new proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem}. First, for the full definition of
degeneracy in Section~15, we determine the sharp first-order density of
degenerate $d$-arrangements. For fixed $k\ge1$, $d\ge2$ and primes $p\to\infty$,
this density is $(k+C_d)/p+O_{k,d}(p^{-2})$, where
$C_d=\tfrac12(T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1)$ and $T_n$ is a central trinomial
coefficient. In particular $C_8=2\,585\,444$. The proof uses paired horizontal
and vertical moment equations and gives explicit finite bounds and a direct
improvement of the ambient-size hypothesis in Lemma~15.5.
Second, we compute the complete fourth- and fifth-order expansion of real
cube moments in every dimension, over every finite abelian group. The
formula identifies all corrections from characters of orders two and three,
and yields a sharp fourth-order leading bound, including sharpness for
indicator sets. Third, we give an elementary transfer from simultaneous
monomial recurrence to partitions on which several polynomial phases have
small oscillation. Existing recurrence theorems yield a polynomial dependence
on the number of phases in place of the exponential dependence displayed
in Lemma~5.9; a shared-leading-coefficient quadratic family admits a stronger
source-internal specialization. An independent volume argument proves a
necessary exponent frontier for every polynomial degree. Complete proofs,
exact finite checks, a source-level Lean integration plan, and further
research questions are included. These are local mathematical results; the
report does not claim a new global Szemer\'edi bound or priority over the
entire literature.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Gowers norms; Boolean cube circuits; additive
arrangements; polynomial recurrence; finite-field rank; Szemer\'edi's theorem.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:18:sec:overview}

The aim is to improve particular statements in Gowers' proof while retaining
enough information to say exactly what has been gained. The three parts of
this report address different losses: the treatment of exceptional
arrangements in Section~15, the triangle inequality for cube counts in
Section~3, and the repeated refinement of polynomial partitions in
Section~5. Each produces a theorem with a full proof, and each has a
different consequence for the surrounding argument.

Throughout, references such as ``Lemma~15.4'' refer to Gowers'
paper~\cite{gowers}, not to the numbering of the present article. The
repository supplied with the research request contains both a reconstructed
\LaTeX\ source and a substantial Lean development~\cite{repo18}. We read
the relevant source files and compared the formulations with the published
paper. The reconstructed source includes corrections and explicit
hypotheses absent from some printed statements; these are relevant when a
local improvement is substituted into a later lemma.

\subsection{A sharp asymptotic for degenerate arrangements}

A $d$-arrangement in $\F_p^{k+1}$ consists of $2d$ labelled $k$-cubes with
common side vector, whose last coordinates satisfy an additive relation.
It has
\[
 D=(2d+1)k+2d-1
\]
free scalar parameters. There is a universal alternating dependence among
its vertices. Degeneracy means that some other ternary dependence annihilates
every coordinate monomial in the definition. Gowers' Lemma~15.4 bounds the
number of degenerate arrangements by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:old-degeneracy-overview}
 k\,3^{2d\,2^k}p^{D-1}.
\end{equation}
The full definition, rather than the weaker list of tests mentioned after
the lemma, permits the following substantially more precise conclusion:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:sharp-degeneracy-overview}
 \#\{\hbox{degenerate $d$-arrangements}\}
 =(k+C_d)p^{D-1}+O_{k,d}(p^{D-2}),
 \qquad
 C_d=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 T_n=[z^0](z^{-1}+1+z)^n.
\]
The coefficient $k+C_d$ is optimal. Its $k$ part counts zero-side
hyperplanes, and its $C_d$ part counts distinct additional relations among
the last coordinates. Every other kind of certificate contributes only at
second order or smaller. This separation is what the general polynomial
zero estimate in the original proof does not record.

For the $8$-arrangements used later in the proof, put
\[
 M=2^{k+4},\qquad E_k=2^{M+k+3},\qquad
 \lambda=(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k}\beta^{15}.
\]
In the usual range $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$, a sufficient condition for
the degeneracy absorption in Lemma~15.5 is improved from
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:threshold-comparison-overview}
 \lambda p\ge k3^M
 \quad\hbox{to}\quad
 p\ge17,\qquad \lambda p\ge k+2\,585\,445.
\end{equation}
The very large sampling exponent $E_k$ remains the same. Thus the report
improves a specific finite threshold, and identifies its asymptotically
correct first-order coefficient, without attributing a further consequence
to parts of the proof that have not been re-estimated.

\subsection{Exact cube coefficients in every dimension}

For a real function $g$ on a finite abelian group $G$, let
\[
 \mathcal C_\ell(g)=
 \E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_\ell\in G}
 \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^\ell}g(x+v\cdot h)
 =\norm{g}_{U^\ell}^{2^\ell}.
\]
We use $\ell$ here to avoid confusing cube dimension with the arrangement
parameter $d$. If $\E f=0$ and $m=2^\ell$, the first three nonconstant
coefficients in $\mathcal C_\ell(\delta+t f)$ vanish. The fourth coefficient
is an explicit combination of the ordinary Fourier fourth moment and its
restriction to characters of order two. The fifth is a combination of a
five-circuit Fourier correlation and an order-three correction. The four
counting constants are
\begin{align*}
 R_\ell&=\frac{6^\ell-2\cdot4^\ell+2^\ell}{8},&
 B_\ell&=\frac{2^\ell(2^\ell-1)(2^\ell-2)}{24},\\
 Q_\ell&=\frac{8^\ell-3\cdot6^\ell+3\cdot4^\ell-2^\ell}{6},&
 S_\ell&=\frac{10^\ell-4\cdot8^\ell+6\cdot6^\ell-4\cdot4^\ell+2^\ell}{24}.
\end{align*}
These formulas count the relevant four- and five-vertex configurations in
the Boolean cube. Smith normal form explains why only orders two and three
can enter at these orders. The result is valid for every finite abelian
group; excluding small torsion is a corollary, rather than a tacit
assumption in the proof.

For an indicator $\ind_A=\delta+f_A$ with
$\norm{f_A}_{U^\ell}\le\varepsilon$, the resulting estimate begins at
$B_\ell\delta^{m-4}\varepsilon^4$ instead of the linear term in
$(\delta+\varepsilon)^m$. For odd-order groups the fourth coefficient can
be bounded using $R_\ell$ instead. The all-group coefficient $B_\ell$ is
sharp, even along sequences of indicator sets with density tending to any
fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$. The proof first gives an exact order-two-character
example for real weights, and then transfers it to sets by independent
rounding with a quantified Gowers-norm error.

\subsection{Partitions and their quantitative limits}

The polynomial part keeps the near-prescribed lengths of Lemma~5.9:
every cell has length $v-1$ or $v$. It replaces repeated induction on the
number $q$ of phases by an induction on polynomial degree which treats all
$q$ leading coefficients together. A recurrence-radius function is the
only analytic input, so the elementary partition argument can be combined
with either the source's scalar estimate or later simultaneous recurrence
theorems~\cite{maynard,lau}.

For arbitrary quadratic phases, Lau's stated recurrence estimate gives
every strict exponent
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:quad-rate-overview}
 a<\frac{1}{126q^2+129q+2}
\end{equation}
for lengths $v-1,v$ with $v\le r^a$ and containing-arc diameter at most
$r^{-2a}$, once $r$ is sufficiently large. The displayed quadratic case of
Gowers' lemma uses $a=1/(2\cdot2048^q)$. The new conclusion has an
unspecified coefficient-independent threshold inherited from the cited
recurrence theorem. Its numerical exponent should not be confused with a
small or fully numerical threshold for $r$.

For quadratics whose leading coefficients are bounded integer multiples of
one common frequency, the scalar estimate in Gowers' own Lemma~5.5 instead
gives every $a<1/(99q+98)$, with an explicit, though enormous, threshold.
Arbitrary lower coefficients are permitted in this specialization.

There is also a rigorous obstruction. If a universal degree-$k$, $q$-phase
partition theorem guaranteed all cell lengths $\gg r^a$ and all
oscillations $\ll r^{-b}$, with $b>0$, it would necessarily satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:necessary-frontier-overview}
 \left(\frac{qk(k+1)}2+1\right)a+kqb\le1.
\end{equation}
For quadratics and $b=2a$, this says $a\le1/(7q+1)$. The sufficient
$q^{-2}$ rate and this $q^{-1}$ obstruction leave a substantive research
gap. No optimality assertion for the general quadratic partition exponent
is made.

\subsection{What is established, imported, and left open}

The rank arguments, coefficient counts, cube expansion, rounding
sharpness, recurrence-to-partition transfer, and polynomial obstruction
are proved in this article. Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz, Fourier orthogonality,
Smith normal form, and the cited recurrence estimates are established
inputs. The familiar twenty circuits of the three-dimensional cube were
explicitly described in earlier literature, for example
Beerenwinkel--Pachter--Sturmfels~\cite{bps}; the low-dimensional
configuration itself is not presented as a discovery of this report.

The article extends the earlier local calculations to precise
all-dimensional statements and pursues the Section~15 and nonlinear
partition questions further. The statements can be assessed from their
proofs independently of a claim of historical priority. A targeted
literature check does not establish that no equivalent result appears
elsewhere.

Nor does a collection of local improvements establish a new best bound for
Szemer\'edi's theorem. For context, Leng--Sah--Sawhney proved, for each
$k\ge5$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\!\bigl(- (\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),
 \qquad c_k>0,
\]
using quantitative inverse theorems and a density-increment
strategy~\cite{lssbounds}. The results here have a different, explicitly
local purpose. Their value includes sharp information about exceptional
sets, exact spectral expansions, and more effective interchangeable
components for proofs and formalizations.

\subsection{Conventions}

Finite averages are normalized. A finite group has at least one element.
Characters are written additively in the dual group; $j\chi=0$ means that
the character's order divides $j$. A cube is a labelled affine map, so
coincident vertices are included in cube counts. In the arrangement part,
$d\ge2$ is the number of cubes on either side of the additive relation,
and $k\ge1$ is their horizontal dimension. In the partition part, $k$ is
polynomial degree and $q$ is the number of phases. These parameters are
reintroduced at the start of each part. Polynomial oscillation always means
the length of a containing circle arc, as in Gowers' diameter convention.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Source 19: Scope and principal results}]{Source 19. Scope and principal results}\label{gsr:fm:19:sec:d1}\label{gsr:fm:19:sec:scope}
\srcnote{19}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title page.} ``Research article / Additive combinatorics / Efficient Interpolation in Gowers' Szemer\'edi Framework / Exact sampling losses, shared refinements, and simultaneous polynomial recurrence / Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``ChatGPT, research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. Archive \file{gowers\_interpolation\_article.zip} (arrival \texttt{82bc38a30}), manuscript \file{gowers\_interpolation.tex} (2,505 lines, 32 pages), pin \texttt{dca9f0638} (its \file{provenance/source-audit.json}, shipped as \file{data/19-shared-interpolation-source-audit.json}). Printed below: the abstract, the closing statement of its title page and Section~1; Sections~2--5 and~8 are in Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sections1516}), Section~6 in Part~I, Sections~7, 9 and~10 in Part~V. Its `question' environment (printed ``Research question'') is set in this report's `Research question' style; its macro \texttt{\textbackslash commit} (its own pin) is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash commitnineteen}; its \texttt{cleveref} references are written out as cleveref prints them.}
\begin{partabstract}{19}
We strengthen the interpolation mechanism in Section~16 of Gowers' proof
of Szemer\'edi's theorem and give a complementary refinement of its
polynomial phase partition lemma.  A common sample of
$\min\{n,\lceil qd/\sigma\rceil-1\}$ distinct columns recovers all but
$\sigma$ of the ambient mass in any family of partial rows containing
at most $q$ polynomial classes of degree at most $d-1$.  We determine
the exact finite minimax loss by a hypergeometric optimization and prove
its sharp sparse-sampling asymptotic.  For affine interpolation the
constant is $\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}=0.839962094657\ldots$, where
$\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$.  Refining the sampled cross-sections once, before
forming their interpolants, replaces a quadratic number of structural
refinement steps by a linear number and reduces the list count to an
elementary symmetric polynomial in the slice list sizes.  The result
extends to arbitrary fixed degree in the final variable and includes a
proper-box synchronization argument.  Separately, Maynard's established
simultaneous recurrence theorem yields polynomial rather than
exponential dependence on the number of polynomial phases, for fixed
degree.  A self-contained volume obstruction gives a necessary
degree-sensitive frontier for any such partition theorem.  Full written
proofs, exact finite diagnostics, a source audit, and a research agenda
are supplied.  These are local refinements; neither a new global
Szemer\'edi bound nor a new Lean kernel certification is asserted.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent The source comparison is pinned to ProveIt commit\par
\noindent\commitnineteen.\par
\noindent The original 2001 publication and the repository's edited
transcription are distinguished throughout.  The article is a research
report; historical priority for its exact formulations is not claimed.
\end{quote}

The difficult part of the inverse machinery in Gowers' argument is not
merely finding many local affine pieces.  Those pieces must be related
across different fibres, and the resulting descriptions must remain
economical after repeated partitioning.  Section~16 uses sampled
cross-sections and interpolation to make that transition.  This is the
main target of the present article \cite{gowers,repo19paper}.

Two losses can be treated separately.  First, the sampling argument
discards small classes and then insists on a small failure probability
for every remaining class.  Averaging the \emph{mass} of failed classes
gives a better estimate.  Second, once interpolation candidates have
been formed, treating them as independent functions causes the same
sampled data to be refined repeatedly.  A common refinement of the
sampled cross-sections allows all interpolants to be formed afterward.

These changes are independent of the more difficult global inverse
theorem.  They give explicit local statements with transparent inputs,
and they also suggest exact extremal questions.  We solve the finite
sampling optimization for the specified interpolation recovery rule
and identify its sharp asymptotic constant.  A separate part of the
article uses modern recurrence theory to improve the dependence on the
number of phases in Lemma~5.9.

\subsection{The main conclusions at a glance}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\Alph*.}]
\item \textbf{Exact finite sampling loss.}  For an $n$-point column set,
at most $q$ disjoint classes per row, and interpolation order $d$, define
\[
 W_{n,r,d}(s)=\frac{s}{n\binom nr}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,s)-1}\binom{s}{j}\binom{n-s}{r-j}.
\]
The worst possible loss of the best common $r$-column sample is exactly
\[
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)=
 \max_{\substack{s_1,\ldots,s_q\in\Z_{\ge0}\\s_1+\cdots+s_q\le n}}
 \sum_{i=1}^{q} W_{n,r,d}(s_i).
\]
The loss is at most $\min\{1,qd/(r+1)\}$ and is zero for $r=n$.
The equality statement is a genuine finite minimax theorem for the
specified common-anchor recovery mechanism.

\item \textbf{Sharp asymptotic constant.}  For fixed $d$, as
$r\to\infty$, $r/n\to0$, and $q/r\to0$,
\[
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)\sim\frac{qC_d}{r},\qquad
 C_d=\max_{\lambda\ge0}
 \lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}.
\]
In the affine case, $d=2$, this is
$C_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$.  The order $q/\sigma$ is therefore
optimal within this sampling model in the sparse-sampling limit.

\item \textbf{Shared interpolation refinement.}  If the $r$ sampled
cross-sections have list sizes $M_1,\ldots,M_r$ on a common partition,
then all degree-at-most-$d-1$ interpolants require at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}e_j(M_1,\ldots,M_r)
\]
candidate graphs, where $e_j$ is the $j$th elementary symmetric
polynomial.  With a common list size $M$, the affine count is
$rM+\binom r2M^2$.  The partition is refined once per sampled
cross-section, rather than once for every interpolation pair.

\item \textbf{A degree-sensitive recurrence transfer.}  Let $q_j$ count
the phases whose degree is at least $j$, and let $\kappa_j$ be a valid
simultaneous recurrence constant of degree $j$, with $\kappa_1=1$.
Define $F_0=1$, $G_0=0$, and
\[
 F_j=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)F_{j-1},\qquad
 G_j=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)G_{j-1}+\kappa_jq_j.
\]
For $F_ka+G_kb<1$, every sufficiently long integer interval can be
partitioned into progressions of length at least $N^a$ on which all
phase diameters are at most $N^{-b}$.  Maynard's published theorem
supplies the constants; its recurrence assertion is an external input
\cite{maynard}.  For fixed degree, $F_k+G_k=O_k(q^k)$ when $q_j=q$.

\item \textbf{A necessary polynomial frontier.}  If the prescribed
phase degrees are $d_1,\ldots,d_q$, set
$D=\sum_i d_i$ and $S=\sum_i d_i(d_i+1)/2$.  A universal progression
partition with length exponent $a$ and diameter exponent $b$ must satisfy
\[
 (S+1)a+Db\le1.
\]
The proof uses finite differences and a volume estimate, not an
unproved Diophantine approximation conjecture.  For nonlinear phases
the gap between this obstruction and the sufficient frontier remains
open in the present approach.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{How the results differ from earlier project refinements}

This article concentrates on the conversion of fibrewise polynomial
descriptions into compatible descriptions in all variables, and on
simultaneous recurrence for several nonlinear phases.  It does not
repackage the project's earlier cube expansions, energy inequalities,
Bohr extension estimates, or sharp linear phase-density selection
results.  The relevant source targets are Lemmas~16.9--16.10 and the
nonlinear part of Lemma~5.9.  The original and edited source statements,
and the live Lean interfaces, are examined in section~\ref{gsr:fz:19:audit:section}.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{What this ``does not repackage''.} At the pin the report directory held source~04's manuscript as \file{article.tex}; sources~05 and~13 (linear phase partitions) were not visible to this source. Within this report, Section~\ref{gsr:dt:19:sec:d6} meets source~18's Sections~4--5 (the same theorem, proved independently: note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:quadratic-polynomial-q}) and extends source~13's linear results; Sections~\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d5} are new ground: no other source treats Section~16 of the paper.
\end{writenote}


\subsection{Novelty, attribution, and the scope of the conclusions}

The tools used here have substantial precedents.  Missing-mass
optimization and occupancy estimates are established subjects
\cite{missingmass,occupancy}.  Lagrange interpolation, finite averaging,
and common refinement of partitions are classical.  Maynard's
recurrence theorem is imported with attribution; the optional numerical
specialization from Lau is explicitly identified as a preprint input
\cite{maynard,lau}.

The contributions claimed here are the precise finite minimax
formulation, its interpolation-compatible endpoint, the sharp
asymptotic analysis for that model, the more economical lifting theorem,
and the proved recurrence transfer and obstruction.  These results
improve the specified local procedures.  A complete priority search
would be needed before claiming that every individual formulation is
new to the literature.  No well-known open global conjecture is claimed
to be resolved.

For perspective, substantially stronger global bounds than the 2001
estimate are already available.  Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove, for each
$k\ge5$, a bound of the form
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$, where $c_k>0$ and $r_k(N)$
is the largest size of a $k$-term-progression-free subset of $[N]$
\cite{lssbounds}.  The local comparisons here do not improve that result.
More fundamentally, the explicit closing graph-budget comparison in
the supplied Section~16 proof requires repair; reducing a sampling
constant does not discharge it.

\begin{partabstract}{20}
\noindent
We refine the counting stage of Gowers's proof by retaining two functions
through the Cauchy--Schwarz argument. For surjective homomorphisms from a
finite abelian parameter group, the resulting bound is a product of two
directional Gowers seminorms and one ordinary $L^2$ norm. A sharp
finite-index comparison converts the directional norms to global norms,
with explicit constants that record torsion rather than hiding it behind
a prime-modulus hypothesis. A second-order telescoping identity then gives
quadratic, rather than linear, error in the balanced uniformity norm.
For a set of density $\delta$ and admissible $k$-term progressions,
\[
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le B_k(\delta)\,\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1}^{\,2},
 \qquad B_k(\delta)\le \frac{\sqrt\delta}{(1-\delta)^2}.
\]
We give a sharper explicit formula for $B_k$, unequal-density versions,
and supersaturation consequences. An exact quadratic-phase construction,
followed by probabilistic rounding, proves that the exponent two cannot
be increased for three-term counts, even for indicator sets on growing
$\F_{29}$-vector spaces. The article includes proofs, limitations,
10,389 exact finite checks, a formalization plan, and twelve research
questions. The improvements are relative to specified local estimates;
worldwide priority and a new best global Szemer\'edi bound are not asserted.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent Research article and reproducibility package. The supplied proofs are
human-readable mathematical proofs; no new Lean kernel verification is claimed.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:20:sec:intro}

The target is the passage from uniformity to counting in Section~3 of
Gowers's paper \cite{gowers}. In normalized notation, its Theorem~3.2
controls a progression average by the $U^{k-1}$ norm of one function.
Corollary~3.3 expands balanced functions and obtains a counting estimate
with a factor $2^k$. Its hypotheses are asymmetric: the first two sets
need not be uniform. The ProveIt transcription makes the coefficient
invertibility conditions explicit \cite{repo20lean}.

The inspected research article in the repository already improves this
expansion by density-weighted, first-order telescoping \cite{repo20research}.
For a single set $A$ of density $\delta$, that argument gives
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le S_{k-2}(\delta)u,
 \qquad
 u=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1},\quad
 S_{k-2}(\delta)=\sum_{r=0}^{k-3}\delta^r.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:old}
\end{equation}
The improvement developed here is not another reordering of this linear
estimate. We retain a second uniformity factor before estimating the
balanced expansion.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Framing within this report.} The ``inspected research article'' is source~04's delivered manuscript (blob \texttt{45b408f}, staged as \file{article.tex} by \texttt{aefb0b44a} and inspected at the checkpoint \texttt{1bd57e91c}, three minutes before the first write replaced it). Against that text the sentence is accurate. But the quadratic estimate is not new in this report: source~06's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:homogeneous} proves $|\Lambda-\delta^k|\le\sqrt\delta\,B^{(06)}_k(\delta)\varepsilon^2$ with the same norm, and its Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:three-term} the sharp three-term coefficient $\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$, which is this source's $B_3$. Source~06 was placed (\texttt{ad37962c4}) as a merge member whose manuscript was not staged, so this source could not see it; the two are independent. New here: a coefficient strictly smaller than source~06's for every $k\ge3$ and $0<\delta<1$ (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric}), the generality of surjective homomorphisms with torsion constants, the sharp finite-index comparison, the pair correction, and quadratic sharpness at fixed density for indicator sets.
\end{writenote}


\subsection{A concrete statement to keep in view}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, $|G|=N$, and let
\[
 \La_k(a)=\E_{x,y\in G}\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}a(x+ry).
\]
Call the progression system \emph{admissible} when multiplication by every
integer $1,\ldots,k-1$ is an automorphism of $G$. In a cyclic group this
means $\gcd(N,(k-1)!)=1$, not necessarily that $N$ is prime.

For $0<\delta<1$, write $\sigma=\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$ and define
\begin{align}
 R_m(\delta)
 &=\min\left\{\sqrt\delta,
       \sigma\frac{1-\delta^m}{1-\delta}\right\},\qquad m\ge1,
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:Rm-intro}\\
 B_k(\delta)
 &=\sum_{j=2}^{k-1}(j-1)\delta^{j-2}R_{k-j}(\delta).
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-intro}
\end{align}
We prove
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}\le B_k(\delta)u^2.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline}
\end{equation}
The coefficient is explicit, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 B_3(\delta)=\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)},\qquad
 B_k(\delta)\le\frac{\sqrt\delta}{(1-\delta)^2}.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-simple}
\end{equation}
For $0<\delta\le1/2$ there is the simpler exact expression
\begin{equation}
 B_k(\delta)
 =\sqrt\delta\sum_{r=0}^{k-4}(r+1)\delta^r
 +(k-2)\delta^{k-3}\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-small}
\end{equation}
An empty sum, here and below, is zero. The cases $\delta=0,1$ have zero
error and are treated separately.

The two estimates \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:old} and \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline} can be used
together by taking their minimum. The quadratic estimate is particularly
useful when $u$ is small. It requires uniformity at two marked positions
in each surviving term. Consequently it is a strengthening for the
symmetric counting problem, not a replacement of the asymmetric
Corollary~3.3 under unchanged hypotheses.

\subsection{What is proved, and what remains distinct}

The principal structural result is Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two}, for arbitrary
surjective homomorphisms of finite abelian groups. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index}
determines the optimal constant in a directional-to-global norm
comparison for every fixed tuple of subgroups. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:count}
and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric} give the counting refinements.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness} establishes sharpness of the exponent
two for actual three-term counts on a specified family of groups.

These statements resolve several local questions posed by the argument:
linear dependence on the balanced norm is not intrinsic to symmetric
counting; torsion can be included quantitatively; the subgroup norm
conversion has an exact sharp constant; and, for three-term counts,
quadratic dependence cannot be replaced uniformly by any higher power.
The last assertion is about finite abelian groups in a growing-dimensional
family. We do not claim the corresponding sharpness construction here for
prime cyclic groups, or for $k\ge4$.

The underlying tools---Cauchy--Schwarz, Fourier orthogonality, and
quadratic Gauss sums---are classical. Directional Gowers norms have an
established theory, including the substantially deeper concatenation
results of Tao and Ziegler \cite{taoziegler}. Our comparison concerns
finite-index subgroups and needs no concatenation theorem. A targeted
source check does not establish worldwide priority for the exact
formulations below; they should be viewed as proved refinements relative
to the specified source estimates.

Nor does a sharper counting lemma by itself establish a new record for
$r_k(N)$. For perspective, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$ for $k\ge5$, using
quasipolynomial inverse bounds and a density-increment strategy
\cite{lssbounds}. We make no global bound claim beyond the local implications
proved in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:20:sec:super}.

\begin{partabstract}{21}
Let $G$ be a nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five, let $f:G\to\R$
have mean zero, and put $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$.  We prove, with absolute constants
$c,C>0$ and without a pointwise bound on $f$, that
\[
 \|\delta+f\|_{U^3}^8
 \le \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
      +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+Cu^8
 \qquad(\delta>0,\ u\le c\delta).
\]
The coefficient at $u^6$ is optimal even on a fixed five-point quotient.
This closes the characteristic-five coefficient gap in an earlier
project report, which established the exponent and a matching lower
candidate but only an unspecified upper constant.

The proof strengthens the treatment of the sixth- and seventh-degree
terms in the centered cube expansion.  A positive cubic convolution
statistic controls both terms, and its Fourier-tail estimate permits
their absorption against a retained norm deficit.  Four further
Fourier squares yield the sharp phase-dependent coefficient
\[
 \frac{2^{3/4}}3\,
 \frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi},\qquad
 \theta=2\arg\widehat f(\xi)-\arg\widehat f(2\xi),\quad
 \phi=3\arg\widehat f(\xi)+\arg\widehat f(2\xi),
\]
when $\{\pm\xi\}$ is a largest conjugate Fourier pair.
Near equality forces a second harmonic of size
$2^{1/4}u^2/(6\delta)$ and the phase condition
$e^{10i\arg\widehat f(\xi)}\to-1$.

On $G=\Z/5\Z$, an exact six-row Fourier formula and analytic
optimization determine the next term of the weighted supremum:
\[
 M_{\delta,5}(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8
       +O_\delta(u^{10}).
\]
We transfer sharpness to indicator sets in growing exponent-five groups,
give explicit finite profile inequalities, explain the interface with
Gowers's Lemmas~3.8--3.10 and the repository, and distinguish the
remaining higher-dimensional eighth-order problem from the questions
resolved here.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Principal result.} On every nontrivial finite abelian group
of exponent five, the sharp next coefficient after
$6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$ in the centered three-cube problem is
$2^{3/4}\delta^2/3$, at order $u^6$.  The uniform error is $O(u^8)$.
On the five-point group the following coefficient is exactly $20/9$.

\smallskip
\noindent Based on the supplied Ramsey development in
\texttt{VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt}, inspected at commit

it does not assert bibliographic priority or a new global quantitative
Szemer\'edi bound.  The new proofs have not been certified by Lean.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:21:sec:introduction}

Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem develops higher uniformity norms
to measure additive structure \cite{gowers}.  Lemma~3.10 bounds the
number of $d$-dimensional additive cubes in a set of density $\delta$ by
\[
       (\delta+\alpha^{1/2^d})^{2^d}N^{d+1},
\]
where $\alpha$ is the degree-$(d-1)$ uniformity parameter.  Its proof
uses the triangle inequality from Lemma~3.9, itself a consequence of
the cube Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in Lemma~3.8.  This is an effective
general estimate, but it does not exploit the real-valued, mean-zero
structure of the balanced function.

The Ramsey research collection in the supplied repository
\cite{repo21} already contains extensive local improvements.
In particular, the quartic leading term in the real, centered
three-cube problem and its Fourier concentration mechanism are prior
project results.  An additional manuscript, \emph{Sharp Extremal
Refinements in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Framework} \cite{prior21extremal},
determines a secondary $u^{16/3}$ term over suitable odd-order groups.
Its Section~3 shows that exponent five changes the next exponent to
$6$ and constructs the lower coefficient $2^{3/4}/3$, while explicitly
leaving the optimal upper coefficient unresolved.

The present report develops that unresolved direction.  It does not
relabel the existing quartic estimate or the previous lower example as
new.  Instead, it proves a matching uniform upper coefficient, a sharp
phase envelope, a stronger error estimate, and an exact further term
on the smallest group.  Background inequalities are reproved because
their precise constants and equality defects are needed.

\subsection{Statements at a glance}

All averages in this report are probability averages.  For real $W$,
write
\[
 Q_3(W)=\E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3\in G}
        \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}W(x+\omega\cdot h)
        =\|W\|_{U^3}^8.
\]
The constants used repeatedly are
\begin{equation}
 C_5=\frac{2^{3/4}}3=0.5605976101\ldots,
 \qquad \beta_5=\frac{2^{1/4}}6=0.1982011858\ldots.
 \label{gsr:fm:21:eq:constants}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform characteristic-five expansion]
\label{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}
There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that, for every nontrivial
finite abelian group $G$ of exponent five, every real mean-zero $f$,
and every $\delta>0$, putting $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$, one has
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le
 \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+C_5\delta^2u^6+Cu^8
 \quad\text{if }u\le c\delta.
 \label{gsr:fm:21:eq:main-upper}
\end{equation}
For every fixed $0<\delta<1$ and every fixed nontrivial such group,
$[0,1]$-valued weights of mean $\delta$ attain the displayed coefficients
through order $u^6$.  Both the constants in the upper bound and the
smallness condition are independent of the dimension of $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route, and a check.} Source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main} is the same statement, with the supremum over weights on every fixed group and over all such groups; its constants are cruder (its sextic tail term $84t^6\sqrt D$ against $42\sqrt3\,t^6D^{1/2}$ here), and its rigidity statement is equivalent to Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity} (note there). The coefficient was re-derived at the write: $\sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\cdot2^{1/4}b^2+4\sqrt2\,b\}=(4\sqrt2)^2/(48\cdot2^{1/4})=2^{3/4}/3$, attained at $b=2^{1/4}/6=\beta_5$. The theorem answers source~14's Question~1, including its sub-question on the rank of the group: the bound is uniform, and the coefficient is attained on every fixed group (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}).
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase} refines $C_5$ to an explicit function of two
Fourier phases.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity} gives necessary conditions
for asymptotic equality.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next} proves the
additional coefficient $20/9$ on $\Z/5\Z$, including a proof that the
formula describes the global maximum for small $u$.

\subsection{Scope and comparison with the literature}

The optimization problem is local in the uniformity norm.  It asks how
large the cube count of a small perturbation of a constant can be when
the norm of that perturbation is fixed.  Eisner and Tao
\cite{eisnertao} study a different extremizer problem: Gowers--Host--Kra
seminorms that are large under $L^\infty$ or critical $L^p$ constraints.
Hatami \cite{hatami} develops norm geometry and Hanner inequalities for
generalizations of Gowers norms.  These works provide appropriate
context for rigidity and convexity, but their constraints should not be
identified with the fixed-mean, small-centered-norm problem here.

The literature search did not establish bibliographic priority for
the new formulas.  Accordingly, ``sharp'' always means that the stated
inequality has matching examples in its specified mathematical class;
it does not mean that no related observation exists elsewhere.
The unresolved question settled here is explicitly the coefficient
question in the earlier project report.

No new bound for the largest progression-free subset of
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is obtained.  As a quantitative benchmark, Leng,
Sah, and Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} prove for each fixed $k\ge5$ a bound
$r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_k})$ with $c_k>0$.
The present characteristic-five results concern a different local
step and do not propagate through a new global density-increment
argument.  In particular, a group of exponent five has no progression
with more than five distinct points; its cube geometry remains
meaningful independently of that restriction.

\subsection{What is counted}

A three-cube is an ordered parameter tuple $(x,h_1,h_2,h_3)\in G^4$.
Its vertices may coincide, and a sidelength may be zero.  Thus
$|G|^4Q_3(1_A)$ is an integer count of parameterized cubes, not a count
of unlabelled eight-point subsets.  This convention is the one relevant
to the uniformity norm and to Lemma~3.10.

Every nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five is a finite
dimensional vector space over $\F_5$.  We use additive notation for
both $G$ and its character group $\widehat G$; a dual element $r$
is also the character $x\mapsto r(x)$ when it occurs in Fourier
inversion.  No coordinate basis is needed in the proofs.

\section[{Source 22: Purpose, results, and scope}]{Source 22. Purpose, results, and scope}\label{gsr:fm:22:sec:d1}

\begin{partabstract}{22}
We develop two degree-sensitive refinements connected with Gowers' proof of
Szemer\'edi's theorem. First, we stratify the exceptional certificates in
Section~15 by the Boolean degree left after removing parity. A degree-$t$
certificate has success probability at most $p^{-t-1}$ for $t\ge2$.
For degree one we count exactly the certificate classes satisfying the
necessary balance constraints. Their number is a polynomial in the cube
dimension $k$ of degree $2d$, rather than an exponential in $2^k$.
For $d=2$ it is
$30k^4+204k^3+111k^2+114k$.
This yields a fully explicit finite replacement for the exceptional-set
estimate, with degree-sensitive sufficient field-size conditions for its
absorption step. We also settle the first-order degeneracy count for the
previously excluded two-cube case: its optimal coefficient is $k^2+3k$.

Second, for any prescribed equality pattern on a finite set of field
parameters, we determine the exact minimum number of successful directions
at a prescribed center among polynomial colorings of given degrees.
The answer is $q^{\max(n-B,0)}$, where $B$ is a maximum-weight column-basis
sum of an explicit evaluation matrix. This removes the earlier degree
restriction for symmetric progressions and gives a monochromatic analogue.
Norm forms attain the pointwise bound. We prove that a complete low-degree
norm construction cannot be extended by adding an arbitrary independent
summand; in the four-term case we give an exact count in terms of third
differences of that summand. Quantitative constant-line counts explain a
further obstruction in the characteristic-divisible norm layers.
All principal statements have proofs; exact finite verification and
integration notes accompany the source. No improved global Szemer\'edi
bound or resolution of the global quintic avoidance problem is asserted.
\end{partabstract}

The useful question behind this report is whether the degree actually
present in an auxiliary object can replace the worst possible degree
implicit in a large counting argument. We answer this in two settings.
In Gowers' exceptional-arrangement argument, degree controls the number of
independent restrictions imposed by a certificate. In polynomial coloring,
degree controls the number of variables that can be constrained by the
evaluation equations. Both arguments become substantially more precise
when they retain a filtration by degree.

Our direct source is Section~15 of Gowers' 2001 paper
\cite{gowers}, as transcribed and studied in the Ramsey part of
ProveIt \cite{repo22}. We use repository snapshot \texttt{43306653afaa};
the full revision identifier appears in the references and source ledger.
The earlier project reports \cite{prior22degeneracy,prior22extremal} already
determined the first-order coefficient for $d\ge2$ arrangements and the
low-degree symmetric-coloring threshold. Those results are prerequisites
and comparison points, not claimed again as new discoveries. The necessary
arguments are reproduced here so that this article can be read alone.

\subsection{The direct Section 15 improvement}

A $d$-arrangement consists of $2d$ parallel $k$-cubes. Its parameter
space has dimension
\[
 D=(2d+1)k+2d-1.
\]
Gowers' Lemma~15.4 bounds the number of degenerate arrangements by
$k3^{2d2^k}p^{D-1}$. The preceding project analysis replaced its leading
coefficient by $k+C_d$, where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:22:eq:Cd-intro}
 C_d=\frac12\left(T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1\right),
 \qquad
 T_{2d}=\sum_{a=0}^{d}\binom{2d}{2a}\binom{2a}{a}.
\end{equation}
It still bounded all nonparity certificates together by a very large
multiple of $p^{-2}$.

The new estimate distinguishes their degrees. The degree-one contribution
has coefficient $\Bal_{k,d}$, given by a constant-term formula in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:balanced-count}. For each fixed $d$ it is a polynomial in
$k$ of degree $2d$. Certificates of higher degrees are assigned progressively
smaller probabilities. The resulting finite bound is
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:filtration-bound}. Its proof includes the necessary
summation by parts; subtracting two unrelated cumulative upper bounds
would not be a valid way to bound an individual degree stratum.

The case $d=1$ has different geometry. We identify all its divisorial
exceptions and prove
\[
 \delta_{k,1}(p)=\frac{k^2+3k}{p}+O_k(p^{-2}),
\]
with an explicit finite remainder. This answers a specific question left
open by the preceding report, including the exact formula
$\delta_{1,1}(p)=4/p-3/p^2$.

\subsection{Exact pointwise polynomial questions}

Let $\Pi$ prescribe which colors on a finite parameter set must agree.
Given a polynomial coloring $Q:\F_q^n\to\F_q^r$, write $S_z(Q)$ for
the directions $h$ realizing that pattern from the base point $z$;
the zero direction is included. We prove an exact formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:22:eq:pattern-intro}
 \min_Q |S_z(Q)|=q^{\max\{n-B,0\}}.
\end{equation}
The integer $B$ is computed by descending Gaussian elimination on a small
matrix of parameter powers. This is an exact extremal answer at every
\emph{prescribed} center: the minimizing polynomial is allowed to depend
on that center. It is generally a different question to minimize the sum
over all centers using one polynomial.

For symmetric $\ell=2m$ term progressions and degree caps $D_a$, put
$s_a=\lceil D_a/2\rceil$ and $t_a=\min(m,s_a)$. The answer uses
\[
 B_{\rm sym}=\sum_a t_a(2s_a-t_a).
\]
For monochromatic $\ell$-term progressions it uses
\[
 B_{\rm mono}=\sum_a \frac{r_a(2D_a-r_a+1)}2,
 \qquad r_a=\min(D_a,\ell-1).
\]
Both statements hold for arbitrarily large degree caps in characteristic
$p>\ell$; a bound on the field size alone would be insufficient.

For symmetric four-term progressions, the scalar quintic and sextic
pointwise budget is exactly eight. We exhibit the sharp example
$N_3+N_5$ at the origin. Thus a universal prescribed-center theorem
cannot lower eight to seven. We also prove concrete obstructions to two
natural ways of promoting such local examples to globally avoiding
colorings.

\begin{partabstract}{23}
We establish precise local refinements and sharpness results for three
parts of Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem.  First, simultaneous
linear-phase partitions with cell lengths in a finite set $\mathcal S$
are controlled by the numerical-semigroup conductor $C(\mathcal S)$.
A torus-packing upper bound and a mixed-radix lower construction give
asymptotically matching constants when the permitted lengths are close.
In particular, the eventual universal threshold for cell lengths
$L,L+1$ is $L^{q+2}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i\,(1+o(1))$.
This proves the necessity of the extra tiling cost left open in an
earlier project report, even when different cells may use different
steps.  We also compute an exact exceptional-set profile for the
obstructions and a sharp almost-partition threshold.

Second, for real centered functions on groups of exponent five, we prove
the sharp cube-counting expansion
\[
 \|\delta+f\|_{U^3}^8
 \le\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
 +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+O(u^8),
 \qquad u=\|f\|_{U^3}\ll\delta,
\]
with an absolute, dimension-independent error constant.  An exact
five-point model and indicator approximations attain the secondary
coefficient; a rigidity theorem determines the necessary harmonic
phase alignment.  Third, a localization to width at least $m/3$ lets
common slice refinements extend to full product boxes without further
width loss.  Paired interpolation and retained observations give an
explicit conditional replacement for the geometric part of Lemma~16.10.

Every principal new statement is proved in the article.  Exact finite
certificates accompany the proofs.  We distinguish these local results
from the remaining global parameter comparison and from Lean
formalization; no new general bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem is claimed.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent Source revision: \snapshottwentythree.\\
Status: research draft with complete written proofs and reproducible finite checks.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:23:sec:introduction}

Gowers's 2001 proof develops several interacting quantitative mechanisms:
uniformity norms control configuration counts; phase approximation turns
algebraic structure into useful progressions; and repeated structural
refinements make fibre information compatible across coordinates
\cite{gowers}.  These mechanisms contain local questions whose answers
can be sharpened independently of the full density-increment iteration.
The present article concentrates on three such questions and proves
explicit results for each.

The reference repository already contains extensive earlier refinements,
and several changes to its transcription address the difference between
the printed paper and statements suitable for formalization
\cite{repo23source,repo23research,repo23status}.  We treat those results as
prior project work.  In particular, the previously obtained upper
exponent for prescribed linear-phase cell lengths is reproduced with
attribution; the new contribution is a matching obstruction, a sharp
leading constant, and the extension to arbitrary admissible length sets.
Similarly, the leading centered three-cube coefficient was known in the
project; here the order-five secondary coefficient is determined.

\subsection{Three principal conclusions}

\paragraph{Exact lengths have an unavoidable arithmetic cost.}
Let $T_{\mathcal S}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$ be the eventual universal
interval threshold for a partition into progressions of lengths in
$\mathcal S$, on which $q$ affine phases have arc diameters at most
$\varepsilon_i$.  If $L=\min\mathcal S\ge2$, $H=\max\mathcal S$,
$\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$ and $C=C(\mathcal S)$, then
\begin{equation}
 C\prod_i\left(\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1\right)
 \le T_{\mathcal S}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \le C\left(\left\lceil\frac{(H-1)^q}{\prod_i\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1\right).
 \label{gsr:fm:23:eq:intro-threshold}
\end{equation}
For $\mathcal S=\{L,L+1\}$ this yields
$T\sim L^{q+2}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i$, uniformly in the tolerances for
fixed $q$ as $L\to\infty$.  This answers the prescribed-length
sharpness question posed in \cite[Question~11.1]{prior23linear}.
The lower example allows cell-dependent steps and persists for phases
coming from a prime cyclic ambient group.

\paragraph{Order five selects a different secondary coefficient.}
For $G=\F_5^n$, $\E f=0$, and $u=\|f\|_{U^3}\ll\delta$, the sharp
first two nonconstant terms of the weighted cube supremum are
\[
 6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u^6.
\]
The proof retains the positive cost of the doubled dominant frequency
and controls the incomplete cubes by the fourth-power Fourier tail.
This turns the previous order estimate into a sharp coefficient with
an $O(u^8)$ remainder.  It also forces the dominant Fourier phase
$\theta$ to satisfy $\cos(5\theta)\to0$ in any family attaining the
secondary term.

\paragraph{A common base refinement can keep its full width.}
For a proper prime-field box $T\times J$ of width at least $m$, a
preliminary partition of $T$ into short index boxes leaves width at
least $m/3$.  Any subsequent common-step base refinement of width $W>1$
extends to a true partition of its product with $J$ into boxes of width
at least $W$.  This uses full residue chains on the final axis.
Combined with common slice covers and affine interpolation, it gives
complete geometric and sampling conclusions under explicit inputs.
The final Section~16 comparison of control functions remains a separate
problem.

\subsection{Scope of the mathematical and computational claims}

The article proves finite theorems and local asymptotics, including two
answers to questions explicitly posed in the preceding project reports.
We do not assert historical priority for all of the combined formulations.
Dirichlet approximation, numerical-semigroup conductors, cube
Cauchy--Schwarz, and two-point affine interpolation are established
ingredients.  The new arguments and the precise comparison with the
earlier reports are identified where they occur.

These results do not constitute a new best general bound for
$r_k(N)$, the largest size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no
nonconstant $k$-term arithmetic progression.  For context, Leng, Sah,
and Sawhney proved the stronger general estimate
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$ for $k\ge5$ in their 2024
paper \cite{lssbounds}.  Our local results are not compared against that
bound as if they were an alternative global theorem.

The repository snapshot is \snapshottwentythree, retrieved on 6 October 2026.
Its status record explicitly separates completed formal components
from unresolved statements and control-function comparisons
\cite{repo23status}.  We inspected the relevant source and proof
interfaces but did not compile a new Lean development.  The accompanying
Python programs check finite arithmetic and polynomial identities;
the proofs in the article establish the quantified mathematical claims.

\subsection{Reading guide}

Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:23:sec:phase-model}--\ref{gsr:dt:23:sec:partial} form a self-contained
treatment of the phase-partition problem, including exact witnesses and
algorithms.  Section~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:section} is independent of the partition
argument and proves the characteristic-five cube result.
Section~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:sec} supplies the geometric gluing theorem and its
conditional Section~16 specialization.  The final sections give a
verification record, integration recommendations, and further research
questions.

For reference, on a finite abelian group we use normalized averages and
the Gowers norm convention
\[
 \|f\|_{U^s}^{2^s}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_s}
 \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^s}\mathcal C^{|v|}f(x+v\cdot h),
\]
where $\mathcal C$ is complex conjugation.  Fourier coefficients are
$\widehat f(\xi)=\E_xf(x)\overline{\xi(x)}$.  Fourier sums have no
normalizing factor.  For real functions the conjugations in the
physical-space cube product are immaterial.  The cube
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality used below is Gowers's Lemma~3.8
\cite{gowers}; in normalized form it bounds a mixed cube average by the
product of the $U^s$ norms of its $2^s$ vertex functions.

\begin{partabstract}{24}
We develop explicit, self-contained refinements of the structural reductions
in Section~7 of Gowers's \emph{A new proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem}.
First, a cubic supporting-line argument replaces the five-sample
intersection lemma by a three-sample theorem: the retained fraction
$\delta^5/\sqrt2$ becomes $7\delta^3/(3\sqrt6)$, with the same
$90\%$ good-pair conclusion and the same intersection threshold.
We determine the sharp constant in the corresponding scalar moment
relaxation and identify exactly why its two-sample analogue fails.
Second, retaining the actual edge mass of the popular-difference graph
through a one-sample argument yields an elementary energy-to-structure
bound with a linear retained fraction and relative doubling
$2^{17}\kappa^{-6}$.
Third, an injective vertical-fibre argument replaces the loss
$8kC^{4k}$ in the Freiman-restriction lemma by $kC^{2k+1}$.
The two structural improvements combine to replace the order-eight
restriction bound $2^{-1882}\gamma^{1164}|B_0|$ by
$2^{-295}\gamma^{103}|B_0|$.
We also prove weighted and higher-arity selection statements, a
finite-field-vector codomain extension, profile-dependent certificates,
and an optimized threshold formula.
The article separates these local improvements from stronger published
Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers results and from global quantitative
Szemer\'edi bounds. It includes complete proofs, a repository-specific
formalization plan, exact finite regression tests, and further research
questions. No new global record or literature-priority claim is made.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small

\label{gsr:fm:24:sec:scope}

The question addressed here is not whether the entire 2001 proof should
be replaced by contemporary higher-order Fourier analysis. It is more
specific: which losses in its elementary structural machinery can be
removed while retaining transparent statements, explicit constants, and
a short dependency chain suitable for formalization?
The answer developed below concerns Gowers's Lemma~7.4,
Proposition~7.3, Lemma~7.5, and Corollary~7.6~\cite{gowers}.
The corresponding statement and proof modules in the supplied
repository were also inspected~\cite{repo24}.

\subsection{The compiled improvement}

For a function $\phi:B_0\to H$ between subsets of abelian groups, a
\emph{respected additive quadruple} is an ordered tuple
$(a,b,c,d)\in B_0^4$ for which
\[
 a+b=c+d,\qquad \phi(a)+\phi(b)=\phi(c)+\phi(d).
\]
Repeated entries are allowed. A Freiman homomorphism of order $k$
preserves every equality between two sums of $k$ domain elements,
again with repetitions allowed.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit order-$k$ restriction]\label{gsr:fm:24:thm:headline}
Let $G$ be an abelian group, $p$ a prime, $B_0\subset G$ a nonempty
finite set of size $m$, and $\phi:B_0\to\F_p$ a function.
Suppose that at least $\gamma m^3$ additive quadruples are respected,
where $\gamma>0$. For every integer $k\ge1$, there is a subset
$B\subseteq B_0$ on which $\phi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:24:eq:headline-general}
 |B|\ge \frac{2^{-(34k+20)}}{k}\,\gamma^{12k+7}m.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $k=8$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:24:eq:headline-eight}
 \boxed{\quad |B|\ge 2^{-295}\gamma^{103}|B_0|.\quad}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Weaker than source~10 by $2^{10k+6}$} (checked at the write). Source~10's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:10:cor:improved-order-eight} gives, under the same hypotheses, $|B|\ge2^{-(24k+14)}\gamma^{12k+7}m/k$; the ratio to the bound here is $2^{(34k+20)-(24k+14)}=2^{10k+6}$, which is $2^{86}$ at $k=8$ ($2^{-209}\gamma^{103}$ against $2^{-295}\gamma^{103}$). Both come from a Proposition~7.3-type step followed by a fibre extraction with $Q_k\le C^{2k+1}$; source~10's energy step has the better constants. Like source~10's, this bound implies the conclusion of the formal \file{corollary_7_6} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~197) where the hypotheses agree, since $\gamma\le1$ gives $2^{-295}\gamma^{103}\ge2^{-1882}\gamma^{1164}$; not formalized.
\end{writenote}

The hypotheses imply $\gamma\le1$: a graph with $m$ points has additive
energy at most $m^3$. The theorem therefore improves the source's lower
bound throughout its meaningful parameter range. Its proof is completed
in Section~\ref{gsr:en:24:sec:compiler}; no asymptotic qualification such as
``$p$ sufficiently large'' is needed.

\subsection{What is classical, what is derived, and what is not claimed}

Dependent random choice, popular-difference graphs, path counting, and
Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa growth inequalities are established tools
\cite{gowers,foxsudakov,petridis}. Our contribution here is an explicit
reorganization and sharpening of these particular interfaces, including
the scalar certificates and the vertical-fibre bookkeeping. The proofs
establish the stated inequalities independently of any assertion that
their individual formulations have not appeared elsewhere.

Stronger published Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers theorems already exist.
For example, Reiher and Schoen obtain a subset of size
$(1-\varepsilon)\kappa^{1/2}|A|$ with relative difference-set bound
$C_\varepsilon\kappa^{-4}$~\cite{reiherschoen}. We explicitly import
that theorem in Section~\ref{gsr:en:24:subsec:modern} to derive a further
restriction estimate, with its dependence on the imported theorem
visible. Thus the elementary energy bound here is not advertised as a
new extremal record.

Nor is a local improvement automatically a new quantitative Szemer\'edi
bound. As a published modern benchmark, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove,
for every fixed $\ell\ge5$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_\ell(N)\ll N\exp\bigl(- (\log\log N)^{c_\ell}\bigr)
 \qquad(c_\ell>0)
\]
by substantially different machinery~\cite{lssbounds}.
We do not re-run Gowers's Sections~8--18 with the constants below, and
we make no claim about the best currently available global estimate.
The sharpness result proved here concerns a precisely defined scalar
relaxation, not an unrestricted graph or additive-combinatorial
extremal problem.

\section[{Source 25: Scope, main theorem, and relation to the source}]{Source 25. Scope, main theorem, and relation to the source}\label{gsr:fm:25:sec:d1}
\srcnote{25}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``The Codimension-One Degeneracies of Gowers Arrangements / An asymptotically sharp replacement for Lemma 15.4 and explicit random-selection thresholds / Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / Mathematical development and computational checks with ChatGPT / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``Research prepared with ChatGPT for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. Archive \file{gowers\_arrangement\_degeneracy.zip} (arrival \texttt{d7c4aa399}), manuscript \file{arrangement\_degeneracy.tex} (1,207 lines, 17 pages), pin \texttt{568d1802e} (its \file{SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}, shipped as \file{25-codimension-one-SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--8 are in Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:degeneracy}), Sections~9--11 in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash card} (an absolute value, not this report's operator) is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash cardtwentyfive}; its `question' environment (``Question'', numbered on its own counter there) is set in this report's `Question' style, numbered within its section (its Questions~1--8 keep their indices).}
\begin{partabstract}{25}
We study the full ternary-moment degeneracy condition in Section 15 of
Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem.  For a $d$-arrangement of $k$-cubes,
put $D=(2d+1)k+2d-1$ and $n=2d\,2^k$.  Over a finite field of cardinality
$q$ and characteristic greater than $2d$, with $k\ge1$ and $d\ge2$, we prove
that the number of degenerate labelled arrangements is
\[
 (k+H_d)q^{D-1}+O_{k,d}(q^{D-2}),\qquad
 H_d=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
\]
where $T_m$ is the central trinomial coefficient.  All constants in the
error term are explicit.  In particular, $H_8=2\,585\,444$.  The coefficient
$k+H_d$ is exact: the codimension-one components are precisely the zero
sidelength hyperplanes and a projective family of balanced ternary
cross-section hyperplanes.  Outside those hyperplanes, every remaining
witness has codimension at least two.  The key step is a minimal-Walsh-layer linearization, followed
by use of the moment equations involving the last coordinate that the
original counting argument does not need to retain.  A sharp single-witness
probability, a genuine second-order obstruction, and a small-characteristic
counterexample accompany the classification.  We also prove a finite-field,
arbitrary-$d$ random-selection theorem with exact Riesz-product parameters
and a better explicit ambient-size requirement.  The package includes
reproducible exact finite checks and a ProveIt integration plan.  These are
local refinements, not a claimed improvement of the final quantitative
Szemer\'edi theorem; no proof-assistant verification or literature-priority
claim is made.
\end{partabstract}
\label{gsr:fm:25:sec:main}

Gowers's Lemma 15.4 bounds exceptional arrangements before the random
selection in Lemma 15.5.  In the original notation, its estimate is
\begin{equation}
 \cardtwentyfive{\Dg_{k,d}(\F_N)}\le k\,3^{2d2^k}
 N^{(2d+1)k+2d-2}.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:gowers}
\end{equation}
The proof chooses one nonconstant multilinear moment for each ternary
coefficient pattern, uses a polynomial fibre bound, and then takes a
union bound \cite[pp.~562--565]{gowers}.  The resulting constant treats
all witnesses as though they defined hypersurfaces.  This is the point
we sharpen.

The full definition of degeneracy uses \emph{every} coordinate monomial,
including monomials that contain the last, cross-section coordinate.
Gowers remarks after Lemma 15.4 that his argument could use fewer such
monomials.  For the present purpose, retaining them is decisive: they
usually give a second independent equation.

The ProveIt interface inspected here is
\texttt{Sections14\_15.lean} at commit \sha.  It defines degeneracy by a
ternary coefficient function which is not a \emph{modular} multiple of the
distinguished parity coefficient, and requires all arrangement moments
to vanish \cite{repo25lean}.  Our definition agrees with that interface,
after an invertible change from Boolean to centred sign coordinates.
The existing research README was also inspected to separate this project
from its density-transfer, phase-partition, energy, cube-counting and
floor-pattern developments \cite{repo25research}.

\subsection{Parameters}
Throughout the main results,
\begin{equation}
 k\ge1,\quad d\ge2,\quad q=\cardtwentyfive{\F_q},\quad
 p=\operatorname{char}\F_q>2d,
 \qquad n=2d\,2^k,\quad D=(2d+1)k+2d-1.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{align}
 T_m&=[z^0](z^{-1}+1+z)^m
     =\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\binom mj\binom{m-j}{j},
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:trinomial}\\
 H_d&=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
 &L_{k,d}&=k+H_d,
 &U_{k,d}&=\frac{3^{2d2^k}-3^{2d}}{2}.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:constants}
\end{align}
The arrangement count is a count of labelled parameter tuples, including
repeated vertices when these occur.  There are exactly $q^D$ such tuples
satisfying the cross-section relation.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit sharp first-order count]
\label{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}
Under \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}, the number $Z_{k,d}(q)$ of degenerate
arrangements satisfies
\begin{equation}
 L_{k,d}q^{D-1}-\binom{L_{k,d}}2q^{D-2}
 \ \le\ Z_{k,d}(q)\ \le\
 L_{k,d}q^{D-1}+U_{k,d}q^{D-2}.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:mainbounds}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for fixed $k,d$,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{\substack{q\to\infty\\ \operatorname{char}\F_q>2d}}
 \frac{Z_{k,d}(q)}{q^{D-1}}=k+H_d.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:limit}
\end{equation}
Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero or greater than
$2d$, the codimension-one irreducible components of the same degeneracy
locus are exactly $k+H_d$ explicitly described hyperplanes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (checked at the write). \file{lemma_15_4} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~402) bounds the count by $k3^nq^{D-1}$, $n=2d2^k$, for prime $q$. Here $L_{k,d}+U_{k,d}/q\le k3^n$ for $d\ge2$, $q\ge5$: $H_d\le(3^{2d}+1)/2\le(3^{n/2}+1)/2$ because $n\ge4d$, and $U_{k,d}/q<3^n/10$, so $L_{k,d}+U_{k,d}/q<k+(3^{n/2}+1)/2+3^n/10\le k3^n$ (already for $k=1$, since $0.9\cdot3^n-1\ge(3^{n/2}+1)/2$ for $n\ge8$). So the theorem implies the formal bound for $d\ge2$ and primes $q>2d$, as source~18's does; not formalized. Its predicate is the formal one (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:25:sec:d9}).
\end{writenote}

The proof occupies Sections~\ref{gsr:en:25:sec:walsh}--\ref{gsr:en:25:sec:global}.
The leading constant cannot be reduced.  For the $8$-arrangements actually
used by Gowers, \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:mainbounds} gives
\begin{equation}
 Z_{k,8}(q)\le
 (k+2\,585\,444)q^{17k+14}
 +\frac{3^{2^{k+4}}-3^{16}}2\,q^{17k+13}.
 \label{gsr:fm:25:eq:d8}
\end{equation}
Thus the enormous ternary-pattern count has moved from the leading
$q^{-1}$ term to a $q^{-2}$ error term.  This does not eliminate the
large error constant, and it is not a dimension-uniform asymptotic.

\subsection{What is, and is not, established}
The main contributions developed here are the minimal-layer rank bound,
the separation of parity and non-parity degeneracies, the exact projective
hyperplane count, and their combination into \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:mainbounds}.
Section~\ref{gsr:en:25:sec:selection} gives a self-contained quantitative application
to the selection step.  The hypotheses $d\ge2$ and $p>2d$ are substantive;
we show what fails without them.

The proofs are conventional mathematical proofs, supplemented by finite
exact computations.  They have not been independently refereed or
formalized in Lean.  A targeted source search does not establish priority
for the classification in the broader literature.  In particular, the
standard finite-field viewpoint on hyperplane arrangements is classical
\cite{athanasiadis}; it is not presented here as a new method.  Nor do we
claim to have propagated these local savings through Sections 16--18 to
obtain a new bound for progression-free sets.

Source~27 re-derives the leading coefficient a third time and determines the second coefficient for $d=2$.

\section[{Source 26: The question and the scope}]{Source 26. The question and the scope}\label{gsr:fm:26:sec:d1}
\srcnote{26}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Threshold free affine density increments on cyclic groups / Report275 / Research report prepared for Vladimir / 6 October 2026''; the PDF author field reads ``Research report prepared for Vladimir''. Archive \file{Report275\_Threshold\_Free\_Affine\_Density\_Increments.zip} (arrival \texttt{7e827c6f3}), manuscript \file{article.tex} (494 lines, 12 pages), pin \texttt{c94998a5d} (its \file{SOURCES.md}, shipped as \file{26-threshold-free-affine-SOURCES.md}). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--4 and Appendix~A form a chapter of Part~I (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:cor58}), Sections~5--6 are in Part~V.}
\begin{partabstract}{26}
A family of local affine correlations on disjoint modular progressions covering a set yields a density increment with no scale threshold. We keep the exact balanced mass of the cover. If its shortest progression has length $r$, the set has density $\delta$, the normalized balanced mass is $\mu$, and the summed correlation is at least $\alpha N$, then a proper progression has density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$ and length at least
\[
 \min\left\{\left(\frac{r(1-\delta)}{128\mu}\right)^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\right\}.
\]
A complementary, parent-contained progression has the same density increment and length at least $\sqrt{\alpha r/(24\pi\mu)}$, over every cyclic modulus. For every cyclic modulus and $M$ pairwise two-comparable parents, the resulting guarantees are $(N/M)^{1/3}/8$ and $\sqrt{\alpha(N/M)/(96\pi(1-\delta))}$. This strengthens the full degree-one specialization of a specified repository version of Corollary 5.8. The proofs combine a subgroup-coset moment bound, removal of nonproper directions, and phase-flat residue partitions. A separate appendix records a common-step integer-box almost-cover, with its exact scope. The companion checks bounded identities and regressions; no formal verification, global Ramsey bound, or literature-priority claim is made.
\end{partabstract}

The local density-increment step is a useful place to separate an actual quantitative improvement from a change of hypotheses. The target here is the degree-one part of the repository predicate \texttt{corollary\_5\_8} at the source pin specified in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:26:sec:source}. Its displayed premises do not include a lower-scale assumption. A phase-partition argument alone can demand a minimum parent length that is not supplied by those premises. We avoid this issue by using a second-moment increment when the requested correlation gain is small, and phase refinement when it is large.

The principal results below are self-contained written theorems over cyclic groups. Their strongest form uses the actual balanced mass on the cover and does not require comparable parent lengths. Comparability enters only to express the answer through $N/M$. All progressions in the main body are modular and injectively parameterized. Integer representatives are treated separately in Appendix~\ref{gsr:dt:26:app:boxes}.

The cube-root scale, Dirichlet phase partitioning, and progression moments have classical precedents. Section~\ref{gsr:fz:26:sec:source} gives a narrow source comparison. The claims concern the explicit local interfaces proved here; they do not close the general-degree catalogue statement, change the repository's formal status, or improve a final Szemer\'edi or Ramsey bound.
