\begin{proposition}[A larger allowance at the same factor-two interface]
\label{gsr:en:07:prop:120}
Retain the local factor-two assumptions and
\(\theta=10\eta^{1/5}\). The condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:120}
 0\le\eta\le120^{-5}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for \(\psi\in\Fr_2(D,H)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Now \(\theta\le1/12\), so
\(q(\theta)\le23/144\). Therefore
\[
 6\Delta\le\frac{23}{24}+\frac6{120^5}<1.
\]
The case \(k=2\) of \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:gowers-kappa} proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

The ratio of this explicit allowance to \(360^{-5}\) is
\((360/120)^5=243\). This compares sufficient conditions for the local
step only; it does not assert a factor-243 improvement in any final
progression-length or density estimate.

\subsection{Retaining the full ambient invariance}

The construction in Section~10 supplies stronger fiber control than the
minimal shift-regular interface records. For its application here, the
needed inequalities are the following \cite{repo07statements}:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:full-package}
 \begin{gathered}
 R_g\ge\alpha^2M/16\quad(g\in S),\qquad
 |R_{g+d}-R_g|\le\sigma M\quad(g\in G,d\in B),\\
 0<\alpha\le1,\quad M>0,\quad
 0\le\rho\le\alpha^2/32,\quad
 0\le\sigma\le\eta\rho\alpha^2/16.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The relevant transport parameter is consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:tau-eta}
 \tau=\frac{16\sigma}{\alpha^2}\le\eta\rho\le\eta.
\end{equation}
Only these displayed consequences, not a new construction of \(W\), are
used in this subsection.

\begin{theorem}[An explicit higher-order range]\label{gsr:en:07:thm:order-k}
Assume the local model, the factor-two regularity, and
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:full-package}. Set \(\theta=10\eta^{1/5}\). For every integer
\(k\ge2\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:40k}
 0\le\eta\le(40k)^{-5}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi\in\Fr_k(D,H).
\end{equation}
More precisely, in the range \(\eta\ge0\) and \(0\le\theta\le1\), it
suffices that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:full-k-exact}
 [2k+\eta k(k-1)]\bigl(2\theta-\theta^2+\eta\bigr)<1.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The precise criterion follows from \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:tau-eta} and
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:gowers-tau}. To verify the convenient allowance
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:40k}, observe that
\[
 \theta\le\frac1{4k},\qquad
 \Delta\le\frac1{2k}-\frac1{16k^2}+\eta.
\]
Using \(k(k-1)\le k^2\) and expanding gives
\begin{align*}
 [2k+\eta k(k-1)]\Delta
 &\le(2k+\eta k^2)
       \left(\frac1{2k}-\frac1{16k^2}+\eta\right)\\
 &=1-\frac1{8k}+\frac52k\eta-\frac\eta{16}+k^2\eta^2\\
 &\le1-\frac1{8k}+\frac52k\eta+k^2\eta^2.
\end{align*}
The hypothesis implies \(\eta\le1/(64k^2)\), since
\((40k)^5\ge64k^2\). Hence the last two positive terms are at most
\[
 \frac5{128k}+\frac1{4096k^2}
 \le\frac{161}{4096k}<\frac1{8k}.
\]
The strict inequality needed for \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:full-k-exact} follows, including
at the endpoint \(\eta=(40k)^{-5}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Order nine in the original parameter range]\label{gsr:en:07:cor:nine}
Under the full assumptions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:order-k}, the original
condition \(6\sqrt{10\eta^{1/5}}<1\) implies
\(\psi\in\Fr_9(D,H)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
It gives \(\eta<360^{-5}=(40\cdot9)^{-5}\), so use
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:order-k} with \(k=9\).
\end{proof}

The distinction between Corollaries~\ref{gsr:en:07:cor:five} and \ref{gsr:en:07:cor:nine} is
important. Order five follows from the assumptions exposed in the recorded
local shift interface. Order nine additionally retains ambient invariance
and a fiber lower bound from the construction. Omitting those extra
hypotheses from an order-nine theorem would not be justified by this proof.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
\emph{Order nine is not a corollary of the Lean statement.} Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:order-k} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:07:cor:nine} use, besides the hypotheses of \file{lemma_10_9} listed in the previous note, the package \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:full-package}: fibre sizes at least $\alpha^2M/16$ on $S$; $|R_{g+d}-R_g|\le\sigma M$ for \emph{all} $g\in G$ and $d\in B$; $0<\alpha\le1$, $M>0$, $0\le\rho\le\alpha^2/32$ and $0\le\sigma\le\eta\rho\alpha^2/16$. None of these is a hypothesis of \file{lemma_10_9}. In \file{Section10.lean} they occur in other places: the fibre lower bound in \texttt{IsSection10RegularComponent}, the ambient invariance as \texttt{DomainInvariant D B (sigma * M)} and the bounds on $\alpha$, $M$ in \texttt{Section10Setup}, and $\rho\le\alpha^2/32$, $\sigma\le\eta\rho\alpha^2/16$ as hypotheses of \file{lemma_10_6} (there with $\sigma>0$ and no explicit sign condition on $\rho$). A formal order-nine theorem therefore needs a new statement carrying these assumptions, for example one under the hypotheses of \file{lemma_10_6}, not a corollary of \file{lemma_10_9}. The order-five and order-nine statements are kept separate here, as the source keeps them.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A larger order-two allowance with ambient invariance}

\begin{proposition}[The allowance \(75^{-5}\)]\label{gsr:en:07:prop:75}
Under the full local and ambient assumptions of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:order-k}, the condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:75}
 0\le\eta\le75^{-5}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for \(\psi\in\Fr_2(D,H)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We have \(\theta\le2/15\), so \(q(\theta)\le56/225\). It follows that
\begin{align*}
 (4+2\eta)\Delta
 &\le(4+2\eta)\left(\frac{56}{225}+\eta\right)\\
 &=\frac{224}{225}+
       \left(4+\frac{112}{225}\right)\eta+2\eta^2.
\end{align*}
Because \(\eta\le75^{-5}<1/4\), the last two terms are at most
\(5\eta\). Indeed, \(4+112/225+1/2<5\). Finally
\(5\eta\le5/75^5<1/225\), so the total is strictly below one. This is
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:full-k-exact} for \(k=2\).
\end{proof}

The two explicit endpoints and their ratio are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:allowance-comparison}
 \begin{aligned}
 360^{-5}&=\frac1{6046617600000}\approx1.65382\times10^{-13},\\
 75^{-5}&=\frac1{2373046875}\approx4.21399\times10^{-10},\\
 \frac{75^{-5}}{360^{-5}}&=\left(\frac{24}{5}\right)^5
                          =2548.03968.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These are transparent, rounded sufficient thresholds, not optimized roots.
The exact inequalities \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:gowers-kappa} and
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:full-k-exact}, or the profiles themselves, should be used when
constant-level optimization matters.

\paragraph{What does not follow.}
The earlier extraction of a large regular component, the size of \(B'\),
subsequent Bohr-set shrinkage, and the final density iteration all retain
their own requirements. Enlarging the allowance at this one compatibility
step does not remove them. In particular, neither the number 243 nor
2548.03968 is a claimed improvement factor in a global Szemer\'edi bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Choosing the initial law by a rational linear program\srctag{07}}]{Choosing the initial law by a rational linear program}\label{gsr:en:07:sec:d7}
\srcnote{07}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:07:sec:optimization}

The original source law \(\mu\) is useful because it is the law for which
local errors are known. It need not be the best law from which to start a
particular pair of paths. The distinction can be handled exactly.

Let \(\nu\) be any probability law supported on \(S\). Keep the same local
functions \(F_d\) and their \(\mu\)-means \(\delta_d\), but define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:root-profile}
 \trans_s^{\nu}(t)=\max\left\{
    \sum_{g\in S}\nu(g-s)a_g:
    0\le a_g\le1,\quad\sum_{g\in S}\mu(g)a_g\le t\right\}.
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Alternative-root certificate]\label{gsr:en:07:prop:root}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:polygon} remains valid after replacing every
\(\trans_s\) by \(\trans_s^\nu\), provided that the same law \(\nu\) is used
for both paths. The choice of \(\nu\) may depend on the relation being
verified.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Start the common initial index with law \(\nu\), still choosing uniformly
within its fiber. The source-index weight for an edge of prefix \(s\) is
bounded by \(\nu(g-s)\), while \(F_d\) still has known \(\mu\)-mean
\(\delta_d\). Thus \eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:edge-budget} becomes the corresponding bound
with \(\trans_s^\nu\). All other steps are unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[An exact dual expression]\label{gsr:en:07:lem:dual}
For every supported law \(\nu\), shift \(s\), and \(0\le t\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:dual}
 \trans_s^\nu(t)=
 \min_{\lambda\ge0}\left[
     \lambda t+\sum_{g\in S}\pos{\nu(g-s)-\lambda\mu(g)}\right].
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For any feasible vector \(a\) and any \(\lambda\ge0\),
\begin{align*}
 \sum_g\nu(g-s)a_g
 &=\lambda\sum_g\mu(g)a_g+
      \sum_g[\nu(g-s)-\lambda\mu(g)]a_g\\
 &\le\lambda t+
      \sum_g\pos{\nu(g-s)-\lambda\mu(g)}.
\end{align*}
This proves one inequality. For the reverse, order the ratios
\(\nu(g-s)/\mu(g)\) and use the filling construction in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:profile}. Choose \(\lambda\) to be the ratio of the
possibly fractional final coordinate. Every positive coefficient in the
second sum is then fully filled, every negative one is unfilled, and the
remaining coordinate has zero coefficient. This makes the displayed bound
an equality. At \(t=0\), choose \(\lambda\) at least the largest ratio; at
\(t=1\), choose \(\lambda=0\). Budget boundaries and tied ratios give
the same equality by the identical argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimizing the root is a finite linear program]\label{gsr:en:07:thm:lp}
Fix two equal-total words. Index all their edges by a finite set \(I\),
and let edge \(i\) have prefix \(s_i\) and direction \(d_i\). The smallest
alternative-root budget equals the optimum of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:lp}
 \begin{aligned}
 \text{minimize}\quad&
   \sum_{i\in I}\left[\lambda_i\delta_{d_i}
                         +\sum_{g\in S}z_{i,g}\right],\\
 \text{subject to}\quad&
   \nu(g)\ge0\ (g\in S),\quad \sum_{g\in S}\nu(g)=1,
        \quad\nu(g)=0\ (g\notin S),\\
 &\lambda_i\ge0,\quad z_{i,g}\ge0,\quad
   z_{i,g}\ge\nu(g-s_i)-\lambda_i\mu(g)
       \quad(i\in I,g\in S).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
An optimum below one certifies the image relation. When the input laws and
budgets are rational, an optimal rational certificate exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For fixed \(\nu\), independently minimizing over each \(\lambda_i\) and
\(z_{i,g}\) gives exactly the sum of the dual expressions
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:dual}. Minimizing also over \(\nu\) therefore gives the desired
smallest budget. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:root} proves the certificate claim.

For attainment and rationality, let \(\mu_{\min}=\min_{g\in S}\mu(g)>0\).
One may restrict \(0\le\lambda_i\le1/\mu_{\min}\) without worsening the
objective: at the upper endpoint every coefficient
\(\nu(g-s_i)-\lambda_i\mu(g)\) is already nonpositive. Likewise one may
restrict \(0\le z_{i,g}\le1\), since the minimal feasible positive part
never exceeds one. The resulting feasible set is a nonempty compact
polytope. With rational data it is a rational polytope, and a linear
objective attains its minimum at a rational vertex.
\end{proof}

Taking \(\nu=\mu\) recovers the earlier theorem, so this optimization never
weakens that certificate. It is not claimed that every compatible relation
admits a budget below one. The profiles optimize over arbitrary bounded
error functions with the specified means; the errors of an actual map
\(\phi\) satisfy additional simultaneous constraints that this relaxation
need not exploit.

For a computation one can use any candidate feasible rational solution of
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:lp}; an optimality proof is unnecessary when its objective is
already below one. This separates discovering a certificate from checking
one. The supplied script checks the exact primal--dual profile identity
for many finite instances, but does not include a general LP solver.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further proved extensions\srctag{07}}]{Further proved extensions}\label{gsr:en:07:sec:d8}
\srcnote{07}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:07:sec:extensions}

\subsection{Recovering labels from collision probabilities}

So far the labels \(\psi(d)\) were given. They can instead be selected from
a concentrated directional difference distribution. For \(h\in H\), define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:histogram}
 p_d(h)=\sum_{\substack{g\in S\\g+d\in S}}\mu(g)
   \frac{\#\{(x,y)\in X_g\times X_{g+d}:\phi(y)-\phi(x)=h\}}
        {R_gR_{g+d}}.
\end{equation}
This distribution has finite support even if \(H\) is infinite, and total
mass \(s_d=1-b_d\).

\begin{proposition}[Collision-to-mode exactification]\label{gsr:en:07:prop:collision}
Assume \(s_d>0\) and put
\[
 C_d=\sum_{h\in H}\left(\frac{p_d(h)}{s_d}\right)^2.
\]
Choose \(\psi(d)\) to maximize \(p_d(h)\). Its directional defect satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:07:eq:collision-bound}
 \delta_d=1-\max_h p_d(h)\le1-s_d C_d.
\end{equation}
In particular, if \(C_d\ge1-\varepsilon_d\), then
\[
 \delta_d\le b_d+(1-b_d)\varepsilon_d.
\]
Substituting these budgets into Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:polygon} or
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:07:cor:freiman} gives the corresponding exact relations among
the selected modes.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For \(q_h=p_d(h)/s_d\), the values \(q_h\) are a probability distribution.
Hence
\[
 C_d=\sum_hq_h^2\le (\max_hq_h)\sum_hq_h=\max_hq_h.
\]
Multiplying by \(s_d\) and using the definition of the defect proves the
claim. If a selected label has defect below \(1/2\), it is the unique
label with that property, since two disjoint success events cannot both
have probability greater than \(1/2\).
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
Source~12's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority} gives the sharp form of this collision-to-mode step, mode at least $1-\chi(\eta)$ with $\chi(\eta)=(1-\sqrt{1-2\eta})/2$; source~11's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} uses the coarser $\sum p^2\le\max p$.
\end{writenote}

The collision experiment is two independent samples from the normalized
internal difference law. It is not automatically the same as a raw
additive-energy statistic, which weights pairs of fibers differently.
An application starting from energy must separately prove the necessary
normalization or comparison. This proposition does not bypass that step.

\subsection{Weighted conditional fiber laws}

The finite uniform model is not essential to the main theorem. More
generally, put any probability law \(\pi_g\) on each nonempty usable fiber,
and any positive probability law \(\mu\) on the finite support \(S\).
Define \(F_d(g)\) by sampling independently from \(\pi_g\) and
\(\pi_{g+d}\) on internal edges, and again set it equal to one on exits.
Define \(\delta_d\) by its \(\mu\)-mean and keep the same transport profiles.

\begin{proposition}[Weighted version]\label{gsr:en:07:prop:weighted}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:polygon} and \ref{gsr:en:07:thm:lp} remain valid for these arbitrary
conditional laws. The fiber-size estimates of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:07:lem:prefix} are
replaced, where needed, by direct bounds on \(\mu(g-s)/\mu(g)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose the initial index with the stated law and every formal fiber point
with its prescribed conditional law, still sharing the endpoints and
keeping distinct formal internal positions independent. The conditional
edge-failure probability is the newly defined \(F_d(g)\). The proof of
\eqref{gsr:en:07:eq:edge-budget} and all transport optimizations depend only on its
range and mean, not on uniformity of the fiber samples.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Nonabelian source and target groups}

\begin{theorem}[Ordered word relations]\label{gsr:en:07:thm:nonabelian}
Let \(G\) be a finite group and \(H\) any group, now written
multiplicatively. Use right steps \(g\mapsto gd\), and test
\(\phi(x)^{-1}\phi(y)=\psi(d)\) on an internal edge. Define the transport
profile with coefficient \(\mu(gs^{-1})\) for prefix \(s\). For two
nonempty words with the same ordered product in \(G\), a total profile
budget below one forces equality of their ordered image products in
\(H\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a prefix \(s\), the equation \(g=rs\) gives starting index
\(r=gs^{-1}\), so the edge marginal has precisely the claimed coefficient.
Choose shared initial and terminal samples exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:07:thm:polygon}. On the event that all edge equations hold,
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^m\psi(d_j)
 =\bigl[\phi(x_0)^{-1}\phi(x_1)\bigr]
  \bigl[\phi(x_1)^{-1}\phi(x_2)\bigr]\cdots
  \bigl[\phi(x_{m-1})^{-1}\phi(x_m)\bigr]
 =\phi(x_0)^{-1}\phi(x_m),
\]
with products in their original order. Both paths have the same endpoints.
The identical union bound now proves the result without any commutativity
assumption.
\end{proof}

This is a relation-wise, direction-wise statement. It should again be
distinguished from a theorem deriving closeness to a global homomorphism
from one averaged multiplication test, as in \cite{bclr}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An explicit weighted replacement for the energy extraction step\srctag{10}}]{An explicit weighted replacement for the energy extraction step}\label{gsr:en:10:sec:d7}
\srcnote{10}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:10:sec:weighted-bsg}

The rather large powers in Proposition~7.3 of the source paper are not
intrinsic to the energy extraction step.  Two intermediate thresholding
operations can be removed by retaining the representation multiplicities
as weights.  We give all constants, including the finite-size correction
caused by diagonal pairs.  This is a self-contained quantitative
replacement for that proposition, not a claim to improve the modern
Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers theorem.

For a nonempty finite subset $A$ of an abelian group, write
\[
 m=|A|,\qquad
 r_A(d)=|\{(a,b)\in A^2:a-b=d\}|,\qquad
 E(A)=\sum_d r_A(d)^2.
\]
The ambient group need not be finite or torsion-free.

\begin{theorem}[An explicit weighted energy extraction]
\label{gsr:en:10:thm:weighted-bsg}
Suppose $0<c\leq1$ and $E(A)\geq cm^3$.  Then there is a nonempty
subset $A_*\subseteq A$ such that
\[
 |A_*|\geq \frac{c}{4}m,
 \qquad
 |A_*-A_*|\leq 2^{10}c^{-5}m.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $m\leq32c^{-2}$, take $A_*=A$.  Indeed,
$|A-A|\leq m^2\leq32c^{-2}m\leq2^{10}c^{-5}m$.
We henceforth assume $m>32c^{-2}$.

Define the symmetric matrix of weights
\[
 w(a,b)=\frac{r_A(a-b)}{m}\in[0,1]\quad(a,b\in A)
\]
and its weighted codegrees
\[
 T(a,b)=\sum_{v\in A}w(v,a)w(v,b).
\]
Here diagonal pairs are retained throughout.  The normalization was
chosen so that
\[
 \sum_{a,b\in A}w(a,b)=\frac{E(A)}m\geq cm^2.
\]
Call a pair $(a,b)$ bad if $T(a,b)<c^2m/16$.

Choose $v$ uniformly from $A$ and, conditional on $v$, form a random
subset $K\subseteq A$ by including each $a$ independently with
probability $w(v,a)$.  If $d(v)=\sum_aw(v,a)$, then
\[
 \mathbb E(|K|^2\mid v)
 =d(v)^2+\sum_a w(v,a)(1-w(v,a))\geq d(v)^2.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb E|K|^2\geq\frac1m\sum_vd(v)^2\geq c^2m^2.
\]
Let $Z$ be the number of ordered bad pairs in $K^2$.  For $a\ne b$,
the probability that $a,b\in K$ is $T(a,b)/m$, hence is less than
$c^2/16$ for a bad pair.  There are at most $m$ diagonal pairs, and each
contributes at most one to the expectation.  Consequently
\[
 \mathbb EZ\leq\frac{c^2m^2}{16}+m.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \mathbb E(|K|^2-8Z)
 \geq\frac{c^2m^2}{2}-8m
 >\frac{c^2m^2}{4}.
\]
Fix one outcome with
$|K|^2-8Z\geq c^2m^2/4$.  This implies
\[
 |K|\geq cm/2,\qquad Z\leq |K|^2/8.
\]
Let $A_*$ consist of those $a\in K$ for which at most $|K|/4$ elements
$b\in K$ make $(a,b)$ bad.  Counting bad pairs by their first coordinate
shows that $|A_*|\geq|K|/2\geq cm/4$.  Moreover, for every
$a,b\in A_*$ there are at least $|K|/2$ elements $z\in K$ for which
\[
 T(a,z)\geq c^2m/16,
 \qquad T(b,z)\geq c^2m/16.
\]

Let $R(t)$ count the representations of $t$ in the form
$(p-q)-(r-s)$ with $p,q,r,s\in A$.  For fixed $a,z\in A$,
\[
 R(a-z)\geq\sum_{u\in A}r_A(a-u)r_A(z-u)=m^2T(a,z).
\]
For completeness, the inequality involves no multiplicity error:
each choice of $u$, a representation $p-q=a-u$, and a representation
$r-s=z-u$ supplies a quadruple representing $a-z$; that quadruple
recovers $u$ from $u=a-(p-q)$.

For each of the above good choices of $z$, there are at least
$c^4m^6/2^8$ pairs of quadruples representing $a-z$ and $b-z$.
Combining them gives representations of $a-b$ by ordered eight-tuples
in $A^8$.  Representations coming from different $z$ are disjoint:
the first quadruple determines $a-z$ and hence determines $z$.
Thus every $a-b$ with $a,b\in A_*$ has at least
\[
 \frac{|K|}{2}\frac{c^4m^6}{2^8}
 \geq\frac{c^5m^7}{2^{10}}
\]
representations of this form.  Choose one pair of endpoints $(a,b)$
for every distinct member of $A_*-A_*$.  An ordered eight-tuple has a
unique value of the displayed alternating sum, so tuples counted for
different differences are disjoint.  There are only $m^8$ eight-tuples
in total.  Dividing proves
$|A_*-A_*|\leq2^{10}c^{-5}m$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What is improved, and what is already known.}
The source paper gives $|A_*|\geq2^{-20}c^{12}m$ and
$|A_*-A_*|\leq2^{38}c^{-24}m$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:weighted-bsg}
improves both quantitative guarantees and applies to arbitrary abelian
groups.  The mechanism is familiar: weighted dependent random choice,
followed by counting many representations of each surviving difference.
It should not be described as a new best theorem in additive
combinatorics.  For example, Reiher and Schoen prove that for every
$\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ one can obtain
\[
 |A'|\geq(1-\varepsilon)c^{1/2}m,
 \qquad
 |A'-A'|\leq2^{33}\varepsilon^{-9}c^{-4}|A'|.
\]
Their theorem is a substantially stronger modern benchmark
\cite[Theorem 1.2]{reiherschoen}.  The
advantage of the present replacement is a short proof with small,
completely explicit constants that can be inserted directly into the
source paper's chain of lemmas.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
Source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:03:drc:elementary-bsg} is the other elementary replacement, with $(c/8,\,2^{19}c^{-9})$; this theorem is stronger in both conclusions for $0<c\le1$ (note after source~03's theorem). Both imply the formal \file{proposition_7_3} bounds (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~135; exact companion \file{proposition_7_3_holds}); neither is formalized.
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{A parameterized version for later optimization.}
The same proof can retain its choices.  Let
$0<\beta<\eta<1/2$, $0<\theta<\beta$, and $0<\sigma<1$ satisfy
$\sigma^2<1-\theta/\beta$.  Put
\[
 M_0=\frac{1}{\beta(1-\theta/\beta-\sigma^2)c^2}.
\]
If $m>M_0$, the proof with bad threshold $\theta c^2m$ and potential
$|K|^2-\beta^{-1}Z$ gives
\[
 |A_*|\geq(1-\beta/\eta)\sigma cm,
 \qquad
 |A_*-A_*|\leq
 \frac{c^{-5}m}{(1-2\eta)\sigma\theta^2}.
\]
For $m\leq M_0$ one can simply take $A_*=A$ and use
$|A-A|\leq M_0m$.  The choice
$(\beta,\eta,\theta,\sigma)=(1/8,1/4,1/16,1/2)$ gives the theorem.
The explicit $m$ term in the random-pair calculation is essential:
independence of the two membership events is available only off the
diagonal.  Omitting that term would leave a genuine gap for small sets.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharper obstruction-fibre form of the Freiman extraction\srctag{10}}]{A sharper obstruction-fibre form of the Freiman extraction}\label{gsr:en:10:sec:d8}
\srcnote{10}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:10:sec:fibre-freiman}

We next refine Lemma~7.5 of the source.  This stage does not require the
domain to be a cyclic group.  What matters is that the \emph{codomain}
is the field of prime order.

\begin{theorem}[Extraction controlled by the vertical obstruction fibre]
\label{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction}
Let $G$ be an abelian group, let $p$ be prime, let $B\subseteq G$ be
finite and nonempty, and let $\phi:B\to\mathbb F_p$.  Fix an integer
$k\geq1$, write $\Gamma=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\}$, and define
\[
 H_k=\{y\in\mathbb F_p:(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\},
 \qquad h_k=|H_k|.
\]
Then $\phi$ restricts to a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$ on a
subset $B'\subseteq B$ of size at least
\[
 |B'|\geq\frac{|B|}{k(h_k-1)+1}.
\]
If, in addition, $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\leq C|\Gamma|$, then
\[
 h_k\leq C^{2k+1},
 \qquad
 |B'|\geq\frac{|B|}{kC^{2k+1}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The set $H_k$ is symmetric and contains zero.  If $h_k=1$, then every
relation between two sums of $k$ elements of $B$ already has zero
vertical defect, so $\phi$ itself is a Freiman homomorphism of order
$k$.  Suppose henceforth that $h_k\geq2$, and set
\[
 a=k(h_k-1),\qquad L=\left\lfloor\frac{p-2}{a}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each integer $j$ with $1\leq j\leq kL$ and each
$y\in H_k\setminus\{0\}$, the equation $jd=y$ excludes at most one
$d\in\mathbb F_p^\times$.  Indeed $kL\leq p-2$, so $j$ is invertible.
There are at most $kL(h_k-1)=aL\leq p-2$ excluded nonzero choices of
$d$, and there are $p-1$ nonzero choices available.  Choose an allowed
$d$.  Symmetry of $H_k$ ensures
\[
 jd\notin H_k\quad\text{whenever }0<|j|\leq kL.
\]

For every $b\in\mathbb F_p$, consider
\[
 B_b=\{x\in B:\phi(x)\in b+d\{0,1,\ldots,L\}\}.
\]
Since $L<p$ and $d\ne0$, each $x\in B$ is counted in exactly $L+1$
of these sets.  Some $b$ thus satisfies
$|B_b|\geq(L+1)|B|/p$.  We claim
\[
 \frac{L+1}{p}\geq\frac{1}{a+1}.
\]
If $a\geq p-1$, then $L=0$ and the assertion is immediate.  If
$a\leq p-1$, Euclidean division of $p-2$ by $a$ gives
$L+1\geq(p-1)/a$, while
$(p-1)/a\geq p/(a+1)$ because $p-1\geq a$.

Take $B'=B_b$.  For each $x\in B'$ there is a unique integer
$j(x)\in[0,L]$ such that $\phi(x)=b+dj(x)$.  If
$x_1+\cdots+x_k=x'_1+\cdots+x'_k$, then
\[
 d\left(\sum_{i=1}^kj(x_i)-\sum_{i=1}^kj(x_i')\right)\in H_k.
\]
The integer in parentheses lies in $[-kL,kL]$, and the chosen step
$d$ forces it to vanish.  Hence the corresponding sums of $\phi$
values are equal, proving the Freiman property and the first bound.

For the small-doubling assertion, the map
\[
 H_k\times\Gamma\longrightarrow(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma,
 \qquad(y,\gamma)\longmapsto(0,y)+\gamma
\]
is injective.  Its first coordinate recovers $\gamma$ because
$\Gamma$ is a graph, and then its second coordinate recovers $y$.
The standard Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa inequality gives
\[
 |(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma|\leq C^{2k+1}|\Gamma|.
\]
For a small-difference hypothesis this follows by applying the
sum-difference form of that inequality to the pair
$-\Gamma,\Gamma$; see \cite{petridis}.
Consequently $h_k\leq C^{2k+1}$.  Finally,
$k(h_k-1)+1\leq kC^{2k+1}$ for $k\geq1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
Source~24's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction} is a second route with the prefactor $|B|/(kQ_k)$, $Q_k=h_k$, never better than the one here; its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:hash} treats codomains $\F_p^d$ by linear hashing.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~31's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman} is this theorem with arbitrary nonnegative weights and the progression length $\lfloor p/(kq)\rfloor$, never longer than the one in the proof here (note there).
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Why the fibre is the appropriate invariant.}
The set $H_k$ records exactly the possible failures to respect
length-$k$ additive relations.  The global size of a high sum-difference
set is used only to bound $h_k$ when no more specific information is
available.  In examples where the vertical defects occupy few values,
the first bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction} can be much
stronger than its small-doubling corollary.  If $H_k=\{0\}$ it correctly
returns all of $B$, independently of the doubling constant.
The dilation proof requires a prime codomain; the displayed argument
does not extend unchanged to arbitrary composite cyclic groups.

\begin{corollary}[An explicit replacement for Corollary~7.6]
\label{gsr:en:10:cor:improved-order-eight}
Let $B_0$ be a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group, let
$\phi:B_0\to\mathbb F_p$, and suppose the graph of $\phi$ has at least
$\gamma|B_0|^3$ additive quadruples, where $0<\gamma\leq1$.  For every
integer $k\geq1$ there is $B\subseteq B_0$ on which $\phi$ is a Freiman
homomorphism of order $k$ and
\[
 |B|\geq\frac{2^{-24k-14}}{k}\,
       \gamma^{12k+7}|B_0|.
\]
In particular, for order eight,
\[
 |B|\geq2^{-209}\gamma^{103}|B_0|.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:weighted-bsg} to the graph, obtaining a subgraph
$\Gamma_1$ with
\[
 |\Gamma_1|\geq\frac\gamma4|B_0|,
 \qquad
 |\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|\leq2^{10}\gamma^{-5}|B_0|
 \leq2^{12}\gamma^{-6}|\Gamma_1|.
\]
Set $C=2^{12}\gamma^{-6}$ and use
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction}.  The retained proportion is at least
\[
 \frac{\gamma/4}{k(2^{12}\gamma^{-6})^{2k+1}}
 =\frac{2^{-24k-14}}k\gamma^{12k+7}.
\]
When $k=8$, $24k+14+\log_2k=209$ and $12k+7=103$.
\end{proof}
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
\emph{Checked at the second write.} The retained proportion is $(\gamma/4)/(k(2^{12}\gamma^{-6})^{2k+1})=2^{-2-12(2k+1)}k^{-1}\gamma^{12k+7}$, which at $k=8$ is $2^{-209}\gamma^{103}$. \emph{Against the formal statements} (HEAD \texttt{764740f07}): \file{corollary_7_6} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~197) assumes $N$ prime, $|B_0|=\alpha N$ and $\gamma(\alpha N)^3\le$ the number of additive quadruples of the graph, and concludes a Freiman homomorphism of order eight on $B$ with $|B|\ge2^{-1882}\gamma^{1164}\alpha N$. Likewise Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction} implies \file{lemma_7_5}'s $|B|/(8kC^{4k})$, since $C\ge1$ when $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$ and $B\ne\emptyset$ (for $B=\emptyset$ the formal conclusion holds with $B'=\emptyset$) \textup{(corrected after the independent check of 6~October 2026; the first wording omitted the empty case)}. Neither is formalized (exact companions \file{corollary_7_6_holds}, \file{lemma_7_5_holds} prove the printed constants).
\end{writenote}

This partly answers source~17's Question~7 (exactness from quadruple energy with polynomial loss; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:exactness}).
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{A modern-input alternative.}
If the Reiher--Schoen theorem \cite{reiherschoen} is admitted as an external input instead
of the self-contained energy extraction, the same fibre argument gives
\[
 |B|\geq
 \frac{(1-\varepsilon)\varepsilon^{9(2k+1)}}
      {k\,2^{33(2k+1)}}\,
 \gamma^{8k+9/2}|B_0|
 \quad(0<\varepsilon<1/2).
\]
For $k=8$ the power of $\gamma$ is $137/2$ rather than $103$.
This is a corollary of a published result plus the preceding extraction
calculation, and must be labelled as such.  The self-contained and
modern-input versions have different useful roles: the former has a
short complete proof here, while the latter records a better presently
available exponent.  Neither by itself yields a new overall bound for
Szemer\'edi's theorem; the later structural and iterative stages still
have to be checked with their own quantified hypotheses.

\paragraph{Further questions arising specifically from these refinements.}
The obstruction fibres $H_k$ may permit data-sensitive structure
theorems stronger than replacing them immediately by $C^{2k+1}$.
Natural precise projects are to bound $|H_k|$ from a graph's vertical
energy profile, to study its growth with $k$, and to determine when an
order-$k$ homomorphism extends with small additional loss to order
$k+1$.  The next subsection extends the prime-codomain dilation
argument to a general finite abelian codomain by retaining the exact
number of solutions of $jd=y$.
For formalization, the two finite counting injections in the energy
proof and the injection $H_k\times\Gamma\to(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma$ are
particularly suitable intermediate lemmas.

% Szemeredi, and Gowers, Combinatorica 44 (2024), 691--698.

\subsection{A torsion-sensitive extraction for general finite codomains}
\label{gsr:en:10:subsec:torsion-fibre-extraction}

The prime-codomain dilation argument admits an explicit extension when
the sizes of the multiplication fibres are retained.  The resulting
criterion records how the vertical defects meet the images $jV$.

\begin{theorem}[Extraction from a torsion and defect budget]
\label{gsr:en:10:thm:torsion-fibre-extraction}
Let $G$ be an abelian group, let $B\subseteq G$ be finite and nonempty,
let $V$ be a finite abelian group of order $n\geq2$, and let
$\phi:B\to V$.  Fix an integer $k\geq1$, and put
\[
 \Gamma=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\},\qquad
 F=\{y\in V:(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\}.
\]
For an integer $L\geq0$ define
\[
 \mathcal B_{k,V,F}(L)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{kL}
    \bigl(|V[j]|\,|F\cap jV|-1\bigr),
 \qquad V[j]=\{v\in V:jv=0\}.
\]
If
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal B_{k,V,F}(L)\leq n-2,
 \label{gsr:en:10:eq:torsion-defect-budget}
\end{equation}
then $\phi$ restricts to a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$ on a
subset $B'\subseteq B$ of size at least
\begin{equation}
 |B'|\geq\frac{L+1}{n}|B|.
 \label{gsr:en:10:eq:torsion-defect-retention}
\end{equation}
The subset can be chosen so that its image lies in
$a+d\{0,\ldots,L\}$ for some $a\in V$ and some $d\ne0$.
If $L>0$, this step has order greater than $kL$.
If $F=\{0\}$, the original map $\phi$ is already a Freiman
homomorphism of order $k$ on all of $B$, independently of the budget.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The defect set $F$ is symmetric and contains zero.  For $j\geq1$ let
\[
 E_j=\{d\in V\setminus\{0\}:jd\in F\}.
\]
Multiplication by $j$ has image $jV$, and every nonempty fibre has
$|V[j]|$ elements.  Because $0\in F$, the zero element is one of the
preimages being counted.  Removing it gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 |E_j|=|V[j]|\,|F\cap jV|-1.
 \label{gsr:en:10:eq:torsion-defect-bad-step-count}
\end{equation}
The union bound and \eqref{gsr:en:10:eq:torsion-defect-budget} leave at least one
nonzero $d$ outside $\bigcup_{j=1}^{kL}E_j$.  It satisfies
\[
 jd\notin F\quad\text{for }1\leq j\leq kL.
\]
By symmetry of $F$, the same holds for $-kL\leq j\leq-1$.
When $L>0$, the inclusion $0\in F$ also implies that the order of $d$
is greater than $kL$.  Hence the $L+1$ elements of
$P=d\{0,\ldots,L\}$ are distinct; this is immediate when $L=0$.

For each $a\in V$ let
\[
 B_a=\{x\in B:\phi(x)\in a+P\}.
\]
Every $x\in B$ occurs in exactly $L+1$ of these sets, since the possible
translations are $a=\phi(x)-jd$ with $0\leq j\leq L$.  Thus
\[
 \sum_{a\in V}|B_a|=(L+1)|B|.
\]
Choose a translate attaining at least this average, and put $B'=B_a$.
For every $x\in B'$ there is a unique integer $t(x)\in[0,L]$ with
$\phi(x)=a+dt(x)$.

Suppose
$x_1+\cdots+x_k=x'_1+\cdots+x'_k$ with all the points in $B'$.
Its vertical defect belongs to $F$ and equals
\[
 dJ,\qquad
 J=\sum_{i=1}^kt(x_i)-\sum_{i=1}^kt(x'_i),\qquad |J|\leq kL.
\]
The choice of $d$ rules out every nonzero such integer $J$.  Therefore
$J=0$, and the sums of the corresponding $\phi$ values agree.  This
proves the Freiman property and \eqref{gsr:en:10:eq:torsion-defect-retention}.
Finally, if $F=\{0\}$, every length-$k$ relation in the original domain
has zero vertical defect by definition, proving the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
On $V=\F_p^d$ source~24's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:hash} is strictly better whenever $Q_k\le p^{d-1}$ and $k\ge2$, because a multiple of $p$ costs $p^d-1$ in the budget here (proved in the note after that theorem).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Recovery of the prime-codomain estimate]
\label{gsr:en:10:cor:torsion-fibre-prime-recovery}
Under the hypotheses above, let $V=\mathbb F_p$ and $h=|F|$.
There is a subset on which $\phi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order
$k$ and whose cardinality is at least
\[
 \frac{|B|}{k(h-1)+1}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $h=1$, use all of $B$.  Otherwise set
\[
 a=k(h-1),\qquad L=\left\lfloor\frac{p-2}{a}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then $kL\leq p-2$, so multiplication by each $1\leq j\leq kL$ is
invertible.  Every summand of the budget is $h-1$, and
\[
 \mathcal B_{k,\mathbb F_p,F}(L)=kL(h-1)\leq p-2.
\]
The theorem gives $(L+1)|B|/p$.  The integer inequality
$p-2<a(L+1)$ implies
\[
 p\leq a(L+1)+1\leq(a+1)(L+1),
\]
which proves the claimed bound, including the case $L=0$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope of the criterion.}
The budget always allows $L=0$, giving the constant-fibre bound
$|B|/|V|$.  Positive $L$ requires a step of order greater than $kL$.
For example, if $\exp(V)\leq k$, no positive $L$ satisfies the budget:
the summand with $j=\exp(V)$ is already $n-1$.  The separate case
$F=\{0\}$ still returns the whole domain.  Thus the theorem is a
data-dependent extension of the dilation argument; it does not assert
a uniform large-subset guarantee for every torsion profile.  Sharper
estimates for unions of the sets $E_j$, rather than their sum, are a
natural way to improve this criterion.

\section{Source~11's chapter: affine rigidity at the Section~6 endpoint \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:affine}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the third write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections are source~11, a manuscript on one interface of Gowers's Section~6: after Proposition~6.1 supplies many respected additive quadruples and Lemma~6.2 identifies them with additive quadruples of the graph of the frequency-selection map, the observation before Lemma~6.2 says that \emph{full} graph energy forces an affine map. Source~11 quantifies this endpoint. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~02's Sections~\ref{gsr:en:02:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:02:sec:d5}}, which strengthen the energy lower bound of Proposition~6.1 itself; it is printed here, at the end of Part~II, because no number printed earlier may move. Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:11:sec:d1}; its verification, formalization plan, questions, conclusion and reproduction notes are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:11:sec:d12}--\ref{gsr:fz:11:sec:dA}).

\emph{Reading conventions.} $\Energy(f)$ counts ordered additive quadruples respected by $f:G\to W$, $\defect(f)=1-\Energy(f)/N^3$, $d(f)$ is the proportion of points where $f$ differs from the nearest affine map, $\kappa=1$ exactly when $W$ has an element of order two, and $\Psi_\kappa(t)=4t-(10+2\kappa)t^2+(6+2\kappa)t^3$; the table at the head of this Part lists the clashes.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For errors on a set of density $t$ below $1/7$ (odd targets) or $1/3$ (targets with an involution) the defect is at least $\Psi_\kappa(t)$, with equality exactly for one error value on a subgroup coset (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainlocal}); if $\defect(f)<1/9$ the nearest affine map is unique and $d(f)\le D_\kappa(\defect(f))$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability}); for $|G|\ge34$ the largest non-affine graph energy is $N^3-4N^2+(10+2\kappa)N-(6+2\kappa)$, attained exactly by one-point modifications, and for maps between vector spaces over the same prime field without the cutoff (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}). The radii $1/7$, $1/3$ and the cutoff $34$ are sufficient, not claimed optimal (the source's non-claims); Remark~\ref{gsr:en:11:rem:cutoff} shows that the cutoff cannot simply be dropped for general groups. The correction step is the classical Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld majority decoding, credited by the source.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}). \file{proposition_6_1} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~37; exact companion \file{proposition_6_1_holds}, \file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~505) and \file{lemma_6_2} (line~47; \file{lemma_6_2_holds}, \file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~589, with \texttt{Finset.addEnergy} of \file{functionGraph}) are the interface. The exact endpoint itself is a remark of the paper, not a numbered statement or a Lean declaration. Nothing in this chapter is formalized; the source's plan is in Part~V and in \file{11-affine-rigidity-formalization\_plan.md}.

\section[{Graph energy, derivatives, and the exact endpoint\srctag{11}}]{Graph energy, derivatives, and the exact endpoint}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:basics}
\srcnote{11}{Section 2}

\begin{lemma}[Derivative collision identity]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:derivative}
Put $\Delta_h f(x)=f(x+h)-f(x)$ and
\[
 r_h(w)=|\{x\in G:\Delta_hf(x)=w\}|.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:derivative}
\Energy(f)=\sum_{h\in G}\sum_{w\in W}r_h(w)^2.
\end{equation}
Moreover, adding or subtracting an affine map from $f$ does not change
$\Energy(f)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pairs $x,y$ with $\Delta_h f(x)=\Delta_h f(y)$ correspond bijectively to
respected quadruples $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$. Conversely, from any respected
quadruple one recovers $h=x_1-x_3=x_4-x_2$, $x=x_3$, and $y=x_2$.
For an affine map $\ell(x)=L(x)+b$, the derivative $\Delta_h\ell(x)=L(h)$
is independent of $x$. Subtracting it just permutes the labels of each
histogram $r_h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Full energy]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:full}
One has $\Energy(f)\le N^3$, with equality if and only if $f$ is affine.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each $h$, the nonnegative integers $r_h(w)$ sum to $N$, so their
squares sum to at most $N^2$. Equality holds precisely when the derivative
is constant. If all derivatives are constant, let their values be $L(h)$.
The identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle}
\Delta_{h+k}f(x)=\Delta_hf(x+k)+\Delta_kf(x)
\end{equation}
implies $L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$. Also $f(x)=L(x)+f(0)$.
The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

In the derivative-imbalance normalization used in \cite{ffwc}, if
$M=|W|$, the corresponding quantity is
\[
 NB_f=\Energy(f)-N^2-(N-1)N^2/M.
\]
The ambiguity statistic is
\[
 \sum_{h\ne0}\sum_w\binom{r_h(w)}2
   =\frac{\Energy(f)-2N^2+N}{2}.
\]
These formulas allow the results here to be translated into those
normalizations without confusing componentwise Fourier nonlinearity with
the distance from a vector-valued map to a single affine map.

\subsection{A basic fact about error supports}
For a subset $S\subseteq G$ let
\[
 E(S)=\#\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in S^4:x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\}.
\]
This is set energy, as distinct from the graph energy $\Energy(f)$.

\begin{lemma}[Maximum set energy and its equality case]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}
If $|S|=s$, then $E(S)\le s^3$. If $S\ne\varnothing$, equality holds if
and only if $S$ is a coset of a subgroup of $G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $c_h=|S\cap(S-h)|$. Then
$E(S)=\sum_hc_h^2$ and $\sum_hc_h=s^2$. Since $0\le c_h\le s$,
$E(S)\le s\sum_hc_h=s^3$. Equality forces each $c_h$ to be either $0$ or
$s$. Let $T=\{h:S+h=S\}$, a subgroup. Fix $a\in S$. For every $x\in S$,
$c_{x-a}>0$, so $x-a\in T$. Thus $S\subseteq a+T$, while
$a+T\subseteq S$ follows from translation invariance. A subgroup coset
plainly attains equality.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact counting for a one-valued error\srctag{11}}]{Exact counting for a one-valued error}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:onecolor}
\srcnote{11}{Section 3}

Let $S\subseteq G$, $|S|=s$, and $b\ne0$ in $W$. Consider
$g=b\one_S$. Every additive quadruple has four positions, with signs
$+,+,-,-$. Let $J$ denote the set of positions whose coordinates belong
to $S$.

Any choice of three coordinates uniquely determines the fourth, and any
choice of two coordinates has exactly $N$ completions. This remains true
when coordinates coincide or $G$ has torsion. Consequently, fixing three
specified positions in $S$ gives $s^3$ quadruples, fixing two gives $s^2N$,
and fixing one gives $sN^2$.

\begin{lemma}[Support-pattern counts]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:patterns}
The numbers of additive quadruples with exactly one, exactly three, or
exactly two same-side positions in $S$ are, respectively,
\begin{align}
 Q_1&=4sN^2-12s^2N+12s^3-4E(S),\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q1}\\
 Q_3&=4s^3-4E(S),\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q3}\\
 Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}&=2s^2N-4s^3+2E(S).\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q2}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For one prescribed position in $S$ and the remaining three outside $S$,
inclusion--exclusion gives
$sN^2-3s^2N+3s^3-E(S)$; sum over the four positions.
For a prescribed triple of positions in $S$ and the remaining position
outside, the answer is $s^3-E(S)$; again there are four choices.
The two same-side pairs are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. For either pair,
requiring the other two positions to lie outside $S$ gives
$s^2N-2s^3+E(S)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact one-valued defect]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:onecolor}
If $2b\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oneodd}
 N^3-\Energy(b\one_S)=4sN^2-10s^2N+12s^3-6E(S).
\end{equation}
If $2b=0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwo}
 N^3-\Energy(b\one_S)=4sN^2-12s^2N+16s^3-8E(S).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
When $2b\ne0$, the rejected support patterns have exactly one position,
exactly three positions, or exactly two positions on the same side.
Patterns with two opposite-side positions have equal contributions on
both sides, and patterns with zero or four positions also pass.
Thus the defect is $Q_1+Q_3+Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}$.

When $2b=0$, the same-side two-position patterns pass as well. The rejected
patterns are exactly those with an odd number of positions in $S$, giving
$Q_1+Q_3$.
\end{proof}

Write $t=s/N$ and $e_S=E(S)/N^3$. The two formulas become
\begin{align}
\defect(b\one_S)&=\Psi_0(t)+6(t^3-e_S),&&2b\ne0,\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oneoddnorm}\\
\defect(b\one_S)&=\Psi_1(t)+8(t^3-e_S),&&2b=0.\label{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwonorm}
\end{align}
The set-energy gap is therefore visible without any asymptotic notation.

\begin{example}[One corrupted point]\label{gsr:en:11:ex:spike}
Take $S=\{x_0\}$. Then $E(S)=1$, and
\[
 \Energy(b\one_{\{x_0\}})=
 \begin{cases}
 N^3-4N^2+10N-6,&2b\ne0,\\
 N^3-4N^2+12N-8,&2b=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For $h\ne0$, the derivative histogram has entries $N-2,1,1$ in the first
case and $N-2,2$ in the second. This gives an independent check of the
counting formulas. The distinction depends on the target, not merely on
the parity of the domain size.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Replacing many error values by one: odd targets\srctag{11}}]{Replacing many error values by one: odd targets}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:odd}
\srcnote{11}{Section 4}

Subtract an affine map and suppose now that $g$ is zero outside $S$ and
nonzero on $S$. For $b\ne0$ put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:colorstats}
 c_b=|\{x:g(x)=b\}|,\qquad
 M=\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^2,\qquad
 A=s^2-M,\qquad C=\sum_{b\ne0}c_bc_{-b}.
\end{equation}
The quantity $A$ counts ordered pairs of errors with different nonzero
values. It is zero exactly when all errors have one value.

\begin{lemma}[Two elementary color inequalities]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:color}
Let $T=s^3-\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^3$, the number of ordered non-monochromatic
triples of error positions. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Tbound}
 T\le\frac32sA.
\end{equation}
For every target $W$, $C\le M$. If $W$ has no nonzero element of order two,
one also has $C\le A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A non-monochromatic triple has at least two unequal pairs among its three
pairs of positions. Counting unequal pairs together with the third entry
gives $3sA$, which proves \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:Tbound}.
The inequality $C\le M$ follows from
\[
 M-C=\frac12\sum_{b\ne0}(c_b-c_{-b})^2\ge0.
\]
When $b\ne-b$ for every nonzero $b$, the ordered pairs counted by $C$ form
a subset of the unequal-value ordered pairs counted by $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Odd-target error-value comparison]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:oddmono}
Suppose that $W$ has no nonzero element of order two. Choose any $b_0\ne0$
and put $g_0=b_0\one_S$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmono}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)\ge2(N-7s)A.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Separate additive quadruples according to the exact number of positions
in $S$. With zero positions, both maps pass; with one position, both fail;
with four positions, $g_0$ always passes and therefore cannot lose.
Only the cases with two or three positions need attention.

For two opposite-side positions, $g_0$ passes, whereas $g$ passes exactly
when the two nonzero values agree. There are four opposite-side pairs.
For one fixed pair and one of its $A$ unequal-value assignments, the
remaining coordinates have $N$ possible completions. For either remaining coordinate, at most $s$ completions put that
coordinate in $S$, since it varies bijectively with the free parameter. Thus at least
$N-2s$ completions have exactly these two errors. The total gain is at
least $4(N-2s)A$.

For two same-side positions, $g_0$ fails. The map $g$ can pass only when
the values are negatives of one another. Ignoring the restriction on the
other positions gives an upper bound $2NC$ for this loss, because there
are two same-side pairs.

For exactly three error positions, $g_0$ fails. If all three nonzero
values of $g$ are equal, $g$ fails as well: the signed sum is that value
or its negative. Therefore a gain for $g$ requires a non-monochromatic
triple. There are four triples of positions, and dropping the restriction
on the fourth position bounds this loss by $4T$.

Combining the three estimates and applying Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:color},
\[
\begin{split}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)
 &\ge4(N-2s)A-2NC-4T\\
 &\ge4(N-2s)A-2NA-6sA\\
 &=2(N-7s)A.
\end{split}
\]
Repeated coordinates create no missing cases: the fixed-position
parametrizations count them with their proper multiplicities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Odd-target deficit decomposition]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:oddmaster}
Let $W$ have no nonzero element of order two, let $g=f-\ell$ for an affine
$\ell$, and use the notation above. Put
$a=A/N^2$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(t)+6(t^3-e_S)+2(1-7t)a.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $0<t<1/7$, the lower bound $\Psi_0(t)$ holds, and equality
is equivalent to $S$ being a subgroup coset and $g$ having one nonzero value.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Affine invariance, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:11:prop:onecolor}, and
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:11:prop:oddmono} give \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}.
If $t<1/7$, both remainder terms are nonnegative. Equality forces
$A=0$ and $E(S)=s^3$, giving the description by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}. Conversely, that description attains equality
by \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oneoddnorm}.
\end{proof}

The comparison inequality is stronger than merely proving a cubic upper
bound for graph energy. It gives two independently meaningful certificates
of failure to be extremal: the support may have insufficient additive
energy, and the errors may use too many different values.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Targets with two-torsion, including mixed targets\srctag{11}}]{Targets with two-torsion, including mixed targets}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:two}
\srcnote{11}{Section 5}

It is not necessary for the target to have characteristic two. In this
section $W$ may, for example, be $\Z/6\Z$; the hypothesis is only that it
contains a nonzero involution $b_0$. Keep $M,A,C$ as in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:colorstats}, and put
\[
 J=M-C\ge0.
\]
The extra statistic $J$ measures the asymmetry between the multiplicities
of $b$ and $-b$.

\begin{proposition}[Error-value comparison with an involution]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:twomono}
If $s<N/3$ and $g_0=b_0\one_S$, with $2b_0=0$ and $b_0\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:twomono}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)
 \ge6(N-3s)A+2(N-2s)J.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For exactly two errors, $g_0$ always passes. For an opposite-side pair,
$g$ fails on $A$ ordered assignments; for a same-side pair it fails on
$s^2-C=A+J$ assignments. Requiring the other two positions to be outside
$S$ leaves at least $N-2s$ completions for each assignment. Hence the
two-error gain is at least
\[
 (N-2s)\bigl(4A+2(A+J)\bigr).
\]
For exactly three errors, the loss is bounded by $4T\le6sA$ just as
before. With zero, one, or four errors, $g_0$ cannot lose. Subtraction
proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-torsion deficit decomposition]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:twomaster}
Under these hypotheses, with $a=A/N^2$ and $j=J/N^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:twomaster}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_1(t)+8(t^3-e_S)
       +6(1-3t)a+2(1-2t)j.
\end{equation}
If $0<t<1/3$, equality with $\Psi_1(t)$ holds precisely when the error is
one involution-valued constant on a subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwonorm} and \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:twomono}.
At equality all three remainder terms vanish. The condition $A=0$ says
that exactly one nonzero value $b$ occurs. In this case $J=0$ is equivalent
to $b=-b$. The support condition again follows from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}. The converse follows from the exact counting
formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why an odd-target assertion cannot simply ignore torsion]
For a one-point error into a target containing an involution,
Example~\ref{gsr:en:11:ex:spike} exceeds the odd-target extremal energy by $2N-2$.
The odd-target cubic is therefore false in this setting, not just
nonoptimal. The distinction has been incorporated at the level of the
hypotheses rather than hidden in a proof convention.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Quantitative information about near-extremizers\srctag{11}}]{Quantitative information about near-extremizers}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:near}
\srcnote{11}{Section 6}

The preceding theorems also describe how an almost extremizer can fail to
be an exact extremizer. This does not require any compactness argument.

\begin{corollary}[Two separate defects in the odd case]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:nearodd}
Assume $0<t<1/7$ and
$\defect(f)\le\Psi_0(t)+\eta$. Then
\begin{align}
 t^3-e_S&\le\eta/6,\label{gsr:en:11:eq:nearsupport}\\
 \frac{A}{N^2}&\le\frac{\eta}{2(1-7t)}.\label{gsr:en:11:eq:nearcolor}
\end{align}
There is a nonzero value $b$ such that the proportion of domain points
with nonzero error different from $b$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:minority}
 \frac{\eta}{2t(1-7t)}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first two claims follow by dropping the other nonnegative term in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}. If $m=\max_b c_b$ and $u=s-m$, then
$M\le sm$, so $A=s^2-M\ge su$. Divide by $N^2$ and use
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:nearcolor}.
\end{proof}

For a target with an involution, \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:twomaster} similarly gives
\[
 t^3-e_S\le\eta/8,\qquad
 \frac A{N^2}\le\frac{\eta}{6(1-3t)},\qquad
 \frac J{N^2}\le\frac{\eta}{2(1-2t)}.
\]
The minority-value estimate follows by dividing the second inequality by
$t$. The third inequality is additional information not present in the
odd-target case.

These estimates do not by themselves state that $S$ is close in symmetric
difference to a subgroup coset. They reduce that remaining stability issue
to a precise high-energy question about $S$, with
$E(S)/s^3\ge1-\eta/(6t^3)$ in the odd case. That normalization matters:
an additive error small compared with one need not be small compared with
$t^3$. A full relative stability statement would have to retain this
scale.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Removing the assumption of proximity to an affine map\srctag{11}}]{Removing the assumption of proximity to an affine map}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:correction}
\srcnote{11}{Section 7}

We now prove a correction lemma rather than taking it as a black box.
The method is classical; its role here is to enter the range where the
sharp cubics apply.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary correction of a nearly additive map]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:blr}
Let $F:G\to W$ and suppose
\[
 \Prb_{x,y}\bigl(F(x+y)\ne F(x)+F(y)\bigr)=\rho<1/6.
\]
Then there is a homomorphism $L:G\to W$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}
 \Prb_x(F(x)\ne L(x))\le\frac{\rho}{1-2\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $h\in G$ and consider the random value
$Z_h(y)=F(h+y)-F(y)$. For independent uniform $y,z$, both equations
\[
 F(h+y)+F(z)=F(h+y+z),\qquad
 F(y)+F(h+z)=F(h+y+z)
\]
hold except with probability at most $2\rho$. Each tested pair is uniformly
distributed on $G^2$, even for fixed $h$. When both equations hold,
$Z_h(y)=Z_h(z)$. Hence the collision probability of $Z_h$ is at least
$1-2\rho$.

For any probability distribution $(p_w)$, $\sum_wp_w^2\le\max_wp_w$.
Thus $Z_h$ has a unique modal value $L(h)$ of probability at least
$1-2\rho>1/2$. For fixed $h,k$, the three identities
\[
 Z_{h+k}(x)=L(h+k),\quad Z_h(x+k)=L(h),\quad Z_k(x)=L(k)
\]
hold simultaneously for some $x$, since their total failure probability
is at most $6\rho<1$. The exact derivative identity
$Z_{h+k}(x)=Z_h(x+k)+Z_k(x)$ then proves additivity of $L$.

If $F(h)\ne L(h)$, at least a proportion $1-2\rho$ of the values $Z_h(y)$
differ from $F(h)$. Averaging this observation over $h$ gives
\[
 \rho=\Prb_{h,y}(Z_h(y)\ne F(h))
 \ge(1-2\rho)\Prb_h(F(h)\ne L(h)),
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit and comparison.} The majority step $\sum_wp_w^2\le\max_wp_w$ used here is the coarsest of three collision-to-mode bounds in this report: source~07's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:collision} and source~12's sharp Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}, whose mode bound $1-\chi(\eta)$, $\chi(\eta)=(1-\sqrt{1-2\eta})/2\le\eta$, is optimal. Inserting source~12's lemma into this proof (with $\eta=2\rho$) would give disagreement at most $\rho/(1-\chi(2\rho))$ in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}; the consequence for the cutoff $34$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} is recorded as a marked question, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}, because neither source writes it.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Passing from graph energy to the correction test]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:anchor}
There is an anchor $a\in G$ such that
$F_a(x)=f(a+x)-f(a)$ fails the test in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} with
probability at most $\defect(f)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The average over $a,x,y$ of the acceptance condition is the probability
of
\[
 f(a+x)+f(a+y)=f(a)+f(a+x+y).
\]
The parametrization
$(a,x,y)\mapsto(a+x,a+y,a,a+x+y)$ is a bijection onto the ordered additive
quadruples. Its acceptance probability is exactly $1-\defect(f)$.
One anchor is at least as good as the average.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability}]
Write $\defect=\defect(f)$. Applying Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:anchor} and
\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} gives an affine map with disagreement proportion at most
\[
 \frac{\defect}{1-2\defect}<\frac17
 \qquad(\defect<1/9).
\]
In original coordinates this map is
$x\mapsto L(x-a)+f(a)$. The closest affine map has disagreement proportion
$d(f)<1/7$ as well, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainlocal} gives
$\defect\ge\Psi_\kappa(d(f))$. Monotonicity on $[0,1/7]$ yields
\eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:mainstability}.

Two distinct affine maps agree either nowhere or on a coset of the kernel
of a nonzero homomorphism. Such a coset has size at most $N/2$.
Their mutual Hamming distance is therefore at least $N/2$.
Two affine maps each at distance less than $N/7$ from $f$ cannot be
distinct. This proves uniqueness. Finally, equality in the inverse
inequality is equality in the corresponding local profile, whose equality
cases have already been classified.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A deterministic reconstruction algorithm}
The proof gives an explicit, though not optimized, algorithm for a finite
input table. Count the failed tests for each anchor $a$, select an anchor
with failure at most the average, and compute the modal derivative value
$L(h)$ for every $h$. Output $L(x-a)+f(a)$ and count its disagreements with
$f$. With group operations available by tables, straightforward enumeration
uses $O(N^3)$ elementary operations for the anchor search and $O(N^2)$
for the histograms, with sparse counters for target values. These operation
counts describe this implementation, not a claim of optimal complexity.
The cubic gives a certificate stronger than the preliminary
$\defect/(1-2\defect)$ estimate.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact inversion and sharp recovery constants\srctag{11}}]{Exact inversion and sharp recovery constants}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:inverse}
\srcnote{11}{Section 8}

The odd-target cubic factors as
\[
 \Psi_0(t)=4t(1-t)(1-3t/2).
\]
The analytic inverse at zero therefore has a particularly explicit series.

\begin{proposition}[All-orders odd-target inverse]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:inverse}
For sufficiently small $u$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:lagrange}
 D_0(u)=\sum_{n\ge1} a_nu^n,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:an}
 a_n=\frac{1}{n4^n}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \binom{n+j-1}{j}\binom{2n-j-2}{n-1-j}
 \left(\frac32\right)^{n-1-j}.
\end{equation}
In particular all the coefficients are positive, and the first eight are
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac14,\quad\frac5{32},\quad\frac{11}{64},\quad\frac{475}{2048},\\
\frac{1427}{4096},\quad\frac{36645}{65536},\quad
\frac{123051}{131072},\quad\frac{13661175}{8388608}.
\end{gathered}
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inverse equation is
\[
 t=u\,\frac{1}{4(1-t)(1-3t/2)}.
\]
The formal Lagrange coefficient identity gives
\[
 a_n=\frac1{n4^n}[z^{n-1}](1-z)^{-n}(1-3z/2)^{-n}.
\]
Expanding the two binomial series gives \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:an}.
Since $\Psi_0'(0)=4$, the analytic inverse function theorem identifies the
formal expansion with a convergent inverse in a neighborhood of zero.
The exact rational substitution check through degree eight is included in
the verification script.
\end{proof}

No radius of convergence is needed for the quantitative theorem:
$D_0$ is defined there by the unique root in $[0,1/7]$. For numerical use,
bisection on that interval gives a certified value without relying on a
truncated asymptotic series. The beginning of the other branch is
\[
 D_1(u)=\frac u4+\frac{3u^2}{16}+\frac{u^3}{4}+O(u^4).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness along vanishing-density families]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:sharpinverse}
For either target type there are finite examples with $d(f)\to0$ and
\[
 d(f)=D_\kappa(\defect(f)).
\]
Consequently, no coefficient in the full small-$u$ expansion can be
decreased while keeping all preceding coefficients unchanged and an
error of smaller order, uniformly over finite groups.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take a one-point error in cyclic groups of increasing order, or a coset
error of increasing index, using an involution when required. Let the
error density be $t$. Once $t<1/4$, the zero affine map is uniquely closest:
any other affine map differs from it on at least half the domain and
therefore differs from the error map on more than $tN$ points.
The exact defect is $\Psi_\kappa(t)$. For sufficiently large index this
defect is below $1/9$, and equality in the inverse follows. Comparison
along this sequence proves the coefficient assertion.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The largest non-affine energy in arbitrary large finite groups\srctag{11}}]{The largest non-affine energy in arbitrary large finite groups}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:global}
\srcnote{11}{Section 9}

We first prove the unrestricted-group part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}.
The key additional ingredient is merely the discreteness of Hamming
distance.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} for $N\ge34$]
For $N\ge34$,
\[
 \Psi_\kappa(1/N)\le\Psi_0(1/34)
 =\frac{4290}{39304}<\frac19.
\]
Suppose a non-affine $f$ had graph energy larger than the right-hand side
of \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax}. Its defect would be smaller than
$\Psi_\kappa(1/N)$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability} would imply
$d(f)<1/N$, impossible for a non-affine function on an $N$-point set.

At equality the same theorem gives $d(f)\le1/N$. Non-affinity forces
$d(f)=1/N$, and the equality description of the small-error theorem gives
a one-point modification, of the required target order.
Conversely, such a modification has exactly the asserted energy by
Example~\ref{gsr:en:11:ex:spike}. It is non-affine because two distinct affine maps
cannot differ on only one point when $N\ge34$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact affine certification threshold]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:certificate}
For $N\ge34$, if
\[
 \Energy(f)>N^3-4N^2+(10+2\kappa)N-(6+2\kappa),
\]
then $f$ is affine. The strict inequality cannot be weakened.
\end{corollary}

This assertion is a complete extremal statement for this finite problem,
not just a stability estimate with an unspecified constant. It is also
uniform in the structures and cardinalities of the target groups, except
for the stated two-torsion distinction. The cutoff $34$ is a convenient
consequence of the correction radius, not a demonstrated optimal cutoff.

\begin{writeremarkc}[The cutoff cannot simply be dropped; added at the third write, 6~October 2026]\label{gsr:en:11:rem:cutoff}
For general finite abelian groups the formula \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax} can fail for $N<34$ (it holds for some such $N$ and fails for others); the smallest failure found has $N=4$. Take $G=\Z/12\Z$, $W=\Z/2\Z$ (so $\kappa=1$), and $f(x)=1$ if $x\bmod4\in\{0,1\}$, $f(x)=0$ otherwise. Then $f$ is not affine and
\[
 \Energy(f)=1296>1288=N^3-4N^2+12N-8\qquad(N=12).
\]
\emph{Proof.} Write $f=g\circ\pi$ with $\pi:\Z/12\Z\to\Z/4\Z$ the reduction and $g=\one_{\{0,1\}}$ on $\Z/4\Z$. Every additive quadruple of $\Z/12\Z$ maps to one of $\Z/4\Z$, and over each quadruple of $\Z/4\Z$ there are exactly $3^3=27$ (the lifts of $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are free and $x_4$ is then determined, and lies over the right point); whether $f$ respects a quadruple depends only on its image. Hence $\Energy(f)=27\,\Energy(g)$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:derivative}, $\Energy(g)=\sum_h\sum_wr_h(w)^2$: the derivatives in directions $0$ and $2$ are constant ($\Delta_2g\equiv1$), contributing $16$ each, and those in directions $1$ and $3$ take each value twice, contributing $8$ each; so $\Energy(g)=48$ and $\Energy(f)=1296$. The derivative $\Delta_1f$ takes both values ($\Delta_1f(0)=0$, $\Delta_1f(1)=1$), so $f$ is not affine by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:full}. \emph{Exhaustive check at the write} (all maps, exact integers): the largest non-affine energies of maps $\Z/n\Z\to\Z/m\Z$ against the value of \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax} are $48$ against $40$ for $\Z/4\to\Z/2$, $85$ against $77$ for $\Z/5\to\Z/2$, $231$ against $223$ for $\Z/7\to\Z/2$, $162$ against $126$ for $\Z/6\to\Z/3$, $513$ against $489$ for $\Z/9\to\Z/3$ and $1296$ against $1288$ for $\Z/12\to\Z/2$, while the formula holds for $\Z/10$, $\Z/14$, $\Z/15$ and $\Z/16\to\Z/2$ (the intake found the same table, dossier \texttt{dossier116\_GOWERS}). This does not contradict the theorem, which assumes $N\ge34$, or its vector-space part ($\Z/12\Z$ and $\Z/4\Z$ are not vector spaces over a prime field). It shows that the cutoff cannot be removed for general groups and that its exact value is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}).
\end{writeremarkc}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All finite vector-space sizes: a second proof\srctag{11}}]{All finite vector-space sizes: a second proof}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:vector}
\srcnote{11}{Section 10}

Let $V=\F_p^n$, $W=\F_p^m$, and $N=p^n$. Assume throughout this section
that $f$ is non-affine. The proof has no high-energy correction hypothesis. It explains exactly where
prime-field structure helps with the small cardinalities.

\subsection{Constant-derivative directions and quotienting}
Define
\[
 H=\{h\in V:\Delta_hf\text{ is constant on }V\}.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle}, $H$ is a subspace, and the constant derivative
values form a linear map $\lambda:H\to W$. Extend $\lambda$ to a linear
map $L:V\to W$ by extending a basis of $H$ to a basis of $V$.
The map $f-L$ is constant on each coset of $H$, so it factors through
$\bar f:V/H\to W$.

\begin{lemma}[Energy under quotienting]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:quotient}
Let $q=|V/H|$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:quotient}
 \frac{\Energy(f)}{N^3}=\frac{\Energy(\bar f)}{q^3}.
\end{equation}
The map $\bar f$ has no constant derivative in a nonzero direction.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every additive quadruple in the quotient lifts to exactly $|H|^3$
additive quadruples in $V$, and respect for the function is unchanged
under this lift and subtraction of $L$. A nonzero constant-derivative
direction in the quotient would lift to a direction in $H$, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The odd-characteristic histogram bound}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:11:lem:oddhist}
Let $p$ be odd, $q$ a positive power of $p$, and let a nonconstant
$q$-term list in $\F_p^m$ have sum zero. Its value multiplicities satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddhist}
 \sum_w r(w)^2\le(q-2)^2+2.
\end{equation}
Equality holds precisely when the three nonzero multiplicities are
$q-2,1,1$; the values are of the form $a,a+b,a-b$ with $b\ne0$.
For $q=3$ these three multiplicities are all one.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A multiplicity $q-1$ would give $(q-1)a+b=0$. Since $qa=0$, this forces
$b=a$, contradicting nonconstancy. If a value has multiplicity $q-2$,
the remaining two entries cannot be equal: equality to $b$ would give
$2(b-a)=0$. Thus they are distinct, and their sum must be $2a$.
This gives the asserted equality configuration.

If the maximum multiplicity is at most $q-3$ and $q\ge7$, convexity
(or transferring units from smaller counts to larger counts) bounds the
sum of squares by $(q-3)^2+3^2$, which is strictly less than
$(q-2)^2+2$. For $q=5$, a cap of two gives at most $2^2+2^2+1^2=9<11$.
For $q=3$, a nonconstant zero-sum list must have three distinct entries,
which is exactly the asserted configuration.
\end{proof}

For each derivative of $\bar f$, the sum of its values is zero, since
translation permutes the domain. Applying the lemma in every nonzero
direction and using the constant zero derivative in direction zero gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:quotoddgap}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(1/q).
\end{equation}
For real $q\ge4$, the function
$\Psi_0(1/q)=4/q-10/q^2+6/q^3$ is strictly decreasing; its derivative has
numerator $-4q^2+20q-18<0$ there. The only additional comparison needed
among powers of an odd prime is
$\Psi_0(1/3)>\Psi_0(1/9)$.
Thus if $q<N$, the inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:quotoddgap} is strictly stronger
than $\defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(1/N)$.
This proves the odd-characteristic bound and shows that equality requires
$H=\{0\}$ and equality in every nonzero-direction histogram.

\subsection{Equality for odd characteristic}
Assume first that $N\ge7$. For each nonzero $h$, let $L(h)$ be the unique
modal derivative value, attained $N-2$ times, and put $L(0)=0$.
For any $h,k$, the three modal identities in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle} exclude at most six choices of $x$. Since $N>6$, there
is a choice where all hold. Hence $L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$, and $L$ is linear.

Put $g=f-L$. For every $h\ne0$, exactly $N-2$ values of $x$ satisfy
$g(x+h)=g(x)$. If $t_w=|g^{-1}(w)|$, summing these equality counts gives
\[
 \sum_wt_w^2=N+(N-1)(N-2)=(N-1)^2+1.
\]
For a nonconstant map on $N$ points, the largest sum of squared fiber
sizes is $(N-1)^2+1$, and equality forces the fiber sizes $N-1,1$.
Indeed, among partitions of $N$ into at least two positive parts, moving
mass to the largest part increases the sum of squares until these two
parts remain. Thus $g$ is constant except at one point.

If $N=5$, take a generator and write its derivative values as
$a,a,a+b,a-b$, with $b\ne0$. After subtracting the linear map $x\mapsto ax$,
the derivative is zero except for one $b$ and one $-b$. Going around the
five-cycle, the function has two values on complementary cyclic intervals.
If either interval is a singleton, the required conclusion follows.
Otherwise their sizes are two and three; the step-two derivative then has
multiplicities $1,2,2$, whose squared sum is $9<11$, contradicting equality.

If $N=3$, subtract the affine map interpolating any two of the three
points. A non-affine map then differs at exactly the remaining point.
This completes the equality proof for every odd characteristic.

\subsection{Characteristic two}
If $p=2$, each derivative obeys
$\Delta_hf(x+h)=\Delta_hf(x)$, so for $h\ne0$ every histogram multiplicity
is even. On a quotient of size $q$, a nonconstant histogram therefore has
squared sum at most $(q-2)^2+4$, attained by multiplicities $q-2,2$.
A non-affine map cannot have quotient size two, since every map from
$\F_2$ to $W$ is affine. Thus $q\ge4$, and
\[
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_1(1/q).
\]
The function $\Psi_1(1/q)$ is decreasing for real $q\ge8$, and
$\Psi_1(1/4)>\Psi_1(1/8)$. Hence it is strictly decreasing along the powers
of two that arise here. Equality at the $N$-point bound again forces
$H=\{0\}$ and extremal histograms in every nonzero direction.

For $N\ge8$, the modal values have exactly two exceptions, so the same
six-exception argument makes them a linear map. The fiber-square argument
then gives a one-point modification. For $N=4$, interpolate a linear-affine
map through $0,e_1,e_2$ and subtract it. Only the point $e_1+e_2$ remains,
so every non-affine map has the required form. This proves the remaining
part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Partial domains and the interface with Proposition 6.1\srctag{11}}]{Partial domains and the interface with Proposition 6.1}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:partial}
\srcnote{11}{Section 11}

Gowers's frequency-selection map is naturally defined on a subset rather
than the entire group. The full-energy normalization, not a normalization
by the subset size, gives a clean extension.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical affine recovery from a partial graph]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:partial}
Let $B\subseteq G$, $\phi:B\to W$, and let $\Gamma_B$ be its graph.
Suppose
\[
 E(\Gamma_B)\ge(1-\defect)N^3,\qquad 0\le\defect<1/9.
\]
There is a unique affine map $\ell:G\to W$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr}
 |\{x\in B:\phi(x)\ne\ell(x)\}|\le D_\kappa(\defect)N.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:holes}
 |G\setminus B|/N\le1-(1-\defect)^{1/3}.
\end{equation}
The same affine map is recovered by applying the full-domain theorem to
any completion of $\phi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $\beta=|B|/N$. A graph with $|B|$ points has energy at most $|B|^3$,
so $\beta^3\ge1-\defect$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:holes}.
Extend $\phi$ arbitrarily to $f:G\to W$. Every respected quadruple of the
partial graph is also a respected quadruple of the full graph, so
$\defect(f)\le\defect$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability} and monotonicity of
$D_\kappa$ give an affine map satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr}.

If two affine maps satisfy this inequality, their agreement set has size
at least $(\beta-2D_\kappa(\defect))N$. Here $D_\kappa(\defect)<1/7$,
while $\beta>(8/9)$, unless $\defect=0$, when the conclusion is immediate.
Thus
\[
 \beta-2D_\kappa(\defect)>\frac89-\frac27=\frac{38}{63}>\frac12.
\]
Distinct affine maps cannot agree on more than half the domain. This proves
uniqueness and independence from the completion.
\end{proof}

The error in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr} is normalized by $N$, not by $|B|$.
The statement requires a graph energy close to $N^3$. It does not assert
that an arbitrary sparse partial homomorphism with energy close to
$|B|^3$ extends to an affine map on the ambient group.

\begin{corollary}[A high-correlation refinement of the Section 6 output]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61}
Let $N$ be an odd prime, $F:\Z/N\Z\to\mathbb C$ satisfy $|F|\le1$,
and let $\phi:B\to\Z/N\Z$ for $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$. Use the unnormalized
Fourier transform $\widehat u(r)=\sum_xu(x)\exp(-2\pi i rx/N)$ and put
$\partial_hF(x)=F(x)\overline{F(x-h)}$. Suppose $\alpha>0$ and
\[
 \sum_{h\in B}|\widehat{\partial_hF}(\phi(h))|^2\ge\alpha N^3,
 \qquad \alpha^4>8/9.
\]
Then the frequency-selection map $\phi$ agrees on $B$ with a unique
affine map, except on at most
\[
 D_0(1-\alpha^4)N
\]
points. Also $|B|\ge\alpha^{4/3}N$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Proposition 6.1 gives at least $\alpha^4N^3$ respected quadruples, and the
graph identity in Lemma 6.2 converts this to the hypothesis of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:11:thm:partial}. The target $\Z/N\Z$ has no nonzero involution.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~31's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:graph} treats selected graphs on every finite abelian group, partial graphs included and with no amplitude bound: graph errors at most $\varepsilon$ and quadratic infidelity at most $(1-\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon})/2$ for score $1-\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\le1/400$, both separately sharp.
\end{writenote}

The approximation error begins
\[
 \left(\frac{1-\alpha^4}{4}
 +\frac5{32}(1-\alpha^4)^2
 +\frac{11}{64}(1-\alpha^4)^3+O((1-\alpha^4)^4)\right)N.
\]
This corollary genuinely strengthens the structural information obtained
from that proposition in its high-correlation range. It does not improve
the exponent four in the original energy lower bound. In the usual
small-$\alpha$ inverse-theorem regime, its hypothesis is unavailable; this
is the precise reason it does not automatically improve the global
Szemer\'edi bound.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Scope (intake observation, checked at the write).} The hypothesis that $N$ is an odd prime is not needed for the argument. The formal \file{proposition_6_1} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~37; exact companion \file{proposition_6_1_holds}, \file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~505, at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}) assumes only $N\ge1$, $0<\alpha$, $|F|\le1$ and the displayed Fourier hypothesis with the unnormalized transform and the same derivative $F(x)\overline{F(x-h)}$, and concludes at least $\alpha^4N^3$ respected quadruples; the graph identity of Lemma~6.2 and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:11:thm:partial} hold for every finite abelian group. So the corollary holds for every odd $N$ as stated, and for even $N$ with $D_1$ in place of $D_0$ (then $\Z/N\Z$ contains the involution $N/2$). Not formalized. \emph{Relation to source~02.} Source~02's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:02:thm:main} strengthens the energy \emph{lower bound} of Proposition~6.1; this corollary uses that bound's output in the range $\alpha^4>8/9$. The two results are complementary and share no theorem.
\end{writenote}
