\section{Source~12's chapter: Freiman extension and Bohr radii in Section~10 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:bohr}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the third write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next nine sections are source~12, a manuscript on the second half of Gowers's Section~10, Lemmas~10.10--10.14: extending a Freiman homomorphism from a dense subset of a Bohr set to a smaller Bohr set, choosing the Bohr radii, and the local model of Theorem~10.13. \emph{Logically the chapter continues source~07's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:transport}), which treats Lemma~10.9, the step just before: together they cover Section~10 from Lemma~10.6 to Corollary~10.14, and they share no statement. It is printed here, at the end of Part~II, because no number printed earlier may move. Its notation follows the Section~10 table at the head of this Part. Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}; its formalization interfaces, checks, questions and parameter ledger are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:12:sec:d10}--\ref{gsr:fz:12:sec:dB}). Its Appendix~A, the fixed-domain repair of the extraction input, is printed at the end of this chapter, beside the theorem that uses it.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} If $S\subseteq B$ misses at most a fraction $\varepsilon$ of $B$ and every shift in $C$ loses at most a fraction $\kappa$ of $B$, a Freiman homomorphism on $S$ induces one on $C$ whenever $3\varepsilon+2\kappa<1$, and every rational boundary point has a counterexample (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}, \ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}); the collision-to-mode bound $1-\chi(\eta)$ is sharp (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}); a finite pigeonhole among $m$ radii selects an ambient radius with overlap $4^{-d/m}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}); a fourth-moment estimate enlarges the initial radius from $2^{-148}\alpha^{18}/\pi$ to $2^{-74}\alpha^9/\pi$ with the same spectrum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}); and Theorem~10.13 holds on a Bohr set of radius at least $\alpha^{19}/(3\pi2^{149})$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}). The component-extraction input (Lemmas~10.3--10.9) is borrowed, with its hypotheses stated (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input}); sharpness is universal over groups, not for prime cyclic groups with the same target (the source's non-claims).

\section[{Translation loss and intersections along a tree\srctag{12}}]{Translation loss and intersections along a tree}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d2}
\srcnote{12}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:boundary}

Throughout the algebraic parts, $G$ and $H$ are abelian groups written additively. The ambient group $G$ need not be finite, but $B\subseteq G$ is finite and nonempty. For $t\in G$, $B-t=\{x:x+t\in B\}$. All missing densities are measured relative to $|B|$, not $|G|$.

\begin{definition}
A function $\phi:S\to H$ is a \emph{Freiman homomorphism of order two} if
\[
 a+b=c+d,\quad a,b,c,d\in S
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \phi(a)+\phi(b)=\phi(c)+\phi(d).
\]
Repeated elements are permitted. A Freiman homomorphism of order $r$ preserves all equalities between sums of $r$ elements of its domain.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary properties of translation loss]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:boundary-properties}
For every $u,v\in G$,
\[
 b_B(0)=0,\quad b_B(-u)=b_B(u),\quad
 0\le b_B(u)\le1,\quad b_B(u+v)\le b_B(u)+b_B(v).
\]
Also $|B\mathbin\triangle(B-u)|=2b_B(u)|B|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Finite translates have equal cardinality, so each one-sided difference has half the cardinality of the symmetric difference. Translation gives symmetry. For subadditivity, use
\[
 B\setminus(B-u-v)\subseteq
 [B\setminus(B-u)]\cup[(B-u)\setminus(B-u-v)]
\]
and count. The other claims follow directly from the definition.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Intersection bound along a tree]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:tree}
Let $t_0,\dots,t_m\in G$, and let $T$ be a tree on the labels $0,\dots,m$. Suppose $S_i\subseteq B$ and $|B\setminus S_i|\le\eps_i|B|$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\bigcap_{i=0}^m(S_i-t_i)\right|
 \ge\left(1-\sum_{i=0}^m\eps_i
              -\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}b_B(t_i-t_j)\right)|B|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:tree}
\end{equation}
The right side may be negative; its useful content is when it is positive.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Root the tree at 0 and add its vertices in an order in which each parent precedes its children. Before adding a child $j$ with parent $i$, the current intersection of ambient translates is contained in $B-t_i$. Imposing membership in $B-t_j$ therefore removes at most
\[
 |(B-t_i)\setminus(B-t_j)|=b_B(t_j-t_i)|B|
\]
points. Starting with a translate of $B$ proves the bound with all $S_i=B$. Replacing $B-t_i$ by $S_i-t_i$ removes at most $\eps_i|B|$ further points. Summing these losses proves \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:tree}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:tree} is this lemma (with losses counted in points), proved again without citation.
\end{writenote}

This formulation records the geometry of the configuration. One pays for the edges of a spanning tree, and can choose the tree of least total translation loss. It avoids charging every displacement independently from a single base point.

\begin{corollary}[Two and three translated copies]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:triangle}
If $S\subseteq B$ and $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, then
\begin{align}
 |S\cap(S-t)|&\ge(1-2\eps-b_B(t))|B|,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:pair}\\
 |S\cap(S-c)\cap(S-c-d)|
 &\ge(1-3\eps-b_B(c)-b_B(d))|B|.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle}
\end{align}
In the second inequality, $b_B(c)+b_B(d)$ can be replaced by
\[
 \tau_B(c,d)=\min\{b_B(c)+b_B(d),\ b_B(c)+b_B(c+d),\ b_B(d)+b_B(c+d)\}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:tree} to the vertices $0,t$ or $0,c,c+d$. The three possible trees on the latter vertices give the stated minimum.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp theorem for induced Freiman homomorphisms\srctag{12}}]{A sharp theorem for induced Freiman homomorphisms}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d3}
\srcnote{12}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:exact}

\begin{lemma}[The canonical difference map]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:difference}
If $S\ne\varnothing$ and $\phi:S\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism, there is a unique map $D:S-S\to H$ satisfying
\[
 D(y-x)=\phi(y)-\phi(x)\qquad(x,y\in S).
\]
It obeys $D(0)=0$ and $D(-t)=-D(t)$. If $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$, then
\begin{equation}
                       D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle-add}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $y-x=v-u$, then $y+u=v+x$, so the Freiman property gives $\phi(y)-\phi(x)=\phi(v)-\phi(u)$. This proves well-definedness and uniqueness. Swapping the ordered pair gives oddness. The three-point identity follows by telescoping the two successive increments.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp density--overlap extension]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}
Let $S\subseteq B$ with $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, and let $C\subseteq G$ be symmetric with $0\in C$. Suppose
\[
 b_B(c)\le\kappa\quad(c\in C),\qquad 3\eps+2\kappa<1.
\]
Then, for every Freiman homomorphism $\phi:S\to H$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $C+C\subseteq S-S$;
\item its canonical difference map satisfies $D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d)$ for every $c,d\in C$;
\item $D|_C$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order two and $D(0)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
More precisely, every ordered pair $c,d\in C$ has at least $(1-3\eps-2\kappa)|B|$ witnesses $x$ with $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The witness count is \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle}. It is positive, so for each $c,d$ a witness exists. Its endpoints show that $c+d\in S-S$, and lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:difference} gives (ii). If $c_1+c_2=c_3+c_4$, with all $c_i\in C$, both sums of $D$-values equal the same well-defined value $D(c_1+c_2)$. This proves (iii).
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:extension} needs $4\varepsilon+3\kappa<1$ at order two, which implies the condition here; with source~30's fixed-radius estimate this theorem gives the larger fixed radius of the note after its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:extension-only}.
\end{writenote}

Only losses for shifts in $C$ are required. Imposing the same loss bound on $C+C$ would unnecessarily shrink the eventual Bohr radius. The proof also explains why one does not need to find one base point supporting two entire decompositions of a sum: the canonical difference at their common endpoint makes two separate triangles sufficient.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness on the whole boundary]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}
Every rational pair $(\eps,\kappa)$ with $0\le\eps\le1/3$, $0\le\kappa\le1/2$, and $3\eps+2\kappa=1$ occurs in a finite example satisfying the size and overlap hypotheses of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} but not its conclusion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $K$ be a finite abelian group of size $m$, choose $T\subseteq K$ of size $t$, $0\le t\le m$, and put
\[
 G=\Z/3\Z\times K,\quad
 S=\{0,1\}\times K,\quad
 B=S\cup(\{2\}\times T),\quad
 C=\Z/3\Z\times\{0\}.
\]
Define $\phi:S\to\Z$ by $\phi(a,k)=a$ using the representatives $a=0,1$. This is a Freiman homomorphism: the sum of two first coordinates is one of $0,1,2$, and equality modulo 3 of such sums is equality as integers.

We have $|B|=2m+t$, $|S|=2m$, and, for either nonzero $c\in C$, $|B\cap(B-c)|=m+2t$. Therefore
\[
 \eps=\frac{t}{2m+t},\qquad
 \kappa=\frac{m-t}{2m+t},\qquad
 3\eps+2\kappa=1.
\]
Writing $e=(1,0)$, the induced values are $D(e)=1$, $D(2e)=-1$, and $D(0)=0$. But $e+e=2e+0$, whereas $1+1\ne-1+0$. Thus $D|_C$ is not a Freiman homomorphism. Finally, every rational $\eps\in[0,1/3]$ is obtained by taking $t/m=2\eps/(1-\eps)$ and clearing denominators.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of sharpness]
This is a sharp universal statement over abelian ambient and target groups. It does not assert an optimal threshold when both groups are the same prime cyclic group. The example uses a target in which three times a nonzero value need not vanish. Symmetric ambient examples are also available by using the two slices $\{-1,1\}\times K$ and a symmetric subset of the zero slice, with the corresponding integer-valued map.
\end{remark}

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.76\textwidth]{figures/12-bohr-extension-extension_frontier.pdf}
\caption{The universal sufficient region is below the line $3\eps+2\kappa=1$. The construction in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness} supplies counterexamples densely along the boundary. The diagram records an exact theorem, not an empirical fit.}
\label{gsr:en:12:fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

\begin{corollary}[Global extension above two thirds]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:global}
If $G$ is finite, $|S|>2|G|/3$, and $\phi:S\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism, then there are a unique homomorphism $D:G\to H$ and a unique $h_0\in H$ such that
\[
                         \phi(x)=h_0+D(x)\quad(x\in S).
\]
The constant $2/3$ cannot be reduced uniformly over $G,H$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $B=C=G$ and $\kappa=0$. The canonical difference map is additive on all of $G$. Fix $x_0\in S$ and put $h_0=\phi(x_0)-D(x_0)$. The difference identity gives the formula for all $x\in S$. Since $S-S=G$, any affine extension has this same difference map and then the same constant. Set $t=m$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness} for the endpoint obstruction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Higher-order local extension]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:higher}
Let $r\ge2$ be an integer. Under the same set hypotheses, replace the numerical condition by $3\eps+r\kappa<1$. Then $rC\subseteq S-S$, and the canonical difference map satisfies
\[
 D(c_1+\cdots+c_j)=D(c_1)+\cdots+D(c_j)
 \quad(1\le j\le r,\ c_i\in C).
\]
In particular, $D|_C$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subadditivity gives $b_B(t)\le r\kappa$ for $t\in rC$. The pair bound is positive since $1-2\eps-r\kappa>0$, so $rC\subseteq S-S$. For a partial sum $u=c_1+\cdots+c_{j-1}$, the triangle loss is at most $b_B(u)+b_B(c_j)\le j\kappa$. Thus \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle-add} applies and proves the identity inductively. Two equal sums of $r$ elements have the same canonical difference value. We make no optimality claim for this higher-order numerical condition.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Correction from concentrated directional increments\srctag{12}}]{Correction from concentrated directional increments}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d4}
\srcnote{12}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:robust}

The exact Freiman hypothesis can be weakened in a way that separates algebraic errors from missing points. This is useful for local repair, although a global average over all additive quadruples does not by itself give the uniform directional hypothesis below.

For any function $\phi:S\to H$ and any $t\in S-S$, let
\[
 E_t=\{x\in S:x+t\in S\},\qquad
 p_t(h)=\frac{|\{x\in E_t:\phi(x+t)-\phi(x)=h\}|}{|E_t|}.
\]
These distributions have finite support even when $H$ is infinite. Their collision probabilities are
\[
 Q_t=\sum_{h\in H}p_t(h)^2.
\]
Equivalently, $Q_t$ is the fraction of ordered pairs of $t$-edges with the same increment label.

\begin{lemma}[Sharp collision-to-majority bound]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}
For $0\le\eta<1/2$ define
\[
                  \chi(\eta)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2\eta}}2.
\]
If a finite probability distribution $p$ has $\sum p_i^2\ge1-\eta$, its largest atom is unique and has mass at least $1-\chi(\eta)$. This bound is sharp.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a=\max p_i$. Since $\sum p_i^2\le a$, we have $a\ge1-\eta>1/2$. Also
\[
 \sum p_i^2\le a^2+(1-a)^2.
\]
Solving $a^2+(1-a)^2\ge1-\eta$ on the interval $a>1/2$ gives the asserted lower bound. A two-atom distribution with masses $1-\chi(\eta)$ and $\chi(\eta)$ attains equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} This is the sharpest of the report's collision-to-mode bounds: source~07's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:collision} and source~11's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} (which uses $\sum p_i^2\le\max p_i$, mode at least $1-\eta$) are weaker, since $\chi(\eta)\le\eta$. Source~14's envelope $\tau(\varepsilon)=(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2$ is the same function, $\tau(\varepsilon)=\chi(2\varepsilon)$, in a different problem.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Directional repair]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:repair}
Let $S\subseteq B$, $C=-C$, $0\in C$, $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, and $b_B(c)\le\kappa$ for $c\in C$. Suppose
\begin{equation}
                         3\eps+2\kappa+3\chi(\eta)<1,
 \qquad 0\le\eta<1/2.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget}
\end{equation}
Assume $Q_t\ge1-\eta$ for every $t\in C+C$. Then the majority increment $D(t)$ is well defined on $C+C$, and
\[
              D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d)\qquad(c,d\in C).
\]
Consequently $D|_C$ is an exact Freiman homomorphism, $D(0)=0$, and at least $1-\chi(\eta)$ of the $t$-edges carry label $D(t)$ for every $t\in C+C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The strict budget first implies $3\eps+2\kappa<1$, so the geometric triangle bound shows $C+C\subseteq S-S$ without any algebraic assumption on $\phi$. Thus the distributions in the hypothesis exist. By lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}, each majority label is unique and at most $\chi(\eta)|E_t|$ of its edges are bad.

Fix $c,d\in C$ and put $s=c+d$. There are at least $(1-3\eps-2\kappa)|B|$ points $x$ with $x,x+c,x+s\in S$. Among these witnesses, at most $\chi(\eta)|E_c|$ have a bad first edge, at most $\chi(\eta)|E_d|$ have a bad second edge (translate its starting point by $c$), and at most $\chi(\eta)|E_s|$ have a bad direct edge. Each $|E_t|\le|B|$, so \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget} leaves a witness with all three edges good. Telescoping its actual $\phi$-increments proves the additive identity. The remaining conclusions follow as in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}; the zero increment is identically zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The exact nonuniform budget]
For a fixed triangle, one may instead require
\[
 1-3\eps-\tau_B(c,d)
 >\frac{\chi(\eta_c)|E_c|+\chi(\eta_d)|E_d|+
              \chi(\eta_{c+d})|E_{c+d}|}{|B|},
\]
where $Q_t\ge1-\eta_t$ and each $\eta_t<1/2$. This follows from precisely the same witness count. The three equal error allowances in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget} are a convenient uniform specialization, not an asserted optimal repair threshold.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Global affine repair]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:global-repair}
Take $B=C=G$ finite, $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|G|$, and assume $3\eps+3\chi(\eta)<1$ and $Q_t\ge1-\eta$ for every $t\in G$. Then the majority increments give a homomorphism $D:G\to H$, and some $h_0\in H$ satisfies
\[
 |\{x\in S:\phi(x)=h_0+D(x)\}|
 \ge [1-\chi(\chi(\eta))]|S|.
\]
In particular the weaker, simpler proportion $1-\chi(\eta)$ also holds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The repair theorem makes $D$ additive everywhere. Put $F(x)=\phi(x)-D(x)$ on $S$. Every ordered pair $(x,y)\in S^2$ appears in exactly one direction $t=y-x$. It has $F(y)\ne F(x)$ exactly when its directional edge is bad. Hence
\[
 |\{(x,y)\in S^2:F(x)\ne F(y)\}|
 \le \chi(\eta)\sum_t|E_t|=\chi(\eta)|S|^2.
\]
The distribution of $F$ therefore has collision probability at least $1-\chi(\eta)$. A second application of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority} gives the result.
\end{proof}

The error parameter is conditional on a direction. Replacing this by the assertion that a $1-\eta$ fraction of all additive quadruples is respected is a different problem: directions with few representations can have large conditional error. The component-extraction stage of Gowers's proof is designed to cope with this difficulty. Our repair theorem does not silently remove that stage.

\section[{A finite selection argument for Bohr radii\srctag{12}}]{A finite selection argument for Bohr radii}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d5}
\srcnote{12}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:bohr}

Let $G$ now be a finite abelian group of order $N$, and identify characters with homomorphisms $\gamma:G\to\T=\R/\Z$. Write $\|u\|_\T$ for distance to the nearest integer. For a finite set $\Gamma$ of $d$ characters and $r>0$, set
\[
 \Bohr(\Gamma,r)=\{x\in G:\|\gamma(x)\|_\T\le r
                                      \text{ for every }\gamma\in\Gamma\}.
\]
These are closed Bohr sets, matching the weak inequalities in the repository. The case $\Gamma=\varnothing$ gives $G$ and reduces to the global extension theorem; below $d\ge1$.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary size and doubling bounds]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:bohr-cover}
For $0<r\le1/2$,
\begin{align}
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,r)|&\ge \frac{N}{\lceil1/r\rceil^d}
                    \ge (r/2)^dN,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-size}\\
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,r)|&\le4^d|\Bohr(\Gamma,r/2)|.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-double}
\end{align}
Also $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)+\Bohr(\Gamma,s)\subseteq\Bohr(\Gamma,r+s)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Map $x$ to its $d$ character values in $\T^d$. Divide each circle into $\lceil1/r\rceil$ half-open intervals of equal length at most $r$. Some product cell has at least $N/\lceil1/r\rceil^d$ preimages. Subtract a fixed preimage from all others in that cell; the differences belong to $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$. The weaker bound follows from $\lceil1/r\rceil\le2/r$.

For \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-double}, represent all character values of $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$ in $[-r,r]$. Partition this cube into $4^d$ cells of side length $r/2$, assigning boundary points consistently. In each occupied cell choose one preimage. Subtraction from that preimage injects the cell's preimages into $\Bohr(\Gamma,r/2)$. Sum over the cells. The final assertion is the triangle inequality on $\T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-scale radius selection]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}
Let $0<\rho\le1/2$ and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $s=\rho/(2m)$. There is
\[
 r\in\left\{\frac\rho2+js:1\le j\le m\right\}\subseteq(\rho/2,\rho]
\]
such that, for $B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$,
\begin{equation}
 |B\cap(B-c)|\ge4^{-d/m}|B|
                 \qquad(c\in\Bohr(\Gamma,s)).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:one-scale}
\end{equation}
More generally, replace $4^d$ by the actual ratio
\[
             R=\frac{|\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)|}{|\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/2)|}
\]
and replace $4^{-d/m}$ by $R^{-1/m}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $r_j=\rho/2+js$, $0\le j\le m$, and $a_j=|\Bohr(\Gamma,r_j)|$. The product of $a_{j-1}/a_j$ is $a_0/a_m=R^{-1}\ge4^{-d}$. Therefore some ratio is at least $R^{-1/m}\ge4^{-d/m}$. Choose that $j$ and $r=r_j$. If $x\in\Bohr(\Gamma,r-s)$ and $c\in\Bohr(\Gamma,s)$, both $x$ and $x+c$ belong to $B$. Thus the inner set is contained in $B\cap(B-c)$, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

This proves the needed overlap at one scale with a finite pigeonhole argument. It does not assert that $B$ is regular at every smaller relative change of radius in the standard sense. Full regularity is available from the classical theory \cite{greentaoUthree}, but is unnecessary here.

\begin{corollary}[A replacement for Corollary 10.11]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:bohr-extension}
Given $\Gamma$, $d\ge1$, and $0<\rho\le1/2$, there exists $r\in(\rho/2,\rho]$ such that every $S\subseteq B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$ with $|S|\ge7|B|/8$ and every Freiman homomorphism $\phi:S\to H$ induce a Freiman homomorphism on
\[
                         C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(8d)).
\]
In fact $C+C\subseteq S-S$ and the induced difference map is additive on pairs from $C$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $m=4d$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}. Then $\kappa=1-1/\sqrt2$ is admissible, and
\[
 3\cdot\frac18+2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
                  =\frac{19}{8}-\sqrt2<1.
\]
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Scope.} As the remark ``Why the order of selection matters'' in Section~\ref{gsr:en:12:sec:bohr} and the caption of Table~\ref{gsr:fm:12:tab:overview} say, the ambient radius $r$ is \emph{selected} in $(\rho/2,\rho]$ before the dense subset is chosen. So this corollary is an alternative to Corollary~10.11 with a changed quantifier order, not a replacement for it at a prescribed radius; the abstract's word ``replaces'' (Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}) should be read this way. \emph{Observation (intake, checked at the write):} the hypotheses $C=-C$ and $0\in C$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} are not used by its proof: for $c,d\in C$ the witness count gives $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$, hence $c,d,c+d\in S-S$, and the conclusions follow; $D(0)=0$ holds since $S\ne\varnothing$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
At a prescribed radius $\rho\le1/4$ source~30 gives $\rho/(8(3^r-1))$ with the same margins (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}; $r$ here is $d$), and shows that a fixed-radius estimate must depend exponentially on the rank (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}); this corollary's $\rho/(8d)$ uses the selected radius.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[General density and extension order]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:bohr-general}
Let $0\le\eps<1/3$ and $q\ge2$. If the integer $m$ satisfies
\[
                         3\eps+q(1-4^{-d/m})<1,
\]
the selected radius in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius} makes every Freiman homomorphism on a $(1-\eps)$-dense subset of $B$ induce a Freiman homomorphism of order $q$ on $\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(2m))$. In particular, one can take any integer
\[
 m>\frac{d\log4}{-\log\left(1-(1-3\eps)/q\right)}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:higher} with $\kappa=1-4^{-d/m}$. Rearranging the strict inequality gives the displayed sufficient choice.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the order of selection matters]
The radius $r$ depends only on $\Gamma,\rho,m$, not on the later subset or map. This is exactly the quantifier order required in the application. If a dense subset of $\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)$ has already been fixed, shrinking the ambient radius can concentrate all its missing points in the smaller set. Its relative density need not survive. We therefore select $r$ before invoking component extraction.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Why a factor of the rank is natural]
In $G=(\Z/L\Z)^d$, take the $d$ coordinate characters and $\rho<1/4$. For large $L$, the Bohr set is a product of intervals of length about $2\rho L$. A shift whose every coordinate is about $sL$ has overlap ratio tending to
\[
                           \left(1-\frac{s}{2\rho}\right)^d.
\]
Keeping this uniformly above a fixed positive constant requires $s=O(\rho/d)$. Thus the inverse-rank scale in the overlap method is necessary for this family; the example does not assert optimality of the constants 6 or 8.
\end{example}

\section[{Fourier smoothing with the full fourth moment\srctag{12}}]{Fourier smoothing with the full fourth moment}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d6}
\srcnote{12}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:fourier}

We use unnormalized Fourier transforms and convolutions in this section:
\[
 \widehat g(\gamma)=\sum_{x\in G}g(x)e^{-2\pi i\gamma(x)},\qquad
 (f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in G}f(y)g(x-y).
\]
Thus $g(x)=N^{-1}\sum_\gamma\widehat g(\gamma)e^{2\pi i\gamma(x)}$ and $\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2=N\sum_x|g(x)|^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Fourth-moment smoothing]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}
Let $0\le g(x)\le M$ and $\sum_xg(x)=\alpha MN$, where $M>0$ and $0<\alpha\le1$. Put
\[
 L=\alpha^3M^4N^3,\quad
 h=g*\widetilde g*g*\widetilde g,\quad
 \widetilde g(x)=g(-x),
\]
and, for $\lambda>0$, let
\[
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\},\qquad d=|\Gamma|.
\]
Then, for every $\rho>0$,
\begin{align}
 d&\le\frac{\alpha}{\lambda^2},\label{gsr:en:12:eq:rank}\\
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4&\le LN,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:fourth}\\
 \sup_x|h(x+t)-h(x)|
 &\le\left(2\pi\rho+\frac{2\lambda^2}{\alpha^2}\right)L
       \quad(t\in\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}
\end{align}
More precisely, if $\xi=(LN)^{-1}\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4$, then $\alpha\le\xi\le1$ and $2\pi\rho$ in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth} can be replaced by $2\pi\rho\xi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Parseval and $g^2\le Mg$ give
\[
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
       =N\sum_xg(x)^2\le\alpha M^2N^2.
\]
Each element of $\Gamma$ contributes at least $\lambda^2M^2N^2$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:rank}. Since $|\widehat g(\gamma)|\le\alpha MN$,
\[
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4
 \le(\alpha MN)^2\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
 \le\alpha^3M^4N^4=LN.
\]
The zero-frequency term alone is $\alpha^4M^4N^4=\alpha LN$, proving the lower bound for $\xi$.

The convolution identity is $\widehat h(\gamma)=|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4$. On $\Gamma$, membership of $t$ in the Bohr set gives
\[
 |e^{2\pi i\gamma(t)}-1|\le2\pi\rho.
\]
On the complement, use the bound 2 and
\[
 \sum_{\gamma\notin\Gamma}|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4
 \le\lambda^2M^2N^2\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
 \le\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^4.
\]
Fourier inversion, with its factor $1/N$, now yields
\[
 |h(x+t)-h(x)|
 \le2\pi\rho\xi L+2\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^3
 =\left(2\pi\rho\xi+\frac{2\lambda^2}{\alpha^2}\right)L.
\]
This proves all the claims.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The precise improvement over the original estimate}

The original large-spectrum estimate bounds the sum of fourth powers on $\Gamma$ by $d(\alpha MN)^4$, and then bounds $d$ by $\alpha/\lambda^2$. The available moment estimate \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:fourth} is stronger by a factor $\alpha^2/\lambda^2$. To achieve the same total translation error $4\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^3$, one may therefore replace
\[
 \rho_{\rm old}=\frac{\lambda^4}{\pi\alpha^4}
 \quad\hbox{by}\quad
 \rho_{\rm new}=\frac{\lambda^2}{\pi\alpha^2}.
\]
With $\lambda=2^{-37}\alpha^{11/2}$, this is the change
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2^{-148}\alpha^{18}}\pi
 \quad\longrightarrow\quad
 \frac{2^{-74}\alpha^9}\pi.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:initial-gain}
\end{equation}
No character has been added or removed from $\Gamma$. The gain comes entirely from a better estimate of the same Fourier expression.

\begin{proposition}[Optimal allocation within the moment bounds]
\label{gsr:en:12:prop:allocation}
Fix a desired relative translation error $0<\sigma\le1$, with the spectrum and rank defined as in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}, and use only the bounds \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:rank} and \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}. Among positive choices of $\lambda,\rho$ satisfying
\[
                     2\pi\rho+2\lambda^2/\alpha^2\le\sigma,
\]
the lower bound for $\rho/d$ obtained by substituting $d\le\alpha/\lambda^2$ is maximized at
\[
 \lambda^2=\frac{\sigma\alpha^2}{4},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi}.
\]
Its maximum is $\sigma^2\alpha/(16\pi)$. After the $3d$ radius-selection step, the resulting guaranteed inner radius is $\sigma^2\alpha/(96\pi)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $\lambda^2=q\sigma\alpha^2$, $0<q<1/2$. Saturating the error budget gives $\rho=\sigma(1-2q)/(2\pi)$, so
\[
 \frac\rho d\ge\frac{\rho\lambda^2}{\alpha}
        =\frac{q(1-2q)\sigma^2\alpha}{2\pi}.
\]
The quadratic $q(1-2q)=1/8-2(q-1/4)^2$ is maximized at $q=1/4$. Divide by 6 for the selected inner radius.
\end{proof}

This is an optimization of the guaranteed expression furnished by these estimates. It does not claim optimality of the actual radius for each input function. If the measured fourth moment is smaller, the factor $\xi$ yields the further admissible choice $\rho=\sigma/(4\pi\xi)$, provided it is within the range used for radius selection.

\section[{Synchronizing a local model across fibres\srctag{12}}]{Synchronizing a local model across fibres}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d7}
\srcnote{12}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:synchronization}

The extension theorem concerns a map on a set of directions. Gowers's argument also requires it to agree with differences between elements of another, possibly multivalued, domain. The next lemma makes this second use of overlap explicit.

Let $\Omega$ be a finite set with an index map $r:\Omega\to G$ and a value map $F:\Omega\to H$. Write $\Omega_a=r^{-1}(a)$ for its fibres. Let $S\subseteq B\subseteq G$, $|S|=a|B|$, and let $\psi:S\to H$ be a Freiman homomorphism with canonical difference map $D$.

\begin{lemma}[Common-fibre synchronization]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:sync}
Let $W_1\subseteq\Omega$. Suppose that for each $w\in W_1$ there is a set $T_w\subseteq S$ with $|T_w|\ge(1-q)|S|$, and for each $d\in T_w$ the fibre $\Omega_{r(w)+d}$ is nonempty and
\[
 |\{z\in\Omega_{r(w)+d}:F(z)-F(w)=\psi(d)\}|
                  \ge(1-\theta)|\Omega_{r(w)+d}|.
\]
For $w_1,w_2\in W_1$, if $c=r(w_1)-r(w_2)$ satisfies $b_B(c)\le\kappa$ and
\begin{equation}
              2(1-q)a>1+\kappa,\qquad 2\theta<1,
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:sync-budget}
\end{equation}
then $c\in S-S$ and
\[
                         F(w_1)-F(w_2)=D(c).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Both $T_{w_1}\subseteq B$ and $T_{w_2}-c\subseteq B-c$. The two-set form of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:tree}, or direct subtraction of their complements, gives
\[
 |T_{w_1}\cap(T_{w_2}-c)|
 \ge[2(1-q)a-1-\kappa]|B|>0.
\]
Choose $d$ in this intersection, so $d\in T_{w_1}$ and $d+c\in T_{w_2}$. Their fibres coincide because
\[
                    r(w_1)+d=r(w_2)+(d+c).
\]
This common fibre is nonempty. The two subsets on which the required value equations hold have combined missing fraction at most $2\theta<1$, so they contain a common $z$. Subtracting the two equations gives
\[
 F(w_1)-F(w_2)=\psi(d+c)-\psi(d)=D(c).
\]
The same choice of $d$ also establishes $c\in S-S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:compatibility} is this lemma, with the same condition $2(1-\sigma)a_0>1+\kappa$, proved again without citation.
\end{writenote}

If $a\ge1-\eps$, the convenient sufficient condition is $2(1-q)(1-\eps)>1+\kappa$. This retains the actual relative density and improves the coarse overlap bookkeeping used in the source's Lemma 10.12.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A strengthened version of the Section 10 local-model theorem\srctag{12}}]{A strengthened version of the Section 10 local-model theorem}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d8}
\srcnote{12}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:main}

We now specialize to $G=\Z/N\Z$, $N\ge2$. Primality is unnecessary until the later scalar-linearity corollary. A \emph{multifunction domain} is a finite set $X$ with an index map $r:X\to G$, or equivalently a partition $X=\bigsqcup_{s\in G}X_s$. A function $\phi:X\to G$ is a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order $j$ if at least a $1-\eta$ fraction of all ordered tuples
\[
 (x_1,\dots,x_{2j})\in X^{2j},\qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^{j}r(x_i)=\sum_{i=j+1}^{2j}r(x_i),
\]
also satisfy the analogous equality of their $\phi$-values. The denominator counts all such tuples, including repeated elements.

\subsection{The established component-extraction input}

Fix, for the remainder of this section,
\begin{equation}
 \eta=2^{-43},\qquad \theta=10\eta^{1/5},\qquad q=\sqrt\theta.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:eta}
\end{equation}
One has
\begin{equation}
                   \theta<1/36,\qquad q<1/6.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:theta-small}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\theta<1/36$ is equivalent to $360^5<2^{43}$, an integer inequality.

\begin{lemma}[Gowers's component input, with explicit hypotheses]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input}
Let $\Omega=\bigsqcup_{s\in G}\Omega_s$, with $|\Omega|=\alpha LN$, $|\Omega_s|\le L$, where $L$ is a positive integer and $0<\alpha\le1$. Let $F:\Omega\to G$ be a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order two. Suppose $B=-B$ is nonempty and
\[
           \big||\Omega_{s+b}|-|\Omega_s|\big|\le\sigma L
                           \quad(s\in G,\ b\in B).
\]
Let $\varrho>0$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 \varrho&\le\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\},\label{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho}\\
 0<\sigma&\le\min\{\eta\alpha^2,
               \eta\varrho^4\alpha/384,
               \eta\varrho\alpha^2/16\},\qquad
 \sigma<\alpha^2/16.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma}
\end{align}
Then there exist $W_1\subseteq W\subseteq\Omega$, $S\subseteq B$, and a Freiman homomorphism $\psi:S\to G$, such that
\begin{align}
 |W|&\ge\varrho^2\alpha^2 LN/16,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound}\\
 |W_1|&\ge(1-q)|W|,\qquad |S|\ge(1-\theta)|B|,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:W1-bound}
\end{align}
and the hypotheses about the sets $T_w$ and the good fibre fractions in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync} hold with this $W_1$, $S$, $q$, and $\theta$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Source and deduction]
This is the required output of Gowers's Lemmas 10.3--10.9, in the corrected form recorded in \cite{repo12section10,repo12extraction}. Lemma 10.3 selects an anchor under $\sigma\le\eta\alpha^2$. Lemma 10.5 selects a fibre-saturated component $W$ under \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho} and $\sigma\le\eta\varrho^4\alpha/384$, with \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound} and fibre sizes at least $\alpha^2L/16$ on $W$. Lemma 10.6 supplies $S$ and the nested $1-\theta$ difference model under the remaining extraction bound. Lemma 10.7 reverses the two outer counting quantifiers, losing $q=\sqrt\theta$ and defining $W_1$. Lemmas 10.8--10.9 give the exact Freiman property using $6q<1$ and $W\ne\varnothing$.

The fibre sizes needed in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync} are positive: for $w\in W$ and $d\in S\subseteq B$,
\[
 |\Omega_{r(w)+d}|\ge|\Omega_{r(w)}|-\sigma L
                 \ge(\alpha^2/16-\sigma)L>0.
\]
This last point is a necessary hypothesis of the synchronization argument, not a consequence of a proportionate statement on a possibly empty fibre.

The printed proof of Lemma 10.6 has an ambiguity involving a set depending on the direction and a later exchange of quantifiers. The corrected proof used here works on a fixed product of a low-error set with $B$ and chooses each direction's value from an anchor-fibre mode. Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:12:sec:repair-audit} records the count behind this repair. No Bohr-specific property of $B$ is used in this component input.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The parameterized theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Local model with a polynomial radius]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:main}
Let $X=\bigsqcup_{s\in\Z/N\Z}X_s$ be finite, $M\ge1$ an integer, $|X_s|\le M$, and $|X|=\alpha MN$ with $0<\alpha\le1$. Suppose $\phi:X\to\Z/N\Z$ is a $(1-2^{-43})$-homomorphism of order eight. Choose $\varrho,\sigma$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho}--\eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma}, let $\lambda>0$, and put
\begin{equation}
 \lambda^2=\frac{\sigma\alpha^2}{4},\qquad
 \rho=\frac\sigma{4\pi},\qquad
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\},
 \quad g(s)=|X_s|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters}
\end{equation}
Then $1\le d=|\Gamma|\le4/(\sigma\alpha)$. On
\begin{equation}
 C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta),\qquad
 \zeta=\frac{\sigma}{24\pi d}
           \ge\frac{\sigma^2\alpha}{96\pi},
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:new-zeta}
\end{equation}
there is a Freiman homomorphism $\psi_1:C\to\Z/N\Z$ with $\psi_1(0)=0$, and there is $Y\subseteq X$ with
\begin{equation}
               |Y|\ge\frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}|X|,
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:Y-exact}
\end{equation}
such that, whenever $y,z\in Y$ and $r(y)-r(z)\in C$,
\begin{equation}
           \phi(y)-\phi(z)=\psi_1(r(y)-r(z)).
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We give the full parameter propagation.

\textbf{1. The fourfold domain.}
Let $\Omega=X^4$, with
\[
 r_\Omega(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=r(x_1)+r(x_2)-r(x_3)-r(x_4)
\]
and the identical signed expression defining $F$ from $\phi$. Set
\[
                     L=M|X|^3=\alpha^3M^4N^3.
\]
Each fibre of $\Omega$ has at most $M|X|^3=L$ elements: after choosing three entries, the index of the fourth is determined, and at most $M$ elements have that index. Moreover
\begin{equation}
                 |\Omega|=|X|^4=\alpha LN.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:omega-density}
\end{equation}
An additive quadruple in $\Omega$ expands, after a permutation of its 16 entries, into an equality between two sums of eight indices in $X$. This is a bijective rearrangement of all tested tuples, and the same rearrangement applies to values. Thus $F$ is a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order two.

\textbf{2. Fourier control and nonempty spectrum.}
The fibre-count function of $\Omega$ is $h=g*\widetilde g*g*\widetilde g$. By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing} and \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters}, it is $(\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho),\sigma L)$-invariant. The rank bound is $d\le4/(\sigma\alpha)$. The parameter conditions imply $\sigma<1$, hence $\lambda<\alpha$, so the zero character belongs to $\Gamma$ and $d\ge1$. They also imply $0<\rho<1/2$.

\textbf{3. Choose the ambient Bohr set before extraction.}
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius} with $m=3d$. It provides $r_0\in(\rho/2,\rho]$ such that $B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r_0)$ satisfies
\[
 b_B(c)\le\kappa:=1-4^{-1/3}<3/8
                    \quad(c\in C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(6d))).
\]
Since $B\subseteq\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)$, the already established invariance holds on $B$. Now, and only now, apply lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input} to obtain fresh $W,W_1,S,\psi$. The character set is unchanged.

\textbf{4. Extend the directional model.}
The actual missing density of $S$ is at most $\theta<1/36$. Therefore
\[
 3\theta+2\kappa<\frac1{12}+\frac34=\frac56<1.
\]
By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}, the canonical difference map of $\psi$ induces a Freiman homomorphism $\psi_1$ on $C$, with zero value at zero.

\textbf{5. Synchronize values on the selected component.}
For the parameters of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync}, $a\ge1-\theta>35/36$, $1-q>5/6$, and $1+\kappa<11/8$. Thus
\[
 2(1-q)a>2\cdot\frac56\cdot\frac{35}{36}
            =\frac{175}{108}>\frac{11}{8}>1+\kappa,
\]
and $2\theta<1$. The synchronization lemma gives
\[
 F(w_1)-F(w_2)=\psi_1(r_\Omega(w_1)-r_\Omega(w_2))
\]
for $w_1,w_2\in W_1$ with index difference in $C$.

\textbf{6. Retain the full slice count.}
By \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound}--\eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:omega-density},
\[
 |W_1|\ge(1-q)\frac{\varrho^2\alpha^2LN}{16}
          =\frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}|X|^4.
\]
Average over the last three coordinates. Some $(x_2,x_3,x_4)\in X^3$ leaves at least the fraction in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:Y-exact} of $X$ in the fibre
\[
 Y=\{y\in X:(y,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in W_1\}.
\]
On this slice, differences of indices and of values are exactly $r(y)-r(z)$ and $\phi(y)-\phi(z)$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}. Finally, the bound on $d$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:new-zeta}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~28's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main} replaces the component selection by logarithmic windows: retained fraction $\alpha p(\alpha)/20$, $O(\alpha^{-3})$ original-domain frequencies, radius $\Omega(\alpha^5)$, input defect $2^{-21}$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:section10}); it credits this theorem's $\alpha^5$ retention, extension and smoothing.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Keeping exactly the original large spectrum}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit sparse-density specialization]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}
Under the hypotheses on $X,\phi$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, suppose $0<\alpha\le1/6$. Keep Gowers's threshold
\[
 \lambda=2^{-37}\alpha^{11/2},\qquad
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\}.
\]
Then $d=|\Gamma|\le2^{74}\alpha^{-10}$, and one can take
\begin{equation}
 C=\Bohr\left(\Gamma,\frac{2^{-74}\alpha^9}{6\pi d}\right),
 \qquad |Y|\ge\frac{\alpha^5}{20000}|X|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:fixed-spectrum}
\end{equation}
The local model identity \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model} holds on $C$, whose radius is at least $\alpha^{19}/(3\pi2^{149})$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\varrho=\alpha^2/32$ and $\sigma=2^{-72}\alpha^9$. The bound $\varrho\le\alpha/192$ is exactly $\alpha\le1/6$. The most restrictive smallness comparison is
\[
 \sigma=2^{-72}\alpha^9
 \le\frac{2^{-70}}3\alpha^9
       =\frac{\eta\varrho^4\alpha}{384}.
\]
The other conditions in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma} follow directly from $\alpha\le1$; for example $\sigma\le\eta\varrho\alpha^2/16$ reduces to $\alpha^5\le2^{20}$. Then \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters} gives exactly the displayed $\lambda$. Also
\[
 \frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}
 >\frac{5\alpha^5}{98304}\ge\frac{\alpha^5}{20000}.
\]
Substitute the rank bound into the radius and simplify.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}). \file{theorem_10_13} (\file{Section10.lean}, line~473; exact companion \file{theorem_10_13_holds}, \file{Proofs10Main.lean}, line~1292) concludes $|Y|\ge\alpha^6|X|/20000$ on the Bohr set of radius \texttt{section10Zeta}, under $0<\alpha\le1/6$. The fraction $\alpha^5/20000$ here is below the $5\alpha^5/98304$ that the formal proof already establishes internally (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}), so the improvement in the retained fraction is a proof-level fact of the development, not new; the polynomial radius is new. Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{An all-density schedule and a moment-sensitive version}

\begin{corollary}[All densities]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:all-density}
For every $0<\alpha\le1$, the choices
\begin{equation}
 \varrho=\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\},\qquad
 \sigma=\frac{2^{-43}\alpha\varrho^4}{384}
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:all-density}
\end{equation}
satisfy the conditions of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}. Thus its explicit radius and retained-fraction conclusions hold without the restriction $\alpha\le1/6$. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} This schedule is Gowers's own printed choice (transcription \file{sz-thm-gowers-proof.tex}, line~2201: $\rho=\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\}$, $\sigma=\eta\rho^4\alpha/384$); it is new relative to the formal statement, which assumes $\alpha\le1/6$.

On the branch $\alpha\le1/6$, these choices give
\[
 \sigma=\frac{2^{-70}}3\alpha^9,\quad
 \lambda^2=\frac{2^{-72}}3\alpha^{11},\quad
 d\le3\cdot2^{72}\alpha^{-10},\quad
 \zeta\ge\frac{2^{-145}}{27\pi}\alpha^{19}.
\]
This last constant is $16/9$ times the radius lower bound in corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}, but uses a slightly different spectral threshold.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The only remaining comparisons are $\varrho^4\le384\alpha$, $\varrho^3\le24\alpha$, and $\eta\varrho^4<24\alpha$. They follow from $\varrho\le\alpha/192$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and $\eta<1$. These inequalities give the three conditions on $\sigma$ and fibre positivity. The sparse-branch formulas follow by substituting $\varrho=\alpha^2/32$ and simplifying powers of 2 and 3.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Using the measured fourth moment]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:measured-moment}
In theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, let $\xi=(LN)^{-1}\sum|\widehat g|^4$. If $\rho_*:=\sigma/(4\pi\xi)\le1/2$, the same spectrum and retained fraction work on the larger Bohr set of radius
\[
                \zeta_* =\frac{\sigma}{24\pi\xi d}
                          \ge\frac{\sigma^2\alpha}{96\pi\xi}.
\]
For the schedule \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:all-density}, the required bound on $\rho_*$ is automatic.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the precise version of \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}. Nothing after the smoothing step changes. For the final assertion, $\xi\ge\alpha$ gives $\rho_*\le\eta\varrho^4/(1536\pi)<1/2$.
\end{proof}

\section[{Consequences and the size of the improvement\srctag{12}}]{Consequences and the size of the improvement}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d9}
\srcnote{12}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:consequences}

\subsection{The volume cost changes from quadratic to linear in the rank}

Let $k=\lceil2^{74}\alpha^{-10}\rceil$ and compare the explicit rank-based radius
\[
 \zeta_{\rm old}=2^{-155k}\alpha^{18k}/k
 \quad\hbox{with}\quad
 \zeta_{\rm new}=\frac{\alpha^{19}}{3\pi2^{149}}.
\]
The latter is a guaranteed smaller radius inside the actual set in corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}; hence the local model also holds on $\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm new})$. The size bound \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-size} gives
\begin{align*}
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm old})|
 &\ge 2^{-E_{\rm old}}N,\\
 E_{\rm old}
 &=k\bigl[1+155k+18k\log_2(1/\alpha)+\log_2 k\bigr],\\
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm new})|
 &\ge 2^{-E_{\rm new}}N,\\
 E_{\rm new}
 &=k\bigl[150+\log_2(3\pi)+19\log_2(1/\alpha)\bigr].
\end{align*}
Here using $k$ rather than the actual $d$ only weakens a lower bound because the base is below one. Thus the certified logarithmic volume cost changes from
\[
 O\bigl(k^2[1+\log(1/\alpha)]\bigr)
 \quad\hbox{to}\quad
 O\bigl(k[1+\log(1/\alpha)]\bigr).
\]
The large rank itself remains. This is a substantial improvement at this stage of the proof, but the resulting numerical constants are still enormous.

\begin{example}[Density $\alpha=1/8$]
Then $k=2^{104}$. The old negative base-two logarithm of the radius is
\[
                  \log_2(1/\zeta_{\rm old})=209\cdot2^{104}+104.
\]
The new guaranteed radius has
\[
                  \log_2(1/\zeta_{\rm new})
                   =206+\log_2(3\pi)\approx209.2365.
\]
The retained fraction improves by a factor of 8 relative to the corrected $\alpha^6/20000$ statement. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} Relative to what the formal proof already establishes ($5\alpha^5/98304$, note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}) there is no gain in the fraction; the gain is in the radius. These are parameter comparisons; they do not assert that a set of feasible computational size meets the full theorem's worst-case volume bound.
\end{example}

\subsection{Long progressions of locally linear directions}

\begin{corollary}[Scalar linearity along short Bohr progressions]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:linearity}
Let $N=p$ be prime, and suppose $Y,\psi_1,C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta)$ satisfy theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}. If $m\ge1$, $0\ne h\in\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)$, and $m<p$, then there is $a\in\Z/p\Z$ such that
\[
 \phi(y)-\phi(z)=a(r(y)-r(z))
\]
whenever $y,z\in Y$ and $r(y)-r(z)\in\{jh:-m\le j\le m\}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
All $jh$, $|j|\le m$, belong to $C$ by the triangle inequality. Since $\psi_1$ is a Freiman homomorphism and $\psi_1(0)=0$, the relations
\[
                      jh+h=(j+1)h+0
\]
give $\psi_1(jh)=j\psi_1(h)$ by induction for nonnegative $j$, and oddness gives the negative values. Take $a=\psi_1(h)/h$, which is legitimate since $h\ne0$ in the prime field. Then use \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit supply of nonzero directions]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:progression-size}
If $0<\zeta\le1/2$ and $\zeta p^{1/d}\ge4$, put
\[
                     m=\left\lfloor\zeta p^{1/d}/4\right\rfloor.
\]
Then $\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)$ contains a nonzero $h$, and the progression $P=\{jh:-m\le j\le m\}\subseteq C$ is proper. A single scalar governs all index differences of pairs from $Y$ which belong to $P$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
We have $m\ge1$ and
\[
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)|
       \ge\left(\frac{\zeta}{2m}\right)^dp\ge2^d>1.
\]
The elementary size bound remains valid if $\zeta/m=1/2$. Also $m\le p/8$, since $d\ge1$ and $\zeta\le1/2$. Thus $2m<p$, so the distinct integers $-m,\ldots,m$ give distinct multiples of a nonzero element in $\Z/p\Z$. Apply corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:linearity}.
\end{proof}

This supplies the direct analogue of Gowers's Corollary 10.14 with the larger radius. It does not assert that $Y$ itself contains a progression of this length; it asserts that differences in the displayed progression are governed by one scalar.

\subsection{What does not yet follow}

The later proof still requires compatible multilinear structure, partitions with controlled widths, recurrence thresholds, and an iteration which pays for the density lost when changing cyclic models. The current repository records unresolved obligations in Sections 13, 16, and 18 \cite{repo12status}. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14] Incomplete list:} the ledger at the pin also had open statements in Sections~1, 5, 7 and~8, and at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99} the 20 open statements are \file{theorem_1_2}, \file{theorem_1_3}, \file{corollary_5_8}, \file{theorem_7_1}, \file{theorem_7_2}, \file{theorem_8_2}, \file{corollary_8_3}, \file{lemma_13_5}--\file{lemma_13_7}, \file{lemma_13_9}, \file{corollary_13_10}, \file{theorem_13_12}, \file{theorem_16_2}, \file{lemma_16_4}, \file{lemma_16_10}, \file{corollary_16_11}, \file{theorem_18_1}, \file{theorem_18_2} and \file{corollary_18_7}. A local radius improvement cannot be substituted into every later theorem without checking these dependencies.

In particular, the theorem established here is a complete replacement of the Section 10 local-model output under its stated assumptions. It does not prove a better final $r_\ell(N)$ bound. Determining how much of the local gain survives the entire argument is one of the proposed research projects below.
