\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Equality in the collision cap\srctag{15}}]{Equality in the collision cap}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:equality}
\srcnote{15}{Section 7}

We now determine the geometric meaning of saturating the cubic estimate.
For a coordinate group product $X$, write $\pi_i:X\to X$ for projection
onto coordinate $i$, with all other coordinates set to zero.

\begin{theorem}[Exact Cartesian classification]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian}
For a nonempty set $A\subseteq X$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $Q(A)=|A|^3$;
\item $A=c+H$ for a subgroup $H\le X$ invariant under every $\pi_i$;
\item $A=c+(H_1\times\cdots\times H_k)$ for subgroups $H_i\le G_i$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equality in the injection of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:cubic} makes that injection
surjective. Hence for every $r,t,s\in A$, the two cubes with common side
$t-r$ and bases $r,s$ lie in $A$. In particular their all-one corner gives
$s+t-r\in A$. Choose $c\in A$ and let $H=A-c$. This set contains zero
and is closed under the ternary operation $u+v-w$; it is consequently a
subgroup, using that operation with one or two inputs zero.

The single-coordinate corners also give
$r+\pi_i(t-r)\in A$. Taking $r=c$ shows $\pi_iH\subseteq H$.
If $H_i$ is the $i$th coordinate projection of $H$, then every element of
$H$ belongs to $\prod_iH_i$, and every coordinate-supported element from
$H_i$ belongs to $H$. Adding them proves $H=\prod_iH_i$.

Conversely, in a Cartesian coset every triple $(r,t,s)\in A^3$ gives
admissible cubes with side $t-r$: every coordinate of every vertex remains
in its corresponding coordinate coset. The injection is therefore
surjective, proving $Q(A)=|A|^3$.
\end{proof}

The label condition has an equally explicit description. An arbitrary
function that omits a coordinate has zero full mixed derivative, so such
functions must be allowed in any correct classification.

\begin{theorem}[Labels at exact collision equality]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:exactlabels}
Let $A\ne\varnothing$ and $\phi:A\to V$. The respected parallel
cube-pair count on $A$ equals $|A|^3$ if and only if $A$ is a Cartesian
coset and, after translating it to $H=\prod_iH_i$, the map has the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:labelclassification}
 \phi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=L(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
   +\sum_{i=1}^k\psi_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_k),
\end{equation}
where $L:H\to V$ is additive separately in every coordinate and the
$\psi_i$ are arbitrary functions on the indicated smaller products.
For $k=1$, the final sum is simply a constant.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equality forces equality in both inequalities
$C_A\le Q(A)\le|A|^3$, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian} applies.
For each $h\in H$, every base is admissible. Equality of all collisions
therefore says that $D_h\phi(y)$ is independent of $y\in H$.

Define the anchored mixed part by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:anchored}
 L(x)=D_x\phi(0)
 =\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}(-1)^{k-|S|}\phi(x_S),
\end{equation}
where $x_S$ agrees with $x$ on $S$ and is zero elsewhere.
For a coordinate translation $T_a$ and difference
$\Delta_a=T_a-I$, the identity
\[
 \Delta_{a+b}=\Delta_a+T_a\Delta_b
\]
holds. Apply it to one of the coordinate increments in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:anchored}, keeping the other differences fixed. The translated
full mixed difference equals its unshifted value because of the base-point
independence just proved. Thus $L$ is additive in that coordinate.
The same argument applies to every coordinate.

Solving \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:anchored} for the term with $S=[k]$ gives
\[
 \phi(x)-L(x)=\sum_{S\subsetneq[k]}(-1)^{k-|S|+1}\phi(x_S).
\]
Every summand omits at least one coordinate. Assign each proper $S$ to one
chosen missing coordinate and collect the assigned terms to obtain the
functions $\psi_i$ in \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:labelclassification}.

Conversely, the full mixed derivative of a function omitting a coordinate
is zero. Separate additivity gives $D_hL(y)=L(h)$, independently of $y$.
Hence every admissible pair with the same side has equal mixed values,
and the count is $Q(A)=|A|^3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian} and~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactlabels} are source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-equality} (equality with labels), which adds that the top interaction is unique; proved independently. At $k=1$ the set statement is source~11's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}.
\end{writenote}

No division by factorials or scalar-field hypothesis enters this proof.
It applies to arbitrary finite abelian value groups, including groups with
small torsion. It describes a multiadditive top component modulo
coordinate-omitting functions, not necessarily an ordinary polynomial over
a field. Globally, $C=\Gamma$ holds precisely when every nonempty fibre
satisfies this description, with possibly different subgroups and functions
in different fibres.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dimension-free Cartesian stability\srctag{15}}]{Dimension-free Cartesian stability}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:Cartesianstability}
\srcnote{15}{Section 8}

The exact theorem has a robust counterpart with a linear error term. The
proof first finds an almost-period subgroup using ordinary additive energy,
then uses the axis-cube condition to force that subgroup to split by
coordinates. The latter step is what ordinary energy alone would not give.

\begin{lemma}[A small-difference-set fact]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:smalldifference}
If a nonempty finite subset $P$ of an abelian group satisfies
$|P-P|<\tfrac32|P|$, then $P-P$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D=P-P$. For $t=u-v\in D$, the sets $P-u$ and $P-v$ are both
subsets of $D$, so their intersection has size at least
$2|P|-|D|>|P|/2$. Thus
\[
 r_P(t):=|\{x\in P:x+t\in P\}|>|P|/2.
\]
For any $s,t\in D$, the two subsets
$\{x\in P:x+s\in P\}$ and $\{x\in P:x-t\in P\}$ each contain more
than half of $P$ and therefore intersect. For a point in the intersection,
$(x+s)-(x-t)=s+t\in D$. Since $D$ also contains zero and is symmetric,
it is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} The same classical fact is source~14's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:14:lem:three-halves} (note there); both prove it.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Linear-error Cartesian stability]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:stability}
Let $A\ne\varnothing$ be a subset of $X=\prod_{i=1}^kG_i$, and put
$a=|A|$. Suppose
\[
 Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)a^3,\qquad
 0\le\varepsilon\le\frac1{100}.
\]
There is a Cartesian coset
$\mathcal C=c+(H_1\times\cdots\times H_k)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:stabilitydetails}
 |A\cap\mathcal C|\ge(1-8\varepsilon)a,
 \qquad |\mathcal C|\le(1+2\varepsilon)a,
 \qquad |A\symdiff\mathcal C|\le18\varepsilon a.
\end{equation}
All constants are independent of $k$ and of the coordinate-group orders.
The same conclusion follows if the respected cube-pair count for any
labelling of $A$ is at least $(1-\varepsilon)a^3$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\textit{Step 1: almost maximal additive energy.}
Let $r(t)=|\{x\in A:x+t\in A\}|$. We have $\sum_tr(t)=a^2$.
Every cube pair counted by $Q(A)$ has its four extreme endpoints in $A$,
so
\[
 Q(A)\le E(A):=\sum_tr(t)^2\le a^3.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:energydeficit}
 \sum_t r(t)(a-r(t))=a^3-E(A)\le\varepsilon a^3.
\end{equation}

\textit{Step 2: a subgroup of popular differences.}
Set $P=\{t:r(t)>7a/8\}$. This set contains zero and is symmetric.
For $t\notin P$, $r(t)(a-r(t))\ge (a/8)r(t)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:popularmass}
 \sum_{t\in P}r(t)\ge(1-8\varepsilon)a^2,
 \qquad |P|\ge(1-8\varepsilon)a.
\end{equation}
The translation distance $a-r(t)=\tfrac12|A\symdiff(A-t)|$ obeys the
triangle inequality. Hence for $s,t\in P$,
$r(s-t)>3a/4$. It follows that
\[
 |P-P|<\frac43a
 <\frac32(1-8\varepsilon)a\le\frac32|P|,
\]
where the strict middle inequality uses $\varepsilon\le1/100$.
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:smalldifference}, $H=P-P$ is a subgroup.
Write $m=|H|$; then $m<4a/3$ and $P\subseteq H$.

\textit{Step 3: one coset captures nearly all of $A$.}
The identity
\[
 \sum_{h\in H}r(h)=\sum_{\mathcal D\in X/H}|A\cap\mathcal D|^2
\]
and \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:popularmass} imply that one coset
$\mathcal C=c+H$ has intersection size
$b=|A\cap\mathcal C|\ge(1-8\varepsilon)a$.
For every $h\in H$, two subsets of the same $m$-point coset give
\[
 r(h)\ge2b-m>
 \left(\frac23-16\varepsilon\right)a\ge\frac a2.
\]
Use this lower bound in \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:energydeficit}, restricting the sum to $H$:
\begin{align*}
 \varepsilon a^3
 &\ge \frac a2\left(ma-\sum_{h\in H}r(h)\right)\\
 &=\frac a2\left(ma-\sum_{\mathcal D\in X/H}|A\cap\mathcal D|^2\right)
 \ge\frac{a^2}{2}(m-a).
\end{align*}
The final inequality uses $\sum_{\mathcal D}|A\cap\mathcal D|^2\le a^2$.
It follows that $m\le(1+2\varepsilon)a$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:cosetdistance}
 |A\symdiff\mathcal C|=a+m-2b\le18\varepsilon a.
\end{equation}
At this point $H$ need not yet be a Cartesian subgroup.

\textit{Step 4: the axis condition forces a Cartesian subgroup.}
Fix a coordinate projection $\pi_i$ and define
$L_i(r,t)=r+\pi_i(t-r)$. The injection underlying $Q(A)\le a^3$
shows that at least $(1-\varepsilon)a^2$ ordered pairs $(r,t)\in A^2$
satisfy $L_i(r,t)\in A$: a pair failing this condition can support none
of the at most $a$ third entries in that injection.
Thus at least $b^2-\varepsilon a^2$ pairs from
$(A\cap\mathcal C)^2$ satisfy this condition.

For uniformly chosen $(r,t)\in\mathcal C^2$, the value $L_i(r,t)$ is
uniform on the coset $c+K_i$, where
\[
 K_i=(I-\pi_i)H+\pi_iH=H+\pi_iH.
\]
If $\pi_iH\nsubseteq H$, then $|K_i|\ge2m$, and the number of pairs
in $\mathcal C^2$ with $L_i(r,t)\in A$ is at most $am/2$.
On the other hand,
\[
 b^2-\varepsilon a^2
 \ge\bigl((1-8\varepsilon)^2-\varepsilon\bigr)a^2
 \ge(1-17\varepsilon)a^2\ge\frac{83}{100}a^2,
\]
whereas
\[
 \frac{am}{2}\le\frac{1+2\varepsilon}{2}a^2
 \le\frac{51}{100}a^2.
\]
This is a contradiction. Hence $\pi_iH\subseteq H$ for every $i$, and
$H$ is a product subgroup by the argument in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian}. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:stabilitydetails}.
The labelled version follows because its count is at most $Q(A)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{A weaker second route} (checked at the write). Source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} has the same hypothesis and gives a unique closest coordinate-product coset $\mathcal C$ with $|A\symdiff\mathcal C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)a$, $\tau(\varepsilon)=(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2$. Since $\tau(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$ increases on $[0,1/100]$ and $\tau(1/100)=0.010102\ldots$, $\tau(\varepsilon)\le1.0102\,\varepsilon\le2\varepsilon$ there, so source~14's coset satisfies all three bounds of \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:stabilitydetails}: $|A\cap\mathcal C|\ge(1-\tau)a$, $|\mathcal C|\le(1+\tau)a$, $|A\symdiff\mathcal C|\le\tau a$. The theorem here is correct; its constants are not sharp. The method is the same (this source's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:smalldifference} is source~14's three-halves lemma, and the coordinate-mixing step is source~14's), and Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:linearsharp} is source~14's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{example}[The linear order is necessary]\label{gsr:en:15:ex:linearsharp}
Let $k=1$, take $G_1=\Z/p\Z$ with $p\ge101$ prime, and let
$A=G_1\setminus\{0\}$. Put $a=p-1$. Then $r(0)=a$ and
$r(t)=a-1$ for every $t\ne0$. Since $Q(A)=E(A)$ in dimension one,
\[
 Q(A)=a^2+a(a-1)^2=a^3-a^2+a,
 \qquad \varepsilon=\frac1a-\frac1{a^2}.
\]
The closest coset of a subgroup is the whole group, at symmetric-difference
distance $1$. Its relative distance $1/a$ is asymptotic to $\varepsilon$.
Thus no uniform $o(\varepsilon)$ replacement for the error term is possible.
Taking the product with whole additional coordinate groups gives the same
relative deficit and relative distance in higher dimensions.
This does not establish optimality of the numerical constant $18$.
\end{example}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
With source~14's theorem this example settles the leading constant asked for in the first question of Section~\ref{gsr:fz:15:sec:questions}: at $\varepsilon=1/a-1/a^2$ one has $1-4\varepsilon=(1-2/a)^2$, so $\tau(\varepsilon)a=1$, the distance here. The optimal $\delta(\varepsilon)$ is therefore $\tau(\varepsilon)$ along this sequence, with leading constant $1$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}).
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Stability of the amplification inequality\srctag{15}}]{Stability of the amplification inequality}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:spectral}
\srcnote{15}{Section 9}

The preceding theorem describes near equality in the \emph{geometric cap}
$C\le\Gamma$. Near equality in the \emph{moment interpolation} has a
different consequence: the spectrum has nearly constant magnitude on the
part that carries its collision mass.

Assume $C>0$ and put, with $i=(h,\alpha,\psi)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:spectralprob}
 t_i=|F_h(\alpha,\psi)|^2,\qquad
 p_i=\frac{t_i}{nqC},\qquad
 \lambda=\frac{R_2}{C},\qquad W_i=\frac{t_i}{\lambda}.
\end{equation}
Then $(p_i)$ is a probability distribution and $\E_pW=1$.

\begin{theorem}[Spectral plateau stability]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:spectral}
For $d\ge3$, define the nonnegative interpolation defect
\[
 \mathcal D_d=\frac{R_dC^{d-2}}{R_2^{d-1}}-1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:spectralvariance}
 \E_p(W-1)^2\le\frac{\mathcal D_d}{d-2}.
\end{equation}
For every $\tau>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:spectraltail}
 p\{i:|W_i-1|\ge\tau\}
 \le\frac{\mathcal D_d}{(d-2)\tau^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The moment identity gives
$\mathcal D_d=\E_pW^{d-1}-1$. For $w\ge0$ the exact polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:polynomialgap}
 w^{d-1}-1-(d-1)(w-1)
 =(w-1)^2\sum_{j=0}^{d-3}(d-2-j)w^j
 \ge(d-2)(w-1)^2
\end{equation}
holds. Taking expectations and using $\E_pW=1$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:spectralvariance}. Markov's inequality applied to $(W-1)^2$
proves \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:spectraltail}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Source~14's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:moment-spectral-stability} bounds the same variance (in its notation $\eta=\mathcal D_d$) by $(1+\eta)^{1/(d-2)}-1$, which is at most $\eta/(d-2)$ by Bernoulli's inequality; so this theorem is a weaker second route (at $d=8$, $\mathcal D_8=1$: $0.1225$ against $1/6$). Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:15:cor:band}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:15:prop:profile} and Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:diagonal} are new in this report.
\end{writenote}

For eight-arrangements, the coefficient in \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:spectralvariance} is
$1/6$. This estimate concerns collision-weighted spectral mass, not the
uniform proportion of all frequencies. Small or zero Fourier coefficients
can occupy many indices without affecting it appreciably.

\begin{corollary}[Size of the near-flat band]\label{gsr:en:15:cor:band}
Define
\[
 K_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{nqC^2}{R_2},\qquad
 I_\tau=\{i:|W_i-1|\le\tau\},\qquad 0<\tau<1,
\]
and let $\eta=\mathcal D_d/((d-2)\tau^2)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:band}
 \frac{\max(0,1-\eta)}{1+\tau}K_{\mathrm{eff}}
 \le |I_\tau|\le\frac{K_{\mathrm{eff}}}{1-\tau}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
On $I_\tau$, $\lambda(1-\tau)\le t_i\le\lambda(1+\tau)$.
Its $p$-mass is at least $1-\eta$, while its total $t$-mass is at most
$nqC$. Divide these two bounds by the appropriate endpoints of the band.
Since $nqC/\lambda=K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the conclusion follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The additional gain from the side-vector profile}
\begin{proposition}[Disintegrated amplification]\label{gsr:en:15:prop:profile}
For $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:profile}
 R_d\ge\sum_{h:C_h>0}\frac{R_2(h)^{d-1}}{C_h^{d-2}}
 \ge\frac{R_2^{d-1}}{C^{d-2}}.
\end{equation}
For $C>0$, put $w_h=C_h/C$, $\lambda_h=R_2(h)/C_h$ on occupied sides,
and $\lambda=R_2/C$. The ratio of the middle expression in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:profile} to the final expression equals
\[
 \E_w\left(\frac{\lambda_h}{\lambda}\right)^{d-1}.
\]
For $d\ge3$, this ratio is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:profilevariance}
 1+(d-2)\Var_w\left(\frac{\lambda_h}{\lambda}\right).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply the moment interpolation with $h$ fixed and sum over $h$.
Since $R_2(h)=0$ whenever $C_h=0$, no term is lost.
The middle expression is $C\E_w\lambda_h^{d-1}$, and
$\E_w\lambda_h=\lambda$. Jensen proves the second inequality and the
ratio identity. Formula \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:polynomialgap} proves the variance bound.
\end{proof}

The full spectral distribution disintegrates over $h$ with weights $w_h$.
The law of total variance gives the useful identity
\[
 \Var_p(W)=\E_w\Var(W\mid h)
 +\Var_w(\lambda_h/\lambda).
\]
Thus a near extremizer must have both approximately flat conditional
spectra and approximately aligned scales across the collision-carrying
side vectors.

\begin{example}[Spectral equality is not Cartesian equality]\label{gsr:en:15:ex:diagonal}
Let $X=(\Z/p\Z)^2$, let $T$ and $V$ be trivial groups, and take the
horizontal domain $A=\{(u,u):u\in\Z/p\Z\}$ with the zero label.
The only admissible side vector is $h=0$, because a nonzero single-coordinate
corner leaves the diagonal. Hence $R_d=p^{2d}$ and $C=p^2$.
Moment amplification is an equality for every $d$, and the spectrum has
one nonzero magnitude. But $A$ is not a Cartesian coset for $p>1$, and
$Q(A)/|A|^3=1/p$. Near equality in the interpolation alone therefore cannot
replace the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:stability}.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A complete normal form for joint equality\srctag{15}}]{A complete normal form for joint equality}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:joint}
\srcnote{15}{Section 10}

There is a useful stronger conclusion when both the moment inequality and
the cubic collision cap are equalities. We first translate flat Fourier
magnitudes into a statement about the nonnegative measures $m_h$.

\begin{lemma}[Positive flat spectra]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:positiveflat}
Let $K$ be a finite abelian group and $\mu:K\to[0,\infty)$ a nonzero
function of total mass $s$. Every Fourier coefficient has magnitude either
$0$ or $s$ if and only if
\[
 \mu=\frac{s}{|L|}\one_{z+L}
\]
for some subgroup $L\le K$ and some coset $z+L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $z\in\supp\mu$ and let $L$ be the subgroup generated by
$\supp\mu-\supp\mu$. Equality in the triangle inequality
$|\widehat\mu(\xi)|\le s$ holds exactly when $\xi$ is constant on
$\supp\mu$, equivalently when $\xi\in L^\perp$.
For such characters the coefficient is $s\xi(z)$; for other characters,
the hypothesis forces it to be zero. Fourier inversion and character
orthogonality therefore give $(s/|L|)\one_{z+L}$.
The converse follows by summing a character over that coset.
\end{proof}

For a nonempty domain and $d\ge3$, equality in moment amplification is
therefore equivalent to the following description: every occupied $m_h$ is
a constant multiple of a subgroup-coset indicator in $T\times V$, and
\emph{all occupied measures have the same total mass}. The common mass
condition is needed because the interpolation combines different $h$.

\begin{theorem}[Joint extremizers]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:joint}
For a nonempty labelled domain $B\subseteq X\times T$, the following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $C=\Gamma$ and $R_dC^{d-2}=R_2^{d-1}$ for some integer $d\ge3$;
\item there exist a Cartesian subgroup $H=\prod_iH_i\le X$, a subgroup
$J\le T$, a coset $S=x_0+J$, and representatives $c_x\in X$ for $x\in S$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:jointdomain}
 B_x=c_x+H\quad(x\in S),\qquad B_x=\varnothing\quad(x\notin S),
\end{equation}
and, for $u\in H$ and $x\in S$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:jointlabel}
 \phi(c_x+u,x)=L_0(u)+A(u,x-x_0)
       +\sum_{i=1}^k\psi_{i,x}(u_1,\ldots,\widehat{u_i},\ldots,u_k).
\end{equation}
Here $L_0:H\to V$ is separately additive in the $k$ horizontal variables,
$A:H\times J\to V$ is separately additive in all $k+1$ variables,
and the functions $\psi_{i,x}$ are arbitrary.
\end{enumerate}
For all these domains and every integer $r\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:jointcounts}
 R_r=|H|^{2r+1}|J|^{2r-1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, equality then holds in moment amplification for every $r\ge2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assume (i). Since $k\ge1$, the zero side has zero mixed value and
$m_0(x,v)=b_x\one_{\{v=0\}}$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:positiveflat} and the
moment equality, the nonempty vertical fibres form a coset $S=x_0+J$,
and all their sizes equal some positive integer $b$.
The total mass of $m_0$ is $b|S|$, so every other occupied $m_h$ has this
same mass.

The equality $C=\Gamma$ holds fibre by fibre. By
Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian} and~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactlabels}, each
$B_x$ is $c_x+H_x$ for a Cartesian subgroup $H_x$, and its mixed value
$L_x(h)$ is independent of the base whenever $h\in H_x$.
For any $h$ that lies in at least one $H_x$,
\[
 \sum_{x,v}m_h(x,v)=b\,|\{x\in S:h\in H_x\}|.
\]
This is an occupied side, so its mass must equal $b|S|$. Thus such an $h$
lies in every $H_x$, proving that all the subgroups $H_x$ coincide with
one Cartesian subgroup $H$.

For each $h\in H$, the measure $m_h$ is now $b$ times the indicator of
\[
 \{(x,L_x(h)):x\in S\}\subseteq T\times V.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:positiveflat}, this graph is a subgroup coset. Projection
onto $T$ is one-to-one on it, so its subgroup is the graph of a homomorphism
from $J$ to $V$. Consequently
\[
 L_{x_0+t}(h)=L_{x_0}(h)+A(h,t),\qquad t\in J,
\]
where $A(h,\cdot)$ is additive. Each $L_x$ is separately additive in the
horizontal variables by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactlabels}; hence their difference
$A(\cdot,t)$ is also separately additive. Put $L_0=L_{x_0}$ and use the
coordinate-omitting decomposition in each fibre to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:jointlabel}.

Conversely, suppose (ii) holds. For $h\in H$, every base in every occupied
fibre gives an admissible cube, and its mixed value is
$L_0(h)+A(h,x-x_0)$; for $h\notin H$, no cube is admissible.
Whenever the vertical coordinates satisfy the additive relation, these
mixed values also satisfy it, by additivity of $A$ in its last variable.
Thus all vertical additive tuples are respected. Choosing the common side,
the $2r$ bases, and the vertical tuple gives \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:jointcounts}.
Also $C=|H|^3|J|=\Gamma$, and substituting these counts proves all the
moment equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} This normal form is source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:joint-geometric-equality} (same freedom in the representatives $c_x$, the same additive and lower-order terms, the same counts \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:jointcounts}); proved independently. The intake checked both statements against each other on groups that neither package uses (no mismatch).
\end{writenote}

The representatives $c_x$ need not depend additively on $x$, and the
coordinate-omitting functions may vary arbitrarily from fibre to fibre.
These freedoms are invisible to the mixed-value arrangement test. Omitting
them would give an incorrect rigidity statement. This normal form classifies
joint equality, not all extremizers of the product-property lower bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A geometry--amplification dichotomy\srctag{15}}]{A geometry--amplification dichotomy}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:dichotomy}
\srcnote{15}{Section 11}

The quantitative results also provide an alternative that distinguishes two
reasons an arrangement estimate can be useful: either collisions are
substantially below their cubic cap, improving amplification, or most of the
cubic fibre mass lies on nearly Cartesian fibres.

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy with explicit weights]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:dichotomy}
Let $B\ne\varnothing$, $0<\eta<1$, and
$0<\varepsilon\le1/100$. At least one of the following alternatives holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),itemsep=0.3em]
\item $C\le(1-\eta)\Gamma$, and therefore
\[
 R_8\ge(1-\eta)^{-6}\frac{R_2^7}{\Gamma^6};
\]
\item the fibres satisfying $C_x\ge(1-\varepsilon)b_x^3$ carry at least
$(1-\eta/\varepsilon)\Gamma$ of the total cubic mass $\sum_xb_x^3$.
Every such nonempty fibre is within $18\varepsilon b_x$ points of a
Cartesian coset, with the intersection and size bounds in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:stabilitydetails}.
\end{enumerate}
The lower bound in (ii) is informative when $\eta<\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If (i)'s collision inequality holds, apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification}. Otherwise,
$\sum_x(b_x^3-C_x)<\eta\Gamma$. A bad fibre with
$C_x<(1-\varepsilon)b_x^3$ contributes more than $\varepsilon b_x^3$
to this deficit. Their total cubic mass is consequently at most
$\eta\Gamma/\varepsilon$. On every remaining nonempty fibre,
$Q(B_x)\ge C_x\ge(1-\varepsilon)b_x^3$, so
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:stability} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} A weaker restatement of source~14's cubic-weight split in Section~\ref{gsr:en:14:sec:d4} (with $\tau(\theta)$ in place of $18\varepsilon$) together with its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:14:cor:joint-equality}.
\end{writenote}

Taking $\eta=\varepsilon^2$ gives a particularly simple statement: either
there is a factor $(1-\varepsilon^2)^{-6}$ improvement over the cubic-cap
bound, or at least $1-\varepsilon$ of the cubic fibre mass has the stated
Cartesian approximation. This mass is not point mass $\sum_xb_x$ and not
uniform mass on the set of fibres. A claim about either of those would
require an additional fibre-size comparison.

The theorem gives geometric information about the domain. It does not
supply a quantitative repair of the labels to the exact multiadditive form.
The latter is a separate research problem in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:15:sec:questions}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Vertex weights and other extensions\srctag{15}}]{Vertex weights and other extensions}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d12}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:weights}
\srcnote{15}{Section 12}

The moment method is naturally a method for nonnegative measures, not only
for subsets. There are two different levels of generality.

\subsection{Arbitrary cube measures}
Let each $m_h:T\times V\to[0,\infty)$ be any nonnegative real measure,
and define $R_d$ as its additive $2d$-tuple count, summed over $h$.
The moment identity, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification}, the spectral stability
estimates, and the side-vector profile inequality continue to hold verbatim.
No vertex representation is needed for these statements.
An arbitrary collection of measures does not, however, have a meaningful
bound $C\le\sum_xb_x^3$ unless suitable additional data and hypotheses are
given.

\subsection{Weights arising from vertices}
Let $f:X\times T\to[0,1]$, with $\phi$ defined on $\supp f$.
Give a supported cube the weight
\[
 w(y,h,x)=\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}f(y+\omega h,x),
\]
and define $m_h(x,v)$ by summing this weight over cubes of mixed value $v$.
The arrangement count is now the sum of the products of the $2d$ cube
weights. Put
\[
 b_x=\sum_y f(y,x),\qquad
 \beta_x=b_x/M,\qquad\beta=\E_x\beta_x.
\]
The same normalizations for $a_d,\chi,\rho_3$ apply.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted collision and coupling bounds]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:weighted}
For vertex-product weights in $[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:weightedcap}
 C\le\sum_xb_x^3.
\end{equation}
Thus all density-sensitive amplification bounds remain valid.
If the map on $\supp f$ has $\PP_\gamma$, then the configuration lower
bound, the collision lower bound, and the coupled bounds
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledchi}--\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledbeta} also remain valid, with these
weighted densities and counts.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First discard the label-equality condition. For each pair of cubes, retain
only the formal vertex factors at $y$, $y+h$, and $z$ in the product
$w(y,h,x)w(z,h,x)$. There are three distinct formal positions because
$k\ge1$, even if their actual values coincide. All remaining factors are
at most one. Thus
\[
 w(y,h,x)w(z,h,x)\le f(y,x)f(y+h,x)f(z,x).
\]
Summing over $h,y,z$ and using the bijection $h\leftrightarrow y+h$ gives
$b_x^3$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:weightedcap}.

For the configuration induction, give a configuration the product of $f$
over its $4^j$ formal vertices and impose the same face-respect conditions.
At a fixed lower-dimensional configuration $\zeta$, replace
$\one_{E_\zeta}$ in the proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:configuration} by the
product of its vertex weights at that level, set to zero where a lower face
fails. The product property allows every such nonnegative weight.
All sums and Jensen steps are unchanged. The zero-dimensional base is
$\mathcal F_0=f$, so it is valid for fractional values as well.
The injection from configurations to cube pairs preserves the selected
$2^{j+1}$ formal vertex factors; discarding the others can only increase the
weight. Hence it gives the required inequality of weighted counts.

For the pair bound, replace the reference weight in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:PPcollision} by
\[
 \widetilde w_y(x)=w(y,h,x)\,m_h(x,D_h\phi(y,x)),
\]
with zero value on unsupported cubes. Its sum over $y,x$ is exactly $C_h$.
The weighted quadruple output is bounded by the weighted $R_2(h)$ because
the four additional reference-cube factors are at most one.
The two averaging steps therefore give the same inequality
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:globalPP}. Combining it with the weighted collision lower bound
and the unchanged moment interpolation proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact saturation forces hard vertex weights]
For $k\ge1$, equality in \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:weightedcap} implies that every
$f(y,x)$ is zero or one. Indeed, in the cap proof consider the term with
$h=0$ and $z=y$. Its left-hand weight is
$f(y,x)^{2^{k+1}}$, its retained right-hand weight is $f(y,x)^3$, and the
label condition is automatically satisfied. These are strictly unequal for
$0<f(y,x)<1$. Since every termwise difference is nonnegative, equality of
the sums rules out all fractional values. The exact set classifications then
apply. This observation alone gives no useful dimension-free quantitative
rounding theorem for near equality; a single diagonal term can be tiny
relative to the full cubic sum.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Which extensions require new work?}
The group generalization above allows composite moduli, unequal coordinate
sizes, noncyclic groups, and finite abelian value groups. It does not assert
an analogous theorem for nonabelian value groups, where an alternating
additive relation has no canonical interpretation. Nor does it automatically
handle a requirement that all vertices of an entire arrangement be distinct.
Weights on side vectors are compatible with the Fourier argument, but their
normalizations and geometric caps must be tracked separately.

\section{Source~17's chapter: polynomial-loss restriction at Section~9 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:restriction}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next seven sections are source~17, a manuscript on Gowers's random restriction in Section~9 (Lemmas~9.2--9.3 and Corollary~9.4): from many respected additive sixteen-tuples, pass to a subset on which almost all are respected. Source~17 replaces the long product of degree-one cosine filters by one Fej\'er kernel and keeps the exact second moment. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~04's Sections~\ref{gsr:en:04:sec:d3}--\ref{gsr:en:04:sec:d4}}, which prove the same moment lifting and a complementary restriction theorem over prime fields; source~04's text was in the repository at this source's pin and is not cited by it. It is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:17:sec:d1}; its Lean relation, audits, questions, conclusion and appendices are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:17:sec:d9}--\ref{gsr:fz:17:sec:dB}). Its notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} Over a prime field, with $L=\lceil(m+1)/(\alpha\eta)\rceil$ and $N\ge2L^m(2L-1)^{m-1}\beta^{-(m-1)}$, a set whose map respects $\alpha|B|^{m-1}$ balanced $m$-tuples has a subset on which a $1-\eta$ proportion is respected and which keeps $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}|B|^{m-1}/(2(m+2)^m)$ tuples, for weights and vector-valued maps too (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:main}); at $m=16$ the retention is $\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}/(2\cdot18^{16})$, in place of $(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}$. The moment lifting $G_{2r}\ge\gamma^{r-1}|B|^{2r-1}$ without a density loss is source~04's (M2)--(M5) (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:moments}). The best retention a scalar filter certificate can give is determined (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:methodbarrier}, sharpening source~04's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:method-bound}), and a random-linear-map construction treats arbitrary systems in fixed characteristic with a rank gap (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap}; new in this report). Against source~04's restriction theorem: a better constant for $d\le97$, a worse threshold; both are printed (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:main}). Prime moduli only: composite moduli need a new argument (Section~\ref{gsr:en:17:sec:d8}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}). \file{lemma_9_3} and \file{corollary_9_4} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, lines~77, 91) hold for every $N$, with exact companions (\file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, lines~376, 416) and the retention $(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}$; the definitions match this chapter's $T_{16}$, $G_{16}$ and $1-\eta$ exactly. The theorem here proves their prime case with an explicit threshold and a far better constant (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:17:sec:d1}); it is not formalized.

\section[{Notation and elementary counting facts\srctag{17}}]{Notation and elementary counting facts}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:notation}
\srcnote{17}{Section 2}

Let $V$ and $H$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a prime field
$\F_p$.  Write $N=|V|$.  A map $\phi:V\to H$ need not be linear.
Let $m=2r\ge4$, and write
\[
 \varepsilon=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{r},
              \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{r})\in\F_p^m.
\]
For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in V^m$, the notation
$\varepsilon\cdot x=0$ means $\sum_j\varepsilon_jx_j=0$ in $V$.
We call such a tuple \emph{additive}.  It is \emph{respected} if also
$\sum_j\varepsilon_j\phi(x_j)=0$ in $H$.

For a weight $w:V\to[0,1]$, define
\begin{align}
 T_m(w)&=\sum_{\varepsilon\cdot x=0}\prod_{j=1}^m w(x_j),\label{gsr:en:17:eq:Tdef}\\
 G_m(w,\phi)&=\sum_{\substack{\varepsilon\cdot x=0\\
                       \varepsilon\cdot\phi(x)=0}}
                       \prod_{j=1}^m w(x_j).\label{gsr:en:17:eq:Gdef}
\end{align}
For $w=\one_B$, abbreviate these quantities to $T_m(B)$ and
$G_m(B,\phi)$.  The word ``proportion'' in the conclusion always refers
to $G_m(B',\phi)/T_m(B')$, not to normalization by $|B'|^{m-1}$.
The theorem guarantees $T_m(B')>0$.

\begin{lemma}[The free-variable bound]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:free}
If $b=\sum_xw(x)$, then
\[
 0\le G_m(w,\phi)\le T_m(w)\le b^{m-1}.
\]
In particular, $T_m(B)\le |B|^{m-1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After choosing $x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1}$, the additive relation determines
$x_m$ uniquely because its coefficient is $-1$.  Its weight is at most
one.  Summing the product of the first $m-1$ weights gives $b^{m-1}$.
The first two inequalities follow from nonnegativity and restriction of
the summation set.
\end{proof}

The parameter $\alpha$ in the main theorem therefore measures the number
of respected tuples against the maximal scale $b^{m-1}$.  It is not merely
a lower bound for their fraction among whatever additive tuples happen
to be present.  This distinction is important in sparse or highly
structured examples.

We use normalized averages over random parameters, but unnormalized
counts of tuples.  On $\T=\R/\Z$ let $\e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$.
On $\F_p$ write $\e_p(a)=\exp(2\pi i a/p)$, which is well-defined
independently of the integer representative of $a$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Moment lifting without a density loss\srctag{17}}]{Moment lifting without a density loss}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:moments}
\srcnote{17}{Section 3}

The following elementary result is useful independently of the
restriction theorem.  We prove it in an arbitrary finite abelian group
so that the normalization is visible.

\begin{proposition}[Density-sensitive graph moment inequality]
\label{gsr:en:17:prop:moments}
Let $A$ be a nonempty subset of a finite abelian group $K$, let $b=|A|$,
and let
\[
 E_r(A)=\#\{(a_1,\ldots,a_{2r})\in A^{2r}:
              a_1+\cdots+a_r=a_{r+1}+\cdots+a_{2r}\}.
\]
For each integer $r\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:moment}
 E_r(A)\ge\frac{E_2(A)^{r-1}}{b^{r-2}}.
\end{equation}
For $r>2$, equality holds exactly when $A$ is a coset of a subgroup of $K$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $Q=|K|$, and use the unnormalized Fourier transform
$\widehat{\one_A}(\chi)=\sum_{a\in A}\overline{\chi(a)}$.
Character orthogonality gives
\[
 E_r(A)=\frac1Q\sum_{\chi\in\widehat K}
                  |\widehat{\one_A}(\chi)|^{2r},
 \qquad
 b=\frac1Q\sum_\chi|\widehat{\one_A}(\chi)|^2.
\]
For $r>2$, apply H\"older to
\[
 z^4=(z^2)^{(r-2)/(r-1)}(z^{2r})^{1/(r-1)},\qquad z\ge0.
\]
Using normalized sums yields
$E_2(A)\le b^{(r-2)/(r-1)}E_r(A)^{1/(r-1)}$.
Raising to the power $r-1$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:moment}; for $r=2$ it is an
identity.

For equality with $r>2$, equality in H\"older says that all nonzero
$|\widehat{\one_A}(\chi)|$ are the same.  The trivial character has
value $b$, so that common magnitude is $b$.  Fix $a_0\in A$ and put
$J=\langle A-A\rangle$.  Equality in the triangle inequality shows that
$|\widehat{\one_A}(\chi)|=b$ exactly when $\chi$ is constant on $A$,
equivalently $\chi$ annihilates $J$.  Thus the Fourier support is $J^\perp$.
Parseval gives
\[
 b=\frac{|J^\perp|b^2}{Q}=\frac{b^2}{|J|},
\]
so $b=|J|$.  Since $A\subseteq a_0+J$, equality of cardinalities makes
$A=a_0+J$.  Conversely, the Fourier transform of a subgroup coset has
magnitude either zero or $b$, so all the inequalities are equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} This is source~04's (M2) with its coset equality case (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:interpolation}), and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:17:cor:momentgraph} is source~04's (M3) (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:graph}); the remark on $N^2|B|$ is source~04's (M4)--(M5), and source~04's (M1) with complex weights contains the remark on fractional weights. Source~04's (M6) (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:residual}) is stronger. The arrangement analogues are source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality} and source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification}. Proved independently; the source does not claim the inequality as new.
\end{writenote}

Apply this proposition to the graph
$A=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\}\subseteq V\oplus H$.
Its size is $|B|$, and $E_r(A)=G_{2r}(B,\phi)$.

\begin{corollary}[From quadruples to arbitrary even order]
\label{gsr:en:17:cor:momentgraph}
If $G_4(B,\phi)\ge\gamma|B|^3$, with $0<\gamma\le1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:gamma-moment}
 G_{2r}(B,\phi)\ge\gamma^{r-1}|B|^{2r-1}
 \qquad(r\ge2).
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute $E_2(A)\ge\gamma|B|^3$ and $b=|B|$ into
\eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:moment}.  The exponent of $|B|$ is
$3(r-1)-(r-2)=2r-1$.
\end{proof}

For the original absolute normalization
$G_4(B,\phi)\ge\delta N^3$ and $|B|=\beta N$, the order-eight consequence
is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:absolute-moment}
 G_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\delta^7\beta^{-6}N^{15}.
\end{equation}
Putting $\delta=\gamma\beta^3$ gives precisely
$\gamma^7\beta^{15}N^{15}$, rather than
$\gamma^7\beta^{21}N^{15}$.
The equality behind the improvement is the exact second moment
$N^2|B|$, before it is bounded by $N^3$.
The inspected Lean proof contains that exact equality inside the proof
of \codeseventeen{section9_second_moment_le}; it is therefore a natural point at
which to expose a stronger reusable lemma \cite{repo17moments}.

\begin{remark}[Fractional graph weights]
For a nonnegative graph weight $f$ with values at most one, the same
interpolation has denominator $(\sum f^2)^{r-2}$.  Since
$\sum f^2\le\sum f$, a hypothesis $E_2(f)\ge\gamma(\sum f)^3$
again implies $E_r(f)\ge\gamma^{r-1}(\sum f)^{2r-1}$.
No equality classification for fractional weights is asserted here.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A single Fej\'er filter\srctag{17}}]{A single Fej\'er filter}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:fejer}
\srcnote{17}{Section 4}

\subsection{The kernel and its signal}
For an integer $L\ge2$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:kernel}
 K_L(t)=\frac1{L^2}\left|\sum_{a=0}^{L-1}\e(at)\right|^2
       =\frac1L\sum_{n=-(L-1)}^{L-1}
                   \left(1-\frac{|n|}{L}\right)\e(nt).
\end{equation}
This normalization has $0\le K_L(t)\le1$, so it is an admissible
inclusion probability.  Its mean is $1/L$, and its Fourier coefficients
are nonnegative.

\begin{lemma}[Exact relation signal]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:signal}
For $m\ge2$ let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:signal}
 S_{m,L}=\sum_{n=-(L-1)}^{L-1}
              \left(1-\frac{|n|}{L}\right)^m
        =1+2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}\left(\frac jL\right)^m.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:signalbounds}
 \frac{2L}{m+1}\le S_{m,L}\le L.
\end{equation}
For fixed $m$, $S_{m,L}/L\to2/(m+1)$ as $L\to\infty$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the lower bound apply the trapezoidal inequality for the convex
function $f(t)=(1-t/L)^m$ on $[0,L]$:
\[
 \frac12 f(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}f(j)+\frac12f(L)
 \ge\int_0^L f(t)\,dt=\frac{L}{m+1}.
\]
Twice the left side is $S_{m,L}$.  For the upper bound use
$u^m\le u$ for $0\le u\le1$ and sum the triangular coefficients, whose
sum is $L$.  The limit is the corresponding Riemann-sum limit.
\end{proof}

The signal in a one-layer degree-one filter is only
$1+2^{1-m}$.  In contrast, the signal \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:signal} grows linearly
with $L$.  Choosing $L$ proportional to $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ gives the
whole needed amplification in one layer.  Its cost is the controlled
increase in the set of possible short Fourier relations.

\subsection{Bounded affine degeneracy}
The independent random translation used below is useful: it forces
Fourier coefficient vectors to have coordinate sum zero.  This saves
one power in the elementary count of exceptional coefficient vectors.
All coefficient sums in this definition are interpreted modulo $p$.

\begin{definition}[Exceptional tuples]\label{gsr:en:17:def:degenerate}
Suppose $p>2L-2$.  An additive tuple $x\in V^m$ is
\emph{$L$-degenerate} if there is an integer vector
$n=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\in[-L+1,L-1]^m$ such that
\[
 \sum_j n_j=0\text{ in }\F_p,\qquad
 \sum_j n_jx_j=0\text{ in }V,
\]
and whose reduction modulo $p$ does not belong to
$\Span_{\F_p}(\varepsilon)$.  A tuple that is not $L$-degenerate is
\emph{$L$-generic}.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exceptional-set bound]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:degcount}
The number of $L$-degenerate additive tuples in $V^m$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:D0}
 D_0=(2L-1)^{m-1}N^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
Every $L$-generic additive tuple has pairwise distinct entries.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are at most $(2L-1)^{m-1}$ vectors $n$ under consideration with
$\sum n_j=0$ modulo $p$: after choosing the first $m-1$ entries, the last
entry is determined modulo $p$, and the interval of $2L-1$ allowed
integers contains at most one representative because $p>2L-2$.
For an $n$ outside $\Span(\varepsilon)$, the two equations with rows
$n$ and $\varepsilon$ are independent over $\F_p$.  They have exactly
$N^{m-2}$ solutions in $V^m$, as is seen by row reduction in each
coordinate of $V$.  A union bound proves \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:D0}.

If $x_i=x_j$ for $i\ne j$, the vector $e_i-e_j$ gives an additional
allowed affine relation.  It is not a multiple of $\varepsilon$,
since $m\ge4$ and every coordinate of $\varepsilon$ is nonzero.
Thus any repeated-entry tuple is degenerate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Short vectors on the principal relation line]
\label{gsr:en:17:lem:shortline}
If $p>2L-2$ and $n\in[-L+1,L-1]^m$ reduces modulo $p$ to a multiple of
$\varepsilon$, then $n=t\varepsilon$ as an integer vector for a unique
integer $t\in[-L+1,L-1]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take $t=n_1$, since $\varepsilon_1=1$.  For each $j$,
$n_j-\varepsilon_jt$ is divisible by $p$ and has absolute value at most
$2L-2<p$.  It must therefore be zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact survival probabilities}
Choose independently and uniformly
\[
 u\in V^*,\qquad v\in H^*,\qquad c\in\F_p.
\]
Conditioned on these choices, include each $x\in V$ in a random subset
$B'$ independently with probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:selection}
 w(x)K_L\left(\frac{u(x)+v(\phi(x))+c}{p}\right).
\end{equation}
The notation denotes evaluation through $\e_p$; it does not require a
preferred lift of the numerator.  Points with $w(x)=0$ are never chosen.

\begin{lemma}[Good and bad tuples separate exactly]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:survival}
Set $a=L^{-m}$.  For an $L$-generic additive tuple $x$, its probability
of being contained in the random subset is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:survival}
 \begin{cases}
   aS_{m,L}\prod_jw(x_j),&\varepsilon\cdot\phi(x)=0,\\
   a\prod_jw(x_j),&\varepsilon\cdot\phi(x)\ne0.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The entries are distinct by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:degcount}; hence conditional
independence really does give the product of the $m$ inclusion
probabilities.  Expand all the factors using \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:kernel}.
Averaging over $u,v,c$ leaves exactly the coefficient vectors $n$ with
\[
 \sum_jn_jx_j=0,\qquad
 \sum_jn_j\phi(x_j)=0,\qquad
 \sum_jn_j=0.
\]
Indeed, a uniform linear functional on a finite vector space has average
character zero on any nonzero vector and average one at zero.
Genericity and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:shortline} force $n=t\varepsilon$ with
$|t|\le L-1$.  If the tuple is respected, every such $t$ survives, giving
$aS_{m,L}$.  Otherwise its image discrepancy is a nonzero vector in $H$.
Multiplication by a nonzero $t\in\F_p$ cannot annihilate that vector;
thus only $t=0$ survives, giving $a$.
The fixed product of the weights multiplies both expressions.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The restriction theorem with all exceptional tuples included\srctag{17}}]{The restriction theorem with all exceptional tuples included}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d5}
\srcnote{17}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:17:sec:restriction}

It is not enough to obtain a large expected number of good tuples and a
small expected number of bad ones separately.  The same subset must
satisfy both requirements.  A single signed objective gives that
simultaneity directly.

\begin{proposition}[An exact-data restriction certificate]
\label{gsr:en:17:prop:certificate}
In the setting above, let $T=T_m(w)$, $G=G_m(w,\phi)$, and let $D$ be
any upper bound for the number of $L$-degenerate additive tuples in
$(\supp w)^m$.  Let $0<\eta\le1$.  Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:certificate}
 \Psi_L=L^{-m}\bigl[\eta S_{m,L}G-(1-\eta)(T-G)\bigr]-D.
\end{equation}
If $\Psi_L>0$, some $B'\subseteq\supp w$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:certconcl}
 G_m(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B'),\qquad
 T_m(B')\ge\frac{\Psi_L}{\eta}>0.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a realization of the random subset define $X$ to be the number of
respected additive tuples in it and $Y$ the number of unrespected ones.
Consider
\[
 F=\eta X-(1-\eta)Y=X-(1-\eta)(X+Y).
\]
Let $D_G$ and $D_B$ be the numbers of degenerate respected and degenerate
unrespected additive tuples in the initial support.  Thus
$D_G+D_B\le D$.  The total weighted mass of degenerate respected tuples
is at most $D_G$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:survival} gives
\[
 \E F\ge
 \eta aS_{m,L}(G-D_G)-(1-\eta)a(T-G)-(1-\eta)D_B.
\]
The last term bounds the entire possible contribution of degenerate
bad tuples, including those with repeated entries.  Since
$aS_{m,L}\le1$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:signal}, the two exceptional penalties
are at most $D_G+D_B\le D$.  Therefore $\E F\ge\Psi_L$.
There is a realization with $F\ge\Psi_L$.
For that realization $F\ge0$ implies $X\ge(1-\eta)(X+Y)$, and
$F\le\eta(X+Y)$ implies $X+Y\ge\Psi_L/\eta$.
These are exactly \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:certconcl}.
\end{proof}

The proposition is stronger than a worst-case threshold statement: for
a particular input one may count or estimate its actual exceptional
tuples and optimize over $L$.  No union-bound replacement is compulsory.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted, vector-valued polynomial restriction]
\label{gsr:en:17:thm:main}
Let $m=2r\ge4$.  Let $V,H$ be finite-dimensional $\F_p$-vector spaces,
$N=|V|$, $w:V\to[0,1]$, and $\phi:V\to H$.  Write
$b=\sum_xw(x)>0$ and $\beta=b/N$.  Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:mainhyp}
 G_m(w,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
Let $L=\ceil{(m+1)/(\alpha\eta)}$.  If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:mainthreshold}
 p>2L-2,\qquad
 N\ge2L^m(2L-1)^{m-1}\beta^{-(m-1)},
\end{equation}
there is a subset $B'\subseteq\supp w$ such that
\begin{align}
 G_m(B',\phi)&\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B'),\label{gsr:en:17:eq:mainquality}\\
 T_m(B')&\ge\frac{b^{m-1}}{2\eta L^m}
       \ge\frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{2(m+2)^m}b^{m-1}.\label{gsr:en:17:eq:mainmass}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $M=b^{m-1}$ and $a=L^{-m}$.  By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:free}, $T\le M$.
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:signal} and the choice of $L$,
\[
 \alpha\eta S_{m,L}\ge\frac{2\alpha\eta L}{m+1}\ge2.
\]
The coefficient of $G$ in \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:certificate} is positive, so using
$G\ge\alpha M$ and $T\le M$ gives
\begin{align*}
 a[\eta S_{m,L}G-(1-\eta)(T-G)]
 &\ge a[\alpha\eta S_{m,L}-(1-\eta)(1-\alpha)]M\\
 &\ge aM.
\end{align*}
The ambient-size hypothesis is precisely the sufficient inequality
\[
 D_0=(2L-1)^{m-1}N^{m-2}\le\frac12a\beta^{m-1}N^{m-1}
                                  =\frac12aM.
\]
Thus $\Psi_L\ge aM/2>0$.  Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:certificate} gives
\eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:mainquality} and the first part of \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:mainmass}.
Finally, $\alpha\eta\le1$ implies
\[
 L\le\frac{m+1}{\alpha\eta}+1\le\frac{m+2}{\alpha\eta},
\]
which yields the second lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:17:thm:headline}]
Take $V=H=\F_N$ and $w=\one_B$, extending $\phi$ arbitrarily outside $B$.
The size threshold implies the characteristic condition.
The lower bound for $|B'|$ follows from
$T_m(B')\le|B'|^{m-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Against source~04's restriction theorem} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:main}; checked at the write). The normalizations agree ($m=2d$, ordered tuples with repetitions, $\alpha|B|^{m-1}$), and so do the powers $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$. \emph{Constants:} the retention $1/(2(m+2)^m)=1/(2(4(d+1)^2)^d)$ here against source~04's $\kappa_d=1/(2(400d)^d)$; this one is larger exactly when $(d+1)^2<100d$, that is for $d\le97$ (at $d=8$ by the factor $3200^8/18^{16}\approx9.05\cdot10^7$). \emph{Thresholds:} \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:mainthreshold} has degree $2m-1$ in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ and $\beta^{-(m-1)}$, source~04's (R4) degree $m$ and $\beta^{-1}$, far better. At the Corollary~9.4 point $\gamma=\eta=\beta=1/2$ (relative to $\beta^{15}N^{15}$): Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:17:cor:94} retains $2^{-194.72}$ above $N\ge2^{405.71}$; source~04's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:eight} retains $2^{-222}$ above $2^{231}$; \file{corollary_9_4} retains $2^{-8{,}388{,}608}$. Source~04's conclusion ratio $1/(1+\eta)$ is slightly stronger than $1-\eta$; this theorem's weights and vector-valued maps over $\F_p$-spaces are broader than source~04's $B\subseteq\F_p$. Both are printed; neither dominates. A composition of the two (this filter with source~04's per-tuple lower bound and weighted rank-two count) is a marked question of the intake, not proved here (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold}).

\begin{corollary}[A density-sensitive replacement for Corollary 9.4]
\label{gsr:en:17:cor:94}
Let $N$ be prime, $|B|=\beta N>0$, and suppose
$G_4(B,\phi)\ge\gamma\beta^3N^3$ with $0<\gamma\le1$.
Let $0<\eta\le1$ and $L=\ceil{17/(\gamma^7\eta)}$.
If
\[
 N\ge2L^{16}(2L-1)^{15}\beta^{-15},
\]
there exists $B'\subseteq B$ such that
\[
 G_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B'),\qquad
 T_{16}(B')\ge\frac{\gamma^{112}\eta^{15}}{2\cdot18^{16}}|B|^{15}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:17:cor:momentgraph} with $r=8$ gives
$G_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\gamma^7|B|^{15}$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:17:thm:headline} with $m=16$ and $\alpha=\gamma^7$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A limitation of the scalar filter-certificate method\srctag{17}}]{A limitation of the scalar filter-certificate method}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d6}
\srcnote{17}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:17:sec:barrier}

The polynomial exponents have an intrinsic explanation within the
particular expectation argument used here.  The following does not give
an extremal theorem about all possible subsets.

\begin{lemma}[Universal good-tuple moment bound]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:momentbarrier}
Let $h:\T\to[0,1]$ be a trigonometric polynomial, with Fourier
coefficients $c_n$ and mean $q=c_0>0$.  For even $m\ge4$ put
$P_g=\sum_n|c_n|^m$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:barrier-moment}
 P_g\le q^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
In the generic balanced-relation model, the bad-tuple survival is
$P_b=q^m$, so its distinguishing ratio satisfies
$P_g/P_b\le1/q$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $h\ge0$, $|c_n|\le\int h=q$.
Parseval and $h^2\le h$ give $\sum_n|c_n|^2\le q$.
Therefore
\[
 \sum_n|c_n|^m\le q^{m-2}\sum_n|c_n|^2\le q^{m-1}.
\]
For a generic balanced relation the only Fourier vectors are
$n\varepsilon$; their coefficients multiply to
$c_n^{m/2}c_{-n}^{m/2}=|c_n|^m$.  A generic unrespected tuple retains
only the zero vector, giving $q^m$.
\end{proof}

The same inequality holds for a function on a finite abelian group with
normalized Fourier transform.  For the indicator of a subgroup, it is
an equality: all nonzero Fourier coefficients have magnitude $q$.
This explains why the random-linear-map model of the next section can
attain this moment bound exactly.

\begin{proposition}[Best possible powers for this scalar certificate]
\label{gsr:en:17:prop:methodbarrier}
Consider the ideal model with no exceptional tuples, total initial
count $T$, and respected fraction $\rho=G/T$.
Assume $0<\eta<1$ and $0<\rho<1-\eta$.
A certificate using only the exact generic survival probabilities of
one filter and the signed objective in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:certificate} cannot certify a retained count
larger than
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:barriermax}
 \frac{(m-1)^{m-1}}{m^m}
 \frac{\rho^m\eta^{m-1}}
      {(1-\eta)^{m-1}(1-\rho)^{m-1}}\,T.
\end{equation}
The same upper bound applies to any finite product of independent
filters within this scalar-certificate model.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $c=(1-\eta)/\eta$.  The count certified by the signed expectation,
divided by $T$, is
\[
 \rho P_g-c(1-\rho)P_b.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:momentbarrier} bounds this by
\[
 f(q)=\rho q^{m-1}-c(1-\rho)q^m.
\]
Its maximum on $[0,1]$ occurs at
\[
 q_* =\frac{(m-1)\rho}{mc(1-\rho)}.
\]
The hypothesis $\rho<1-\eta$ ensures $q_*<1$.
Substitution gives \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:barriermax}.
For independent filters with means $q_i$, the bad probability is
$(\prod_iq_i)^m$ and the good probability is at most
$(\prod_iq_i)^{m-1}$.  The same calculation applies with
$q=\prod_iq_i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:momentbarrier} is the inequality of source~04's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:method-bound} ($Q_K\le1/b_0$ is $P_g\le q^{m-1}$); this proposition sharpens it to an unconditional optimum of the scalar certificate in terms of the respected fraction $\rho$, where source~04 has only the conditional form ``if $Q_K\ge4/(\alpha\eta)$''.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[The precise scope of the limitation]
For small $\rho$ and $\eta$, the displayed upper bound has powers
$\rho^m\eta^{m-1}$.  The Fej\'er argument achieves these powers, up to
constants depending on $m$ and the exceptional-set requirement.
This does \emph{not} prove that no subset can be larger, that no more
informative probability argument can do better, or that the main theorem
is globally sharp.  In particular, using more information about the
input than $G,T$ can evade this limitation.
\end{remark}

There is a second, simpler constraint: a filter of degree $D$ has at most
$2D+1$ Fourier coefficients, and $|c_n|\le q$.  Hence its distinguishing
ratio is at most $2D+1$.  A one-stage ratio of order
$(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ needs degree of that order.  The present choice
$D=L-1$ has the correct order for fixed $m$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fixed characteristic: arbitrary linear systems and rank profiles\srctag{17}}]{Fixed characteristic: arbitrary linear systems and rank profiles}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d7}
\srcnote{17}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:17:sec:systems}

The Fej\'er theorem requires large characteristic.  A genuinely different
construction gives an analogous restriction theorem over a fixed field
when the domain dimension is large enough.  It also exposes a useful
rank parameter that is invisible for a single relation.

\subsection{The relation space}
Let $\mathcal R\le\F_p^m$ have dimension $d$, where
$1\le d\le m-2$, and assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:translationinvariant}
 \mathcal R\subseteq\one^\perp
   =\{a\in\F_p^m:\sum_ja_j=0\}.
\end{equation}
Thus the system is invariant under translating all entries by the same
vector.  Put $s=m-d\ge2$.
A tuple $x\in V^m$ is a solution if
\[
 \sum_ja_jx_j=0\qquad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal R.
\]
It is respected by $\phi$ if the same equations hold with $\phi(x_j)$.
Let $T_{\mathcal R}(B)$ and $G_{\mathcal R}(B,\phi)$ count these tuples.
Row reduction shows
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:systemfree}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B)\le |B|^s.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $d$ pivot coordinates are determined by the other $s$ coordinates.

\begin{definition}[Affine genericity and error rank]
A solution tuple is affine-generic if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:genericR}
 \left\{a\in\F_p^m:\sum_ja_j=0,\ \sum_ja_jx_j=0\right\}
 =\mathcal R.
\end{equation}
For a generic solution, its \emph{error rank} is the rank of the map
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:errorrank}
 \mathcal R\longrightarrow H,\qquad
 a\longmapsto\sum_ja_j\phi(x_j).
\end{equation}
Write this rank as $j(x)$.  It is zero exactly for respected solutions.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Degeneracy of a system]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:systemdeg}
The number of nongeneric solution tuples in $V^m$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:systemD}
 D_{\mathcal R}=C_{s,p}N^{s-1},\qquad
 C_{s,p}=\frac{p^{s-1}-1}{p-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An extra affine relation is represented by a nonzero element of
$\one^\perp/\mathcal R$, a vector space of dimension $s-1$.
Relations differing by a nonzero scalar or by an element of $\mathcal R$
impose the same additional equation on solution tuples.
There are $(p^{s-1}-1)/(p-1)$ projective classes.
For each representative, adjoining its row increases the rank by one,
leaving exactly $N^{s-1}$ solutions in $V^m$.  Take a union bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Random linear maps see the exact error rank}
Choose a uniform linear map
\[
 A:V\oplus H\oplus\F_p\longrightarrow\F_p^k,
\]
and let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:linearselect}
 B_A=\{x\in B:A(x,\phi(x),1)=0\}.
\end{equation}
Set $q=p^{-k}$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact rank-profile survival]\label{gsr:en:17:lem:ranksurvival}
For an affine-generic solution $x$ of error rank $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:ranksurvival}
 \Pr[x_1,\ldots,x_m\in B_A]=q^{s+j}.
\end{equation}
This formula does not require distinct entries or independent Bernoulli
choices at the points.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Consider the augmented column vectors
$z_i=(x_i,\phi(x_i),1)$.  The relation space among the projected columns
$(x_i,1)$ is $\mathcal R$ by genericity.
The relation space among the full $z_i$ is the kernel of
\eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:errorrank} inside $\mathcal R$, of dimension $d-j$.
Thus the span of the $z_i$ has dimension $m-(d-j)=s+j$.
A uniform linear map to $\F_p^k$ kills a fixed subspace of dimension
$s+j$ with probability $p^{-k(s+j)}$.
This is exactly the event that every selected point belongs to $B_A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A rank-profile certificate]\label{gsr:en:17:prop:rankcertificate}
Let $n_j$ be the number of affine-generic solution tuples in $B^m$
with error rank $j$, and let $D$ bound the nongeneric solution tuples.
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:rankcertificate}
 \Omega(q)=\eta q^s n_0-(1-\eta)\sum_{j\ge1}q^{s+j}n_j-D>0,
\end{equation}
some set $B_A$ has respected proportion at least $1-\eta$ and
\[
 T_{\mathcal R}(B_A)\ge\Omega(q)/\eta.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:ranksurvival} to the signed objective
$G_{\mathcal R}(B_A,\phi)-(1-\eta)T_{\mathcal R}(B_A)$.
The possible negative contribution of nongeneric tuples is at least
$-D$.  The expectation is therefore at least $\Omega(q)$.
The same deterministic inequalities used in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:certificate} finish the proof.
\end{proof}

The profile matters: a tuple breaking several independent relations is
suppressed by several extra powers of $q$.  Collapsing all bad tuples
into a single class throws away this information.

\begin{theorem}[Restriction with a rank gap]\label{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap}
Let $|B|=\beta N>0$ and suppose
\[
 G_{\mathcal R}(B,\phi)\ge\rho|B|^s,
 \qquad 0<\rho,\eta\le1.
\]
Assume that every affine-generic unrespected solution has error rank at
least $h$, where $1\le h\le d$.
Choose the least positive integer $k$ for which, with $q=p^{-k}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:qchoice}
 q^h\le\rho\eta/2.
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:rankthreshold}
 N\ge\frac{8C_{s,p}}{\rho\eta q^s\beta^s},
\end{equation}
there is $B'\subseteq B$ with respected proportion at least $1-\eta$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:17:eq:rankcount}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B')\ge\frac{\rho q^s}{4}|B|^s
 \ge\frac{\rho^{1+s/h}\eta^{s/h}}
          {4\cdot2^{s/h}p^s}|B|^s.
\end{equation}
In particular the theorem always applies with $h=1$ when its size
hypothesis holds.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $M=|B|^s$ and $D_0=C_{s,p}N^{s-1}$.
There are at least $\rho M-D_0$ generic respected tuples, and at most
$M$ generic unrespected tuples in total by \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:systemfree}.
The latter survive with probability at most $q^{s+h}$.
For the signed objective $F$ we therefore have
\begin{align*}
 \E F
 &\ge\eta q^s(\rho M-D_0)-(1-\eta)q^{s+h}M-D_0\\
 &\ge q^s(\eta\rho-q^h)M-2D_0\\
 &\ge\frac12\rho\eta q^s M-2D_0.
\end{align*}
Condition \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:rankthreshold} says
$D_0\le\rho\eta q^sM/8$, so $\E F\ge\rho\eta q^sM/4$.
Choose a realization at least its expectation and divide the resulting
count bound by $\eta$.
Minimality of $k$ gives
$q>p^{-1}(\rho\eta/2)^{1/h}$, including when $k=1$.
This proves the second inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:rankcount} after harmless
weakening from strict to non-strict inequality.
Every unrespected generic solution has positive error rank, so $h=1$
requires no additional hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~29's Section~\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d9} keeps the affine-rank stratification of every tuple, degenerate ones included, which removes the ambient-dimension requirement and makes the threshold linear in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:main}, \ref{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-gap}); that answers Question~2 of this source for fixed fields (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[One balanced relation in fixed characteristic]
\label{gsr:en:17:cor:fixedp}
For $m=2r\ge4$, take $\mathcal R=\Span(\varepsilon)$, so $d=1$ and
$s=m-1$.  Under the size hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap},
$G_m(B,\phi)\ge\rho|B|^{m-1}$ yields a subset with respected proportion
at least $1-\eta$ and
\[
 T_m(B')\ge
 \frac{\rho^m\eta^{m-1}}{4(2p)^{m-1}}|B|^{m-1}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Why this does not replace the prime-cyclic proof}
A generic system tuple requires the augmented vectors $(x_i,1)$ to have
rank $s$.  Necessarily $\dim V+1\ge s$.
For the sixteen-variable single relation, $s=15$; one needs
$\dim V\ge14$ before a generic tuple can even exist.
When $V=\F_N$ is one-dimensional, all such tuples are degenerate in the
full-field sense.  The Fej\'er construction succeeds there because it
only excludes \emph{bounded-coefficient} extra relations, not every
relation over the field.
This distinction is essential to the applicability of the two theorems.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boundary cases, normalization traps, and constructive content\srctag{17}}]{Boundary cases, normalization traps, and constructive content}\label{gsr:en:17:sec:d8}
\srcnote{17}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:17:sec:boundaries}

\subsection{Repeated entries really are different events}
For a repeated tuple, multiplying the point-inclusion probability once
per occurrence is incorrect.  For example, with $L=2$ and a random
translation $c$ over $\F_7$, the event that the tuple $(0,0,0,0)$ is
contained in the selected subset has probability
\[
 \E_cK_2(c/7)=\frac12.
\]
The formal product of four identical probabilities instead gives
\[
 \E_cK_2(c/7)^4=\frac{35}{128}.
\]
Our product formula is only asserted for generic tuples, which have
distinct entries. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} \emph{Precision:} the product with multiplicities is wrong as an identity but valid as a lower bound, since $0\le K_L\le1$ (here $35/128\le1/2$); a lower bound is all a respected-tuple count needs, and source~04's survival lemma (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:survival}) counts all respected tuples, repeated ones included.  The final theorem then pays for every exceptional
tuple, good or bad, so its conclusion is about the original tuple count.

\subsection{Large characteristic cannot be omitted from the filter formula}
For $p=3$ and $L=4$ one has
\[
 K_4(0)=1,\qquad K_4(1/3)=K_4(2/3)=\frac1{16}.
\]
The discrete mean is $3/8$, not $1/L=1/4$.
Fourier coefficients have aliased modulo $p$.
This example refutes the unrestricted use of the intermediate formula,
not the possibility of a different small-characteristic restriction
theorem.  Section~\ref{gsr:en:17:sec:systems} supplies one such theorem with
different hypotheses.

\subsection{Composite cyclic groups require a separate argument}
In $\Z/N\Z$ with composite $N$, a nonzero scalar may annihilate a
nonzero image discrepancy.  Also two formally distinct coefficient rows
need not define a map with fibers of size $N^{m-2}$.
Both issues enter the present proof, respectively in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:survival} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:degcount}.
The prime-cyclic improvement should therefore not be substituted for an
all-moduli proposition without a new torsion analysis. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} \emph{Two precisions} (HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}). The formal all-$N$ proof avoids the issue differently: its height-zero restriction uses degree-one filters with digit coefficients, whose new relations have a coefficient in $\{\pm1,\pm2\}$ with fibres of size at most two in every cyclic group (\file{Proofs15Restriction.lean}, lines~2083--2086). And the obstruction needs a small prime factor: the intake observed that Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:degcount}--\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:survival} carry over verbatim when every prime factor of $N$ exceeds $2L-2$ (the relevant minors are integers of absolute value at most $2L-2$, and every $0<|t|<L$ is a unit); that observation is not written in the source and is recorded as a marked question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}).

\subsection{Trivial successful inputs}
If $G_m(B,\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B)$ already, take $B'=B$; no threshold or
filter is necessary.  Likewise $\eta=1$ imposes no quality restriction.
The uniform theorem remains true at $\eta=1$, but is deliberately not
optimized for that trivial endpoint.
If $B$ is a subgroup coset and $\phi$ is affine on it, every tuple is
respected.  The small retention lower bound is not a description of the
actual best subset on such an input.

\subsection{Existence, derandomization, and running time}
All random objects here take values in finite probability spaces apart
from the notation for the Bernoulli probabilities.  The proof gives a
finite weighted average over subsets and parameter choices, so a subset
with the required signed objective exists.
For the Fej\'er construction, one can enumerate $u,v,c$ and then fix the
Bernoulli choices one at a time by conditional expectation.
For the linear-map construction, enumeration of the finite matrix
space is enough.

These are finite constructive procedures, not efficient algorithms as
stated.  A direct evaluation of the objective may enumerate
$|B|^{m-1}$ tuples, and the full parameter space can itself be very large.
Positive expected surplus does not by itself imply that a satisfactory
subset is found with a substantial probability.  No polynomial-time
claim in $\log N$, or practical sampling guarantee, is made.

\gsrnewfloats
\section{Sources~18 and~19: degenerate arrangements (Section~15) and common sampling (Section~16) \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:sections1516}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next six sections treat two later stages of Gowers's inverse argument that no earlier source of this report touches. \emph{Source~18's Section~\ref{gsr:en:18:sec:d2}} is on Section~15: Lemma~15.4 bounds the number of degenerate arrangements, and Lemma~15.5 needs that bound to absorb them when a Riesz product selects a denser respected set. It continues the arrangement chain from Lemma~14.8 that source~04's Section~\ref{gsr:en:04:sec:d5}, source~14's Section~\ref{gsr:en:14:sec:d5} and source~15's chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:collision}) hold. \emph{Source~19's chapter} (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d5} and its worked comparisons, Section~\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d8}) is on Section~16: Lemma~16.10 samples cross-sections, interpolates the affine pieces through the sampled points and refines the resulting partitions. Both are printed here, at the end of Part~II, because no number printed earlier may move. Source~18's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:18:sec:d1}, source~19's Section~\ref{gsr:fm:19:sec:d1}; their other sections are in Parts~I, III and~V. Their notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} Source~18: for $d\ge2$ and primes $p>2d$ the proportion of degenerate $d$-arrangements is $(k+C_d)/p+O(p^{-2})$ with $C_d=(T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}d+1)/2$, sharp in its first-order constant (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:thm-count}; $C_8=2{,}585{,}444$), and Lemma~15.5 needs only $\lambda p\ge k+2{,}585{,}445$ in place of $\lambda p\ge k3^{2^{k+4}}$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:cor-selection}); the selection exponent is unchanged and nothing is propagated. Source~19: a common sample of $\min\{n,\lceil qd/\sigma\rceil-1\}$ distinct columns loses at most $\sigma$ of the mass (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:anchors}), so order $q/\sigma$ anchors suffice where the paper takes $q\sigma^{-2}$; the finite minimax value is exact (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:minimax}) and $r\mathcal M/q\to C_d$, with $C_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}=0.83996\ldots$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic}); refining the sampled slices once replaces a quadratic number of refinement steps by a linear one, with $\sum_je_j(M_1,\ldots,M_r)$ candidates (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:main}); and a local replacement for the step in Lemma~16.10 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary}), which needs an inherited-coordinate hypothesis. Lemma~16.10 itself is not proved: both displayed closing comparisons fail (Section~\ref{gsr:fz:19:audit:budget}), as the source says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}). \file{lemma_15_4} and \file{lemma_15_5} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, lines~402, 414) have exact companions; the degeneracy predicate is the formal one; source~18's theorem implies the formal bound for $d\ge2$, $p>2d$ (notes there). \file{lemma_16_9} is an exact companion since \texttt{16bbbe5ad}, after source~19's pin; \file{lemma_16_10} (\file{Section16.lean}, line~851) is open. Formal results written after that pin confirm source~19's audit points (the distinct-anchor counterexample, the failure of the same-dimension comparison) and prove a local affine lift with weaker constants (notes after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:anchors} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary}); they are not source~19's statements. Nothing in these sections is formalized.
