\section[{The exceptional two-cube case: a signed-coordinate arrangement\srctag{22}}]{The exceptional two-cube case: a signed-coordinate arrangement}\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d5}
\srcnote{22}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d1-new}

The assumption $d\ge2$ in the codimension-two bound for nonparity
certificates cannot be discarded: when $d=1$, the vertical constraint is
$r_1=r_2$, so the vertical equations supply no independent information.
Nevertheless the first-order count can be determined exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp first-order degeneracy for two cubes]\label{gsr:en:22:thm:twocube}
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p>\max\{3,2k+1\}$ be prime.  Define
\[
 L_k(p)=1-(1-p^{-1})^k\prod_{i=1}^k\left(1-\frac{2i+1}{p}\right),
 \qquad
 R_k=\frac12\left(3^{2^k}-(2k^2+4k+3)\right)^2.
\]
For the proportion $\delta_{k,1}(p)$ of degenerate $1$-arrangements,
\[
 L_k(p)\le\delta_{k,1}(p)
 \le L_k(p)+(1-p^{-1})^kR_kp^{-2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \delta_{k,1}(p)=\frac{k^2+3k}{p}+O_k(p^{-2}).
\]
For $k=1$ the error term in the finite inequality is zero, and hence
$\delta_{1,1}(p)=4p^{-1}-3p^{-2}$ for every prime $p\ge5$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The proportion of arrangements having a zero side is exactly
$1-(1-p^{-1})^k$, and every such arrangement is degenerate.  Condition
on nonzero sides, write $z_i^j=y_i^j/h_i$, and set
$t_i=z_i^1-z_i^2$.
The variables $t_1,\ldots,t_k$ are independent and uniform in
$\mathbb F_p$.  For a slice coefficient pattern
$\eta:\{0,1\}^k\to\{-1,0,1\}$, put
\[
 F_\eta(X)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
            \eta(\epsilon)\prod_{i=1}^k(X_i+\epsilon_i).
\]
The map $\eta\mapsto F_\eta$ is an invertible linear transformation:
in one coordinate its basis is $X,X+1$, and the general transform is
the tensor product of these invertible two-dimensional transforms.
Comparing coefficients of $X_{[k]\setminus A}$ shows that all the
horizontal moment equations are equivalent to
\[
 F_{\eta_1}(X+t)+F_{\eta_2}(X)=0.
 \tag{D1.1}
\]
The vertical equations duplicate them because $r_1=r_2$.

We first describe the solution set of (D1.1) for fixed patterns.
For any multiaffine polynomial $F$, let
\[
 D_u=\sum_i u_i\frac{\partial}{\partial X_i}.
\]
Since $\deg F\le k<p$, Taylor's identity gives
$F(X+u)=\exp(D_u)F(X)$.  On the space of polynomials of degree at most
$k$, the operator $D_u$ is nilpotent.  Therefore
\[
 \exp(D_u)-1
 =D_u\left(1+D_u/2!+\cdots+D_u^{k-1}/k!\right),
\]
and the parenthesized operator is invertible.  It follows that the
translation stabilizer of $F$ is the linear subspace
\[
 \operatorname{Stab}(F)
 =\{u:F(X+u)=F(X)\}
 =\{u:D_uF=0\}.
 \tag{D1.2}
\]
If (D1.1) has one solution, all its solutions form a coset of this
subspace.  Its codimension is
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb F_p}\operatorname{span}
       \{\partial_1F,\ldots,\partial_kF\}.
 \tag{D1.3}
\]

If the dimension in (D1.3) is one, write $\partial_iF=a_iG$ for a
nonzero polynomial $G$.  When $a_i\ne0$, multilinearity implies that
$G$ is independent of $X_i$.  When $a_i=0$, $F$ is independent of
$X_i$, and hence so is $G$.  Thus $G$ is constant and $F$ is affine.
In particular, every nonaffine $F$ has a stabilizer of codimension at
least two.  For each pair of nonaffine slice patterns, (D1.1) consequently
has at most $p^{k-2}$ solutions.

It remains to determine the hypersurfaces supplied by affine $F$.
Write $\pi(\epsilon)=(-1)^{\sum_i\epsilon_i}$ and
$\eta(\epsilon)=\pi(\epsilon)v(\epsilon)$.  The polynomial $F_\eta$
is affine if and only if the unique multilinear representation of
$v$ is affine: direct expansion gives
$F_\eta(X)=(-1)^k\sum_Ta_T\prod_{i\in T}(X_i+1)$ when
$v(\epsilon)=\sum_Ta_T\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_i$, and substitution
$X_i\mapsto X_i+1$ preserves total degree.  More explicitly, if
\[
 v(\epsilon)=c+\sum_i b_i\epsilon_i,
\]
then
\[
 F_\eta(X)=(-1)^k
        \left(c+\sum_i b_i(X_i+1)\right).
 \tag{D1.4}
\]
For $p\ge5$, an affine Boolean function taking values only in
$\{-1,0,1\}$ has one of the following forms:
\begin{itemize}
\item a constant (three choices);
\item one nonzero slope $b_i=\pm1$, with two admissible intercepts;
\item one nonzero slope $b_i=\pm2$, with one admissible intercept;
\item two nonzero slopes $b_i,b_j\in\{-1,1\}$, with one admissible
      intercept.
\end{itemize}
Indeed, after fixing a nonzero slope $a$, the values on the other
coordinates must lie in
$S\cap(S-a)$, where $S=\{-1,0,1\}$.  This set has at most two
elements, and has two only when $a=\pm1$.  An affine Boolean function
with two values can depend on at most one coordinate in odd
characteristic: otherwise the four values
$x,x+b,x+c,x+b+c$, with $b,c\ne0$, force $b=c$ and $2b=0$.
The displayed list and its intercept counts follow.  Thus the number
of affine slice patterns is
\[
 f_k=3+6k+4\binom{k}{2}=2k^2+4k+3.
 \tag{D1.5}
\]

In (D1.1), replace $\eta_2$ by its negative, which is another allowed
pattern.  Formula (D1.4) shows that a successful pair must have the
same slopes $b_i$ and satisfy
$\sum_i b_it_i=c_2-c_1$.  Constant polynomials give only multiples
of the universal certificate.  The remaining cases give exactly
the following distinct affine hyperplanes:
\[
 t_i=0,1,-1\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad
 t_i-t_j=0,\quad t_i+t_j=0\quad(i<j).
 \tag{D1.6}
\]
Each equation is realized by allowed patterns.  A vector outside all
these hyperplanes has nonzero coordinates, none equal to $\pm1$,
and its coordinates belong to distinct unordered sign pairs.
There are $p-3$ choices for $t_1$, $p-5$ for $t_2$, and in general
$p-(2i+1)$ for $t_i$.  Hence the number outside (D1.6) is exactly
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^k(p-2i-1).
 \tag{D1.7}
\]

There are $3^{2^k}-f_k$ nonaffine slice patterns.  Translation
preserves degree, so any successful pair involving a nonaffine slice
has two nonaffine slices.  Simultaneously negating both slices gives
the same solution set and has no fixed point on these pairs.
There are therefore at most $R_k$ such solution sets.  Applying the
codimension-two bound to each proves the asserted finite upper bound;
retaining only (D1.6) and the zero-side loci proves the lower bound.
Finally, the linear coefficient of the complement probability is
\[
 k+\sum_{i=1}^k(2i+1)=k^2+3k.
\]
For $k=1$ every polynomial $F_\eta$ is affine, so $R_1=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answers source~18's question on $d=1$ in its leading coefficient} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}); source~18 set the case aside after its Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp}. Source~27's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:d1} is the case $k=1$, proved independently. The intake computed $\delta_{k,1}(p)$ from the full definition and found it equal to $L_k(p)$ for $k=2$ at $p=7,11,13,17,19,23$ and for $k=3$ at $p=11,13$, beyond this source's checks; that is evidence for its question on exactness (Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:22:sec:d12}.2 here), not a proof.
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Connection with the balanced degree-one count.}
The Laurent-polynomial calculation has a particularly simple
$q=2$ specialization:
\[
 \operatorname{CT}F_k^2=2k^2+8k+9,
 \qquad \operatorname{CT}B_k^2=2k+4.
\]
Thus the number of balanced classes of degree at most one is
$(k+1)^2$.  Removing the one nonconstant degree-zero class gives
$k^2+2k=3k+2\binom{k}{2}$ classes of degree exactly one.
In the present two-cube setting these classes give precisely the
distinct hypersurfaces in (D1.6).  The $k$ zero-side hypersurfaces
account for the remaining $k$ in the coefficient $k^2+3k$.

\paragraph{Scope.}
The theorem determines the optimal leading coefficient for the
two-cube case omitted from the earlier $d\ge2$ argument.  It does
not assert that all higher-codimension degeneracy is contained in
(D1.6), and its explicit remainder is only a union bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Arrangements and their moment relations\srctag{25}}]{Arrangements and their moment relations}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d2}
\srcnote{25}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:arrangements}

Put $m=2d$ and
\[
 w=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{d},
       \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{d}),\qquad
 \W=w^\perp\subseteq\F_q^m.
\]
An arrangement is specified by
\[
 h=(h_1,\ldots,h_k)\in\F_q^k,\quad
 x=(x_{ji})_{1\le j\le m,\,1\le i\le k},\quad r\in\W,
\]
and its vertices are
\begin{equation}
 \rho(\eps,j)=(x_{j1}+\eps_1h_1,\ldots,
 x_{jk}+\eps_kh_k,r_j),\qquad \eps\in\{-1,1\}^k.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:vertices}
\end{equation}
The relation $r\in\W$ is $r_1+\cdots+r_d=r_{d+1}+\cdots+r_{2d}$.
There are $q^k q^{2dk}q^{2d-1}=q^D$ arrangements.
The usual vertices $y_{ji}+e_iH_i$, $e_i\in\{0,1\}$, are obtained by
$x_{ji}=y_{ji}+H_i/2$ and $h_i=H_i/2$.  This is a bijection of parameter
spaces, not an approximation or a restriction.

Write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and
$\pi(\eps)=\prod_{i=1}^k\eps_i$.  The distinguished coefficient pattern is
\begin{equation}
 \eta_0(\eps,j)=w_j\pi(\eps).
\end{equation}
The Boolean convention $(-1)^{\sum e_i}$ differs by the harmless global
factor $(-1)^k$.

For a ternary pattern
$\eta:\{-1,1\}^k\times[m]\to\{-1,0,1\}\subset\F_q$ define
\begin{align}
 M_A(\eta)&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{\eps}
 \eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),\\
 M_{A,r}(\eta)&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j\sum_{\eps}
 \eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),
 \qquad A\subseteq[k].
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:moments}
\end{align}
These are exactly all coordinate-monomial moments in $k+1$ variables.
In particular, $A=\varnothing$ is included.

\begin{definition}
An arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if some ternary $\eta$ outside the
one-dimensional space $\F_q\eta_0$ satisfies
$M_A(\eta)=M_{A,r}(\eta)=0$ for every $A\subseteq[k]$.
Such an $\eta$ is a witness.
A pattern is \emph{block-parity} if
$\eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)$ for every $j$.
\end{definition}

Orthogonality on the sign cube shows that the block moment of $\pi$ is
zero unless $A=[k]$, and is then $2^k\prod_i h_i$.
Thus $\eta_0$ annihilates all moments because both $\sum_j w_j=0$ and
$\sum_jw_jr_j=0$.  Since the values of $\eta_0$ are $\pm1$, its only
ternary scalar multiples are $0,\eta_0,-\eta_0$.

\begin{lemma}[Coincidences and zero sides]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}
Every arrangement with a zero sidelength is degenerate.  Every
nondegenerate arrangement has distinct labelled vertices.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two labelled vertices coincide, put coefficient $1$ at one and $-1$
at the other, and zero elsewhere.  Every monomial moment cancels.
This pattern cannot be a nonzero scalar multiple of $\eta_0$, whose
support consists of all $n\ge8$ labels.  If $h_i=0$, the vertices within
one block whose signs differ only at $i$ coincide, so the first assertion
is a special case of the second argument.
\end{proof}

A function $\phi:B\to\F_q$ \emph{respects} an arrangement in $B$ if
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j,\eps}w_j\pi(\eps)\phi(\rho(\eps,j))=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:respected}
\end{equation}
We will need an elementary upper bound for the total number of
arrangements contained in an arbitrary set.

\begin{lemma}[Density cap]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:densitycap}
If $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ has size $\beta q^{k+1}$, then it contains at
most $\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ labelled $d$-arrangements.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $h$, the all-minus vertex of each of the first $2d-1$ blocks,
and the $k$ spatial coordinates of the all-minus vertex of the last
block.  The cross-section relation determines the remaining coordinate
of the last block.  These choices determine the entire arrangement.
For an arrangement in $B$, the first $2d-1$ selected vertices must be in
$B$.  There are at most
$q^k\cardtwentyfive B^{2d-1}q^k=\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ choices.  Ignoring the other
containment requirements only increases this upper bound.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Minimal Walsh layers give independent linear equations\srctag{25}}]{Minimal Walsh layers give independent linear equations}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d3}
\srcnote{25}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:walsh}

For $S\subseteq[k]$, let $\chi_S(\eps)=\prod_{i\in S}\eps_i$ and put
\begin{equation}
 c_{j,S}=2^{-k}\sum_\eps\eta(\eps,j)\chi_S(\eps).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:walsh}
\end{equation}
Here $2^{-k}$ denotes inversion in the field.  Orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\eps\chi_S(\eps)\chi_T(\eps)
 =\begin{cases}2^k&S=T,\\0&S\ne T,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 \eta(\eps,j)=\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}c_{j,S}\chi_S(\eps).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:inversion}
\end{equation}
Indeed, a coordinate in $S\mathbin\triangle T$ makes the sum cancel in
pairs; otherwise every summand is one.  This proves inversion as well.

Use $h_S=\prod_{i\in S}h_i$ and
$x_{j,S}=\prod_{i\in S}x_{ji}$.  Expanding the product in a block moment
and applying \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:walsh} gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\eps\eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i)
 =2^k\sum_{S\subseteq A}c_{j,S}h_Sx_{j,A\setminus S}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:expansion}
\end{equation}
This identity is valid for arbitrary field-valued patterns, not only
ternary ones.

\begin{lemma}[Minimal-layer linearization]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}
Suppose $h_i\ne0$ for every $i$.  For a nonzero pattern let
\[
 s=\min\{\cardtwentyfive S:c_{j,S}\ne0\text{ for some }j\}.
\]
If $s<k$, then the equations $M_A(\eta)=0$ with $\cardtwentyfive A=s+1$ include
$k-s$ independent affine-linear equations in the $2dk$ base coordinates.
For every fixed $r$, the probability over uniform $x$ that all moments
vanish is therefore at most $q^{-(k-s)}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
All coefficients of degree below $s$ vanish, so
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:expansion}, for $\cardtwentyfive A=s+1$, contains only terms linear in
$x$ and constant terms.  Choose $j_0,S_0$ with $\cardtwentyfive{S_0}=s$ and
$c_{j_0,S_0}\ne0$.  For each $i\notin S_0$, use the equation indexed by
$A_i=S_0\cup\{i\}$, and use $x_{j_0i}$ as its pivot variable.
The coefficient of this variable is
$2^kc_{j_0,S_0}h_{S_0}\ne0$.  If $i'\notin S_0$ and $i'\ne i$,
then $i'\notin A_i$, so $x_{j_0i'}$ does not occur in that equation.
The indicated square minor is diagonal and nonsingular.

After every other base coordinate has been fixed, these $k-s$ equations
determine the pivot coordinates uniquely.  They therefore have exactly
$q^{2dk-(k-s)}$ simultaneous solutions; imposing the remaining moment
equations can only reduce this number.  No polynomial zero-counting
estimate is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Gowers's Lemma 15.3 is sharp for a single arbitrary multilinear polynomial:
a product of $k$ coordinates can vanish on approximately $k/q$ of the
space.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer} does not contradict that fact.  It exploits
the simultaneous moment system, in which a lowest nonzero Walsh layer
provides specially chosen \emph{linear} equations.  It strengthens the
use of Lemma 15.3 inside the arrangement argument, not the original fibre
bound without extra hypotheses.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Non-parity witnesses have codimension at least two\srctag{25}}]{Non-parity witnesses have codimension at least two}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d4}
\srcnote{25}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:witnesses}

Fix nonzero $h$ and a ternary pattern that is not block-parity.  Its
minimal layer has $s\le k-1$.  If $s\le k-2$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}
already gives a $q^{-2}$ bound, uniformly in the cross-sections.  Only
$s=k-1$ needs a second argument.

In this remaining case write
\begin{equation}
 \eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)
       +\sum_{i=1}^k b_{ji}\pi(\eps)\eps_i,
 \qquad
 a_j=c_{j,[k]},\quad b_{ji}=c_{j,[k]\setminus\{i\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:toplayers}
\end{equation}
At least one vector $b_i=(b_{1i},\ldots,b_{mi})$ is nonzero.  The
coefficients $a_j,b_{ji}$ are field elements; they need not be ternary.
The moments indexed by $[k]\setminus\{i\}$ imply
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jb_{ji}=0,\qquad b_i\cdot r=0\quad(1\le i\le k).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:lowerconstraints}
\end{equation}
After division by $2^kh_{[k]}$, the two top moments become
\begin{align}
 \sum_{j,i}b_{ji}\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}+\sum_ja_j&=0,
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:top1}\\
 \sum_{j,i}r_jb_{ji}\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}+\sum_jr_ja_j&=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:top2}
\end{align}
These equations also display why keeping moments containing the final
coordinate is useful.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp single-witness bound]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:single}
Let $d\ge2$, $k\ge1$, and let the field have odd characteristic.
For each fixed nonzero sidelength vector and each non-block-parity
ternary pattern, uniform $r\in\W$ and uniform $x$ satisfy all moment
equations with probability at most
\begin{equation}
 e_d(q)=q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-2d}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:single}
\end{equation}
This bound is attained, for every $k$, by
\begin{equation}
 \eta(\eps,j)=w_j\pi(\eps)\eps_{i_0}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}
\end{equation}
for any fixed $i_0\in[k]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The case $s\le k-2$ follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}.  Suppose $s=k-1$.
If a constant constraint in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:lowerconstraints} fails, there are
no solutions.  Otherwise put
\[
 e=\dim\spanof(w,b_1,\ldots,b_k)-1.
\]
When $e\ge1$, the equations $b_i\cdot r=0$ cut out a subspace of
codimension $e$ in $\W$.  Their probability is $q^{-e}$.  For every
admissible $r$, equation \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1} is a nonconstant affine-linear
equation in $x$, of probability $q^{-1}$.  Thus the simultaneous
probability is at most $q^{-e-1}\le q^{-2}$.

When $e=0$, write $b_i=t_iw$, where some $t_i\ne0$.  The cross-section
constraints are automatic.  The coefficient rows of \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1}
and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top2} are linearly dependent exactly when all $r_j$ are
equal: for an $i$ with $t_i\ne0$, comparison of the coefficients of
$x_{ji}$ forces $r_j$ to be the same scalar for every $j$.  Outside that
one-dimensional diagonal subspace of $\W$, the two equations have
independent rows and hence exactly $q^{2dk-2}$ solutions for any right
hand sides.  On the diagonal they have at most $q^{2dk-1}$ solutions.
The diagonal occupies a proportion $q^{-(2d-2)}$ of $\W$.  Therefore the
probability is at most
\[
 (1-q^{-(2d-2)})q^{-2}+q^{-(2d-2)}q^{-1}
 =q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-2d}.
\]

For \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}, we have $a_j=0$, $b_{i_0}=w$, and $b_i=0$
for $i\ne i_0$.  All nontrivial conditions are exactly
\[
 \sum_jw_jx_{j i_0}=0,\qquad
 \sum_jw_jr_jx_{j i_0}=0.
\]
They have rank two off the diagonal and rank one on it, and they are
always consistent.  Thus equality holds in the displayed count.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} First printed as source~18's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp} (with the same witness up to the Boolean--sign convention); also source~22's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank} at degree one and source~27's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass} (every characteristic).
\end{writenote}

\begin{example}[The restriction $d\ge2$ is necessary]
For $d=1$, the cross-section relation forces $r_1=r_2$.
The same witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness} gives just
$x_{1i_0}=x_{2i_0}$, a probability $q^{-1}$ event.  Consequently a
blanket codimension-two assertion for non-parity witnesses is false
for $d=1$.  This is a structural obstruction, not a weakness of the
proof.  The formula in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:single} itself becomes $q^{-1}$ in
this case.
\end{example}

For the final count it is useful to exclude a set of cross-sections that
will already be counted as degenerate.

\begin{lemma}[Removing the diagonal exception]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:regularwitness}
Let $\mathcal R\subseteq\W$ omit every constant vector.  Under the
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:single}, for each fixed non-parity pattern
and each fixed nonzero $h$,
\begin{equation}
 \Prob_{r\in\W,x}\bigl(r\in\mathcal R
 \text{ and all moments vanish}\bigr)\le q^{-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:regularjoint}
\end{equation}
For the witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}, equality holds with the right
side replaced by $(\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal R}/\cardtwentyfive\W)q^{-2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s\le k-2$ and for $e\ge1$, the corresponding bounds in the previous
proof were already $q^{-2}$.  For $e=0$, the only rank-one exception
was the diagonal, now excluded.  The final assertion follows from the
two independent homogeneous equations for the sharp witness.
\end{proof}

Notice the normalization: \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:regularjoint} is a \emph{joint}
probability with $r$ uniform in all of $\W$.  Conditioning $r$ to belong
to $\mathcal R$ requires division by $\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal R}/\cardtwentyfive\W$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The cross-section hyperplanes and their exact number\srctag{25}}]{The cross-section hyperplanes and their exact number}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d5}
\srcnote{25}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:hyperplanes}

Suppose all sidelengths are nonzero and $\eta$ is block-parity,
$\eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)$.  Since the pattern is ternary, every
$a_j$ belongs to $\{-1,0,1\}$.  Its moment conditions reduce exactly to
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j=0,\qquad a\cdot r=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:parityconditions}
\end{equation}
The first equality follows from the top spatial moment, and the second
from the top moment including the last coordinate.  All other moments
vanish identically.  The condition $p>2d$ makes the first equality
in the field equivalent to the integer equality: its integer sum has
absolute value at most $2d$.

Exclude $a=0,w,-w$, which give the distinguished scalar multiples.
Every remaining balanced ternary vector defines a hyperplane
\begin{equation}
 H_a=\{r\in\W:a\cdot r=0\}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:crosshyperplane}
\end{equation}
Let $\Hh_d$ be the set of \emph{distinct} such hyperplanes.
Each contains the diagonal of constant cross-sections, since $\sum a_j=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Projective enumeration]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:hyperplanes}
For $d\ge1$ and $p>\max(3,2d)$,
\[
 \cardtwentyfive{\Hh_d}=H_d
 =\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2}.
\]
For $d\ge2$, this family is nonempty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Two nonzero restrictions $a|_\W$ and $a'|_\W$ have the same kernel
exactly when
\begin{equation}
 a'=\lambda a+\mu w,\qquad \lambda\ne0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:equivalence}
\end{equation}
This is the elementary fact that two nonzero linear forms with the same
kernel are proportional, together with $\W^\perp=\F_qw$.
Set $z_j=w_ja_j$.  Then $z\in\{-1,0,1\}^{2d}$,
$\sum_jw_jz_j=0$, and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:equivalence} becomes
\begin{equation}
 z'=\lambda z+\mu\ind.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:affineclasses}
\end{equation}
We must count nonconstant balanced ternary vectors modulo affine changes
of their values.

There are $T_{2d}$ balanced vectors: multiplying their coordinates by
$w_j$ bijects them with the integer-balanced vectors $a$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:parityconditions}.  Exactly three are constant, and they
correspond to $a=0,w,-w$.

First suppose $z$ uses exactly two values $u<v$.  If $S$ is the set of
coordinates at the larger value, then
\[
 \sum_jw_jz_j=(v-u)\sum_{j\in S}w_j.
\]
It vanishes exactly when $S$ contains equally many coordinates from the
first and second halves.  The number of nonempty proper such subsets is
\begin{equation}
 B_d=\sum_{t=0}^d\binom dt^2-2=\binom{2d}{d}-2.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:balancedsubsets}
\end{equation}
The binomial identity follows by counting $d$-element subsets of two
disjoint $d$-element sets, according to the number chosen from the first.
There are three choices of a two-element value set, hence $3B_d$ vectors
of this type.  Each affine class consists of six vectors: three choices
of value set and the two choices of which part gets the larger value.
Thus there are $B_d/2$ two-value classes.

If $z$ uses all three values, an affine change preserving ternarity
must permute $\{-1,0,1\}$.  Summing the three images gives $3\mu=0$;
as $p>3$, we have $\mu=0$.  The image of $1$ now forces
$\lambda=1$ or $-1$.  Consequently every three-value class consists
exactly of $z$ and $-z$.  No invertible affine change can alter the
number of distinct values.  The three-value classes therefore number
$(T_{2d}-3-3B_d)/2$.  Adding the two contributions gives
\[
 \frac{B_d}{2}+\frac{T_{2d}-3-3B_d}{2}
 =\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2}.
\]
For $d\ge2$, for example $a=(1,-1,0,\ldots,0)$ is balanced and not a
multiple of $w$, so at least one hyperplane occurs.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} $H_d$ is source~18's $C_d$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-parity-hyperplanes}), source~22's $C_d$ and source~27's $L_d$. The intake counted the distinct kernels by rank tests and found $0$, $4$, $51$ for $d=1,2,3$ over $\F_{101}$, and $57$ for $d=3$ over $\F_5$, as Example~\ref{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar} and source~27's Example~\ref{gsr:en:27:ex:char} say.
\end{writenote}

\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$d$ & $T_{2d}$ & $\binom{2d}{d}$ & $H_d$\\
\midrule
1 & 3 & 2 & 0\\
2 & 19 & 6 & 4\\
3 & 141 & 20 & 51\\
4 & 1\,107 & 70 & 484\\
5 & 8\,953 & 252 & 4\,225\\
6 & 73\,789 & 924 & 35\,971\\
7 & 616\,227 & 3\,432 & 304\,682\\
8 & 5\,196\,627 & 12\,870 & 2\,585\,444\\

\end{tabular}

\subsection{An explicit canonical representative}
Eliminate the last cross-section coordinate using
$r_m=\sum_{i<m}w_ir_i$.  The restricted normal of $H_a$ is
\begin{equation}
 v(a)=(a_i+a_mw_i)_{i<m}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:normal}
\end{equation}
Over the rationals one divides this nonzero integer vector by the gcd
of its entries and chooses its first nonzero entry positive.  Over a
prime field one divides by its first nonzero entry.  These are the two
independent representations used in the supplied enumeration check.
The closed formula does not rely on either computation.

\begin{example}[Why a large field cardinality is not enough]
\label{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar}
For $d=3$ in characteristic $5$, the integer sums $\pm5$ also vanish in
the field.  They arise from five coefficients equal to $1$ and one zero,
or from their negatives.  There are twelve such vectors.  Each gives a
three-value $z=w\cdot a$, so the preceding affine classification groups
them only in opposite pairs; they cannot coincide with integer-balanced
classes.  There are therefore six extra hyperplanes:
\[
 \cardtwentyfive{\Hh_3(\F_5)}=57\ne51.
\]
The same phenomenon persists in every extension field of characteristic
$5$.  The hypothesis is on the characteristic, not merely on $q$.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The global count and the geometry of the exceptional set\srctag{25}}]{The global count and the geometry of the exceptional set}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d6}
\srcnote{25}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:global}

Let
\[
 \mathcal V_d=\bigcup_{H\in\Hh_d}H\subseteq\W,\qquad
 v_d(q)=\frac{\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal V_d}}{q^{2d-1}}.
\]
Call an arrangement \emph{base-exceptional} if some $h_i=0$ or if
$r\in\mathcal V_d$.  The word ``base'' here refers to the explicitly
classified exception set, not to the spatial base coordinates $x$.
The probability of this event is exactly
\begin{equation}
 b_{k,d}(q)=1-(1-q^{-1})^k(1-v_d(q)).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:baseline}
\end{equation}
Every base-exceptional arrangement is degenerate.  For zero sides this
is Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}; for the cross-section part, use the
corresponding block-parity witness, whose moment identities hold for all
spatial bases and all sidelengths.

\begin{theorem}[Residual count after all hypersurfaces are removed]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:residual}
Under \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters},
\begin{equation}
 b_{k,d}(q)+(1-b_{k,d}(q))q^{-2}
 \ \le\ \frac{Z_{k,d}(q)}{q^D}
 \ \le\ b_{k,d}(q)+(1-q^{-1})^kU_{k,d}q^{-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:residual}
\end{equation}
In particular, the residual degeneracy outside the classified
hyperplanes is genuinely of order $q^{-2}$ for fixed $k,d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Outside the base-exceptional set, all sides are nonzero and no
block-parity witness is available.  There are $3^n$ ternary patterns in
all, and precisely $3^{2d}$ block-parity patterns.  The remaining
patterns come in opposite pairs defining identical vanishing events.
Thus there are $U_{k,d}$ sign classes to consider.

The regular cross-section set $\W\setminus\mathcal V_d$ omits the
constant vectors, since $\Hh_d$ is nonempty and all its hyperplanes
contain them.  For each non-parity sign class,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:regularwitness} bounds the joint probability of vanishing
and regular cross-sections by $q^{-2}$ for every nonzero $h$.  Summing
these bounds and multiplying by $(1-q^{-1})^k$ proves the upper bound.
This is a union bound, so overlaps cause no problem.

For the lower bound fix one witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}.  At every
nonzero $h$ and every regular $r$, its two equations have rank two and
have exactly probability $q^{-2}$ over $x$.  All these configurations
are degenerate and none is base-exceptional.  Their probability is
$(1-b_{k,d}(q))q^{-2}$, proving the lower bound.

Finally $v_d(q)\le H_d/q$, so $b_{k,d}(q)=O_{k,d}(q^{-1})$.
The extra term on the lower side is consequently
$q^{-2}+O_{k,d}(q^{-3})$, whereas the extra term on the upper side is
$O_{k,d}(q^{-2})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the counting part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}]
The base-exceptional set is the union of $L_{k,d}=k+H_d$ distinct linear
hyperplanes in the $D$-dimensional parameter space
$\F_q^k\times\F_q^{2dk}\times\W$.
Each hyperplane has probability $q^{-1}$, and each pair of distinct
hyperplanes has intersection probability $q^{-2}$.  The union bound
and the first two terms of inclusion--exclusion give
\begin{equation}
 \frac{L_{k,d}}q-\frac{\binom{L_{k,d}}2}{q^2}
 \le b_{k,d}(q)\le\frac{L_{k,d}}q.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:bonferroni}
\end{equation}
The lower estimate may be negative for small $q$, which does not affect
its validity.  Combine \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:bonferroni} with
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:residual}, and discard $(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$ on the upper
side.  Multiplication by $q^D$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:mainbounds}; division by
$q^{D-1}$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:limit}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Codimension-one components over an infinite field}
The codimension assertion is stronger than a finite counting heuristic,
so we give its geometric justification.  Work over an algebraically
closed field $K$ of characteristic zero or greater than $2d$.  The
ambient space is affine $D$-space after eliminating $r_m$.
For each of the finitely many ternary patterns, its moment-vanishing
locus is a closed algebraic set.  The degeneracy locus is the finite
union of these sets, with the three distinguished patterns excluded.

The zero-side hyperplanes and parity hyperplanes lie in this locus.
On the open set $h_1\cdots h_k\ne0$, a non-parity witness with
minimal layer $s\le k-2$ has at least two independent affine equations
with a nonsingular pivot minor.  Its dimension is at most $D-2$.
For $s=k-1$ and $e\ge1$, the cross-section equations give codimension
at least one and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1} gives another independent condition in
spatial variables.  For $e=0$, the generic cross-section fibre has two
independent spatial equations; the exceptional diagonal has codimension
$2d-2$ in $\W$ and still has one nonconstant spatial equation.  Its total
codimension is at least $2d-1\ge3$.

Thus every non-parity witness has codimension at least two away from
the zero-side hyperplanes.  Taking a finite union cannot create a new
codimension-one component.  Conversely, each of the listed distinct
hyperplanes is irreducible of codimension one and is already contained
in the degeneracy locus.  This proves the remaining assertion of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main} without deriving geometry from point counts.

\subsection{The first nontrivial example}
For $d=2$, on $r_1+r_2=r_3+r_4$ the four hyperplanes can be written
\begin{equation}
 r_1=r_2,\qquad r_3=r_4,\qquad r_1=r_3,\qquad r_1=r_4.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:d2planes}
\end{equation}
Other balanced ternary equations give one of these or the defining
relation.  The four hyperplanes share the diagonal line; in the
quotient by that line, they are four distinct lines in a two-dimensional
space.  Their union has size $4(q^2-q)+q=4q^2-3q$, so
\begin{equation}
 v_2(q)=\frac4q-\frac3{q^2},\qquad
 b_{k,2}(q)=1-(1-q^{-1})^k(1-4q^{-1}+3q^{-2}).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:d2baseline}
\end{equation}
For example, $b_{1,2}(q)=5q^{-1}-7q^{-2}+3q^{-3}$.
This is an exact count of the classified hyperplanes, not an assertion
that all degeneracies have been counted exactly.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit ambient-size savings\srctag{25}}]{Explicit ambient-size savings}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d7}
\srcnote{25}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:cutoff}

Suppose a later argument can tolerate at most a fraction $\tau>0$ of
ambient arrangements being degenerate.  Gowers's bound
\eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:gowers} gives the sufficient condition
$q\ge k3^n/\tau$.  The refined count instead gives the following.

\begin{corollary}[Two-scale sufficient cutoff]
\label{gsr:en:25:cor:cutoff}
Subject to \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}, the condition
\begin{equation}
 q\ge \max\left\{\frac{2L_{k,d}}{\tau},
                   \sqrt{\frac{2U_{k,d}}{\tau}}\right\}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff}
\end{equation}
implies $Z_{k,d}(q)\le\tau q^D$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first requirement makes $L_{k,d}/q\le\tau/2$ and the second makes
$U_{k,d}/q^2\le\tau/2$.  Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}.
\end{proof}

The large ternary count now enters only through its square root, while
the first-order contribution uses the much smaller exact coefficient.
For extremely small $\tau$, the first term in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff} can
dominate; thus it would be inaccurate to describe the entire threshold
as always a square-root improvement.

\midrule
1 & 32  & 21.268 & 12.714 & first-order\\
2 & 64  & 36.837 & 18.268 & second-order\\
3 & 128 & 67.549 & 33.536 & second-order\\

The tolerated fraction $\tau$ in the actual Riesz-product application
can be far smaller than $10^{-6}$, and the resulting sufficient field-size
criterion far larger than this illustration.  The next section supplies
its precise value instead of silently treating
``sufficiently large'' as a parameter-free condition.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A finite-field random-selection theorem with exact parameters\srctag{25}}]{A finite-field random-selection theorem with exact parameters}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d8}
\srcnote{25}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:selection}

We now generalize the selection step to arbitrary $d\ge2$ and finite
fields satisfying \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}.  The construction is the
Riesz-product idea of Gowers \cite[Section 15]{gowers}; the proof below
keeps exact survival probabilities and handles repeated labels explicitly.

Set
\begin{equation}
 a_n=2^{-n},\qquad
 b_n=2^{-n}(1+2^{1-n}),\qquad
 R_n=b_n/a_n=1+2^{1-n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:survival}
\end{equation}
Let $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$.  Define the integer
\begin{equation}
 t=\min\{u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:R_n^u\ge4/(\alpha\eta)\}
 =\left\lceil\frac{\log(4/(\alpha\eta))}{\log R_n}\right\rceil,
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:t}
\end{equation}
and let
\begin{equation}
 \tau=\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\,\beta^{2d-1}b_n^t.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:tau}
\end{equation}
For numerical implementation the minimum characterization avoids any
rounding ambiguity at an integer logarithmic boundary.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit arrangement purification]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:selection}
Let $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ have size $\beta q^{k+1}$, and let
$\phi:B\to\F_q$ respect at least
$\alpha\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ arrangements in $B$.  Suppose
\eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters} holds and
\begin{equation}
 \frac{L_{k,d}}q+\frac{U_{k,d}}{q^2}\le\tau.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}
\end{equation}
Then a subset $B'\subseteq B$ exists which contains at least
\begin{equation}
 \frac\alpha2\,\beta^{2d-1}b_n^t q^D
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:retained}
\end{equation}
respected arrangements, and the number of its non-respected arrangements
is at most $\eta$ times its number of respected arrangements.
In particular, the proportion respected is at least $1/(1+\eta)\ge1-\eta$.
Condition \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff} with \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:tau} is a sufficient explicit
condition for \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}.
\end{theorem}

Numerically $K_n/E_k=0.69315$ already for $k=1,2,3$. Not formalized; \file{lemma_15_5_holds} (\file{Proofs15Restriction.lean}, line~3086) proves the formal statement.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{One Riesz factor}
Choose a nontrivial additive character $\psi:\F_q\to\mathbb C$.
For example, choose a nonzero $\F_p$-linear functional
$\ell:\F_q\to\F_p$ and take $\psi(z)=\exp(2\pi i\ell(z)/p)$,
where the exponential is independent of the integer representative of
$\ell(z)$.  For independent uniform $u$ and $s_A$ in $\F_q$, with
$A\subseteq[k+1]$, put
\begin{equation}
 P(z)=\frac{1+\Re\psi\bigl(u\phi(z)+
             \sum_{A\subseteq[k+1]}s_A z_A\bigr)}2,
 \qquad z_A=\prod_{i\in A}z_i.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszfactor}
\end{equation}
Thus $0\le P(z)\le1$.  The empty monomial is included.
The expansion of this factor is
\begin{equation}
 P(z)=\frac12+\frac14\psi\bigl(u\phi(z)+\sum_As_Az_A\bigr)
             +\frac14\psi\bigl(-u\phi(z)-\sum_As_Az_A\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszexpansion}
\end{equation}
All coefficients are nonnegative.

Orthogonality says that $\E_s\psi(sc)$ is $1$ if $c=0$ and $0$
otherwise.  For $c\ne0$, multiplication by $c$ permutes the field, and
the average of a nontrivial character is zero: translating its sum by
an element on which it is not one multiplies the sum by a scalar different from one without changing it.  Applying this to every $s_A$, the surviving
terms in the product of \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszexpansion} over arrangement labels
are exactly the ternary patterns whose monomial moments vanish.
Averaging over $u$ additionally requires
$\sum_{j,\eps}\eta(\eps,j)\phi(\rho(\eps,j))=0$.

For a nondegenerate arrangement, the only possibilities are
$0,\eta_0,-\eta_0$.  The zero pattern contributes $2^{-n}$.
Each of the two nonzero patterns has full support and contributes
$4^{-n}$ precisely when $\phi$ respects the arrangement.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \E\prod_{j,\eps}P(\rho(\eps,j))=
 \begin{cases}
 a_n,&\phi\text{ does not respect the arrangement},\\
 b_n,&\phi\text{ respects the arrangement}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:onefactor}
\end{equation}
For a degenerate but respected arrangement the expectation is at least
$b_n$: the same three terms still survive, and all additional surviving
terms have nonnegative coefficients.

\subsection{Several factors and repeated vertices}
Take $t$ independent choices of the parameters in
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszfactor}, giving factors $P_1,\ldots,P_t$.
Conditional on these choices, put each \emph{point} $z\in B$ in $B'$
independently with probability
\[
 p(z)=\prod_{\ell=1}^tP_\ell(z).
\]
A nondegenerate arrangement has distinct vertices by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}.  Its conditional survival probability is
therefore the product of $p(z)$ over its labels.  Independence between
the $t$ parameter choices and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:onefactor} give survival
probability $a_n^t$ or $b_n^t$ according as the arrangement is not respected
or respected.

For a repeated-vertex arrangement the conditional survival probability
is a product over \emph{distinct} points.  Since all factors belong to
$[0,1]$, this is at least the product over all labelled occurrences.
The preceding nonnegative Fourier expansion therefore proves that every
respected arrangement, even a degenerate one, survives with probability
at least $b_n^t$.  It would be incorrect to assert equality of the two
products when labels collide.

\subsection{The positive-potential argument}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:selection}]
Let $M=\beta^{2d-1}q^D$.  Let $X$ count respected arrangements in the
selected set and $Y$ count non-respected ones.  By the preceding survival
calculations, the hypothesis, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:densitycap},
\begin{equation}
 \E X\ge\alpha M b_n^t,\qquad
 \E Y\le M a_n^t+Z_{k,d}(q).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:expectations}
\end{equation}
For the second inequality, treat nondegenerate arrangements using their
exact probability $a_n^t$, and bound the total contribution of degenerate
arrangements by their ambient number.

By the definition of $t$, $a_n^t\le(\alpha\eta/4)b_n^t$.
By Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}, \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}, and
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:tau},
$Z_{k,d}(q)\le(\alpha\eta/4)M b_n^t$.  Consequently
\[
 \E\left(X-\eta^{-1}Y\right)
 \ge \alpha M b_n^t-\frac\alpha4M b_n^t-\frac\alpha4M b_n^t
 =\frac\alpha2M b_n^t.
\]
There is an outcome with
$X-\eta^{-1}Y\ge(\alpha/2)M b_n^t$.
For that outcome, $X$ is at least the right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:retained}, and $Y\le\eta X$.
Thus $X/(X+Y)\ge1/(1+\eta)\ge1-\eta$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A power-form bound and the remaining loss}
Put
\begin{equation}
 K_n=\frac{\log(1/b_n)}{\log R_n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:K}
\end{equation}
Since $t<1+\log(4/(\alpha\eta))/\log R_n$ and $0<b_n<1$,
\begin{equation}
 b_n^t\ge b_n\left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{K_n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:powerretention}
\end{equation}
This gives a power-form lower bound for \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:retained} with no
unspecified constants.  Direct expansion of $\log(1+2^{1-n})$ gives
\begin{equation}
 K_n=(\log2)\,n2^{n-1}+O(n)\qquad(n\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Kasymptotic}
\end{equation}
For $d=8$, the exponent recorded in the repository for the original
coarse selection bound is
$2^{2^{k+4}+k+3}=n2^{n-1}$ \cite{repo25lean}.
Keeping the exact logarithm changes the leading numerical factor in
this local exponent, but not its exponential dependence on $n$.
The very small likelihood advantage $R_n-1=2^{1-n}$ remains the main
loss in this particular selection mechanism.

The theorem neither assumes an improved inverse theorem nor silently
imports a result about prime fields into a composite ring.  It is valid
over finite \emph{fields}; the additive character averages are taken over
that field, and the rank calculations are field calculations.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Labelled arrangements and their moment relations\srctag{27}}]{Labelled arrangements and their moment relations}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:setup}
\srcnote{27}{Section 2}

\subsection{The parameter space}

Let $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ have its first $d$ coordinates equal to $1$ and
its last $d$ coordinates equal to $-1$. All signs are interpreted in the field
when the characteristic is two. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:U}
 U=\{u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\in\F_q^n:s\cdot u=0\}.
\end{equation}
It has dimension $n-1$ because $s\ne0$. A labelled arrangement consists of
\[
 h\in\F_q^k,\qquad x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\F_q^k,\qquad u\in U.
\]
Its labelled vertices, indexed by $\eps\in\{0,1\}^k$ and $1\le j\le n$,
are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:vertex}
 v_{\eps,j}=
 (x_{j1}+\eps_1h_1,\ldots,x_{jk}+\eps_kh_k,u_j)\in\F_q^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
There are $q^kq^{nk}q^{n-1}=q^D$ parameter tuples, as asserted in
\eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:dimensions}. All probabilities below refer to the uniform measure on
this parameter space. In particular the bases, side coordinates, and the
uniform cross section in $U$ are independent.

For a coefficient array $\eta=(\eta_{\eps,j})$ and a subset
$A\subseteq[k+1]$, define the squarefree moment
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:moment}
 M_A(\eta)=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^k}
     \eta_{\eps,j}\prod_{i\in A}v_{\eps,j,i}.
\end{equation}
The empty product is $1$; thus $M_\varnothing(\eta)=\sum\eta_{\eps,j}$.

\subsection{The intrinsic relation and the alphabet}

Write
\[
 \pi(\eps)=(-1)^{|\eps|},\qquad e_{\eps,j}=\pi(\eps)s_j.
\]
For $A\subsetneq[k]$, the alternating cube sum of the associated monomial
vanishes. For $A=[k]$ it is $(-1)^k\prod_i h_i$, independent of the base.
The same statement with the final coordinate present acquires the factor
$u_j$. Since $\sum s_j=0$ and $\sum s_ju_j=0$, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:intrinsic}
 M_A(e)=0\qquad(A\subseteq[k+1])
\end{equation}
in every characteristic, including when some $h_i=0$.

Let $D_p\subseteq\F_p\subseteq\F_q$ be the image of $\{-1,0,1\}$. In
characteristic two this alphabet has two elements, not three.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:degen}
An arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if there is an array
$\eta\in D_p^{\{0,1\}^k\times[n]}$ such that
\[
 \eta\notin\F_q e,
 \qquad M_A(\eta)=0\quad\hbox{for every }A\subseteq[k+1].
\]
The quantity $\Delta_{k,d}(q)$ is its degeneracy probability.
\end{definition}

This definition records relations among labelled vertices, so repeated
vertices can themselves generate degeneracy. It also excludes all field
multiples of the intrinsic relation, not only its two signed integer
representatives.

\begin{lemma}[Zero-side degeneracy]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:zeroside}
If $h_i=0$ for some $i$, then the arrangement is degenerate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose two labels differing only in $\eps_i$, with the same $j$. Their
vertices coincide. The coefficient array with entries $1,-1$ on those labels
and $0$ elsewhere annihilates all moments. In characteristic two the two
nonzero entries are both $1$ and still give zero. Its support has size two,
whereas every nonzero multiple of $e$ has full support $m\ge8$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quotienting coefficient arrays before using a union bound}

Suppose $\eta'=a\eta+be$ with $a\ne0$. By \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:intrinsic}, the two
arrays have precisely the same simultaneous moment-zero event. We therefore
identify them whenever both arrays are admissible. On dividing pointwise by
$e$, this is simply affine equivalence of profiles:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:affineq}
 t_{\eps,j}=\eta_{\eps,j}/e_{\eps,j},
 \qquad t'=at+b\one.
\end{equation}
Constant profiles correspond exactly to multiples of the intrinsic relation.

If $t,t'$ are nonconstant prime-field profiles and \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:affineq} holds
with $a,b\in\F_q$, then in fact $a,b\in\F_p$. Indeed, choose two coordinates
where $t$ differs; their differences determine $a$, and either coordinate
then determines $b$. Thus coefficient-class counts depend on the
characteristic $p$, not on the extension degree of $q$.

Only arrays with $M_\varnothing(\eta)=0$ can occur in the exceptional set.
The intrinsic signs have equally many positive and negative entries as
integer signs. Hence the counting problem is the following one: count
nonconstant ternary profiles on an even number of positions with a balanced
signed sum, modulo affine equivalence. We solve that problem in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:classes}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boolean coefficient extraction and a rank lemma\srctag{27}}]{Boolean coefficient extraction and a rank lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:boolean}
\srcnote{27}{Section 3}

The original Walsh argument is naturally adapted to odd characteristic.
For the present purpose the Boolean zeta transform gives a simpler identity
with no division by two.

For $B\subseteq[k]$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:cB}
 c_{B,j}=\sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^k}
                    \eta_{\eps,j}\prod_{i\in B}\eps_i.
\end{equation}
For $A\subseteq[k]$, write
\[
 F_{A,j}(x_j,h)=\sum_{\eps}\eta_{\eps,j}
                       \prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),
 \qquad h_B=\prod_{i\in B}h_i.
\]
Direct expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:booleanexpansion}
 F_{A,j}=\sum_{B\subseteq A}h_B c_{B,j}
                                      \prod_{i\in A\setminus B}x_{ji}.
\end{equation}
The moments in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:moment} can be written
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:pairedmoments}
 M_A(\eta)=\sum_jF_{A,j},\qquad
 M_{A\cup\{k+1\}}(\eta)=\sum_ju_jF_{A,j}.
\end{equation}
It is important that \emph{both} equations are available for every $A$.

\begin{lemma}[Parity detection]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:paritydetect}
For a fixed column $j$, all $c_{B,j}$ with $B\subsetneq[k]$ vanish if and
only if $\eta_{\eps,j}$ is a scalar multiple of $\pi(\eps)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the support of a Boolean vertex is $E\subseteq[k]$, then
$c_{B,j}=\sum_{E\supseteq B}\eta_{E,j}$. Boolean M\"obius inversion gives
\[
 \eta_{E,j}=\sum_{B\supseteq E}(-1)^{|B\setminus E|}c_{B,j}.
\]
If only $c_{[k],j}$ can be nonzero, the right side is
$(-1)^{k-|E|}c_{[k],j}$, a scalar parity column. Conversely, a parity column
has zero sum over every proper upper interval. The inversion matrix has
integer diagonal entries $1$, so the argument is valid over every field.
\end{proof}

Call an array \emph{column-parity} if each of its columns is a scalar parity
column. An array that is not column-parity has a smallest integer $r<k$ for
which $c_A=(c_{A,1},\ldots,c_{A,n})\ne0$ for some $|A|=r$. Fix such an $A$
and set $c=c_A$. Equation \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:booleanexpansion} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:lowest}
 F_{A,j}=h_Ac_j,
\end{equation}
and, for every $i\notin A$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:next}
 F_{A\cup\{i\},j}=h_Ac_jx_{ji}+b_{i,j}.
\end{equation}
Here $b_{i,j}$ can depend on $h$ and on the coordinates of $x_j$ indexed by
$A$, but not on \emph{any} of the variables $x_{1i},\ldots,x_{ni}$. It can
involve other degree-$r$ coefficients, so it must not be replaced by just
$h_{A\cup\{i\}}c_{A\cup\{i\},j}$.

\begin{lemma}[Two necessary equations]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:rank}
Assume all $h_i\ne0$. For a non-column-parity array and the above choice of
$c$, simultaneous vanishing of the moments implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:constantconstraints}
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot u=0,
\end{equation}
and two affine equations in $z=(x_{1i},\ldots,x_{ni})$ with coefficient rows
$c$ and $u\odot c=(u_jc_j)_j$, for each $i\notin A$.

If the $u_j$ are pairwise distinct and $\sum_jc_j=0$, these two rows have
rank two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:pairedmoments} first to \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:lowest}, and then to
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:next}; divide by the nonzero $h_A$. A nonzero $c$ of coordinate sum
zero has support of size at least two. If the rows were dependent, $u_j$
would have the same value on every index in that support, contrary to
pairwise distinctness.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An all-characteristic per-direction bound]\label{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass}
For a fixed non-column-parity coefficient direction, conditional on all
$h_i\ne0$, its moment-zero probability is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:perclass}
 q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the first nonzero coefficient vector $c$ above. If $\sum c_j\ne0$, the
probability is zero. If $c\notin\F_qs$, the equation $c\cdot u=0$ cuts a
codimension-one subspace of $U$, costing a factor $q^{-1}$. The first affine
base equation has a nonzero coefficient row and costs another $q^{-1}$.

If $c=\lambda s\ne0$, the cross-section equation is automatic. The two base
rows have rank two unless all the $u_j$ coincide. The diagonal line lies in
$U$ and has relative size $q^{-(n-2)}$. Off the diagonal the probability is
at most $q^{-2}$; on it the first equation alone gives at most $q^{-1}$.
Averaging gives
\[
 (1-q^{-(n-2)})q^{-2}+q^{-(n-2)}q^{-1}
       =q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}.
\]
The other base variables may be fixed throughout, since the two equations
are affine in the remaining coordinate block.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Counting coefficient directions exactly\srctag{27}}]{Counting coefficient directions exactly}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:classes}
\srcnote{27}{Section 4}

\subsection{Balanced profiles}

For even $\ell\ge2$, let $\Qc_\ell(p)$ count affine classes of nonconstant
profiles $t\in D_p^\ell$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:profilebalance}
 \sum_{i=1}^{\ell/2}t_i-
 \sum_{i=\ell/2+1}^{\ell}t_i=0\quad\hbox{in }\F_p.
\end{equation}
Let $\Uc_\ell(p)$ count affine classes of nonconstant profiles without the
balance condition. Define
\begin{align}
 \Tc_\ell(p)&=\sum_{a\equiv0\ (p)}[z^a](z^{-1}+1+z)^\ell,\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Tp}\\
 \Bc_\ell(p)&=\sum_{j\in\Z}\binom{\ell}{\ell/2+jp},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Bp}
\end{align}
where binomial coefficients outside their ordinary range are zero.

\begin{theorem}[Affine ternary profile counts]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}
For $p\ge5$,
\begin{align}
 \Qc_\ell(p)&=\frac{\Tc_\ell(p)-2\Bc_\ell(p)+1}{2},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Qp}\\
 \Uc_\ell(p)&=\frac{3^\ell-2^{\ell+1}+1}{2}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Up}
\end{align}
For $p=2$ or $3$,
\begin{align}
 \Qc_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-2}-1}{p-1},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Qsmall}\\
 \Uc_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-1}-1}{p-1}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Usmall}
\end{align}
If $p>\ell$, then $\Tc_\ell(p)=\Tc_\ell$ and
$\Bc_\ell(p)=\binom\ell{\ell/2}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First take $p\ge5$. Changing the signs of the last half of the coordinates is
a bijection of the ternary alphabet, so the number of balanced profiles is
$\Tc_\ell(p)$. The number of balanced binary profiles is $\Bc_\ell(p)$:
if $a,b$ positions are selected in the two halves, balance says
$a-b\equiv0\pmod p$, and Vandermonde's identity sums their number to
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Bp}.

There are three constant ternary profiles. For each of the three unordered
pairs of distinct alphabet values, the number of profiles using exactly
that pair and satisfying balance is $\Bc_\ell(p)-2$. All two-valued
profiles are affinely equivalent to binary ones, and the only ambiguity of
the underlying nontrivial subset is complementation. They therefore give
$(\Bc_\ell(p)-2)/2$ classes.

The number of profiles using all three values is
$\Tc_\ell(p)-3-3(\Bc_\ell(p)-2)=\Tc_\ell(p)-3\Bc_\ell(p)+3$.
An affine bijection preserving $\{-1,0,1\}$ in characteristic at least five
is either the identity or negation. To see this, the image of $0$ must be
the midpoint of the images of $-1$ and $1$; the only alphabet element that
is the midpoint of the other two is $0$ when $p\ne3$. Thus these profiles
form classes of size two. Adding the two types gives \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Qp}.
Removing balance replaces $\Tc_\ell(p)$ by $3^\ell$ and $\Bc_\ell(p)$ by
$2^\ell$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Up}.

For $p=2,3$, the alphabet is the entire prime field. Balanced profiles form
an $(\ell-1)$-dimensional vector space containing the constant line.
Quotienting by that line gives dimension $\ell-2$; quotienting nonzero
vectors by nonzero scalar multiplication gives \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Qsmall}. Without
balance the quotient dimension is $\ell-1$, giving \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Usmall}.
The last assertion follows because the relevant integer sums have absolute
value at most $\ell$ (and the binary differences at most $\ell/2$).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The two counts needed for arrangements}

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:LRp}
 L_{d,p}=\Qc_n(p),\qquad
 R_{k,d,p}=\Qc_m(p)-\Uc_n(p).
\end{equation}
The first quantity will count cross-section hyperplanes. The second is the
number of non-column-parity coefficient directions satisfying the constant
moment condition.

Indeed a column-parity array has the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:columnparity}
 \eta_{\eps,j}=\pi(\eps)c_j,\qquad c_j\in D_p.
\end{equation}
Its empty moment vanishes automatically, since $k\ge1$. Dividing by $e$
gives an arbitrary profile $c_j/s_j$ on the $n$ columns, repeated along each
column. The resulting number of nonconstant affine classes is
$\Uc_n(p)$. All balanced arrays on $m$ positions give $\Qc_m(p)$ classes;
subtracting proves the interpretation of $R_{k,d,p}$. In particular it is a
nonnegative integer, even though many of these directions may never vanish
on a particular regular region.

For $p>m$, formulas \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:LRp} reduce exactly to
\eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:Llarge} and \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:Rlarge}. For the two small characteristics they become
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:LRsmall}
 L_{d,p}=\frac{p^{n-2}-1}{p-1},\qquad
 R_{k,d,p}=\frac{p^{m-2}-p^{n-1}}{p-1}.
\end{equation}

\centering
\caption{Some exact large-characteristic constants. Here $p>n2^k$.}
\label{gsr:en:27:tab:constants}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
$d$ & $k$ & $L_d$ & $S_{k,d}$ & $R_{k,d}$\\
\midrule
2&1&4&15&459\\
2&2&4&32&2\,585\,419\\
3&1&51&63&35\,670\\

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All first-order obstructions\srctag{27}}]{All first-order obstructions}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:allchar}
\srcnote{27}{Section 5}

\subsection{The cross-section hyperplanes}

For a column-parity array \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:columnparity}, all its moments vanish
except possibly those indexed by $[k]$ and $[k+1]$. If all sides are
nonzero, these last two moments vanish exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:parityconditions}
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot u=0.
\end{equation}
The excluded intrinsic arrays are precisely $c\in\F_qs$.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:hyperplanes}
Let $\cH_{d,p}$ be the collection of distinct hyperplanes of $U$ of the form
\[
 H_c=\{u\in U:c\cdot u=0\},
 \qquad c\in D_p^n,\quad \sum_jc_j=0,\quad c\notin\F_qs.
\]
Define the regular cross-section set and its density by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:regular}
 U^\circ=U\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\cH_{d,p}}H,
 \qquad g_{d,p}(q)=\frac{|U^\circ|}{q^{n-1}}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:lem:hyperplanecount}
The collection $\cH_{d,p}$ has exactly $L_{d,p}$ members. Every
$u\in U^\circ$ has pairwise distinct coordinates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Two nonzero linear forms on $U$ have the same kernel if and only if they
are scalar multiples as forms on $U$. The annihilator of $U$ is the line
$\F_qs$, so $H_c=H_{c'}$ exactly when
$c'=ac+bs$ for some $a\ne0$. Dividing by $s$ turns this into affine
profile equivalence. The balance condition becomes a balanced signed sum,
so the class count is $\Qc_n(p)=L_{d,p}$.

If $u_i=u_j$ for distinct indices, choose $c$ supported on those two
coordinates with entries $1,-1$. It is balanced and not proportional to
$s$, because $n\ge4$ and $s$ has full support. Thus $u\in H_c$, contradicting
regularity.
\end{proof}

The diagonal translation direction $\one$ is contained in every member of
$\cH_{d,p}$, because $\sum c_j=0$. Thus this is essentially a hyperplane
arrangement in $U/\F_q\one$, of dimension $n-2$. No general theory of
hyperplane arrangements is required for the bounds below; the intersection
structure becomes relevant when higher coefficients are sought.

\subsection{The sharp first-order theorem in every characteristic}

\begin{theorem}\label{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}
For $k\ge1,d\ge2$, over any finite field of characteristic $p$, put
$A_p=k+L_{d,p}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:allcharbound}
 \frac{A_p}{q}-\frac{\binom{A_p}{2}}{q^2}
 \le\Delta_{k,d}(q)
 \le\frac{A_p}{q}
       +R_{k,d,p}\bigl(q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, for fixed $k,d,p$ and $q=p^a\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:fixedcharasy}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)=\frac{k+L_{d,p}}q+O_{k,d,p}(q^{-2}).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $k$ side hyperplanes $h_i=0$ and $L_{d,p}$ cross-section
hyperplanes. Every tuple on any of them is degenerate: use
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:zeroside} or its defining column-parity relation. These hyperplanes
are distinct in the full parameter space. Every pair intersects in
codimension two. The first two terms of inclusion--exclusion therefore give
the lower bound.

For the upper bound, their union has measure at most $A_p/q$. Outside that
union, a degeneracy witness cannot be column-parity. There are
$R_{k,d,p}$ remaining coefficient directions, and
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass} bounds the moment-zero probability of each, conditional
on nonzero sides. Dropping the factor $(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$ gives the upper
bound. Since $n\ge4$, its remaining term is $O(q^{-2})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit and a cross-answer.} For $p>m$ this is source~18's theorem with its lower bound. In small characteristic it gives the first-order count that source~25 asks for (its Question~4; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}): $L_{d,p}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}, for instance $L_{3,5}=57$, as in source~25's Example~\ref{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar}. The classification of the additional components in characteristics two and three is not given.
\end{writenote}

This proves in a concrete counting sense that all order-$q^{-1}$
obstructions have been identified: the complement of their union contains
only $O(q^{D-2})$ degenerate tuples. The word ``first-order'' here refers to
this counting statement; no unproved assertion about geometric
irreducibility is being used.

\begin{example}[Characteristic dependence]\label{gsr:en:27:ex:char}
For $d=3$, the numbers $L_{3,p}$ are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 p&2&3&5& p>6\\\hline
 L_{3,p}&15&40&57&51.
\end{array}
\]
In characteristic five, ternary integer sums equal to $\pm5$
also become zero, increasing the count. Large field size alone does not
remove this effect: it persists in every extension of $\F_5$.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Second-order structure on the regular region\srctag{27}}]{Second-order structure on the regular region}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:second}
\srcnote{27}{Section 6}

From now until the end of Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:dtwo}, assume $p>m$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:G}
 G=(1-q^{-1})^k g_{d,p}(q).
\end{equation}
This is exactly the probability that all sides are nonzero and $u\in U^\circ$.
Its complement is entirely degenerate.

\subsection{Directions that are not second-order}

Fix a non-column-parity direction and let $r<k$ be its smallest nonzero
Boolean coefficient degree, as in Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:boolean}. If some degree-$r$
vector $c_A$ is not proportional to $s$, then its event on the regular
region costs one cross-section equation and two base equations. More
precisely, $c_A\cdot u=0$ defines a codimension-one subspace in $U$; after
fixing such a regular $u$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:rank} gives rank two in any coordinate
block outside $A$. Hence its probability on the regular region, conditional
only on nonzero sides, is at most $q^{-3}$.

Suppose instead that every nonzero degree-$r$ vector is proportional to $s$.
If $r\le k-2$, choose one such $A$ and two different indices $i,\ell\notin A$.
The paired moments for $A\cup\{i\}$ give two affine equations in the $i$th
base-coordinate block; those for $A\cup\{\ell\}$ give two in the $\ell$th
block. Their right sides depend only on the $A$-coordinates and $h$, not on
either other variable block. On regular $u$, each pair has rank two.
Together they have rank four and cost $q^{-4}$.

Thus the only remaining possibility for a direction contributing at the
second order is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions}
 c_{B,j}=0\ (|B|\le k-2),\qquad
 c_{[k]\setminus\{i\},j}=\lambda_i s_j\ (1\le i\le k),
\end{equation}
with at least one $\lambda_i\ne0$.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:core}
A non-column-parity direction satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions} is called
a \emph{core direction}. This term is local to this article.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:27:prop:noncore}
For every non-column-parity direction that is not a core direction, its
moment-zero event on the regular region, conditional on nonzero sides, has
probability at most $q^{-3}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The two cases above exhaust the possibilities. The first gives $q^{-3}$.
The second gives at most $g_{d,p}(q)q^{-4}\le q^{-3}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Classification of all core profiles}

\begin{lemma}[Affine Boolean form]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:affineboolean}
Condition \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:affineboolean}
 \eta_{\eps,j}=e_{\eps,j}
          \left(t_j+\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\eps_i\right)
\end{equation}
for some $t_j,b_i\in\F_p$, with $b\ne0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Divide each column by its parity and by $s_j$. The Boolean coefficient
transform is invertible. Vanishing of the coefficients below degree $k-1$
means that the resulting Boolean function has degree at most one, and
proportionality of its degree-$k-1$ coefficients to $s_j$ says that the
linear coefficients are common to the columns.

For completeness this can also be checked directly: a constant term times
parity has no proper nonzero $c_B$; a term $\eps_i$ times parity has no
nonzero $c_B$ unless $B\supseteq[k]\setminus\{i\}$, and at that set its
coefficient is $(-1)^{k-1}$. These $k+1$ arrays are linearly independent.
Boolean inversion shows that they exhaust the solution space of the stated
vanishing conditions in each column. The common proportionality factors
then give common $b_i$.
\end{proof}

Every value in parentheses in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:affineboolean} must belong to the
three-element alphabet. This severely restricts $b$.

\begin{lemma}[Width two]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:width}
If $p>m$ and a nonconstant affine Boolean function takes values in
$\{-1,0,1\}\subset\F_p$, its slopes have integer representatives $b_i$
with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:width}
 \sum_i|b_i|\le2.
\end{equation}
Consequently it has either one active coordinate, or two active coordinates
with unit slopes.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose the representative $t\in\{-1,0,1\}$ of the value at the zero vertex.
Each slope is a difference of two alphabet values, so has a representative
in $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. At any vertex the integer affine sum differs from the
chosen representative of its field value by an integer of absolute value
at most $2k+2$. Since $p>m\ge4\cdot2^k>2k+2$, no nonzero multiple of $p$
can occur. Thus the ordinary integer affine function really takes all its
values in $[-1,1]$. Its range width is $\sum_i|b_i|$, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The characteristic cutoff in the width argument]
The proof actually requires only $p>2k+2$ (and hence $p\ge5$), not $p>m$.
Accordingly the core count and the resolved bound remain valid in that
range with $L_{d,p},R_{k,d,p}$ in place of their clean large-characteristic
forms. The stronger assumption $p>m$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:main} also removes modular
wraparound from the balanced coefficient-class counts.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The core direction count]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:corecount}
There are exactly
\[
 S=S_{k,d}=k(2^n-1)+2\binom k2
\]
core directions. For fixed nonzero sides and regular $u$, every one of their
moment-zero events has probability exactly $q^{-2}$ in the base variables.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For one active coordinate $i$, divide by its slope and use translation of
the entire profile. A unit slope allows each column offset to be one of two
adjacent values. A nonconstant binary offset pattern gives one direction;
there are $2^n-2$ such patterns. The two constant patterns are equivalent
under translation and contribute one further direction. A slope of
absolute value two forces a constant offset and belongs to that same
constant-pattern direction after affine normalization. This gives $2^n-1$
directions for each $i$.

For two active coordinates $i,\ell$, their slopes have absolute value one.
After common scaling, their ratio is either $1$ or $-1$. The total width is
two, so every column offset is forced to the same value: $-1$ for slopes
$(1,1)$, or $0$ for slopes $(1,-1)$. These give two directions for every
unordered coordinate pair. Distinct slope ratios, coordinate supports, and
nonconstant offset patterns cannot be related by one common affine
transformation. This proves the count.

For a core profile, all moments except the two top ones vanish identically
on $U$. Expanding the top moment shows that the remaining conditions are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations}
 \sum_j s_j\left(t_j+\sum_i b_i\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}\right)=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_j s_ju_j\left(t_j+\sum_i b_i\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}\right)=0.
\end{equation}
To check the expansion, each $\eps_i$ term contributes the factor
$1+x_{ji}/h_i$ after division by the common alternating top-cube factor.
The additional constant $\sum_i b_i$ disappears from both sums because
$\sum s_j=\sum s_ju_j=0$.

At least one $b_i$ is nonzero. In that coordinate block the coefficient rows
are nonzero multiples of $s$ and $s\odot u$. Since the $u_j$ are pairwise
distinct, these rows are independent. Therefore \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations} is
an affine rank-two system and has exactly a $q^{-2}$ fraction of solutions.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Intersections of core events}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:lem:coreintersections}
Fix regular $u$ and nonzero sides. Distinct core directions with parallel
slope vectors have disjoint zero events. Core directions with nonparallel
slope vectors have intersection probability $q^{-4}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Only the one-coordinate families have more than one direction with a given
slope. Normalize both to slope $1$. If their zero events meet, subtracting
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations} gives
\[
 \sum_j s_j(t_j-t'_j)=0,
 \qquad \sum_j s_ju_j(t_j-t'_j)=0.
\]
The differences can be chosen in $\{-1,0,1\}$. For distinct directions the
vector $c_j=s_j(t_j-t'_j)$ is not proportional to $s$, since a constant
difference would make the profiles affinely equivalent. Thus $u$ belongs
to a forbidden hyperplane, a contradiction.

For nonparallel slopes $b,b'$, consider the two independent coordinate
functionals $b_i/h_i$ and $b'_i/h_i$, and the two independent column
functionals $s$ and $s\odot u$. The four tensor-product functionals are
linearly independent. They are exactly the coefficient rows of the four
affine equations defining the intersection, so that system is surjective
onto $\F_q^4$ and has fraction $q^{-4}$ of solutions.
\end{proof}

Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:P}
 P_{k,d}=\binom{S_{k,d}}2-k\binom{2^n-1}2.
\end{equation}
This is the number of unordered pairs of nonparallel core directions.
Bonferroni's inequality and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:coreintersections} show that the
conditional probability of their union lies between
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreunion}
 \frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}-\frac{P_{k,d}}{q^4}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad \frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}.
\end{equation}
There is no $q^{-3}$ loss from intersections of core events on this region.

\begin{theorem}[Hyperplane-resolved bound]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved}
Let $p>m$ and use $G$ from \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:G}. Then
\begin{align}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)&\ge
 1-G+G\left(\frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}-\frac{P_{k,d}}{q^4}\right),\label{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedlower}\\
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)&\le
 1-G+G\frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}
 +(1-q^{-1})^k\frac{R_{k,d}-S_{k,d}}{q^3}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedupper}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The complement of the regular region has measure $1-G$ and is entirely
degenerate. Apply \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreunion} on the regular region. For the upper
bound add the $R_{k,d}-S_{k,d}$ remaining directions, each bounded by
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:noncore}. Their estimates were conditional on nonzero sides, so
the factor $(1-q^{-1})^k$ is retained.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:main}]
The lower bound is the lower bound of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}. For the upper
bound in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedupper}, use $1-G\le(k+L_d)/q$, $G\le1$, and
$(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$. This proves \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:mainbounds}. Its lower and upper
bounds have the same $q^{-1}$ coefficient, proving sharpness.
\end{proof}
