\section{Source~29 at Lemma~9.3: restriction over a fixed field \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:fixedfield}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the sixth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~29's Section~9. It continues source~17's random-linear-map restriction over a fixed characteristic (Section~\ref{gsr:en:17:sec:d7}) and source~04's restriction theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:main}), keeping the affine-rank stratification of every tuple, degenerate ones included. Over a fixed field $\F_q$ and a fixed translation-invariant system with $s$ free coordinates the size threshold becomes $8qS/(\alpha\eta)$, linear in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$, with retention proportional to $\alpha^{s+1}\eta^s|B|^s$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:main}), and a weaker coefficient removes the threshold (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:no-threshold}). This answers source~04's Question~4 and source~17's Question~2 for fixed fields only (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold}). The constants depend on $q$, so the theorem does not replace the all-moduli \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77; companion \file{lemma_9_3_holds}, \file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, line~376, at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}), as the source says (Section~\ref{gsr:fz:29:sec:d10}). Not formalized. Source~29's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:29:sec:d1}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Restriction without discarding affine degeneracies\srctag{29}}]{Restriction without discarding affine degeneracies}\label{gsr:en:29:sec:d9}
\srcnote{29}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:29:gmsr:restriction}

\paragraph{Attribution and scope.}
The random graph-linear selector and the exact survival formula for
\emph{affine-generic} tuples already occur in Section~8 of
\emph{Polynomial-loss restriction in Gowers's Szemer\'edi argument}
\cite{repo29restriction}.  Its proof charges every
nongeneric tuple the upper bound one for its survival probability.  The
new contribution here is to retain the affine-rank stratification of
\emph{all} tuples.  This removes any ambient-dimension requirement from
the ordinary rank-one version, gives a threshold proportional to
$(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ at fixed field and fixed system, and then removes
that threshold entirely at the cost of a smaller constant.  This answers
the fixed-characteristic version of that manuscript's proposed
rank-stratified threshold problem.  It does not solve its separate
prime-cyclic Fej\'er-kernel threshold problem.  The constants below depend
on the field; their dependence is important when comparing the results.

\subsection{Setup and the exact survival polynomial}

Let $\mathbb F_q$ be a finite field, let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional
$\mathbb F_q$-vector spaces, and let
$\mathcal R\leq\mathbb F_q^\ell$ be a relation space satisfying
\[
 \mathcal R\subseteq\mathbf1^\perp,
 \qquad d=\dim\mathcal R,
 \qquad s=\ell-d\geq2.
\]
The first condition says that every prescribed relation has coefficient
sum zero.  Thus the system is invariant under translating all its
entries by the same vector.  A tuple $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)$ is a solution
when
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i x_i=0\quad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal R.
\]
For a nonempty set $B\subseteq V$ and a map $\phi:B\to W$, write
$T_{\mathcal R}(B)$ for the number of ordered solution tuples in $B^\ell$
and $G_{\mathcal R}(B,\phi)$ for the number also satisfying
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i\phi(x_i)=0\quad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal R.
\]
All tuples, including repetitions, are counted.  Put $m=|B|$.
Row reduction chooses $s$ free coordinate positions, and the other
coordinates are uniquely determined by them.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:count-upper}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B)\leq m^s.
\end{equation}
The cases $d=0$ and $s=1$ are harmless: with no relations every tuple is
respected; with $s=1$, translation invariance forces every solution to
be a constant tuple, which every map respects.  We keep $s\geq2$ below.

For each solution tuple define its full affine-relation space and its
augmented domain rank by
\[
 K_x=\left\{a\in\mathbb F_q^\ell:
          \sum_i a_i=0,\quad\sum_i a_i x_i=0\right\},
 \qquad r(x)=\ell-\dim K_x.
\]
Define the full error map
\[
 E_x:K_x\longrightarrow W,\qquad
 E_x(a)=\sum_i a_i\phi(x_i),
 \qquad e(x)=\operatorname{rank}E_x.
\]
The term ``full'' matters: a degenerate tuple can respect all the
prescribed relations in $\mathcal R$ while failing an additional
relation in $K_x$.  Thus for degenerate tuples, being respected need
not be equivalent to $e(x)=0$.  A tuple is affine-generic exactly when
$K_x=\mathcal R$, or equivalently $r(x)=s$; on such tuples $e(x)$ is
the error rank already used in \cite[Section~8]{repo29restriction}.

Choose a uniformly random linear map
\[
 A:V\oplus W\oplus\mathbb F_q\longrightarrow\mathbb F_q^t,
 \qquad \lambda=q^{-t},
\]
and select
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:selector}
 B_A=\{x\in B:A(x,\phi(x),1)=0\}.
\end{equation}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{lemma}[Exact survival, including degeneracies]\label{gsr:en:29:rr:survival}
For every solution tuple $x$,
\[
 \Pr[x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\in B_A]=\lambda^{r(x)+e(x)}.
\]
In particular, a respected tuple survives with probability at least
$\lambda^s$, whereas an unrespected tuple survives with probability at
most $\lambda^{r(x)+1}$.
\end{lemma}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
The relation space among the augmented graph columns
$z_i=(x_i,\phi(x_i),1)$ is precisely $\ker E_x\leq K_x$.  Its dimension is
$\dim K_x-e(x)$, so
\[
 \dim\operatorname{span}\{z_1,\ldots,z_\ell\}=r(x)+e(x).
\]
A uniform linear map to $\mathbb F_q^t$ kills a fixed subspace of
dimension $u$ with probability $q^{-tu}=\lambda^u$.  This event is
exactly the simultaneous selection event, whether or not entries repeat.
If the tuple is respected, $\mathcal R\subseteq\ker E_x$, whence
$r(x)+e(x)\leq\ell-\dim\mathcal R=s$.  If it is unrespected,
$E_x$ is nonzero on $\mathcal R$, so $e(x)\geq1$.  The final inequalities
follow because $0<\lambda\leq1$.
\end{proof}

Let $G_{r,e}$ and $U_{r,e}$ count respectively the respected and
unrespected solution tuples of full rank pair $(r,e)$.  If
$X=G_{\mathcal R}(B_A,\phi)$ and
$Y=T_{\mathcal R}(B_A)-X$, the exact expectation certificate is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:exact-polynomial}
 \mathbb E[\eta X-Y]
 =\sum_{r,e}(\eta G_{r,e}-U_{r,e})\lambda^{r+e}.
\end{equation}
There is no exceptional-set subtraction.  Any positive lower bound
$L$ for the right side yields a realization with
\[
 X+Y\geq X\geq L/\eta,
 \qquad \frac{X}{X+Y}\geq\frac1{1+\eta}.
\]
The lower bound ensures the denominator is nonzero.

\subsection{The rank-weighted counting lemma}

For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_s)\in B^s$, let
\[
 r(u)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{(u_i,1):1\leq i\leq s\},
 \qquad z=m\lambda,
 \qquad S_{q,s}=\sum_{i=0}^{s-2}q^i
              =\frac{q^{s-1}-1}{q-1}.
\]

\begin{samepage}
\begin{lemma}[Weighted rank count]\label{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-count}
For $0<\lambda\leq1$,
\begin{align}
 R_B(\lambda):=\sum_{u\in B^s}\lambda^{r(u)}
 &\leq z\prod_{i=0}^{s-2}(z+q^i),\label{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-product}\\
 \sum_{\substack{u\in B^s\\r(u)<s}}\lambda^{r(u)}
 &\leq z^s\left\{\prod_{i=0}^{s-2}
                   \left(1+\frac{q^i}{z}\right)-1\right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:29:rr:degenerate-product}
\end{align}
If $z\geq2S_{q,s}$, these imply
\begin{align}
 R_B(\lambda)&\leq2\lambda^s m^s,\label{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-simple}\\
 \sum_{r(u)<s}\lambda^{r(u)}
 &\leq2S_{q,s}\lambda^{s-1}m^{s-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:29:rr:degenerate-simple}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
The first point has $m$ choices and raises augmented rank from zero to
one, contributing $m\lambda=z$.  Before the $j$th point is chosen,
where $2\leq j\leq s$, the affine span of the previous points contains
at most $q^{j-2}$ points.  A choice inside that span does not raise the
rank, and has at most $q^{j-2}$ possibilities.  A choice outside has at
most $m$ possibilities and raises the rank by one, contributing at most
$m\lambda=z$.  Summing over these two possibilities at each step proves
\eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-product}.

More explicitly, classify a tuple by the positions after the first at
which the rank rises.  The contribution of any particular pattern is
at most $z$ times a product, with factor $z$ at a rise and factor
$q^{j-2}$ at a non-rise.  The tuples of rank less than $s$ have at least
one non-rise.  Summing only those patterns gives the complete product
minus the all-rise term $z^s$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:degenerate-product}.  This subtraction is from the pattern
upper bounds; it does not subtract an upper bound for generic tuples
from a separate upper bound for all tuples.

For nonnegative $a_i$ with $\sum_i a_i\leq1/2$, one has
\[
 \prod_i(1+a_i)\leq\frac1{1-\sum_i a_i}\leq2,
 \qquad
 \prod_i(1+a_i)-1\leq2\sum_i a_i.
\]
For example, expand the product and bound its degree-$j$ elementary
symmetric sum by $(\sum_i a_i)^j$, then sum the geometric series.
Use $a_i=q^i/z$ to obtain the two simplified bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{lemma}[Free coordinates preserve affine rank]\label{gsr:en:29:rr:free-rank}
Choose the $s$ free positions by row reduction of a basis matrix for
$\mathcal R$.  For every solution tuple, the augmented domain columns
are spanned by those in the free positions.  Thus the domain rank of
the full tuple equals the augmented rank of the free subtuple.
\end{lemma}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Let $M_P$ be the invertible pivot submatrix and $M_F$ the remaining
columns.  The pivot entries satisfy $x_P=-M_P^{-1}M_F x_F$.
Because every row sums to zero,
$M_P\mathbf1_P+M_F\mathbf1_F=0$.  Thus every row of
$-M_P^{-1}M_F$ sums to one.  The same identities therefore hold for
the augmented columns $(x_i,1)$.  The free columns are themselves
among all columns, so the two spans are equal.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A linear threshold in the inverse accuracy}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Restriction with all degeneracies retained]
\label{gsr:en:29:rr:main}
Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\leq1$ and
\[
 G_{\mathcal R}(B,\phi)\geq\alpha m^s.
\]
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:threshold}
 m\geq\frac{8qS_{q,s}}{\alpha\eta},
\end{equation}
there is a subset $B'\subseteq B$ such that
\begin{align}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B')
 &\geq\frac{\alpha^{s+1}\eta^s}{2(4q)^s}\,m^s,
 \label{gsr:en:29:rr:main-retention}\\
 \frac{G_{\mathcal R}(B',\phi)}{T_{\mathcal R}(B')}
 &\geq\frac1{1+\eta}\geq1-\eta.
 \label{gsr:en:29:rr:main-ratio}
\end{align}
One may take $B'$ of the form \eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:selector} with
$t=\lceil\log_q(4/(\alpha\eta))\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{In this report} (checked at the write). This answers source~04's Question~4 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold}) and source~17's Question~2 for fixed fields only: over a fixed $\F_q$ the threshold becomes linear in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ (source~04's is $\Lambda_d(\alpha\eta)^{-2d}$, source~17's of degree $2m-1$), and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:no-threshold} removes it; source~17's fixed-characteristic theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap}) charges every nongeneric tuple probability one and needs a large domain dimension. As Section~\ref{gsr:fz:29:sec:d10} says, the constants depend on $q$, so this does not replace the all-moduli \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77; companion \file{lemma_9_3_holds}, \file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, line~376, at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}); the growing-modulus case stays open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}). Not formalized.
\end{writenote}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Put $a=\alpha\eta$, choose the stated $t$, and set $\lambda=q^{-t}$.
Then
\[
 \frac{a}{4q}<\lambda\leq\frac a4,
 \qquad m\lambda\geq2S_{q,s}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:survival} gives
$\mathbb E X\geq\alpha\lambda^s m^s$.
For each unrespected solution tuple, its survival is at most
$\lambda^{r(x)+1}$.  The free positions determine at most one full
solution tuple, and have the same augmented domain rank by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:free-rank}.  We may sum over all free tuples in $B^s$,
including ones which do not extend to a solution in $B^\ell$, to obtain
\[
 \mathbb E Y\leq\lambda R_B(\lambda)
              \leq2\lambda^{s+1}m^s.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E[\eta X-Y]
 \geq(a-2\lambda)\lambda^s m^s
 \geq\frac a2\lambda^s m^s>0.
\]
Choose a realization at least its expectation.  It satisfies
$Y\leq\eta X$ and
\[
 T_{\mathcal R}(B_A)\geq X
 \geq\frac\alpha2\lambda^s m^s
 \geq\frac{\alpha^{s+1}\eta^s}{2(4q)^s}m^s.
\]
These are the required claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{corollary}[No size or dimension threshold]\label{gsr:en:29:rr:no-threshold}
Under the same input assumption, with any $m>0$, there is $B'\subseteq B$
such that the respected proportion is at least $1/(1+\eta)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:unconditional-retention}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B')
 \geq (8qS_{q,s})^{-s}\alpha^{s+1}\eta^s m^s.
\end{equation}
Consequently the same subset satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:unconditional-size}
 |B'|\geq\frac{\alpha^{1+1/s}\eta}{8qS_{q,s}}\,m.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
If \eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:threshold} holds, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:main}, noting that
$(8qS_{q,s})^{-s}\leq[2(4q)^s]^{-1}$ because $s\geq2$ and
$S_{q,s}\geq1$.
Otherwise take any singleton $B'\subseteq B$.  Translation invariance
makes its unique tuple a respected solution.  Moreover
\[
 (8qS_{q,s})^{-s}\alpha^{s+1}\eta^s m^s
 =\alpha\left(\frac{\alpha\eta m}{8qS_{q,s}}\right)^s
 <\alpha\leq1.
\]
This proves the count and ratio in the remaining case.
Finally apply \eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:count-upper} to $B'$ and take the $s$th root.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What ``no dimension threshold'' means.}
The constants depend on $q$ and $s$, but not on $\dim V$, $\dim W$, the
ambient cardinality, or the density of $B$ in its ambient space.  The
result remains valid when every tuple is nongeneric.  For a growing
prime field with $\dim V=1$, its constants can make it very weak; this
does not supersede the bounded-coefficient prime-cyclic construction.
The use of vector-space rank is essential to the present proof.  No
corresponding bound for all composite cyclic moduli, or for arbitrary
finite abelian groups of mixed exponent, follows from this argument.

\subsection{The higher-error-rank benefit survives}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Generic rank gap with the improved threshold]
\label{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-gap}
In addition to the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:main}, suppose that
every affine-generic unrespected solution tuple has error rank at least
$h$, where $1\leq h\leq d$.  Under the same threshold
\eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:threshold}, there is a subset $B'\subseteq B$ with respected
proportion at least $1/(1+\eta)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-gap-count}
 T_{\mathcal R}(B')
 \geq\frac{\alpha^{1+s/h}\eta^{s/h}}
               {2\,4^{s/h}q^s}\,m^s.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Set $a=\alpha\eta$ and choose the least positive integer $t$ such that
$\lambda=q^{-t}$ satisfies $\lambda^h\leq a/4$.
Then
\[
 q^{-1}(a/4)^{1/h}<\lambda\leq(a/4)^{1/h},
 \qquad \lambda>\frac a{4q}.
\]
The threshold again ensures $m\lambda\geq2S_{q,s}$.
Respected tuples give $\mathbb E X\geq\alpha\lambda^s m^s$.
Generic unrespected tuples contribute at most $\lambda^{s+h}m^s$ to
$\mathbb E Y$.
Nongeneric unrespected tuples have $r(x)<s$ and $e(x)\geq1$.
Using the free-coordinate injection and
\eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:degenerate-simple}, their total expected contribution is at
most
\[
 \lambda\sum_{r(u)<s}\lambda^{r(u)}
 \leq2S_{q,s}\lambda^s m^{s-1}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \mathbb E[\eta X-Y]
 \geq\lambda^s m^s
       \left(a-\lambda^h-\frac{2S_{q,s}}m\right)
 \geq\frac a2\lambda^s m^s.
\]
Indeed $\lambda^h\leq a/4$ and
$2S_{q,s}/m\leq a/(4q)\leq a/4$.
The same positive-potential argument as before gives
$T_{\mathcal R}(B')\geq\alpha\lambda^s m^s/2$ and the asserted ratio.
The lower bound on $\lambda$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:29:rr:rank-gap-count}.
\end{proof}

The singleton argument does \emph{not} remove the threshold while
preserving these stronger exponents for $h>1$: below the threshold,
$\alpha(\alpha\eta)^{s/h}m^s$ need not be bounded by a constant.
No such removal is asserted here.

\subsection{Examples and comparison quantities}

For a single balanced additive relation on $2d_0$ variables, with
$d_0\geq2$, one has $s=2d_0-1$.  Write $T_{d_0}(B)$ for the number of
ordered tuples satisfying
$x_1+\cdots+x_{d_0}=x_{d_0+1}+\cdots+x_{2d_0}$, and
$G_{d_0}(B,\phi)$ for the number also respected by $\phi$.
Thus the no-threshold count is
\[
 c_{q,d_0}\alpha^{2d_0}\eta^{2d_0-1}|B|^{2d_0-1},
 \quad
 c_{q,d_0}=
 \left(8q\frac{q^{2d_0-2}-1}{q-1}\right)^{-(2d_0-1)}.
\]
At order eight over $\mathbb F_2$, $s=15$ and
$S_{2,15}=16383$.  The large-set theorem has the explicit form
\[
 |B|\geq\frac{262128}{\alpha\eta}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 T_8(B')\geq2^{-46}\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}|B|^{15}.
\]
The respected proportion is at least $1/(1+\eta)$.
Without a size condition the coefficient $262128^{-15}$ is valid.
The value $2^{-270}$ is a slightly weaker simple power of two, since
$262128<2^{18}$.

The conversion from graph quadruple energy to the order-eight input is
an established Fourier-moment argument, following Gowers's Lemma~9.2
\cite{gowers} and retaining the exact second moment as in
\cite{repo29restriction}.  We include the short proof to make the
specialization self-contained.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{lemma}[Graph-energy interpolation]\label{gsr:en:29:rr:graph-moments}
Let $B$ be a nonempty finite subset of a finite abelian group and let
$\phi$ take values in another finite abelian group.  For an integer
$j\geq1$, let $G_j(B,\phi)$ count the ordered additive $2j$-tuples in
$B$ that are respected by $\phi$.  If $0<\gamma\leq1$ and
$G_2(B,\phi)\geq\gamma|B|^3$, then
\[
 G_8(B,\phi)\geq\gamma^7|B|^{15}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Let $\Gamma$ be the graph of $\phi$, let $m=|\Gamma|=|B|$, and write
$H$ for the product of the two ambient groups and $N=|H|$.  For
$\chi\in\widehat H$, define the unnormalized character sum
\[
 F_\Gamma(\chi)=\sum_{z\in\Gamma}\overline{\chi(z)}.
\]
Orthogonality and Parseval give
\[
 G_j(B,\phi)=\frac1N\sum_{\chi\in\widehat H}
                        |F_\Gamma(\chi)|^{2j},
 \qquad
 \frac1N\sum_{\chi\in\widehat H}|F_\Gamma(\chi)|^2=m.
\]
Consequently $p_\chi=|F_\Gamma(\chi)|^2/(Nm)$ is a probability
distribution.  For the random variable $Z_\chi=|F_\Gamma(\chi)|^2$,
\[
 \mathbb E_p Z=\frac{G_2(B,\phi)}m\geq\gamma m^2,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_p Z^7=\frac{G_8(B,\phi)}m.
\]
Jensen's inequality for the convex function $t\mapsto t^7$ on
$[0,\infty)$ yields
$G_8(B,\phi)/m\geq(\gamma m^2)^7$, proving the result.
\end{proof}

Substituting $\alpha=\gamma^7$ in the binary order-eight restriction gives
\[
 |B|\geq262128\gamma^{-7}\eta^{-1},\qquad
 T_8(B')\geq2^{-46}\gamma^{112}\eta^{15}|B|^{15}.
\]
These bounds combine the established interpolation with the new
all-tuples restriction estimate.

For $k\geq1$, an additive $k$-cube has $2^k$ entries and a translation-invariant
relation space of dimension $2^k-k-1$, leaving $s=k+1$ free coordinates.
Thus if at least $\alpha|B|^{k+1}$ cubes are respected by $\phi$, the
new theorem retains at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha^{k+2}\eta^{k+1}}{2(4q)^{k+1}}|B|^{k+1}
\]
cubes with respected proportion at least $1/(1+\eta)$ under
$|B|\geq8q(q^k-1)/((q-1)\alpha\eta)$.
For cubes, ``respected'' means that the full system of affine-cube
relations also holds for the images.  Requiring only the alternating
top-degree sum to vanish is a different condition.  The affine-coordinate
matrix of the cube vertices has rank $k+1$ over every field:
its columns at the zero vertex and the $k$ unit vertices form an
invertible affine-coordinate basis, including in characteristic two.

\section{Sources~28 and~30 at Section~10: logarithmic selection and fixed radii \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:section10}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the sixth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next fourteen sections return to Gowers's Section~10, the local Freiman model on a Bohr neighbourhood. \emph{Logically they continue source~12's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:bohr}) \emph{and source~07's} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:transport}), which stay the spines for paths, extension, synchronization and smoothing; they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Sections~\ref{gsr:en:28:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:28:sec:d7} are source~28's, Sections~\ref{gsr:en:30:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:30:sec:d9} source~30's; their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:28:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:30:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved, and what is new in this report.} Source~28 replaces the component selection by random windows in the logarithms of the fibre size and the anchored energy weight, and obtains a local model on $\Bhr(\Gamma,\zeta_\alpha)$ from the original-domain spectrum, retaining $\alpha p(\alpha)/20$ of the domain, $p(\alpha)=(\log2)^2/(\log(32/\alpha)\log(32/\alpha^2))$, with $|\Gamma|\le2^{34}(1+\alpha)/((\log2)\alpha^3)$, radius $\Omega(\alpha^5)$, input defect $2^{-21}$ and order seven (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main}); against the corrected formal statement ($\alpha^6/20000$, $O(\alpha^{-10})$, $2^{-43}$) and source~12 ($\alpha^5/20000$, radius $\alpha^{19}$). New are the logarithmic selection (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lem:log-selection}), the energy-weighted boundary estimate and the parameter chain; the coupled paths, dense extension and smoothing are credited to sources~07 and~12. Source~30 proves a fixed-radius translation estimate $2m\,b_B(d)\le|B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|-|B|\le(3^r-1)|B|$ with both constituents sharp (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic}, \ref{gsr:en:30:thm:main}), a margin-preserving radius $\rho/(8(3^r-1))$ for Corollary~10.11 at the given radius (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}), the $5/14$ compatibility count, and a Chinese-remainder obstruction: in cyclic groups of composite order the dependence on the rank must be exponential (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}). Its tree budget and compatibility inequality are source~12's, and its extension budget a weaker form of source~12's sharp theorem (notes there); composing its escape inequality with source~12's theorem enlarges its extension radius (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:extension-only}). Source~12's radius $\rho/(8d)$ is larger but selected in $(\rho/2,\rho]$; the obstruction explains the price of a fixed radius. Not to be confused: \file{Proofs07BohrHom.lean} uses a related fourth-moment bound for Section~7, not Section~10.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}). \file{lemma_10_10}, \file{corollary_10_11}, \file{lemma_10_12} and \file{theorem_10_13} (\file{Section10.lean}, lines~362, 374, 401, 473) are exact companions (\file{Proofs10Bohr.lean}, lines~277, 607; \file{Proofs10Induced.lean}, line~145; \file{Proofs10Main.lean}, line~1292). Nothing in this chapter is formalized; whether source~28's theorem implies \file{theorem_10_13} with better parameters is a marked question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:logselection}).

\section[{Conventions and finite domains\srctag{28}}]{Conventions and finite domains}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:conventions}
\srcnote{28}{Section 2}

All groups are written additively except that characters take their values
in the unit circle. Expectations over nonempty finite sets are uniform.
For \(G\) of order \(N\), set
\[
 \widehat u(\chi)=\sum_{s\in G}u(s)\overline{\chi(s)},\qquad
 (u*v)(s)=\sum_{t\in G}u(t)v(s-t).
\]
Then
\[
 u(s)=\frac1N\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\widehat u(\chi)\chi(s),
 \qquad
 \sum_\chi|\widehat u(\chi)|^2=N\sum_s|u(s)|^2.
\]
Part II explicitly switches to normalized Fourier coefficients,
\(\widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}\), denoted \(a_\chi\)
in its concentration argument. These conventions are never mixed
inside one calculation.

\begin{definition}[Bohr sets]
For \(\Gamma\subseteq\widehat G\) and \(u\ge0\),
\[
 \Bhr(\Gamma,u)=
 \{s\in G:\|\arg\chi(s)/(2\pi)\|_{\Tcirc}\le u
                       \text{ for every }\chi\in\Gamma\}.
\]
Here \(\|t\|_{\Tcirc}\) is distance to the nearest integer.
Bohr sets are symmetric and contain \(0\).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Relations and exact local models]
An order-\(k\) relation in a domain \((X,r)\) is an ordered tuple
\((x_1,\ldots,x_{2k})\in X^{2k}\) satisfying
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^k r(x_j)=\sum_{j=k+1}^{2k}r(x_j).
\]
It is respected by \(\phi:X\to H\) if the same equality holds with
\(\phi\) in place of \(r\). A \((1-\eta)\)-homomorphism of order \(k\)
respects at least that fraction of all order-\(k\) relations.
Repetition of points is allowed.

A Freiman homomorphism on \(A\subseteq G\) is a map \(F:A\to H\)
respecting all order-two relations. It need not be the restriction of a
homomorphism defined on all of \(G\).
\end{definition}

A domain is \((B,\sigma M)\)-invariant if
\[
 \big||X_{s+d}|-|X_s|\big|\le\sigma M\qquad(s\in G,\ d\in B).
\]
A \emph{fibre-saturated} subset is a union of whole fibres \(X_s\).
For such a subset \(W\), the statement that it survives the shift \(d\)
means that most of its \emph{points}, counted with their fibre
multiplicities, have their destination fibre also inside \(W\).
We use the explicit expression
\[
 W^{(d)}=\{w\in W:r(w)+d\in r(W)\}.
\]
This avoids treating a shift of a multifunction domain as a
pointwise permutation of its points.


\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Weighted local errors and a useful anchor\srctag{28}}]{Weighted local errors and a useful anchor}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:anchor}
\srcnote{28}{Section 3}
\gsrsrcpart{A sharper local model from logarithmic selection}

Fix a nonempty symmetric \(B\subseteq G\) containing \(0\).
In this section
\[
 |X|=\alpha MN,\qquad |X_s|\le M,\qquad
 0<\eta,\qquad 0<\sigma\le\eta\alpha^2,
\]
and \(\phi:X\to H\) is a \((1-\eta)\)-homomorphism of order two
on a \((B,\sigma M)\)-invariant domain.
Put \(n_s=|X_s|\).
For \(x,y\in X\), define
\begin{align}
 q(x,y)&=\sum_{d\in G}n_{r(x)+d}n_{r(y)+d},\\
 b(x,y)&=\sum_{d\in B}n_{r(x)+d}n_{r(y)+d},\\
 e(x,y)&=\#\{(u,v)\in X^2:r(u)-r(x)=r(v)-r(y)\in B,\\[-0.7em]
 &\hspace{42mm}\phi(u)-\phi(x)\ne\phi(v)-\phi(y)\},\nonumber\\
 \epsilon(x,y)&=e(x,y)/b(x,y).
\end{align}
The denominator is positive because \(0\in B\).
Write
\[
 Q(x)=\sum_y q(x,y),\quad
 E(x)=\sum_y\epsilon(x,y)q(x,y),\quad
 R(x)=n_{r(x)},\quad
 T=\sum_xQ(x).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Energy bounds]\label{gsr:en:28:lem:energy}
One has
\[
 q(x,y)\le\alpha M^2N,\qquad
 Q(x)\le\alpha^2M^3N^2,\qquad
 T\ge\alpha^4M^4N^3.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed difference there are at most \(|X|M\) ordered point pairs:
choose one point and then choose the other within a specified fibre.
This proves the first inequality, and summing over \(y\) proves the second.
If \(a_d\) is the number of ordered pairs of difference \(d\), then
\[
 T=\sum_da_d^2\ge\frac1N\left(\sum_da_d\right)^2
   =\frac{|X|^4}{N}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transfer to anchored weighted error]\label{gsr:en:28:lem:transfer}
\[
 \sum_xE(x)\le15\eta T.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is the local error-transfer mechanism of Gowers's Lemma~10.2,
written with explicit finite counts. Let \(L=\eta\alpha^2M\), and call a
point thick if its fibre has size at least \(5L\).
For thick \(x,y\), and any \((u,v)\) with
\(r(u)-r(x)=r(v)-r(y)\in B\), invariance gives
\[
 \frac{b(u,v)}{b(x,y)}
 \le
 \frac{(n_{r(x)}+2L)(n_{r(y)}+2L)}
      {(n_{r(x)}-L)(n_{r(y)}-L)}
 \le \left(\frac74\right)^2<4.
\]
If the increments at \((x,u)\) and \((y,v)\) disagree, then for any
pair \((z,w)\) with \(r(w)-r(z)=r(y)-r(x)\), at least one of the two
equal-base-difference pairs
\[
 ((x,y),(z,w)),\qquad ((u,v),(z,w))
\]
has unequal label differences.
Count the resulting sextuples with weight \(1/b(x,y)\).
For a failure of the first kind, summing over \((u,v)\) has total
weight exactly one. For a failure of the second kind, symmetry of \(B\)
and the displayed ratio bound give total weight at most four.
The order-two defect therefore bounds the thick contribution by
\(5\eta T\).

There are at most \(5\eta\alpha^2MN\) nonthick points.
Since \(\epsilon\le1\), the contribution of pairs with at least one
nonthick endpoint is, by lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lem:energy}, at most
\[
 2(5\eta\alpha^2MN)(\alpha^2M^3N^2)
 =10\eta\alpha^4M^4N^3\le10\eta T.
\]
Adding the contributions proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[An anchor with simultaneous energy and error control]
\label{gsr:en:28:lem:anchor}
There exists \(x\in X\) such that
\[
 R(x)\ge\frac{\alpha^2M}{2},\qquad
 S:=Q(x)\ge\frac{\alpha^3M^3N^2}{4},\qquad
 E(x)\le60\eta S.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let \(A=\{x:R(x)\ge\alpha^2M/2\}\).
The discarded points are at most \(\alpha^2MN/2\), so
\[
 \sum_{x\notin A}Q(x)\le\frac{\alpha^4M^4N^3}{2}\le\frac T2.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_{x\in A}\left(Q(x)-\frac{E(x)}{60\eta}\right)
 \ge\frac T2-\frac{15\eta T}{60\eta}=\frac T4.
\]
Some \(x\in A\) has the summand at least \(T/(4|A|)\), which is at
least \(T/(4|X|)\ge\alpha^3M^3N^2/4\).
Its summand is positive, giving both required conclusions.
\end{proof}

Fix this anchor. Abbreviate \(q(y)=q(x,y)\) and
\(\epsilon(y)=\epsilon(x,y)\), and put \(q_{\max}=\alpha M^2N\).
For points \(y,z\) with \(r(z)-r(y)\in B\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:q-lipschitz}
 |q(z)-q(y)|\le\sigma\alpha M^2N=\sigma q_{\max}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, shift one of the two fibre-count factors in the defining
convolution and use \(\sum_sn_s=|X|\). The same estimate is valid
for the convolution considered at arbitrary base coordinates.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Logarithmic component selection\srctag{28}}]{Logarithmic component selection}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:log-selection}
\srcnote{28}{Section 4}

The next lemma is the central refinement. Additive windows have to be
small enough for the smallest fibres they can encounter. Logarithmic
windows encode the desired ratio bound directly. Moreover, the boundary
is measured by \(q\), the same weight as the useful energy.
The resulting comparison is local to the selected window.

\begin{lemma}[Selection with logarithmic windows]\label{gsr:en:28:lem:log-selection}
Under the anchored hypotheses above, assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:sigma-selection}
 0<\sigma\le
 \frac{\eta(\log2)\alpha^2}{2048(1+\alpha)},
 \qquad 0<\eta\le2^{-21}.
\end{equation}
There is a nonempty fibre-saturated \(W\subseteq X\) with
\begin{align}
 |W|&\ge\frac{p(\alpha)\alpha}{16}|X|,\label{gsr:en:28:eq:W-mass}\\
 \frac{\max_Wq}{\min_Wq}&\le2,\qquad
 \frac{\max_WR}{\min_WR}\le2,\label{gsr:en:28:eq:W-ratios}\\
 \min_Wq&\ge\frac{\alpha q_{\max}}{32},\qquad
 \min_WR\ge\frac{\alpha^2M}{32},\label{gsr:en:28:eq:W-min}\\
 \E_{w\in W}\epsilon(w)&\le960\eta,\label{gsr:en:28:eq:W-error}\\
 |W^{(d)}|&\ge(1-\eta)|W|\qquad(d\in B).\label{gsr:en:28:eq:W-survival}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\textit{Step 1: discard two low-energy tails.}
Put
\[
 a_0=\alpha/16,\qquad b_0=\alpha^2/16,\qquad
 X_*=\{y:q(y)/q_{\max}\ge a_0,\ R(y)/M\ge b_0\}.
\]
Discarding points with \(q(y)<a_0q_{\max}\) loses at most
\[
 a_0q_{\max}|X|=\frac{\alpha^3M^3N^2}{16}
\]
of the \(q\)-weight. Discarding the other small fibres loses at most
\[
 (b_0MN)q_{\max}=\frac{\alpha^3M^3N^2}{16}.
\]
Both estimates are at most \(S/4\). Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:core-energy}
 S_*:=\sum_{y\in X_*}q(y)\ge S/2.
\end{equation}

\textit{Step 2: random multiplicative windows.}
Set \(h=(\log2)/2\). Choose \(u,v\) independently, uniformly on
\[
 I_q=[\log a_0-h,h],\qquad I_R=[\log b_0-h,h].
\]
The random set \(W_{u,v}\) consists of the points \(y\) satisfying
\[
 |\log(q(y)/q_{\max})-u|\le h,\qquad
 |\log(R(y)/M)-v|\le h.
\]
All quantities inside the logarithms are positive. For a fixed point of
\(X_*\), the admissible center interval in each coordinate has length
\(2h\). Hence its inclusion probability is exactly
\[
 p=\frac{(2h)^2}{|I_q||I_R|}
   =\frac{(\log2)^2}{\log(32/\alpha)\log(32/\alpha^2)}.
\]
Every other point has inclusion probability at most \(p\).
Any nonempty selected window automatically satisfies
equations~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:W-ratios} and \eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:W-min}: the ratio inside either coordinate
interval is \(\exp(2h)=2\), while its lowest possible endpoint is
respectively \(a_0/2\) or \(b_0/2\).

\textit{Step 3: a boundary inside the selected window.}
Define
\[
 \Delta_q=\frac{64\sigma}{\alpha},\qquad
 \Delta_R=\frac{64\sigma}{\alpha^2},\qquad
 \beta=\frac{\Delta_q+\Delta_R}{h}
       =\frac{128\sigma(1+\alpha)}{\alpha^2\log2}.
\]
The hypotheses imply \(\sigma\le\alpha^2/128\) and
\(0<\Delta_q,\Delta_R<h\). Let \(V_{u,v}\) be \(W_{u,v}\)
minus the inner window obtained by replacing the half-widths \(h\)
with \(h-\Delta_q,h-\Delta_R\).
For every fixed point of \(X\), even one outside \(X_*\), the
probability of lying in \(V_{u,v}\) is at most \(p\beta\).
To see this, a boundary interval in the first center coordinate has
total length at most \(2\Delta_q\), and the other coordinate has
length at most \(2h\); interchange the coordinates and use the union
bound. Truncation by \(I_q,I_R\) only decreases these lengths.

This choice of boundary has a deterministic consequence.
If \(y\in W_{u,v}\) and \(d\in B\), invariance first gives
\[
 n_{r(y)+d}\ge R(y)-\sigma M
             \ge\alpha^2M/32-\sigma M>0.
\]
Choose \(z\) in that fibre. By equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:q-lipschitz} and the lower
bounds in equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:W-min},
\begin{align*}
 \left|\log\frac{q(z)}{q(y)}\right|
 &\le\frac{\sigma}{\alpha/32-\sigma}
 \le\frac{64\sigma}{\alpha}=\Delta_q,\\
 \left|\log\frac{R(z)}{R(y)}\right|
 &\le\frac{\sigma}{\alpha^2/32-\sigma}
 \le\frac{64\sigma}{\alpha^2}=\Delta_R.
\end{align*}
We used \(|\log a-\log b|\le|a-b|/\min(a,b)\).
Thus every point in \(W_{u,v}\setminus V_{u,v}\) has its
shifted fibre entirely in \(W_{u,v}\), simultaneously for every
\(d\in B\).

\textit{Step 4: one correlated selection inequality.}
For each pair of centers write
\[
 S_{u,v}=\sum_{X_*\cap W_{u,v}}q,\qquad
 E_{u,v}=\sum_{W_{u,v}}\epsilon q,\qquad
 Q_{V,u,v}=\sum_{V_{u,v}}q.
\]
The probability estimates and the anchor inequalities give
\[
 \E S_{u,v}\ge pS/2,\quad
 \E E_{u,v}\le60\eta pS,\quad
 \E Q_{V,u,v}\le p\beta S.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:selection-functional}
 \E\left[
 S_{u,v}-\frac{E_{u,v}}{480\eta}
           -\frac{Q_{V,u,v}}{8\beta}\right]\ge pS/4.
\end{equation}
Choose centers for which the bracket is at least \(pS/4\).
Set \(W=W_{u,v}\), \(V=V_{u,v}\), and \(S_W=S_{u,v}\).
Then
\[
 S_W\ge pS/4,\qquad E_{u,v}\le480\eta S_W,\qquad
 Q_{V,u,v}\le8\beta S_W.
\]
In particular \(W\ne\varnothing\), and
\[
 |W|\ge\frac{S_W}{q_{\max}}
      \ge\frac{p\alpha^2MN}{16},
\]
which is equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:W-mass}.

\textit{Step 5: convert weighted errors only after selecting.}
Since the ratio of the largest and smallest \(q\)-weights in \(W\)
is at most two,
\[
 \E_W\epsilon
 \le\frac{\sum_W\epsilon q}{|W|\min_Wq}
 \le480\eta\frac{\max_Wq}{\min_Wq}\le960\eta.
\]
Similarly, using \(S_W\le\sum_Wq\le|W|\max_Wq\),
\[
 \frac{|V|}{|W|}
 \le\frac{Q_{V,u,v}}{|W|\min_Wq}
 \le16\beta\le\eta.
\]
Step~3 now implies equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:W-survival}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the density powers disappear}

The original additive-window estimate separately replaces the selected
energy by its global upper bound and the selected cardinality by its
global lower bound. That loses their correlation. Localizing the
boundary to the selected window removes another unnecessary loss.
Weighting the boundary by \(q\) then makes it comparable directly with
the selected energy. Finally, multiplicative windows need only sample a
logarithmic range in each coordinate.

The two logarithmic factors have a precise origin: one pays for choosing
a multiplicative scale of the anchored energy, and the other for choosing
a multiplicative scale of the fibre size. All subsequent error bounds
are proportional to the mass in the selected window. They introduce no
additional inverse power of \(\alpha\).
No optimality of the density powers, logarithms, or numerical constants
is asserted.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{From an averaged anchor error to exact local differences\srctag{28}}]{From an averaged anchor error to exact local differences}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d5}
\srcnote{28}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:sec:repair}

The previous transport report already developed coupled paths and
collision-to-mode exactification \cite{repo28seven}. Its collision input is a
normalized directional law; the comparison with a raw additive-energy
statistic is explicitly a separate requirement. We supply that comparison
for the anchored error furnished by the component selection, then carry
the average directly through the final restriction. This avoids imposing
the nested exceptional-set conclusions of the original Lemma~10.6.

Throughout this section, $G$ is a finite abelian group, $H$ is an abelian
group, $U$ is a finite set with a map $r:U\to G$, and
$F:U\to H$. Write $U_s=r^{-1}(s)$ and $R(u)=|U_{r(u)}|$.
The target group need not be finite. Every probability distribution used
below nevertheless has finite support.

\begin{lemma}[Anchored agreement selects a mode]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:mode}
Let $B\subseteq G$ be nonempty, $W\subseteq U$ nonempty, and $x\in U$.
Assume that $U_{r(x)+d}$ and $U_{r(w)+d}$ are nonempty for every
$d\in B$ and $w\in W$. Put
\[
 b_d(w)=|U_{r(x)+d}|\,|U_{r(w)+d}|,
\]
and let $p(d,w)$ be the probability that
\[
 F(y)-F(x)\ne F(z)-F(w),
\]
where $y,z$ are independent uniform elements of
$U_{r(x)+d},U_{r(w)+d}$, respectively. Define
\[
 \epsilon(w)=
 \frac{\sum_{d\in B}b_d(w)p(d,w)}{\sum_{d\in B}b_d(w)}.
\]
Suppose that
\[
 \max_{d\in B}b_d(w)\le4\min_{d\in B}b_d(w)
 \quad(w\in W),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{w\in W}\epsilon(w)\le1024\eta.
\]
If $0<\eta\le2^{-21}$, there are $D\subseteq B$ and
$\psi:D\to H$ such that
\[
 |D|\ge\frac{15}{16}|B|
\]
and, for every $d\in D$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:edge-average}
 \mathbb E_{w\in W}e_d(w)\le\frac1{31},\qquad
 e_d(w)=
 \mathbb P_{z\in U_{r(w)+d}}
       \bigl(F(z)-F(w)\ne\psi(d)\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The weight comparison implies
$\mathbb E_{d\in B}p(d,w)\le4\epsilon(w)$, hence
\[
 \mathbb E_{d\in B,w\in W}p(d,w)\le4096\eta.
\]
Let
\[
 D=\left\{d\in B:
       \mathbb E_{w\in W}p(d,w)\le\frac1{32}\right\}.
\]
Markov's inequality gives
\[
 \frac{|B\setminus D|}{|B|}
 \le2^{17}\eta\le\frac1{16}.
\]
For $d\in D$, let $A_d$ be the distribution of $F(y)-F(x)$
for uniform $y\in U_{r(x)+d}$. Let $Q_d$ be the distribution of
$F(z)-F(w)$ obtained by choosing $w$ uniformly in $W$ and then $z$
uniformly in $U_{r(w)+d}$. Independent samples from $A_d,Q_d$ agree
with probability at least $31/32$. Their agreement probability is no
larger than the greatest atom of $A_d$. That distribution therefore has
a unique atom $\psi(d)$ of mass at least $31/32$.

The event that the first sample equals $\psi(d)$ and the second does not
is contained in the disagreement event. Independence gives
\[
 \frac{31}{32}\,
 Q_d\bigl(H\setminus\{\psi(d)\}\bigr)\le\frac1{32}.
\]
The probability on the left is precisely
$\mathbb E_{w\in W}e_d(w)$, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two paths with a common endpoint]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:paths}
Assume $W$ is a nonempty union of whole fibers and its positive fiber
sizes vary by a factor of at most two. Let $D\subseteq G$ and suppose
that $U_{r(w)+d}$ is nonempty whenever $w\in W,d\in D$. Suppose also
that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:near-invariance}
 |\{w\in W:r(w)+d\in r(W)\}|\ge(1-\eta)|W|
 \qquad(d\in D).
\end{equation}
If $\psi:D\to H$ satisfies
$\mathbb E_{w\in W}e_d(w)\le e$ for every $d\in D$, with $e_d$
defined as in \eqref{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:edge-average}, and
\[
 6e+2\eta<1,
\]
then $\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order two.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose $w$ uniformly in $W$ and $z$ uniformly in $U_{r(w)+a}$,
where $a\in D$. The probability that $z\notin W$ is at most $\eta$.
For any particular $z\in W$, its probability under this sampling law is
\[
 \frac{\mathbf 1_{\{r(z)-a\in r(W)\}}}{|W|}
 \frac{|U_{r(z)-a}|}{|U_{r(z)}|}
 \le\frac2{|W|}.
\]
Consequently every nonnegative function $h$ on $W$ obeys
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:transport-domination}
 \mathbb E\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{z\in W\}}h(z)\bigr]
 \le2\mathbb E_{z\in W}h(z).
\end{equation}

Fix $a,b,c,d\in D$ with $a+b=c+d=s$. Choose one common starting point
$w$ uniformly in $W$ and one common endpoint $u$ uniformly in
$U_{r(w)+s}$. If this endpoint fiber is empty, use a dummy point and
declare both paths unsuccessful. Choose intermediates independently
from $U_{r(w)+a}$ and $U_{r(w)+c}$.

For the path with increments $(a,b)$, the first edge fails with
probability at most $e$, and the intermediate lies outside $W$ with
probability at most $\eta$. When the intermediate is in $W$, the endpoint
fiber is nonempty by hypothesis. The second edge fails with probability
at most $2e$, by \eqref{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:transport-domination}. Thus the total
failure probability is at most $3e+\eta$. The other path has the same
bound. Since $6e+2\eta<1$, both paths succeed with positive probability.
On that event,
\[
 \psi(a)+\psi(b)=F(u)-F(w)=\psi(c)+\psi(d).
\]
This proves the required exact relation. The common endpoint, rather
than two separately sampled endpoint values, is what makes the
conclusion valid.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact modes on a dense set of directions]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:exact-modes}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:mode}, assume in addition that
$W$ is a union of whole fibers with size ratio at most two and that
\eqref{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:near-invariance} holds for every $d\in B$. Then the map
$\psi:D\to H$ produced there is a Freiman homomorphism of order two.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:paths} with $e=1/31$, since
$6/31+2^{-20}<1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Regular Bohr sets and dense difference extension}

We recall the one-scale argument and extension criterion from the prior
Bohr report \cite{repo28twelve}, in the exact form used here. For a finite set
$K$ of characters write
\[
 B(K,\rho)=
 \{g\in G:\|\arg\chi(g)/(2\pi)\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}
                      \le\rho\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[One selected radius]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:bohr-radius}
Let $1\le k=|K|\le R$ and $0<\rho_0\le1/2$. There exists
$\rho\in[\rho_0/2,\rho_0]$ such that, with
\[
 B=B(K,\rho),\qquad
 C=B\left(K,\frac{\rho_0}{6R}\right),\qquad
 \beta=4^{-1/3}>\frac58,
\]
one has $|B\cap(B+t)|\ge\beta|B|$ for every $t\in C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Partition each coordinate interval $[-\rho_0,\rho_0]$ into four
intervals of length $\rho_0/2$. Any two group points in the same product
cell differ by an element of $B(K,\rho_0/2)$. Translating each nonempty
cell by one of its points gives
\[
 |B(K,\rho_0)|\le4^k|B(K,\rho_0/2)|.
\]
Set $\tau=\rho_0/(6k)$. Among the $3k$ adjacent steps from
$\rho_0/2$ to $\rho_0$, some step has cardinality ratio at most
$4^{1/3}$. At its upper endpoint $\rho$,
\[
 |B(K,\rho-\tau)|\ge\beta|B(K,\rho)|.
\]
For $t\in C\subseteq B(K,\tau)$, the inner set is contained in
$B\cap(B+t)$, proving the result.
\end{proof}

The radius in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:bohr-radius} is selected before constructing
the anchor and $W$. The anchor errors are then defined using this actual
$B$; no subsequent restriction of their averaging domain is needed.

\begin{lemma}[Dense Freiman extension]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:dense-extension}
Let $D\subseteq B\subseteq G$, with $B\ne\varnothing$, satisfy
$|B\setminus D|\le|B|/16$.
Suppose $|B\cap(B+t)|\ge\beta|B|$ for $t\in C$, where $\beta>5/8$,
and $\psi:D\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order two. Then
$C\subseteq D-D$, and the difference map induced by $\psi$ restricts
to a Freiman homomorphism $\Psi:C\to H$ of order two. If $0\in C$,
then $\Psi(0)=0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The Freiman property makes
$\Delta(a-b)=\psi(a)-\psi(b)$ well defined on $D-D$. For $t\in C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:dense-overlap}
 |D\cap(D-t)|\ge\left(\beta-\frac18\right)|B|>\frac{|B|}{2}.
\end{equation}
In particular $C\subseteq D-D$, so define $\Psi=\Delta|_C$.

For $c,d\in C$, the intersection
$D\cap(D-c)\cap(D-c-d)$ has size at least
\[
 \left(1-\frac3{16}-2(1-\beta)\right)|B|>\frac{|B|}{16}.
\]
Indeed the chain of ambient translates $B,B-c,B-c-d$ loses at most
the two boundary sizes for $c$ and $d$, and the three translated hole
sets lose at most $3|B|/16$. A point in the intersection proves that
$c+d\in D-D$ and
\[
 \Delta(c+d)=\Psi(c)+\Psi(d).
\]
This statement holds even when $c+d\notin C$. Two equal pair-sums from
$C$ therefore have equal $\Psi$ pair-sums. Also $\Delta(0)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Averaged rows give exact compatibility]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:pullback}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:dense-extension}, suppose $W$ is
nonempty, all fibers $U_{r(w)+d}$ for $w\in W,d\in D$ are nonempty,
and \eqref{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:edge-average} holds. Then there is $W_1\subseteq W$
with
\[
 |W_1|\ge\frac{27}{31}|W|>\frac56|W|
\]
such that
\[
 F(w_1)-F(w_2)=\Psi(r(w_1)-r(w_2))
\]
whenever $w_1,w_2\in W_1$ and $r(w_1)-r(w_2)\in C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set
\[
 W_1=\left\{w\in W:
       \mathbb E_{d\in D}e_d(w)\le\frac14\right\}.
\]
The average row error is at most $1/31$, so Markov's inequality gives
the stated size. Fix $w_1,w_2\in W_1$ and put
$c=r(w_1)-r(w_2)\in C$. For $d\in I=D\cap(D-c)$, the target fibers
$U_{r(w_1)+d}$ and $U_{r(w_2)+d+c}$ coincide. Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{d\in I}\bigl(e_d(w_1)+e_{d+c}(w_2)\bigr)
 \le\frac{|D|}{2}<|I|,
\]
where the strict inequality follows from \eqref{gsr:en:28:lm:eq:dense-overlap}.
For some $d\in I$ the two conditional errors therefore sum to less
than one. Their good subsets of the common nonempty fiber intersect.
At a point $z$ in the intersection,
\[
 F(z)-F(w_1)=\psi(d),\qquad
 F(z)-F(w_2)=\psi(d+c).
\]
Subtracting proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The auxiliary invariance requirement]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:remark:invariance}
Suppose the ambient fibers change by at most $\sigma M_U$ under
directions in $B$, the anchor fiber has size at least
$\alpha^2M_U/2$, and the fibers on $W$ have size at least
$\alpha^2M_U/32$. The nonemptiness and fourfold weight comparison in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:mode} follow from $\sigma\le\alpha^2/96$: each translated
fiber lies between two thirds and four thirds of its original size.
The smaller auxiliary condition appearing in the original Lemma~10.6
is therefore unnecessary for this replacement. The component theorem
supplies the averaged anchor error, and the present lemmas finish the
exactification directly.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A higher-order conclusion at the same parameters}
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:sec:higher-order}

The full ambient invariance in the present application permits the
prefix-sensitive criterion of the prior transport report \cite{repo28seven}.
We give the short specialization, because it strengthens the output
without changing the spectrum, radius, or retained set.

\begin{lemma}[Ambient invariance and longer paths]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:long-paths}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:paths}, write $R_s=|U_s|$ and assume
$R(w)\ge m>0$ for $w\in W$. Suppose in addition that
\[
 |R_{s+d}-R_s|\le L\qquad(s\in G,d\in D),
\]
and put $\tau=L/m$. For any integer $k\ge2$,
\[
 \bigl(2k+\tau k(k-1)\bigr)(e+\eta)<1
\]
implies that $\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use the unnormalized subprobability law of the paths that have survived
each prefix; never condition the law to have total mass one.
At a prefix of $j$ directions, the mass of a point $z\in W$ is at most
\[
 \frac{1}{|W|}\frac{R_{r(z)-s_j}}{R_{r(z)}}
 \le\frac{1+j\tau}{|W|},
\]
where $s_j$ is the sum of those directions. The last inequality follows
by applying the ambient invariance bound $j$ times. Stop a path when it
leaves $W$ or an edge has the wrong label. For a uniformly sampled source
in $W$, the probability of either event on a fixed direction is at most
$e+\eta$. The marginal domination at prefix $j$ therefore bounds the
failure probability of a length-$k$ path by
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1+j\tau)(e+\eta)
 =\left(k+\frac{\tau k(k-1)}2\right)(e+\eta).
\]
Compare two length-$k$ paths with the same initial and terminal indices,
using a common sampled initial point and a common sampled endpoint as
in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:paths}. The displayed hypothesis ensures simultaneous
success with positive probability. Their telescoping label sums agree,
which proves the order-$k$ Freiman property.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Order of the induced difference map]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:difference-order}
If $D$ is nonempty and $\psi:D\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order
$m\ge2$, its induced difference map on $D-D$ is a Freiman homomorphism
of order $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ and takes the value zero at zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Order $m$ implies every lower order by padding the two sides with copies
of one fixed point of $D$. Order two makes the difference map well
defined. A relation between two sums of $q$ differences from $D-D$
expands, after moving their negative terms to the opposite side, into a
relation between two sums of $2q$ points of $D$. Applying the order-$2q$
property proves the conclusion whenever $2q\le m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Order seven on the Bohr neighborhood]
\label{gsr:en:28:lm:order-seven}
Under the parameters of the main construction,
\[
 \eta=2^{-21},\quad e=\frac1{31},\quad
 m=\frac{\alpha^2M_U}{32},\quad L=\sigma M_U,\quad
 \sigma=\frac{(\log2)\alpha^2}{2^{32}(1+\alpha)},
\]
the map $\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order fifteen on $D$.
Its difference map is a Freiman homomorphism of order seven on $D-D$;
in particular, so is the final map $\Psi$ on $C$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Here $\tau=32\sigma/\alpha^2<2^{-27}$ and
\[
 \left(30+210\cdot2^{-27}\right)
 \left(\frac1{31}+2^{-21}\right)<1.
\]
The last inequality is a rational comparison. Apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:long-paths} with $k=15$, followed by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:difference-order}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fourier smoothing and the proof of the main theorem\srctag{28}}]{Fourier smoothing and the proof of the main theorem}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d6}
\srcnote{28}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:28:sec:assembly}

We now apply the component and repair lemmas to a fourfold difference
domain. This is where the order-eight assumption is used.
The Fourier smoothing estimate itself is the full-moment refinement
already present in source~12 \cite{repo28twelve}.

\begin{lemma}[Fourfold smoothing with the original spectrum]
\label{gsr:en:28:lem:smoothing}
Let \(M>0\), \(0<\alpha\le1\), and \(0\le g(s)\le M\) on \(G\),
with \(\sum_sg(s)=\alpha MN\),
and put
\[
 h=g*\widetilde g*g*\widetilde g,\qquad
 \widetilde g(s)=g(-s),\qquad L=\alpha^3M^4N^3.
\]
For \(\lambda>0\), let
\(\Gamma=\{\chi:|\widehat g(\chi)|\ge\lambda MN\}\).
Then
\[
 |\Gamma|\le\alpha/\lambda^2,\qquad
 \sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^4\le\alpha^3M^4N^4.
\]
If \(d\in\Bhr(\Gamma,\rho_0)\), then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:smoothing-bound}
 |h(s+d)-h(s)|
 \le\left(2\pi\rho_0+\frac{2\lambda^2}{\alpha^2}\right)L
 \qquad(s\in G).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since \(g\ge0\), \(|\widehat g(\chi)|\le\alpha MN\).
Also Parseval and \(g^2\le Mg\) give
\[
 \sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^2\le\alpha M^2N^2.
\]
The cardinality bound and the fourth-moment bound follow immediately.
For the small-spectrum tail,
\[
 \sum_{\chi\notin\Gamma}|\widehat g(\chi)|^4
 \le\lambda^2M^2N^2\sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^2
 \le\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^4.
\]
Fourier inversion gives
\[
 h(s+d)-h(s)=\frac1N\sum_\chi
 |\widehat g(\chi)|^4\chi(s)(\chi(d)-1).
\]
Use \(|\chi(d)-1|\le2\pi\rho_0\) on \(\Gamma\), and at most
two on its complement. Division by \(L\) yields
equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:smoothing-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main}]
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:main-schedule}
 \eta_0=2^{-21},\qquad
 \sigma=\frac{(\log2)\alpha^2}{2^{32}(1+\alpha)},\qquad
 \lambda^2=\frac{\sigma\alpha^2}{4},\qquad
 \rho_0=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\sigma=\eta_0(\log2)\alpha^2/[2048(1+\alpha)]\).
In particular
\[
 \sigma\le\eta_0\alpha^2,\qquad
 \sigma<\alpha^2/128,\qquad
 0<\rho_0<1/2.
\]
The threshold \(\lambda\) in equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:main-schedule} is exactly
equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:28:eq:lambda-main}. Moreover
\[
 R_\alpha=\frac{\alpha}{\lambda^2}
          =\frac4{\sigma\alpha},\qquad
 \frac{\rho_0}{6R_\alpha}
          =\frac{\sigma^2\alpha}{96\pi}
          =\zeta_\alpha.
\]
The trivial character is in \(\Gamma\), since
\(\lambda<\alpha\). Thus \(1\le|\Gamma|\le R_\alpha\).

Form the finite domain
\[
 U=X^4,\quad
 r_U(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=r(x_1)+r(x_2)-r(x_3)-r(x_4),
\]
and define \(F:U\to H\) by the same signed expression in \(\phi\).
Its cardinality and fibre bound are
\[
 |U|=|X|^4=\alpha LN,\qquad
 |U_s|\le L,\qquad L=\alpha^3M^4N^3.
\]
For the bound on a fibre, choose any three of the four points and
then choose the fourth in one specified fibre of \(X\).
Its fibre-count function is the \(h\) of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lem:smoothing}.

An order-two relation on \(U\) expands into an order-eight relation
on \(X\). More precisely, reorder its sixteen independent coordinates
to put its eight positive and eight negative occurrences on opposite
sides. This is a bijection between the two sets of tested tuples and
preserves success and failure. Consequently \(F\) is a
\((1-\eta_0)\)-homomorphism of order two.

By lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lem:smoothing} and equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:main-schedule}, the domain \(U\)
is \((\Bhr(\Gamma,\rho_0),\sigma L)\)-invariant. Apply
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:bohr-radius} now, before selecting any anchor, to obtain
\[
 B=\Bhr(\Gamma,\rho),\quad \rho\in[\rho_0/2,\rho_0],
 \qquad |B\cap(B+c)|\ge4^{-1/3}|B|\quad(c\in C).
\]
The same invariance holds on the smaller \(B\).
Apply lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:28:lem:transfer}, \ref{gsr:en:28:lem:anchor} and \ref{gsr:en:28:lem:log-selection} to \(U\),
using \(L\) in place of \(M\). They give an anchor \(x\in U\)
and a component \(W\subseteq U\) with
\[
 |W|\ge\frac{p(\alpha)\alpha}{16}|U|,\quad
 \E_W\epsilon\le960\eta_0,\quad
 R(w)\ge\alpha^2L/32,\quad R(x)\ge\alpha^2L/2.
\]
The positive fibre sizes on \(W\) vary by at most a factor of two,
and every shift in \(B\) preserves at least \(1-\eta_0\) of its points.

The shifted anchor and component fibres are nonempty.
Indeed \(\sigma\le\alpha^2/128\) makes each such fibre size lie
between \(3/4\) and \(5/4\) of its original size.
For every \(w\in W\), the largest and smallest products
\[
 |U_{r_U(x)+d}|\,|U_{r_U(w)+d}|\qquad(d\in B)
\]
have ratio at most \((5/3)^2<4\).
All hypotheses of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:mode} and corollary~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:exact-modes} follow.
We obtain \(D\subseteq B\), \(|D|\ge15|B|/16\), and an exact
Freiman map \(\psi:D\to H\) with average directional edge error at
most \(1/31\).

The extension and row-selection lemmas
lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:dense-extension} and \ref{gsr:en:28:lm:pullback} give a map \(\Psi:C\to H\)
and \(W_1\subseteq W\) satisfying
\[
 |W_1|\ge\frac{27}{31}|W|>
 \frac{5p(\alpha)\alpha}{96}|U|>
 \frac{p(\alpha)\alpha}{20}|U|.
\]
The label difference of any two points of \(W_1\) whose base difference
lies in \(C\) is given by \(\Psi\).
The stronger order-seven conclusion follows from
corollary~\ref{gsr:en:28:lm:order-seven}; its hypotheses are precisely the ambient
invariance and lower fibre size just established.

Finally average the cardinality of
\[
 Y_{x_2,x_3,x_4}=
 \{y\in X:(y,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in W_1\}
\]
over \(X^3\). Some slice has at least
\(|W_1|/|X|^3\ge p(\alpha)\alpha|X|/20\) points.
Fix it and call it \(Y\). The three fixed coordinates cancel from
both the base difference and the label difference. This gives
equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:28:eq:model-main}, and \(\Psi(0)=0\) follows from its
construction as a difference map.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Keeping the older spectrum exactly}

Some later arguments may already be organized around the old threshold.
There is no need to replace that set of frequencies in order to use
the new local model.

\begin{corollary}[Compatibility with the original threshold]
\label{gsr:en:28:cor:old-spectrum}
In the setting of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main}, let
\[
 \Gamma_{\mathrm{old}}=
 \{\chi:|\widehat g(\chi)|\ge2^{-37}\alpha^{11/2}MN\}.
\]
Then the same retained set \(Y\) has an order-seven local difference
model on \(\Bhr(\Gamma_{\mathrm{old}},\zeta_\alpha)\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The ratio of the squares of the new and old thresholds is
\[
 \frac{2^{40}\log2}{(1+\alpha)\alpha^7}>1\qquad(0<\alpha\le1).
\]
Thus \(\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_{\mathrm{old}}\) and the indicated
Bohr set is contained in \(C\). Restrict \(\Psi\).
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Against the formal statement.} The intake observed that this corollary, with Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main}, appears to give the conclusion of the formal \file{theorem_10_13} with the formal spectrum \file{domainLargeSpectrum} at the threshold $\lambda MN$, a larger radius and a larger retained set, provided the order-eight defect $2^{-21}$ here is measured as in the formal \file{DomainApproxHomOfOrder}. That normalization was not checked at the intake or at the write, so the implication is recorded as a marked question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:logselection}), not as a result; \file{theorem_10_13} is already an exact companion, so nothing formal depends on it.
\end{writenote}

The small frequency-count bound belongs to the new spectrum \(\Gamma\).
When the larger \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{old}}\) is retained for an existing
interface, the new radius and mass conclusions remain true, but its
frequency count should not be relabelled \(O(\alpha^{-3})\).

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences, comparisons, and structural limits\srctag{28}}]{Consequences, comparisons, and structural limits}\label{gsr:en:28:sec:d7}
\srcnote{28}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:28:sec:consequences}

\subsection{The retained fraction and the volume estimate}

As \(\alpha\downarrow0\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:p-asymptotic}
 \frac{\alpha p(\alpha)}{20}
 \sim \frac{(\log2)^2}{40}\,
          \frac{\alpha}{(\log(1/\alpha))^2}.
\end{equation}
This is an asymptotic formula for our \emph{guaranteed lower bound},
not an asymptotic formula for the largest possible structured subset.
The elementary Bohr volume estimate also becomes substantially stronger.

\begin{lemma}[Bohr volume]\label{gsr:en:28:lem:bohr-volume}
For \(0<u\le1\) and \(K\subseteq\widehat G\),
\[
 |\Bhr(K,u)|\ge (u/2)^{|K|}N.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Partition each circle coordinate into \(\lceil1/u\rceil\) intervals
of length at most \(u\). Some product cell contains at least
\(N/\lceil1/u\rceil^{|K|}\) group points.
Translate those points by one of them. Their differences lie in
\(\Bhr(K,u)\), and \(\lceil1/u\rceil\le2/u\).
\end{proof}

Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:28:eq:volume-main}
 |C|\ge
 N\exp\left[-R_\alpha\log\left(\frac2{\zeta_\alpha}\right)\right]
 =
 N\exp\left[-O\left(\alpha^{-3}(1+\log(1/\alpha))\right)\right].
\end{equation}
This lower bound may of course be below one at a given finite \(N\);
the actual set always contains zero. The formula records the
density dependence needed for later asymptotic estimates.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/28-log-selection-local_bounds.pdf}
\caption{Explicit sufficient bounds. The left panel compares retained
fractions with the prior fixed-spectrum source~12 bound. The right
compares the corresponding polynomial radii. Both axes are logarithmic.
These curves compare proved guarantees, not observed optimal outputs.}
\label{gsr:en:28:fig:local-bounds}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Local arithmetic progressions}

\begin{corollary}[Linear difference law on short progression segments]
\label{gsr:en:28:cor:progression}
Let \(m\) be a positive integer and
\(d\in\Bhr(\Gamma,\zeta_\alpha/m)\).
There is \(a\in H\) such that
\[
 \phi(y)-\phi(z)=ja
\]
whenever \(y,z\in Y\) and \(r(y)-r(z)=jd\), with
\(j\in\Z\) and \(-m\le j\le m\). One can take \(a=\Psi(d)\).
If \(G=H=\Z/p\Z\) for a prime \(p\), this may be written as
\(\phi(y)-\phi(z)=c(r(y)-r(z))\) for some \(c\in\Z/p\Z\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every \(jd\), \(|j|\le m\), belongs to \(C\).
The order-two Freiman relation
\((j-1)d+d=jd+0\) and \(\Psi(0)=0\) give
\(\Psi(jd)=j\Psi(d)\), by induction; use
\(jd+(-jd)=0+0\) for negative indices.
The model identity finishes the first assertion.
In the prime cyclic case choose \(c=\Psi(d)/d\) if \(d\ne0\).
If \(d=0\), all the tested differences and their labels vanish.
\end{proof}

In an arbitrary abelian group the expression \(ja\) is the correct
conclusion. Division by the direction \(d\) is neither needed nor
generally meaningful.

\subsection{Several domains and a common set of directions}

\begin{corollary}[Simultaneous local models]\label{gsr:en:28:cor:simultaneous}
Suppose \(t\) domains \(X^{(i)}\) over the same \(G\) satisfy the
hypotheses of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main}, with densities
\(\alpha_i\ge\alpha_0>0\), possibly different fibre bounds and targets.
Let \(\Gamma_i\) be their respective original-domain spectra.
For
\[
 C_*=\Bhr\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^t\Gamma_i,\zeta_{\alpha_0}\right)
\]
each domain has an order-seven exact local model on \(C_*\), retaining
at least \(\alpha_0p(\alpha_0)/20\) of its points.
The union of defining frequencies has size at most \(tR_{\alpha_0}\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The functions \(\alpha p(\alpha)\) and
\(\alpha^5/(1+\alpha)^2\) are increasing on \((0,1]\);
\((1+\alpha)/\alpha^3\) is decreasing.
Apply the theorem separately and restrict each difference map to \(C_*\).
\end{proof}

This supplies compatible directions, not identical label maps.
The distinction prevents a false inference of a single common slope
across unrelated domains.

\subsection{What is still required for a global bound}

The theorem gives explicit replacements for a local Section~10 interface.
A new bound for progression-free sets would additionally require an
end-to-end argument propagating these parameters through the
bilinear and multilinear extraction, the phase-removal step, and the
density-increment iteration. The inspected formalization explicitly
records outstanding obligations in those stages \cite{repo28}.

The new spectrum threshold is larger than the old one. This helps
frequency counts, but any later theorem whose parameters were chosen
using the old threshold must be reconsidered or used through
corollary~\ref{gsr:en:28:cor:old-spectrum}. Likewise, an improved local retained fraction
does not automatically repair common partitions, integer representatives
of boxes, or an incorrect closing comparison. The research agenda below
lists those propagation tasks as open work.
