\section[{Sampling, independence, and Fourier normalization\srctag{33}}]{Sampling, independence, and Fourier normalization}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:normalization}
\srcnote{33}{Section 2}

\subsection{Uniform sampling on a balanced relation}

Let $\mathcal X_s\subset G^s$ be the solutions of
\eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:horizontal}. One may sample them by choosing the first
$s-1$ coordinates independently and solving uniquely for the last.
Thus $|\mathcal X_s|=|G|^{s-1}$.

\begin{lemma}[Proper-coordinate independence]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:independence}
For every proper subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\dots,s\}$, the coordinates
$(x_i)_{i\in I}$ of a uniform element of $\mathcal X_s$ are independent
and uniform. Consequently, conditional on any fixed $h$, the pairs
$(x_i,y_i)$ in any proper subset of positions are independent and uniform
on $G\times H$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix the coordinates in $I$. Among the remaining positions choose one,
$j$, to solve for. The other $s-|I|-1$ coordinates may be chosen freely.
The coefficient of $x_j$ in the balanced relation is $1$ or $-1$, both
invertible as endomorphisms of any abelian group. Hence there are exactly
$|G|^{s-|I|-1}$ completions, independently of the specified coordinates.
The statement about pairs follows because the $y_i$ are independent of
all $x_i$ and of one another.
\end{proof}

The total number of ordered arrangements is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:total-count}
 |G|^{s-1}|H|^{s+1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, when $G=H=\Z_N$, it is $N^{2s}$: $N^8$ for $s=4$ and
$N^{32}$ for $s=16$. The $s$ pairs are not generally jointly independent;
the missing last degree of independence will be important in the sharp
local estimate.

\subsection{An exact moment identity}

For a finite abelian group $L$, write $\widehat L$ for its character group,
with characters taking values on the complex unit circle. On $G$ use
\[
 \widehat g(\xi)=\E_{x\in G}g(x)\overline{\xi(x)}.
\]
Thus Fourier coefficients are normalized, while sums over frequencies
below are not. For $\chi\in\widehat K$ and $h\in H$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:kernel}
 g_{\chi,h}(x)=\E_{y\in H}\chi(D_h\phi(x,y)).
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Moment formula]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:moment}
For every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:moment}
 1-\eps_s(\phi)
  =\E_{h\in H}\E_{\chi\in\widehat K}
    \sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^s.
\end{equation}
Consequently $\eps_{s'}(\phi)\ge\eps_s(\phi)$ for even $s'\ge s\ge4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Character orthogonality on $K$ writes the indicator that the signed sum
in \eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:test} is zero as its character average. For fixed $h$ and
$\chi$, averaging the independent $y_i$ leaves
\[
 \E_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X_s}
   \prod_{i\le s/2}g_{\chi,h}(x_i)
   \prod_{i>s/2}\overline{g_{\chi,h}(x_i)}.
\]
Insert the Fourier expansion of each factor. Orthogonality in the
$s-1$ free horizontal coordinates forces the same Fourier frequency in
all factors. The resulting sum is
$\sum_\xi|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^s$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:moment}. Since
$|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|\le\E_x|g_{\chi,h}(x)|\le1$,
each term decreases when the even exponent increases.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The use of a normalized character average over $\widehat K$ but an
unnormalized sum over $\widehat G$ is deliberate. The constant function
has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient, equal to one, so the right side
of \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:moment} is one for a perfectly respected test.
\end{remark}


\subsection{A cycle bound and a direct refinement of Lemma 12.3}

The usual moment interpolation can be supplemented by information that
each individual Fourier square-mass is at most one. This yields a useful
linear bound near complete agreement.

\begin{lemma}[Cycle deficit inequality]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:cycle}
If $a_1,\dots,a_t\ge0$, $\sum_i a_i\le1$, and $r\ge2$ is an integer,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cycle}
 1-\sum_i a_i^r\le\frac r2\left(1-\sum_i a_i^2\right).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First suppose the $a_i$ sum to one. Draw $r$ independent labels
$X_1,\dots,X_r$ with this distribution and set $X_{r+1}=X_1$.
Unless all labels agree, at least two neighboring pairs on this cycle
disagree. This also holds for $r=2$, counting both directed edges.
Therefore
\[
 2\Prob[\text{not all }X_i\text{ agree}]
 \le\sum_{j=1}^r\Prob[X_j\ne X_{j+1}],
\]
which is \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cycle}. For total mass $A\le1$, adjoin one
label of mass $b=1-A$. Applying the probability-vector case and
rearranging gives
\[
 1-\sum_i a_i^r\le\frac r2\left(1-\sum_i a_i^2\right)
                   +b^r-\frac r2b^2.
\]
Since $0\le b\le1$ and $r\ge2$, the last two terms sum to a nonpositive
quantity. This proves the subprobability version without a limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharp cross-order defect factor]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:cross-order}
For every full-domain function and every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cross-order}
 \eps_4(\phi)\le\eps_s(\phi)\le\frac{s}{4}\eps_4(\phi).
\end{equation}
The upper coefficient $s/4$ is optimal, even on common odd prime cyclic
groups. It requires no small-error hypothesis.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first inequality is Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:moment}. For fixed
$h,\chi$, set $a_\xi=|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^2$. Parseval gives
$\sum_\xi a_\xi=\E_x|g_{\chi,h}(x)|^2\le1$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:cycle} with $r=s/2$, then average over $h,\chi$
and use \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:moment}. Optimality follows from either extremal
family of Section~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:examples}, where
$\eps_s/\eps_4\to s/4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Supplement to Gowers's arrangement amplification]
\label{gsr:en:33:ras:cor:gowers-amplification}
Let $A\subset\Z_N^2$, and let $\phi:A\to\Z_N$. Suppose there are
$\theta N^8$ respected pairs of vertical parallelograms, counted with
Gowers's order and repetition conventions. Then there are at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:gowers-improved}
 \max\{\theta^7,\,4\theta-3\}\,N^{32}
\end{equation}
respected eight-arrangements. More generally, if $\theta_s$ denotes the
number of respected $s/2$-arrangements divided by $N^{2s}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-moments}
 \theta_s\ge\max\left\{\theta_4^{s/2-1},\,
                  \frac{s}{4}\theta_4-\left(\frac{s}{4}-1\right)\right\}.
\end{equation}
The $\theta_s$ are ambient-normalized counts, not conditional fractions
among arrangements contained in $A$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:kernel}, replace the summand by zero unless both
$(x,y)$ and $(x,y+h)$ lie in $A$. Orthogonality still gives the moment
formula for $\theta_s$, and $|g_{\chi,h}(x)|\le1$ still holds.
The cycle argument proves the second term of
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-moments}.
For completeness, let $a_\xi=|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^2$ and
$M_j=\E_{h,\chi}\sum_\xi a_\xi^j$. Then $M_1\le1$, $M_2=\theta_4$,
and $M_{s/2}=\theta_s$. H\"older interpolation gives, for $r=s/2>2$,
\[
 M_2\le M_1^{(r-2)/(r-1)}M_r^{1/(r-1)}.
\]
If $M_1=0$ everything is zero; otherwise
$M_r\ge M_2^{r-1}/M_1^{r-2}\ge M_2^{r-1}$. For $r=2$ the statement is
an identity. Taking $s=16$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:gowers-improved}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (checked at the write at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}). \file{lemma_12_3} (\file{Sections12\_13.lean}, line~151) asks $\theta^7N^{32}\le$ \file{respectedArrangementCount}~$8$ from $\theta N^8\le$ \file{parallelogramPairCount}; its exact companion is \file{lemma_12_3_holds} (\file{Proofs12HigherArrangements.lean}, line~334). The linear branch $4\theta-3$ exceeds $\theta^7$ exactly for $\theta\in(0.8045539\ldots,1)$. That this corollary strengthens the formal conclusion under the same hypothesis depends on matching the repetition and $h=0$ conventions of the two formal counts with those here, which is not checked: a formalization candidate, not formalized. The branch $\theta^7$ is Gowers's; source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification} is its collision-sensitive form.
\end{writenote}

The first term in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:gowers-improved} is Gowers's
Lemma 12.3. The second improves its near-one regime without changing
its hypotheses; for instance, at $\theta=9/10$ it gives $3/5$ in place
of $(9/10)^7=4782969/10^7$. The linear coefficient four is sharp at
$\theta=1$, by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:cross-order}. For smaller
$\theta$ the original power bound can be stronger, which is why the
maximum is retained. This elementary cycle estimate is supplementary;
we do not claim it is the optimal complete moment envelope.

\subsection{Exact convolution counts}

For cyclic groups $G=\Z_n$, $H=\Z_m$, $K=\Z_q$, put
\[
 M_h(x,z)=|\{y\in\Z_m:D_h\phi(x,y)=z\}|.
\]
Let convolution on $\Z_n\times\Z_q$ be unnormalized. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:integer-counter}
 \Res_s(\phi)=\sum_{h\in\Z_m}\sum_{(x,z)\in\Z_n\times\Z_q}
       \big(M_h^{*(s/2)}(x,z)\big)^2
\end{equation}
is the exact number of respected arrangements.
Indeed, the convolution coefficient counts ordered half-arrangements
with prescribed horizontal sum and prescribed derivative sum; squaring
matches two halves with the same two sums. Dividing by
$n^{s-1}m^{s+1}$ gives $1-\eps_s$.
This identity permits exact tests with large $s$ without enumerating
all $2s$ point occurrences and without rounding Fourier coefficients.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A noisy homomorphism lemma with auxiliary labels\srctag{33}}]{A noisy homomorphism lemma with auxiliary labels}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:noisy}
\srcnote{33}{Section 3}

The first objective is only a coarse linear repair estimate. The sharp
coefficient will come later from the geometry of a nearest model.
A small technical point matters: each query in an arrangement has an
independent vertical base point. Randomly choosing one representative
value for each horizontal coordinate would not preserve this query law
when coordinates repeat. The next lemma keeps those auxiliary labels
independent throughout.

\begin{lemma}[Noisy homomorphism correction]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:noisy-hom}
Let $U,V$ be finite abelian groups, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set,
and let $F:U\times S\to V$. Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:noisy-error}
 e=\Prob_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
   [F(u,\alpha)+F(v,\beta)\ne F(u+v,\gamma)]<\frac16.
\end{equation}
Then there is a homomorphism $L:U\to V$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:noisy-bound}
 \Prob_{u,\alpha}[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]\le\frac{e}{1-2e}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed $z\in U$, consider the random variable
\[
 A_z(y;\alpha,\beta)=F(z+y,\alpha)-F(y,\beta).
\]
Two independent copies of $A_z$ agree with probability at least $1-2e$.
To prove this, introduce an independent label $\gamma$ and compare
\begin{align*}
 F(z+y,\alpha)+F(y',\beta')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma),\\
 F(y,\beta)+F(z+y',\alpha')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma).
\end{align*}
Each equality has failure probability $e$, since its two group inputs
are independent uniform elements even with $z$ fixed. If both hold,
$A_z(y;\alpha,\beta)=A_z(y';\alpha',\beta')$.

Write $p_z(t)=\Prob[A_z=t]$. Then
\[
 \max_t p_z(t)\ge\sum_t p_z(t)^2\ge1-2e.
\]
In particular, $A_z$ has a unique most likely value $L(z)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:mode-prob}
 \Prob[A_z=L(z)]\ge1-2e\qquad\text{for every }z.
\end{equation}
There is a pointwise identity
\[
 A_{z+z'}(y;\alpha,\beta)
 =A_z(y+z';\alpha,\gamma)+A_{z'}(y;\gamma,\beta).
\]
For fixed $z,z'$, each of these three random variables equals its mode
except with probability at most $2e$. Since $6e<1$, all three are
simultaneously equal to their modes for at least one choice of labels
and $y$. Their identity gives
$L(z+z')=L(z)+L(z')$. Thus $L$ is a homomorphism.

Finally, \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:noisy-error} also says
\[
 e=\Prob_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
       [F(u,\alpha)\ne A_u(v;\gamma,\beta)].
\]
Conditional on $u,\alpha$, whenever $F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)$, the event
$A_u(v;\gamma,\beta)=L(u)$ forces a failure. This event has probability
at least $1-2e$ and its labels are independent of $\alpha$. Therefore
$e\ge(1-2e)\Prob[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]$, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Noisy affine correction]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:noisy-affine}
Let $F:G\times S\to K$. Let $e$ be the probability that
\[
 F(x_1,\alpha_1)+F(x_2,\alpha_2)
 \ne F(x_3,\alpha_3)+F(x_4,\alpha_4),
\]
where $x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4$ is uniformly sampled and all four labels are
independent uniform elements of $S$. There is an affine map
$A:G\to K$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:affine-six}
 \Prob_{x,\alpha}[F(x,\alpha)\ne A(x)]\le6e.
\end{equation}
If $e<1/6$, the stronger bound $e/(1-2e)$ holds.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $e\ge1/6$, any affine map gives \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:affine-six}.
Suppose $e<1/6$. Condition on $(x_4,\alpha_4)=(z,t)$ and choose an
anchor whose conditional error $e_0$ is at most $e$. Conditional on this
anchor, write $x_1=z+u$, $x_2=z+v$, $x_3=z+u+v$, with $u,v$ independent
uniform. The function
$Q(u,\alpha)=F(z+u,\alpha)-F(z,t)$ has noisy homomorphism error $e_0$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:noisy-hom} gives a homomorphism $L$ with error at most
$e_0/(1-2e_0)\le e/(1-2e)$. Translate back:
$A(x)=L(x-z)+F(z,t)$ is affine. For $e<1/6$, the stronger bound is
at most $3e/2$, and in particular at most $6e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Separation of affine maps]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:separation}
If $A,A':G\to K$ are distinct affine maps, then
$\Prob_x[A(x)\ne A'(x)]\ge1/2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The difference has the form $L(x)+c$. If $L=0$ and $c\ne0$, it is
nonzero everywhere. If $L\ne0$, its zero set is either empty or a coset
of $\ker L$. The index of that kernel is at least two. Thus its zero set
has density at most $1/2$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Synchronizing derivatives into one biadditive model\srctag{33}}]{Synchronizing derivatives into one biadditive model}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:coarse}
\srcnote{33}{Section 4}

A separately chosen affine approximation to each derivative need not
initially be compatible with addition of increments. The derivative
cocycle and affine separation supply exactly the required compatibility.

\begin{theorem}[A coarse full-product decoder]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:coarse}
If $\eps_4(\phi)<1/216$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:coarse}
 \dd(\phi)\le
 6\eps_4(\phi)+\frac{36\eps_4(\phi)}{1-72\eps_4(\phi)}
 \le60\eps_4(\phi).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $e_h$ be the conditional failure probability of the $s=4$ test at
increment $h$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:noisy-affine} to
$F_h(x,y)=D_h\phi(x,y)$, with auxiliary-label set $S=H$.
Choose $A_h\in\Aff(G,K)$ such that
\[
 d_h:=\Prob_{x,y}[D_h\phi(x,y)\ne A_h(x)]\le6e_h.
\]
Set $d=\E_h d_h$. Then $d\le6\eps_4(\phi)<1/36$.

The exact derivative identity is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:derivative-cocycle}
 D_{h+k}\phi(x,y)=D_h\phi(x,y+k)+D_k\phi(x,y).
\end{equation}
If all three approximations hold at these three queries, then
$A_{h+k}(x)=A_h(x)+A_k(x)$. Averaging the union bound gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cocycle-error}
 \Prob_{h,k,x}[A_{h+k}(x)\ne A_h(x)+A_k(x)]\le3d.
\end{equation}
For fixed $h,k$, either the two affine maps in this comparison are
identical or their disagreement density is at least $1/2$, by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:separation}. Hence
\[
 \eta:=\Prob_{h,k}[A_{h+k}\ne A_h+A_k]\le6d<1/6.
\]
The affine maps form a finite abelian group under pointwise addition.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:noisy-hom}, now with a singleton label set, gives a
homomorphism
\[
 \mathcal A:H\longrightarrow\Aff(G,K)
\]
whose disagreement fraction with $h\mapsto A_h$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:q-bound}
 q\le\frac{\eta}{1-2\eta}\le\frac{6d}{1-12d}.
\end{equation}

Split each affine map into its constant and homomorphism parts by setting
\[
 \ell(y)=\mathcal A(y)(0),\qquad
 B(x,y)=\mathcal A(y)(x)-\mathcal A(y)(0).
\]
Because $\mathcal A$ is a homomorphism, $\ell$ is additive and $B$ is
additive in $y$; because $\mathcal A(y)$ is affine, $B$ is additive in $x$.
For the residual
$r(x,y)=\phi(x,y)-B(x,y)-\ell(y)$, we have
\[
 \Prob_{h,x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0]\le d+q.
\]
Indeed, outside the $q$-fraction of bad increments, disagreement is
bounded by the original derivative error.

For fixed $x$, write $p_x(t)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=t]$. The pair $(y,y+h)$ is
independent uniform after averaging over $y,h$. Thus
\[
 \Prob_{h,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0]=1-\sum_t p_x(t)^2
 \ge1-\max_t p_x(t).
\]
Choose $a(x)$ to be a most likely value of $r(x,y)$. The resulting model
$a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$ has distance at most $d+q$. Using
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:q-bound} and $d\le6\eps_4$ proves the first inequality in
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:coarse}. Finally,
$1-72\eps_4>2/3$, so the fraction in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:coarse} is at most
$54\eps_4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact classification]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:cor:classification}
For any even $s\ge4$, $\eps_s(\phi)=0$ if and only if
$\phi\in\Vthirtythree(G,H;K)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every model passes every test. Conversely, the moment monotonicity of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:moment} gives $\eps_4\le\eps_s=0$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:coarse} then gives $\dd(\phi)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where the constants are spent]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:rem:constants}
The coarse constant $60$ is not the final repair coefficient. It merely
puts a nearest model in a small neighborhood where a much more precise
counting argument applies. The losses are explicitly localized: the
factor $6$ for derivative-wise affine correction, the three terms in the
cocycle, affine separation by $1/2$, and one more majority correction.
No density exponent or group-size dependence is hidden in this step.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp local defect inequalities\srctag{33}}]{Sharp local defect inequalities}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:sharp}
\srcnote{33}{Section 5}

\subsection{The geometry of a nearest model}

Fix a nearest model $\psi=a+B+\ell$ and let $r=\phi-\psi$.
For fixed $B,\ell$, each row constant can be optimized independently.
We may therefore choose the nearest model so that zero is a most likely
value of $r(x,y)$ in every row. Write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:row-profile}
 p_x(z)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=z],\qquad
 \dd_x=1-p_x(0),\qquad \dd=\E_x\dd_x.
\end{equation}
Adding or subtracting an exact model does not change the outcome of any
arrangement test. Thus $\eps_s(r)=\eps_s(\phi)$.

For each increment put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:t-profile}
 t_h=\Prob_{x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0],\qquad
 \overline t=\E_h t_h.
\end{equation}
The following two simple inequalities capture the difference between
pointwise corruption and concentrated corruption of a few rows.

\begin{lemma}[Derivative profile]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:profile}
The residual of a nearest model satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:profile-bounds}
 0\le t_h\le2\dd\quad\hbox{for every }h,
 \qquad
 \overline t=\E_x\left(1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\right)\ge\dd.
\end{equation}
If in addition $\dd_x\le\kappa$ for every $x$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:row-cap}
 \overline t\ge2(1-\kappa)\dd.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero difference requires at least one of its two endpoint values
to be nonzero, so $t_h\le2\dd$ by translation invariance and the union
bound. Averaging over $h,y$ gives two independent uniform points of each
row and therefore the collision formula in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:profile-bounds}.
Since $p_x(0)=\max_zp_x(z)$,
$\sum_zp_x(z)^2\le p_x(0)$, proving $\overline t\ge\dd$.
Also
\[
 \sum_zp_x(z)^2\le(1-\dd_x)^2+\dd_x^2,
\]
because the total mass outside zero is $\dd_x$. Hence the row's
noncollision probability is at least $2\dd_x(1-\dd_x)$, which is at
least $2(1-\kappa)\dd_x$ under the extra hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exactly one erroneous edge}

\begin{lemma}[One-error probability with one missing independence degree]
\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:one-error}
Let $s\ge4$ be even. Suppose $Z_1,\dots,Z_s$ are Bernoulli random
variables with common mean $t$, and every proper subfamily is independent.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:one-error}
 \Prob\left[\sum_{i=1}^sZ_i=1\right]\ge
 L_s(t):=st(1-t)\big((1-t)^{s-2}-t^{s-2}\big).
\end{equation}
The ratio $L_s(t)/t$, extended continuously at zero, is nonnegative and
nonincreasing on $[0,1/2]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $p_* =\Prob[Z_1=\cdots=Z_s=1]$. Independence of the first $s-1$
variables gives $p_*\le t^{s-1}$. Inclusion--exclusion at a specified
position $i$ gives
\[
 \Prob[Z_i=1,\ Z_j=0\ (j\ne i)]
   =t(1-t)^{s-1}+t^s-p_*.
\]
Here the last sign is negative because $s$ is even. Summing over $i$
and using the upper bound on $p_*$ yields
\begin{align*}
 \Prob\Big[\sum_iZ_i=1\Big]
 &\ge st(1-t)^{s-1}+st^s-st^{s-1}\\
 &=st(1-t)\big((1-t)^{s-2}-t^{s-2}\big).
\end{align*}
For $0\le t\le1/2$ this expression is nonnegative. After division by
$t$, its derivative, divided by $s$, equals
\[
 -(s-1)(1-t)^{s-2}-(s-2)t^{s-3}+(s-1)t^{s-2},
\]
which is nonpositive on that interval. The extension at zero is $s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Profile-sensitive local bound]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:profile-local}
Let $0<\dd(\phi)\le1/4$, and use the collision profile of any nearest
model chosen as in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:row-profile}. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:profile-local}
 \eps_s(\phi)\ge\frac{\overline t}{\dd}\,F_s(\dd)
 \ge F_s(\dd).
\end{equation}
If every row error is at most $\kappa\le1/2$, this strengthens to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:row-sparse}
 \eps_s(\phi)\ge2(1-\kappa)F_s(\dd).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At fixed $h$, let
$Z_i=\ind_{\{D_hr(x_i,y_i)\ne0\}}$. By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:independence}, these variables satisfy the hypotheses
of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:one-error}, with mean $t_h$.
If exactly one difference is nonzero, the signed sum of differences is
nonzero in $K$, so the arrangement fails. Therefore its conditional
failure probability is at least $L_s(t_h)$.

Because $0\le t_h\le2\dd\le1/2$, monotonicity of $L_s(t)/t$ gives
\[
 \eps_s(\phi)\ge\E_h L_s(t_h)
 \ge\frac{L_s(2\dd)}{2\dd}\E_h t_h
 =\frac{\overline t}{\dd}F_s(\dd).
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:profile}. The case $\dd=0$, omitted from the
ratio notation, has $\eps_s=0$ and satisfies the unprofiled bound as well.
\end{proof}

This proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:local-main}, except for its equality
statement, which follows from the explicit family in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:examples}. It also explains the sharp leading
constant. If errors are uniformly sparse in every row, with
$\kappa=o(1)$, the leading lower bound approaches $2s\dd$, not $s\dd$.
The worst examples for the general theorem instead concentrate errors
in a small set of rows with substantial internal disagreement.

\subsection{A quadratic estimate and the global small branch}

The full expression $F_s$ is useful for local information, but a simpler
quadratic has a transparent inverse.

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic local defect]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:quadratic}
If $\dd(\phi)\le1/(2(s-1))$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:quadratic}
 \eps_s(\phi)\ge Q_s(\dd):=s\dd-2s(s-1)\dd^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At fixed $h$, let $Z_i$ be as above and set $Z=\sum_iZ_i$.
For every nonnegative integer $Z$,
$\ind_{\{Z=1\}}\ge Z-Z(Z-1)$. Pairwise independence implies
\[
 \Prob[Z=1]\ge st_h-s(s-1)t_h^2.
\]
Using $t_h\le2\dd$ and then $\overline t\ge\dd$ yields
\[
 \eps_s\ge s(1-2(s-1)\dd)\overline t
 \ge s(1-2(s-1)\dd)\dd.
\]
The last inequality uses the stated upper bound on $\dd$ to ensure that
the multiplier is nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the repair statement in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main}]
Put $\eps=\eps_s(\phi)$. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:moment} and the coarse
decoder give
\[
 \dd\le60\eps_4\le60\eps\le\frac{1}{4(s-1)}.
\]
The coarse decoder applies because $1/(240(s-1))\le1/720<1/216$.
The function $Q_s$ is increasing on
$[0,1/(4(s-1))]$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:quadratic} gives
$Q_s(\dd)\le\eps$, and the smaller root of $Q_s(v)=\eps$ is exactly
$R_s(\eps)$. Its discriminant is positive in the stated range.
Thus $\dd\le R_s(\eps)$. Taylor expansion at zero proves
\eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:main-expansion}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the coarse step cannot be skipped]
A local defect inequality alone need not imply a small distance from
small failure probability: its right side may fall again at larger
$\dd$. In particular, $F_4(1/4)=0$. The coarse decoder chooses the
correct inverse branch before we use a sharper polynomial. Omitting
this step would leave a genuine logical gap.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The cubic inverse for four differences}

\begin{corollary}[Cubic repair modulus]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:cor:cubic-inverse}
For $0\le u\le1/720$, let $\rho_4(u)$ be the unique root in $[0,1/12]$
of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-inverse}
 4v-24v^2+32v^3=u.
\end{equation}
If $\eps_4(\phi)\le1/720$, then
\begin{align}
 \dd(\phi)&\le\rho_4(\eps_4(\phi)),\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-repair}\\
 \rho_4(u)&=\frac{u}{4}+\frac{3u^2}{8}+u^3
                  +\frac{105u^4}{32}+O(u^5).\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-series}
\end{align}
The entire cubic inequality, and hence this inverse at an infinite
sequence of errors tending to zero, is attained by explicit examples.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The cubic is strictly increasing on $[0,1/12]$: its derivative
$4-48v+96v^2$ is positive there. Its endpoint values are $0$ and $5/27$,
so the specified root exists and is unique. The coarse decoder gives
$\dd\le60\eps_4\le1/12$, and the local cubic bound gives
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-repair}. Substitution of a power series in
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-inverse} gives \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cubic-series}; equivalently,
the analytic inverse theorem applies since the derivative at zero is
four. Equality follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:binary-family} below for
all sufficiently large odd $n$.
\end{proof}

For comparison, the quadratic inverse at $s=4$ starts with
$u/4+3u^2/8+9u^3/8$. The sharp cubic reduces its third coefficient from
$9/8$ to $1$. Sharpness here does not mean that every real number $u$ is
a feasible finite-group failure probability; it means that the
inequality is attained at the explicitly specified finite examples,
including examples arbitrarily close to zero.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Extremal families and optimal coefficients\srctag{33}}]{Extremal families and optimal coefficients}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:examples}
\srcnote{33}{Section 6}

\subsection{An exact binary family}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp row-defect family]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:binary-family}
Let $n\ge3$ be odd, and define
\[
 \phi_n:\Z_n\times\Z_2\longrightarrow\Z_2,
 \qquad \phi_n(x,y)=\ind_{\{0\}}(x)y.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-distance}
 \dd_n:=\dd(\phi_n)=\frac{1}{2n},
\end{equation}
and for every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-error}
 \eps_s(\phi_n)=\frac14\left[
 1-\left(1-\frac2n\right)^s-(n-1)\left(\frac2n\right)^s\right].
\end{equation}
For $s=4$ this is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-cubic}
 \eps_4(\phi_n)=\frac2n-\frac6{n^2}+\frac4{n^3}
              =4\dd_n-24\dd_n^2+32\dd_n^3.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every homomorphism $\Z_n\to\Z_2$ is zero, since $n$ is odd.
Consequently every biadditive map $\Z_n\times\Z_2\to\Z_2$ is zero,
and the exact models are $a(x)+cy$ with $c\in\Z_2$. The row at $x=0$
has slope one; the other $n-1$ rows have slope zero. If a row has the
wrong slope, changing its constant can match exactly one of its two
values. The best choice is $c=0$, with just one wrong-slope row, and its
distance is $1/(2n)$.

The increment $h=0$ always passes. At $h=1$, the derivative is
$\ind_{\{0\}}(x)$, independent of $y$. The nontrivial character of
$\Z_2$ produces
$f(x)=(-1)^{\ind_{\{0\}}(x)}$. Its normalized Fourier coefficients on
$\Z_n$ are $1-2/n$ at the trivial character and $-2/n$ at every nontrivial
character. By character orthogonality, conditional failure at $h=1$ is
\[
 \frac12\left[1-\sum_{\xi\in\widehat{\Z_n}}
                      |\widehat f(\xi)|^s\right].
\]
Average over the two increments to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-error}.
Expanding at $s=4$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-cubic}.
\end{proof}

The equality is not a rounding artifact. For this family the residual
has error $1/2$ in exactly one row, so $\overline t=\dd_n$;
$t_0=0$ and $t_1=2\dd_n$. At $s=4$, the all-four-error event has
probability $n^{-3}=t_1^3$, saturating the upper bound in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:lem:one-error}. Three zero horizontal coordinates force
the fourth to be zero. Thus a three-error event is impossible, and the
binary test fails precisely on a one-error event. All the inequalities
in the local cubic proof become equalities.

\begin{corollary}[Sharp first two asymptotic coefficients]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:cor:optimal-two}
Uniformly over finite abelian groups, the coefficients $1/s$ and
$2(s-1)/s^2$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:main-expansion} are optimal in succession.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For fixed even $s\ge4$, expansion of \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-error}, with
$\dd_n=1/(2n)$, gives
\[
 \eps_s(\phi_n)=s\dd_n-2s(s-1)\dd_n^2+O_s(\dd_n^3).
\]
The term $(n-1)(2/n)^s$ first contributes at order $\dd_n^{s-1}$,
which is at least three. Inverting the displayed expansion gives
\[
 \dd_n=\frac{\eps_s(\phi_n)}s+
       \frac{2(s-1)}{s^2}\eps_s(\phi_n)^2
       +O_s(\eps_s(\phi_n)^3).
\]
These are actual examples with errors tending to zero. They rule out a
smaller universal leading coefficient, and, with that leading
coefficient fixed, a smaller universal quadratic coefficient.
For $s=4$, \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-cubic} also attains every coefficient
of the analytic small-branch cubic inverse along this sequence.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The leading constant in Gowers's common prime setting}

The preceding family's second-order sharpness uses two-torsion, but
its leading-order obstruction is not an artifact of characteristic two.
We now keep all three groups equal to the same odd prime field.

\begin{theorem}[Prime cyclic sharpness of the leading constant]
\label{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:prime-family}
For an odd prime $p\ge5$, define
\[
 \phi_p:\F_p\times\F_p\to\F_p,
 \qquad \phi_p(x,y)=\ind_{\{0\}}(x)y.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-distance}
 \dd_p=\frac{p-1}{p^2}.
\end{equation}
Fix even $s=2m\ge4$. As $p\to\infty$ through primes,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-asymptotic}
 \eps_s(\phi_p)=s\dd_p-\frac{s(3s-2)}4\dd_p^2+O_s(\dd_p^3).
\end{equation}
In particular, the coefficient $1/s$ in the repair bound is optimal
already for common odd prime cyclic groups.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A model has the form $a(x)+(bx+c)y$. If its slope at a row agrees with
$\ind_{\{0\}}(x)$, an appropriate row constant matches all $p$ values;
otherwise it matches exactly one. The zero affine slope agrees on
$p-1$ rows. A nonconstant affine slope can agree with the zero slope on
at most one nonzero row and with slope one at $x=0$ on at most one
additional row, hence on at most two rows. Constant nonzero slopes do
no better. Since $p\ge5$, the zero affine slope is optimal and gives
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-distance}.

For the arrangement error, put $\nu=1/p$ and assume $p>m$, which is
sufficient for the asymptotic claim. The derivative is
$D_h\phi_p(x,y)=h\ind_{\{0\}}(x)$.
Let $Z_i=\ind_{\{0\}}(x_i)$. Every proper subfamily of the $Z_i$ is
independent Bernoulli$(\nu)$, whereas
\[
 \Prob[Z_1=\cdots=Z_s=1]=\nu^{s-1}.
\]
Inclusion--exclusion shows that for any subset $I$ of positions, the
probability that its positions are exactly the ones with $Z_i=1$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:pattern-law}
 \nu^{|I|}(1-\nu)^{s-|I|}
 +(-1)^{s-|I|}(\nu^{s-1}-\nu^s).
\end{equation}
For $h\ne0$, the test accepts if the number of ones in the first half
equals the number in the second half modulo $p$. Since $p>m$, this is
ordinary equality of the two integer counts. Summing
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:pattern-law} over the accepting patterns and then averaging
over $h$ gives the exact expression
\begin{align}
 \eps_s(\phi_p)=(1-\nu)\Bigg[1
 &-\sum_{a=0}^{m}\binom ma^2\nu^{2a}(1-\nu)^{s-2a}
 \nonumber\\[-2pt]
 &-\binom{s}{m}(\nu^{s-1}-\nu^s)\Bigg].\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-exact}
\end{align}
We used $\sum_a\binom ma^2=\binom{2m}{m}$.
The sum in brackets expands as
\[
 s\nu-\left(\binom s2+m^2\right)\nu^2+O_s(\nu^3)
 =s\nu-\frac{s(3s-2)}4\nu^2+O_s(\nu^3).
\]
The last correction in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-exact} starts at order
$s-1\ge3$. Since $\dd_p=(1-\nu)\nu$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-asymptotic} and the leading-coefficient claim.
\end{proof}

The prime family also shows that, with leading coefficient $1/s$ fixed,
a repair estimate valid for all sufficiently large common prime fields
cannot have quadratic coefficient smaller than
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-quadratic-obstruction}
 \frac{3s-2}{4s^2}.
\end{equation}
Our general upper bound has coefficient $2(s-1)/s^2$. Determining the
optimal coefficient between these two values in the common-prime
setting is a concrete unresolved refinement of this work, not an
asserted consequence of the binary example.

\subsection{What is, and is not, sharp}

The following distinctions prevent several possible overinterpretations.
The whole polynomial $F_4$ is attained at the distances in
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:binary-distance}. The global inverse statement uses only
its increasing small branch. For $s\ge6$, the full polynomial $F_s$ is
not asserted sharp; the binary example and the proved lower bound need
not have the same cubic term. The all-group quadratic inverse coefficient
is sharp, while only the leading coefficient has been proved sharp here
under the common odd-prime restriction. Finally, none of the convenient
numerical activation thresholds is claimed optimal.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Erasures and almost-full products\srctag{33}}]{Erasures and almost-full products}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:erasures}
\srcnote{33}{Section 7}

\subsection{Repair on a partial domain}

Let $A\subset G\times H$ have density $1-\tau>0$, and let
$\phi:A\to K$. Draw a full-domain arrangement as before and let $V_A$
be the event that all $2s$ queried point occurrences lie in $A$.
Write $\lambda=\Prob[V_A]$. Each point occurrence is uniform on
$G\times H$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:valid-lower}
 \lambda\ge\max\{0,1-2s\tau\}.
\end{equation}
No independence of the $2s$ point occurrences is needed for this union
bound.

\begin{theorem}[Erasure-robust repair]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:erasures}
Suppose $\lambda>0$ and, conditional on $V_A$, the arrangement failure
probability is at most $\eta\in[0,1]$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:effective}
 E=\lambda\eta+(1-\lambda).
\end{equation}
If $E\le1/(240(s-1))$, then there is a model $\psi\in\Vthirtythree(G,H;K)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:erasure-repair}
 \frac{|\{(x,y)\in A:\phi(x,y)\ne\psi(x,y)\}|}{|A|}
 \le\frac{R_s(E)}{1-\tau}.
\end{equation}
A sufficient condition, not requiring the exact value of $\lambda$, is
$\eta+2s\tau\le1/(240(s-1))$; in that case the right side may use
$R_s(\eta+2s\tau)/(1-\tau)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Extend $\phi$ arbitrarily to a function $\widetilde\phi:G\times H\to K$.
Its test agrees with the partial-domain test on $V_A$, and every other
arrangement may pessimistically be counted as a failure. Therefore
$\eps_s(\widetilde\phi)\le E$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main}; monotonicity
of $R_s$ on the relevant interval gives an absolute disagreement density
at most $R_s(E)$. Restricting the set of disagreements to $A$ and
normalizing by $|A|=(1-\tau)|G||H|$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:erasure-repair}. Finally,
\[
 E=\eta+(1-\eta)(1-\lambda)\le\eta+2s\tau
\]
by \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:valid-lower}. Under the sufficient condition,
$1-2s\tau>0$, so validity is automatically nonvacuous.
\end{proof}

For eight-arrangements the simple effective error is $\eta+32\tau$.
This is a near-full-domain result. If $A$ has small density, the upper
bound for invalid arrangements is too large to activate the decoder;
claiming a useful estimate in that regime would be unjustified.

\subsection{Exact counting in the presence of erasures}

For cyclic groups define
\begin{align*}
 R_h(x)&=|\{y:(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A\}|,\\
 M_h^A(x,z)&=|\{y:(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A,\ D_h\phi(x,y)=z\}|.
\end{align*}
Using convolution on $\Z_n$ in the first expression and on
$\Z_n\times\Z_q$ in the second, respectively, gives
\begin{align}
 N_{\mathrm{valid}}&=\sum_{h,x}\big(R_h^{*(s/2)}(x)\big)^2,
 \label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-valid}\\
 N_{\mathrm{respected}}&=\sum_{h,x,z}\big((M_h^A)^{*(s/2)}(x,z)\big)^2.
 \label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-respected}
\end{align}
The proof is the same matching-of-two-halves argument as for
\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:integer-counter}. Thus both $\lambda$ and the conditional
failure probability are exact rational numbers. If
$N_{\mathrm{valid}}=0$, the conditional probability is undefined rather
than silently interpreted as zero.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact cyclic decoding and reproducible checks\srctag{33}}]{Exact cyclic decoding and reproducible checks}\label{gsr:en:33:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:algorithms}
\srcnote{33}{Section 8}

\subsection{A nearest-model algorithm}

The model class contains an arbitrary function $a$, but it need not be
searched exponentially. For fixed bilinear and linear coefficients,
its rows separate.

\begin{proposition}[Exact cyclic decoder]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:prop:cyclic-decoder}
Let $\phi:\Z_n\times\Z_m\to\Z_q$. Every exact model has the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:cyclic-model}
 \psi(x,y)=a_x+(bx+c)y\pmod q,
 \qquad nb\equiv mb\equiv mc\equiv0\pmod q.
\end{equation}
There are $g_b=\gcd(n,m,q)$ choices of $b$ and
$g_c=\gcd(m,q)$ choices of $c$. For each such pair, choose $a_x$ as a
mode of the offsets
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:offsets}
 \phi(x,y)-(bx+c)y\pmod q\qquad(y\in\Z_m).
\end{equation}
The best pair and these modal offsets give an exact nearest model.
The search uses $O(nm g_b g_c)$ modular and histogram operations.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A biadditive map is determined by $b=B(1,1)$, so it must be $bxy$;
well-definedness is exactly $nb=mb=0$ in $\Z_q$. Similarly a homomorphism
in $y$ has the form $cy$ with $mc=0$. The counts of solutions to these
annihilation constraints are the stated greatest common divisors.
For fixed $b,c$, maximizing matches in row $x$ is precisely choosing a
most frequent value in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:offsets}. Rows are independent in
this optimization, so their maximal scores add. Enumerate the $g_b g_c$
pairs and retain the largest total score.
\end{proof}

The implementation uses sparse Python histograms with deterministic tie
breaking; the operation count treats dictionary access in its usual
expected-constant-time model. It does not claim the same number of bit
operations on unbounded integers. In the common prime case the candidate
search is $O(p^4)$ arithmetic/histogram operations.

For exact arrangement counting, binary exponentiation of convolution
in \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:integer-counter} uses
$O(m(nq)^2\log s)$ integer arithmetic operations with a direct dense
convolution bound. The supplied implementation skips zero entries.
This is a verification algorithm, not a claim of an asymptotically best
large-scale counter. Coefficients are nonnegative Python integers, and
probabilities use \texttt{fractions.Fraction}.

\subsection{The shipped verification suite}

The file \texttt{code/verify.py} checks the identities and inequalities
against exact finite examples. The default suite exhausts the first
five families of Table~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:tab:tests}; the \texttt{--extended} option
adds the sixth. The recorded delivery run used that option.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$n$ & $m$ & $q$ & Tables exhausted & Zero-error tables & Literal check\\
\midrule
2&2&2&16&16&yes\\
3&2&2&64&16&yes\\
3&3&2&512&8&no\\
2&3&3&729&27&yes\\
3&4&2&4,096&16&no\\
3&3&3&19,683&243&no\\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Total}&25,100&&\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact full-table enumeration. Every table was tested at $s=4,6,16$.
The last column means that the $s=4$ counter and nearest distance were
also compared with independent literal enumerations.}
\label{gsr:en:33:ras:tab:tests}
\end{table}

For each full table the suite checks exact classification, both cross-order
defect bounds, the local bound $F_s$, the stronger collision-profile
bound, the quadratic inequality when applicable, and the coarse and
small-branch estimates when their hypotheses hold. The smallest groups
were additionally checked against direct enumeration of every arrangement
and of every full model, including all row constants. This independently
checks both the convolution counter and the modal decoder.

There are also 300 seeded sample tables, 100 each for
$(n,m,q)=(4,4,4),(5,4,6),(5,5,5)$, using seed \texttt{20261006}.
The binary family is compared with the exact counter for
$n=3,5,7,9,11$, and its formula is checked at larger values, including
$n=100001$, where the high-agreement estimates are nonvacuous.
The common-prime row family is compared with exact counts for
$p=3,5,7,11,13,17$. The implementation of its formula includes congruence
wraparound and so also handles primes not covered by the simplified
formula \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:prime-exact}.

A separate erasure suite exhausts all $3^6=729$ partial tables on
$\Z_3\times\Z_2\to\Z_2$, allowing each entry to be zero, one, or
missing. It checks \eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-valid}--\eqref{gsr:en:33:ras:eq:partial-respected}
by literal enumeration at $s=4$, tests $s=4,6,16$ and the ambient-normalized moment bounds, and checks both constant
extensions against the effective-error and validity bounds. Only the
fully erased table has no valid arrangement; no conditional failure
probability is assigned to it.

Negative tests reject malformed tables, invalid orders and moduli, and
an intentionally corrupted model score on every full-table test.
A separate small rational-polynomial module verifies the cubic reversion
coefficients and the first two sharp-family coefficients. There is no
floating-point optimization or acceptance of a numerical solver's
feasibility status in these checks.

\begin{example}[An exact reproducible input]\label{gsr:en:33:ras:ex:json}
The included \texttt{data/example.json} is the binary family at $n=5$.
Its nearest-model distance is $1/10$. The four-difference test has
$3232$ respected arrangements out of $4000$, hence failure $24/125$.
The eight-arrangement failure probability is
$7627229088/30517578125$. These values are not in the small-error
activation range; they check the local formula and normalization, not
a purported global inverse outside its hypotheses.
\end{example}

\subsection{What computation establishes}

The checks verify the listed finite claims and expose errors in
normalization, sign conventions, implementation, and polynomial arithmetic.
They do not prove the theorems for arbitrary groups, certify literature
novelty, or replace the arguments in Sections~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:noisy}--\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:examples}.
Most exhaustive small-group tables have either zero error or an error
larger than the conservative activation threshold. The explicit large
sharp-family calculations, rather than those small enumerations, are
what exercise nonzero inputs inside that threshold. The general proof
of the threshold remains analytic and combinatorial.
