\subsection{A torsion-inclusive symmetric statement}

Without pair independence, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:kappa} and
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-torsion} give
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\La_L(1_A,\ldots,1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le C_{L,\delta}u^2,
 \quad
 C_{L,\delta}=\sum_{j=2}^k\delta^{j-2}\kappa_j\sum_{i<j}\kappa_i.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:C-torsion}
\end{equation}
In particular
$C_{L,\delta}\le\kappa_{\max}^2/(1-\delta)^2$.
This is an explicit bound on every finite abelian group. It may be weak
when a direction collapses, and Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:obstruction}
explains why some loss is then unavoidable.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Pair correlations as an exact torsion correction\srctag{20}}]{Pair correlations as an exact torsion correction}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d6}
\srcnote{20}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:pair}

The directional estimate can be complemented by an exact Fourier
description of the first obstruction to a product-density baseline.

\begin{proposition}[Pair correction and its sharp constant]
\label{gsr:cc:20:prop:pair}
Let $f,g:G\to\C$ have mean zero, let $d$ be an integer, and put
$H=dG$, $m=[G:H]$. Then
\begin{align}
 Q_d(f,g)&:=\E_{x,y}f(x)g(x+dy)
 =\sum_{\substack{\chi\in H^\perp\\\chi\ne1}}
       \widehat f(\chi)\widehat g(\chi^{-1}),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-fourier}\\
 |Q_d(f,g)|&\le\sqrt{m-1}\,\Useminorm f2\Useminorm g2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-bound}
\end{align}
For $m>1$, the constant $\sqrt{m-1}$ is optimal, also when the functions
are required to be real and one-bounded.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fourier inversion and averaging $x$ force the two frequencies to be
inverses. Averaging $dy$, uniform in $H$, forces the surviving character
to lie in $H^\perp$. The zero-frequency term vanishes by centering.
H\"older on the remaining $m-1$ frequencies, with exponents $4,4,2$,
and \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2} prove \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-bound}.
For sharpness take
\[
 f=g=t\sum_{\substack{\chi\in H^\perp\\\chi\ne1}}\chi
   =t(m1_H-1),\qquad 0<t\le1/(m-1).
\]
These are real, centered and one-bounded. Their pair correlation is
$(m-1)t^2$, while each fourth power of the $U^2$ norm is $(m-1)t^4$.
The ratio is exactly $\sqrt{m-1}$.
\end{proof}

For $a_i=\delta_i+b_i$, the full balanced expansion separates an exact
pair contribution
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{i<j}\left(\prod_{r\notin\{i,j\}}\delta_r\right)
 Q_{c_j-c_i}(b_i,b_j)
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-baseline}
\end{equation}
from terms with at least three balanced factors. Thus on a non-admissible
cyclic group, keeping \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-baseline} can be preferable to
regarding it as error. In the admissible case every summand is zero.
The finite-index factors and this quotient-frequency correction describe
the same obstruction in different languages: one is suited to
Cauchy--Schwarz iteration, the other isolates the precise pair bias.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Supersaturation and the uniformity parameter\srctag{20}}]{Supersaturation and the uniformity parameter}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d7}
\srcnote{20}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:super}

A \emph{proper ordered progression} is a pair $(x,y)$ whose $k$ entries
$x,x+y,\ldots,x+(k-1)y$ are distinct and belong to $A$.
Let $T_k^*(A)$ denote their number.

\begin{corollary}[Admissible supersaturation]
\label{gsr:cc:20:cor:super}
Suppose the consecutive progression system is admissible, $k\ge3$,
$|G|=N$, and $A\subset G$ has density $0<\delta<1$. With
$u=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1}$,
\begin{equation}
 T_k^*(A)\ge
 N^2\bigl(\delta^k-B_k(\delta)u^2\bigr)-\delta N.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:super}
\end{equation}
In particular $T_k^*(A)>0$ whenever
\begin{equation}
 u^2\le\frac{\delta^k}{2B_k(\delta)},
 \qquad N>2\delta^{1-k}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The normalized count includes all $N^2$ parameter pairs. A repeated
entry implies $(r-s)y=0$ for $0<|r-s|<k$, hence $y=0$ by
admissibility. Exactly $|A|=\delta N$ counted pairs have zero difference.
Subtract these from the lower bound supplied by
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric}. Conditions \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold} make
the resulting lower bound strictly positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Comparison} (at the write). Source~06's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:existence} needs $u^2\le\delta^{k-1/2}/(2B^{(06)}_k(\delta))=\delta^k/(2\sqrt\delta B^{(06)}_k(\delta))$; since $B_k(\delta)\le\sqrt\delta B^{(06)}_k(\delta)$, the condition \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold} is weaker, so this criterion is the stronger one; for the other criteria of this report see the note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:04:prog:super}.
\end{writenote}

In Gowers's degree-$k-2$ convention, the power parameter corresponding
to the normalized cube norm is
\begin{equation}
 \alpha=u^{2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha}
\end{equation}
Thus the new counting error is
$B_k(\delta)\alpha^{1/2^{k-2}}$, and the sufficient condition becomes
\begin{equation}
 \alpha\le
 \left(\frac{\delta^k}{2B_k(\delta)}\right)^{2^{k-2}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-threshold}
\end{equation}
For $0<\delta\le1/2$, the convenient bound
$B_k(\delta)\le4\sqrt\delta$ gives the simpler sufficient condition
\begin{equation}
 \alpha\le
 \left(\frac{\delta^{k-1/2}}8\right)^{2^{k-2}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-simple}
\end{equation}
This improves the local symmetric threshold derived from
\eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:old}, which is
$\alpha\le(\delta^k/(2S_{k-2}(\delta)))^{2^{k-1}}$.
The comparison keeps the same normalized $u$ and distinguishes a
cube norm from its $2^{k-1}$-th power.

\subsection{Removing degenerate progressions with torsion}

For an arbitrary finite abelian group put
\[
 D_k(G)=\abs{\bigcup_{r=1}^{k-1}G[r]}.
\]
The difference $y$ gives a repeated entry precisely when its order is
less than $k$. For each such difference at most $|A|$ starting points
can contribute. Therefore \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:C-torsion} gives
\begin{equation}
 T_k^*(A)\ge
 N^2\bigl(\delta^k-C_{L,\delta}u^2\bigr)-\delta N D_k(G).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:torsion-super}
\end{equation}
For cyclic groups this degeneracy count has the exact formula
\begin{equation}
 D_k(\Z/N\Z)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid N\\d<k}}\varphi(d),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:degenerate}
\end{equation}
since there are $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$. This includes the
zero difference through $d=1$.

\subsection{The no-wrap distinction}

\begin{lemma}[A sufficient lifting condition]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:nowrap}
Suppose $A\subset\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ is embedded in $\Z/N\Z$ and
$2(n-1)<N$. Any nonconstant modular progression of length at least three
contained in $A$ is an ordinary integer progression; reversing its order
if necessary gives positive difference.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}$ be its integer representatives. Their consecutive
differences are congruent modulo $N$. Each lies between $-(n-1)$ and
$n-1$, so the difference between any two has absolute value less than
$N$ and must be zero. They are all the same integer, which is nonzero
for a nonconstant progression.
\end{proof}

The lemma does not show that cutting an arbitrary uniform set down to a
short interval preserves its balanced norm. Such a localization step can
introduce unbalanced cutoff functions at precisely the positions where
our quadratic argument needs small norms. This is one reason
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-threshold} is not silently promoted to a new global
Szemer\'edi estimate. The inverse theorem, density increment, iteration
losses, and localization must all be analyzed together.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp quadratic obstruction for three-term counts\srctag{20}}]{A sharp quadratic obstruction for three-term counts}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d8}
\srcnote{20}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:sharp}

We now prove that quadratic dependence in \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline} is the
correct uniform exponent when $k=3$, not just an artifact of stopping
Cauchy--Schwarz early. The construction is explicit for bounded weights;
a second argument transfers its scale to actual subsets.

\subsection{An elementary even-dimensional Gauss identity}

Let $p=29$, let $G=\F_p^{2m}$, $N=p^{2m}$, and set
$Q(x)=x_1^2+\cdots+x_{2m}^2$. Write $e_p(t)=\exp(2\pi it/p)$.

\begin{lemma}[Gauss averages]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss}
For every nonzero $t\in\F_p$,
\begin{equation}
 \E_{x\in G}e_p(tQ(x))=N^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \abs{\widehat{e_p(tQ)}(\xi)}=N^{-1/2}
 \quad(\xi\in\widehat G).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:gauss}
\end{equation}
More generally, if a quadratic form in two scalar variables over $\F_p$
has rank $r$, its sum over $2m$ independent coordinate copies has
normalized exponential average $N^{-r/2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $g(t)=\sum_{z\in\F_p}e_p(tz^2)$. If $\chi$ is the quadratic
character, counting square roots gives $g(t)=\chi(t)g(1)$ for $t\ne0$.
The change of variables $(z,w)\mapsto(z-w,z+w)$ is invertible and gives
$|g(t)|^2=\sum_{z,w}e_p(t(z^2-w^2))=p$.
Also $\overline{g(1)}=g(-1)=\chi(-1)g(1)=g(1)$ because $p\equiv1$
modulo four. Hence $g(t)^2=p$, irrespective of its possible sign.
The product over $2m$ coordinates is $p^m$, and normalization gives the
first assertion of \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:gauss}. Completing the square for each
linear Fourier twist proves the magnitude assertion.

Every symmetric quadratic matrix over this odd-characteristic field
is diagonalizable by an invertible linear change of variables. A rank-$r$
form has $r$ nonzero diagonal coefficients; zero directions contribute
one. For each nonzero coefficient the $2m$ coordinate copies contribute
$p^{-m}=N^{-1/2}$. Their product is $N^{-r/2}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Four phases and an exact rank census}

Set $a=1/16$ and
\begin{equation}
 h(x)=a\sum_{t\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}}e_p(tQ(x)),\qquad
 f(x)=h(x)-4aN^{-1/2},\qquad w(x)=\tfrac12+f(x).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight}
\end{equation}
The conjugate pairs make $h,f,w$ real. Their means are
$\E h=4aN^{-1/2}$, $\E f=0$, and $\E w=1/2$.
Moreover $|f|\le4a(1+N^{-1/2})\le1/2$, so $0\le w\le1$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact weighted excess]
\label{gsr:cc:20:prop:weight}
For the functions in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight},
\begin{align}
 \Useminorm f2^4&\le (4a)^4/N,\label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u}\\
 \La_3(w)-\tfrac18
 &=a^3\left(2N^{-1/2}+62N^{-1}-64N^{-3/2}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-excess}
\end{align}
Consequently, as $m\to\infty$, $\Useminorm f2\to0$ and
\begin{equation}
 \La_3(w)-\tfrac18\ge\frac1{128}\,\Useminorm f2^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-sharp}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Centering removes the zero Fourier coefficient. Every other coefficient
of $f$ has absolute value at most $4aN^{-1/2}$, by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss}. There are at most $N$ coefficients, so
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2} proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u}.

Expand $\La_3(h)$ by a triple $(t_0,t_1,t_2)\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}^3$.
At each coordinate, the quadratic form in $(x,y)$ has symmetric matrix
\begin{equation}
 M_t=\begin{pmatrix}
 t_0+t_1+t_2&t_1+2t_2\\
 t_1+2t_2&t_1+4t_2
 \end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \det M_t=t_0t_1+4t_0t_2+t_1t_2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:matrix}
\end{equation}
Its determinant has absolute value at most $24$, so vanishing modulo
$29$ is equivalent to integer vanishing. The only vanishing triples are
$(-1,2,-1)$ and $(1,-2,1)$. To check this without a search oracle,
solve
\[
 t_1(t_0+t_2)=-4t_0t_2.
\]
If $t_0+t_2=0$, the right side is nonzero. For equal endpoints the
solution is $t_1=-2t_0$, which is allowed exactly for $t_0=\pm1$.
For unequal endpoints of the same sign the required middle value has
magnitude $8/3$; for unequal endpoints of opposite signs it has magnitude
$8$. Neither is allowed. These exhaust the possible endpoint pairs.
No matrix has rank zero: subtracting its off-diagonal entry from the
bottom-right entry would give $2t_2=0$. Thus two of the $64$ matrices
have rank one and $62$ have rank two. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss} gives
\[
 \La_3(h)=a^3(2N^{-1/2}+62N^{-1}).
\]
Any two progression positions are independent because $p$ is odd.
Expanding the centered triple therefore gives
$\La_3(f)=\La_3(h)-(\E h)^3$. The singleton and pair terms in
$\La_3(1/2+f)$ vanish. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-excess}.
For $N\ge2$, its right-hand side is at least $2a^3N^{-1/2}$, whereas
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u} implies $\Useminorm f2^2\le16a^2N^{-1/2}$.
Their ratio is at least $a/8=1/128$.
\end{proof}

This construction supplies small global $U^2$ norm through the large
rank of the quadratic phase, while the two rank-one combinations in
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:matrix} preserve a larger three-term correlation. Scaling a
fixed cosine alone would not establish the same exponent: it would give
a cubic correlation in its small amplitude.

\subsection{Rounding without losing the critical scale}

A naive assertion that a random rounding is ``close'' is insufficient:
the excess itself is of order $N^{-1/2}$. We need simultaneous control
of a positive count excess and a fourth power of the norm of order
$N^{-1}$. The following argument supplies that control explicitly.

\begin{theorem}[Quadratic sharpness for indicator sets]
\label{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}
There are subsets $A_m\subset\F_{29}^{2m}$, for all sufficiently large
$m$, with densities $\delta_m\to1/2$ and
$u_m=\Useminorm{1_{A_m}-\delta_m}{2}\to0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 \La_3(1_{A_m})-\delta_m^3\ge c_*u_m^2
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:indicator-sharp}
\end{equation}
for an absolute $c_*>0$. Consequently, for every $\eta>0$, no constant
$C_\eta$ can bound all these errors by $C_\eta u_m^{2+\eta}$.
The failure also holds uniformly for densities in any fixed neighborhood
of $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Include each $x$ independently with probability $w(x)$ from
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight}. Let $B_x=1_A(x)$, $\delta_A=\E_x B_x$, and put
\[
 X_A=\La_3(1_A)-\delta_A^3,
 \qquad S_A=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta_A}{2}^{4}.
\]
We first show, for all sufficiently large $N$, that
\begin{equation}
 \E_A X_A\ge cN^{-1/2},\qquad
 \E_A S_A\le C/N,
 \quad c=a^3,\quad C=8((4a)^4+2)=513/32.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:round-moments}
\end{equation}

All three points of a progression are distinct unless $y=0$.
Off that diagonal, independence gives the product of the three
probabilities. On the diagonal, $B_x^3=B_x$ and $w(x)\ge w(x)^3$.
Therefore $\E_A\La_3(1_A)\ge\La_3(w)$.
Writing $\xi_x=B_x-w(x)$ and expanding the cube of their average gives
\begin{equation}
 \E_A\delta_A^3
 =\delta^3+\frac{3\delta}{N}\E_x w(x)(1-w(x))
 +\frac1{N^2}\E_x w(x)(1-w(x))(1-2w(x)),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:density-third}
\end{equation}
where $\delta=1/2$. Since $w(1-w)\le1/4$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:weight}
yields
\[
 \E_A X_A\ge 2a^3N^{-1/2}-\frac{3}{8N}-\frac1{4N^2}
 \ge a^3N^{-1/2}
\]
for sufficiently large $N$.

For the second assertion, note that
$1_A-\delta_A=f+(\xi-\E_x\xi_x)$.
By \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2}, subtracting the mean removes a nonnegative
term from the fourth power of a $U^2$ norm. Also
\begin{equation}
 \E_A\Useminorm\xi2^4\le2/N.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:noise}
\end{equation}
To prove \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:noise}, expand the parallelogram. Independence and
$\E_A\xi_x=0$ kill any term with a point appearing exactly once.
In an odd-order group, a parallelogram with no singleton among its four
vertices must have $h=0$ or $k=0$. Indeed its three possible pairings
give respectively $h=0$, $k=0$, or $h=k$ and $2h=0$; the last case is
also zero. The union has normalized measure at most $2/N$, and the
absolute value of each expected product is at most one.
The triangle inequality and $(v+w)^4\le8(v^4+w^4)$ now give
\[
 \E_A S_A\le8\left(\Useminorm f2^4+\E_A\Useminorm\xi2^4\right)
 \le C/N,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:round-moments}.

The already proved three-term counting inequality implies
$|X_A|\le\sqrt{S_A}$ for every realization (in fact the prefactor is
at most $1/2$). Let
$E=\{X_A\ge c/(2\sqrt N)\}$. By Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 \frac c{\sqrt N}\le\E_A X_A
 \le\frac c{2\sqrt N}+\E_A(1_E\sqrt{S_A})
 \le\frac c{2\sqrt N}+\sqrt{C/N}\sqrt{\Pr(E)}.
\]
Consequently $\Pr(E)\ge c^2/(4C)$.
Set $K=8C^2/c^2$. Markov's inequality gives
$\Pr(S_A>K/N)\le c^2/(8C)$.
Finally $\Var(\delta_A)\le1/(4N)$, so
\[
 \Pr(|\delta_A-1/2|>N^{-1/4})\le1/(4\sqrt N).
\]
For all sufficiently large $N$, these estimates leave a positive
probability of all three events
\[
 X_A\ge c/(2\sqrt N),\qquad S_A\le K/N,\qquad
 |\delta_A-1/2|\le N^{-1/4}.
\]
Choose one such realization for each large $m$.
Then $u_m^2=\sqrt{S_{A_m}}\le\sqrt{K/N}$ and
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:indicator-sharp} holds with
$c_*=c/(2\sqrt K)>0$.
The norm cannot be zero when $X_A>0$. Dividing by $u_m^{2+\eta}$
now yields a lower bound $c_*u_m^{-\eta}\to\infty$, proving the
claimed impossibility.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
New in this report: source~06's three-term coefficient is sharp only at singletons ($\delta=1/N$); this theorem shows that the exponent $2$ cannot be raised at fixed density near $1/2$, for indicator sets on $\F_{29}^{2m}$. Not for prime cyclic groups or $k\ge4$ (the source's non-claims; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:density}).
\end{writenote}

The constant $c_*$ is intentionally crude. The theorem determines an
exponent, not the optimal coefficient in the indicator-set extremal
problem. The finite check of the weight construction uses $m=1$;
the existence proof for the rounded sets is asymptotic and does not
claim that its crude probability thresholds are useful computationally.
