\section{Source~21's chapter: the exponent-five coefficient, with source~23's second route \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:charfive}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections settle the question that source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:exponent-five} left open: on groups of exponent five, the first correction after $6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$ in the centered three-cube problem has exponent six, and its coefficient is now known. Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:d9} are source~21, the main source; Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:23:sec:d7}--\ref{gsr:cc:23:sec:dA} are source~23's Section~7 and Appendix~A, an independent proof of the same theorem, written the same day from a pin three minutes later, printed here as a credited second route. Neither source cites the other; both cite source~14's manuscript. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~14's Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:d3}}; it is printed here, at the end of Part~III, because no number printed earlier may move. Source~21's introduction, with the main theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}), is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:21:sec:d1}; its repository interface, questions and appendices are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:21:sec:d10}--\ref{gsr:fz:21:sec:dB}). Source~23's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:23:sec:d1}. Their notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For real centered $f$ on any nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five and $u=\norm f_{U^3}\le c\delta$, $Q_3(\delta+f)\le\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+C_5\delta^2u^6+Cu^8$ with $C_5=2^{3/4}/3$ and absolute $c$, $C$, sharp on every fixed such group (source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}; source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}). The mechanism is the same in both: a positive cubic statistic controls the sixth- and seventh-degree terms through the Fourier tail, and the order-five resonance makes the cost of the second harmonic quadratic. Source~21 also proves the phase envelope $C_5(\cos\theta)_+^2/(1+\cos^2\phi)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}), rigidity of near-extremizers (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity}; source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:rigidity} is equivalent), the next coefficient $20/9$ on $\Z/5\Z$ for the maximum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}; source~23's Appendix~A computes $20/9$ for one model, a lower bound), indicator sharpness through $u^8$ as lower examples (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:indicator}; source~23 through $u^6$) and a projection consequence of cube Cauchy--Schwarz (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:21:prop:projection}). The universal coefficient of $u^8$ is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}). \file{lemma_3_10} (\file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~340) is an exact companion (\file{lemma_3_10_holds}, \file{Proofs03CubeUpper.lean}, line~82), as source~21 records; no characteristic-five or cube-expansion declaration exists. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fourier identities and the sharp quartic deficit\srctag{21}}]{Fourier identities and the sharp quartic deficit}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d2}
\srcnote{21}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:fourier}

For $f:G\to\C$, our Fourier convention is
\[
 a_r=\widehat f(r)=\E_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{r(x)},
 \qquad f(x)=\sum_{r\in\widehat G}a_r r(x).
\]
Throughout the main argument $f$ is real and centered, so
$a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$ and $a_0=0$.  Set
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\qquad S=\sum_r|a_r|^4=\|f\|_{U^2}^4,
 \qquad M=\sum_r|a_r|^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:fourier-statistics}
\end{equation}
All sums on the dual group are unnormalized.

\begin{lemma}[A sum of Fourier squares]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:fourier-squares}
Define
\begin{equation}
 T(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                 \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:T}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
                 \|f\|_{U^3}^8=\sum_{s,t}|T(s,t)|^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}
\end{equation}
For real $f$, $T(s,t)$ is real, is symmetric in $s,t$, and is unchanged
by replacing either $s$ or $t$ by its negative.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Insert Fourier inversion in the eight-vertex cube.  Averaging over
$x,h_1,h_2,h_3$ imposes the four equations
\[
 \sum_\omega r_\omega=0,
 \qquad \sum_\omega\omega_j r_\omega=0\quad(1\le j\le3).
\]
Their solutions are precisely the parity-adjusted affine frequency
cubes.  Grouping two opposite faces gives the expansion of the
right side of \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}.  Equivalently, one can expand the
right side and use its four free frequencies as parameters for the
same four equations.  This parameterization uses only invertible
integer changes of variables, so the identity holds on every finite
abelian group.

In \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:T}, the substitution $r\mapsto-r-s-t$ pairs each
summand with its complex conjugate because $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$.
Hence $T$ is real.  Interchanging $s,t$ is immediate; shifting the
base $r$ after changing the sign of one increment conjugates $T$,
and so leaves it unchanged in the real case.
\end{proof}

Define the positive energy
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=\sum_{r+s=t+w}
             \lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w
             =\sum_v(\lambda*\lambda)(v)^2,
\]
where the convolution is an unnormalized sum.  Since $\lambda$ is
even, $T(0,t)=\sum_r\lambda_r\lambda_{r+t}$, and $T(0,0)=S$.
The two axes of \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} therefore contribute exactly
\begin{equation}
                 2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:axes}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Quartic comparison and concentration]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap}
For every real centered $f$ on an odd-order finite abelian group,
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge5S^2-6M\ge2S^2,
 \qquad u=\|f\|_{U^3}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:quartic-gap}
\end{equation}
If $f\ne0$, choose a largest conjugate pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ and put
\begin{equation}
 \rho=|a_\xi|,
 \qquad D=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4,
 \qquad S=2\rho^4+D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
             u^8\ge2S^2+3DS.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap}
\end{equation}
In particular, equality in $u^8\ge2S^2$ for nonzero $f$ forces exactly
one conjugate Fourier pair.  In exponent five, every such pair gives
equality.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the energy as a sum over $r+s+t+w=0$.  Retain the union of the
three families obtained by pairing the four entries into opposite
pairs.  Each family has weight $S^2$, every pairwise intersection has
weight $M$, and the triple intersection has weight zero: it requires
$2r=0$, and the zero Fourier coefficient vanishes.  Thus
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\ge3S^2-3M$.  Combine this with
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:axes}.

The nonzero Fourier coefficients come in conjugate pairs.  If their
fourth-power masses are $x_j=2|a_{r_j}|^4$, then
$S=\sum_jx_j$ and $M=\frac12\sum_jx_j^2\le S^2/2$.
This proves the second inequality and its necessary equality case.
Maximality also gives $M\le\rho^4S=(S-D)S/2$, yielding
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap}.  For a pure pair of order five,
directly evaluating \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} gives $u^8=8\rho^8=2S^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} The inequality $u^8\ge2S^2$ for real centered $f$ on odd-order groups is source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap}; source~14 reproves it (its display~\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap}). The refinement \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap} with the tail $D$ is the form used below.
\end{writenote}

The last sufficiency statement was restricted deliberately.  For
example, short resonances at order three change the norm of a pure
pair.  The present report does not silently extend an exponent-five
equality formula to all odd orders.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Higher centered coefficients with a retained Fourier tail\srctag{21}}]{Higher centered coefficients with a retained Fourier tail}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d3}
\srcnote{21}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:centered}

The following exact expansion introduces the terms whose crude
treatment prevented the earlier coefficient from being identified.

\begin{lemma}[Centered cube expansion]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:centered}
On an exponent-five group,
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8+12\delta^4S+8\delta^3B_5(f)
                  +\delta^2 C_6(f)+\delta C_7(f)+u^8,
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered}
\end{equation}
where $C_j$ is the sum of all $j$-vertex centered terms and
\begin{equation}
               B_5(f)=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^{3}a_r.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5}
\end{equation}
The number $B_5(f)$ is real.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the product over subsets of the eight vertices.  One, two,
or three distinct cube forms are jointly uniform, so centering kills
their expectations.  Among the $70$ four-element supports, the $12$
parallelograms have a one-dimensional relation and contribute $S$;
the other $58$ supports are independent over $\F_5$.

Of the $56$ five-element supports, $48$ have a relation with a zero
coefficient, forcing a factor $a_0$ in their Fourier expectation.
The remaining eight are cube-symmetric copies of
$\{000,100,010,001,111\}$.  If the frequency at $111$ is $r$,
the four orthogonality equations force frequencies
$2r,-r,-r,-r,r$ on this support.  This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5}.
Negating $r$ conjugates a summand, so the sum is real.

The support counts may also be checked by row reduction of the
columns $(1,\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$, as described in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:21:app:certificates}.  The nonzero determinants needed for
these classifications have absolute value at most two; in
characteristic five their ranks agree with the stated ranks.
\end{proof}

Cube Cauchy--Schwarz alone gives $|C_6|\le28u^6$ and
$|C_7|\le8u^7$.  The first of these bounds is too large to
determine the coefficient of $u^6$.  We instead use the positive
statistic
\begin{equation}
             H=\sum_{r+s+t=0}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:H}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sextic and septic profile inequalities]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:six-seven}
For every real centered $f$ on an exponent-five group,
\begin{equation}
              |C_6(f)|\le28H,
              \qquad |C_7(f)|\le8u^4\sqrt H.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:six-seven}
\end{equation}
For a largest pair and tail $D$ as in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail},
\begin{equation}
 H\le3\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda)}
       \le\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}u^4\sqrt D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:H-tail}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 |C_6(f)|&\le42\sqrt3\,u^4D^{1/2},\notag\\
 |C_7(f)|&\le8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}\,u^6D^{1/4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven}
\end{align}
No bound on $\|f\|_\infty$ is assumed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Classify a six-vertex support by the two omitted vertices.  Their
Hamming distance is one, two, or three.  The respective numbers of
unordered pairs are $12,12,4$.  Fourier orthogonality gives the
following representatives, with all frequency sums over $\widehat G$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccl@{}}
\toprule
Omitted vertices&Multiplicity&Six-vertex expectation\\
\midrule
$000,001$&$12$&$H$\\
$000,011$&$12$&$\displaystyle J=\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r a_s^2
                                  a_{r-s}\overline{a_{r+s}}$\\
$000,111$&$4$&$\displaystyle K=\sum_{r+s+t=0}a_r^2a_s^2a_t^2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Each formula follows by solving the same four equations used in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:fourier-squares}, now with the omitted frequencies
set to zero.  Clearly $|K|\le H$.  For $J$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{align*}
 |J|&\le\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s
                 \sqrt{\lambda_{r-s}\lambda_{r+s}}\\
 &\le\left(\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r-s}\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r+s}\right)^{1/2}
 =H,
\end{align*}
using evenness of $\lambda$.  This proves the sextic bound.

For the septic bound, replace the zero Fourier coefficient in $T$ by
a real variable $\delta$ and differentiate at $\delta=0$.  The
derivative is
\begin{equation}
 L(s,t)=2\Rea(a_sa_t\overline{a_{s+t}})
       +2\Rea(a_s\overline{a_t}\,\overline{a_{s-t}}).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:L}
\end{equation}
This is the sum of the four terms obtained by choosing which of
the four factors contains the differentiated zero coefficient.
If indices coincide, the extra zero coefficients make the
corresponding terms vanish, so the formula still applies.
Each of these four cubic terms has squared $\ell^2$ norm $H$.
Thus $\|L\|_2\le4\sqrt H$.  Differentiating the sum of squares gives
\[
 C_7(f)=2\Rea\langle T,L\rangle,
 \qquad |C_7(f)|\le2\|T\|_2\|L\|_2\le8u^4\sqrt H.
\]

Finally, no triple drawn from $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ sums to zero because
$\xi$ has order five.  Every nonzero summand in $H$ contains at
least one tail index.  Therefore
\[
 H\le3\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}
            \lambda_r(\lambda*\lambda)(-r)
   \le3\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda)}.
\]
The axes in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} give
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\le(u^8+S^2)/2$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap} gives $S^2\le u^8/2$,
proving \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:H-tail} and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the two improvements must be used together]
The new bounds express the higher coefficients in terms of the
same tail $D$ that lowers the quartic contribution.  A merely
qualitative statement that $C_6$ tends to zero near a pure pair would
give a sharp coefficient with an unspecified little-oh error.  The
powers $D^{1/2}$ and $D^{1/4}$ allow the explicit $O(u^8)$ remainder.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The characteristic-five resonance and a finite bound\srctag{21}}]{The characteristic-five resonance and a finite bound}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d4}
\srcnote{21}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:resonance}

For a largest pair, set $b=|a_{2\xi}|$.  The pair
$\{2\xi,-2\xi\}$ is distinct from $\{\xi,-\xi\}$, so
$2b^4\le D$.  When $b>0$, write
\begin{equation}
 a_\xi=\rho e^{i\alpha},\qquad a_{2\xi}=b e^{i\beta},
 \qquad \theta=2\alpha-\beta,
 \qquad \phi=3\alpha+\beta.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:angles}
\end{equation}
These phases are understood modulo $2\pi$.  Notice the useful
identity $\theta+\phi=5\alpha$.

\begin{theorem}[A joint norm penalty]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:joint-gap}
With the preceding notation,
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}
\end{equation}
Let $D_{\rm out}=\sum_{r\notin\langle\xi\rangle}|a_r|^4$.
If $b>0$, the stronger finite inequality is
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2
       +4\pos{2\rho^3b|\cos\phi|-D_{\rm out}}^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the four-frequency zero-sum representation of
$\mathcal E(\lambda)$, retain, in addition to the three
opposite-pair families, all permutations of
$(\xi,\xi,\xi,2\xi)$ and of its negative.
There are eight such ordered tuples, each with weight
$\rho^6b^2$.  They sum to zero because $5\xi=0$, and none belongs
to a retained opposite-pair family.  Thus
\[
 u^8\ge5S^2-6M+16\rho^6b^2.
\]
Conjugate pairing in the tail gives
$M\le2\rho^8+D^2/2$.  Expanding $S=2\rho^4+D$ now yields
\[
 5S^2-6M\ge8\rho^8+20\rho^4D+2D^2
               =2S^2+12\rho^4D.
\]

For the stronger statement retain the four off-axis slots
$(s,t)=(\pm2\xi,\pm2\xi)$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}.
They are distinct, and all have the same $T$ value.  The contribution
from bases in $\langle\xi\rangle$ is
\[
 T(2\xi,2\xi)=a_\xi^3a_{2\xi}
             +\overline{a_\xi^3a_{2\xi}}+E
             =2\rho^3b\cos\phi+E.
\]
For a base outside $\langle\xi\rangle$, all four shifted indices
remain outside it.  H\"older's inequality therefore gives
$|E|\le D_{\rm out}$.  The four retained squares contribute at
least the final term in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap}.
\end{proof}

The extra term $16\rho^6b^2$ is the decisive order-five resonance.
Without such a quadratic cost in the second harmonic, balancing a
quartic tail cost against the quintic gain can produce fractional
powers, as in the earlier $u^{16/3}$ result.  Here the balance is
quadratic and forces the smaller second harmonic $b\asymp u^2/\delta$.

\begin{proposition}[Explicit finite Fourier-profile bound]
\label{gsr:cc:21:prop:finite-profile}
For every $\delta\ge0$ and every nonzero real centered $f$ on an
exponent-five group,
\begin{align}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le{}&\delta^8+12\delta^4S
       +16\delta^3\rho^4b\cos\theta+8\delta^3\rho D\notag\\
 &+42\sqrt3\,\delta^2u^4D^{1/2}
       +8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}\,\delta u^6D^{1/4}+u^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:finite-profile}
\end{align}
If $b=0$, its cosine term is interpreted as zero.  This bound and
the constraints \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}--\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap} are finite
inequalities, with no asymptotic qualification.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The two selected summands $r=\pm\xi$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5} give
$2\rho^4b\cos\theta$ exactly.  Every other summand has absolute
value at most $\rho|a_r|^4$, because $\rho$ is the largest Fourier
amplitude.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 B_5(f)=2\rho^4b\cos\theta+E_5,
 \qquad |E_5|\le\rho D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5-tail}
\end{equation}
Use this identity and Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:six-seven} in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp uniform optimization and the phase envelope\srctag{21}}]{Sharp uniform optimization and the phase envelope}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d5}
\srcnote{21}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:optimization}

We now prove Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}.  The proof first locates the
Fourier mass and then absorbs the remaining higher-degree terms.
This order is necessary: dropping the negative tail term too early
would lose the eighth-order remainder.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform localization]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:localization}
Let $\|g\|_{U^3}=1$, let $t>0$, and put
\[
 S_0=2^{-1/2},\qquad \eta=S_0-S,\qquad
 F=Q_3(1+tg)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4,
\]
where the Fourier statistics refer to $g$.  If $F>0$ and $t$ is
sufficiently small, then, with absolute implied constants,
\begin{equation}
          \eta=O(t^2),\qquad D=O(t^2),\qquad b=O(t).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:localization}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First $S\le S_0$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap}.  Cube
Cauchy--Schwarz and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered} give
\[
 F=-12\eta t^4+8B_5(g)t^5+R,
 \qquad |R|\le28t^6+8t^7+t^8\le37t^6\quad(t\le1).
\]
Also $|B_5(g)|\le\rho S\le1$.  Thus $F>0$ implies
$\eta=O(t)$, and $S$ is bounded below by a positive constant for
small $t$.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap} yields
\[
 3DS\le1-2S^2=2\eta(S_0+S),
\]
so $D=O(\eta)$.  It follows that
$\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ is bounded below.  The resonance penalty
in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap} now gives $b^2=O(\eta)$.

Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5-tail} gives
$|B_5(g)|=O(\sqrt\eta+\eta)$.  Substituting in the preceding
expression for $F$ gives
\[
 \eta\le A t\sqrt\eta+B t\eta+C t^2
\]
with absolute constants.  For small $t$, absorb $Bt\eta$.
The resulting quadratic inequality in $\sqrt\eta$ implies
$\sqrt\eta=O(t)$, proving all three claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, upper bound]
If $u=0$, the norm property gives $f=0$.  Otherwise set
$g=f/u$ and $t=u/\delta$.  Then
$Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8Q_3(1+tg)$.
If $F\le0$, the asserted upper bound is immediate, so assume $F>0$.
All the following Fourier variables refer to $g$.

By localization,
\[
 \rho^4=2^{-3/2}+O(t^2),\qquad
 \rho^6=2^{-9/4}+O(t^2).
\]
Expand \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}, using
$1-2S^2=2\sqrt2\eta-2\eta^2$, to obtain
\begin{equation}
           \eta\ge\frac32D+2^{1/4}b^2-O(t^4).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:deficit}
\end{equation}
The constants are absolute.  Use
$B_5(g)\le S_0b+D$ and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven} to get
\begin{align}
 F\le{}&-18Dt^4-12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5+8Dt^5
           \notag\\
 &+K_6t^6D^{1/2}+K_7t^7D^{1/4}+O(t^8),
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption}
\end{align}
where $K_6=42\sqrt3$ and $K_7=8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}$.

For sufficiently small $t$, $-18D+8Dt\le-17D$.
Set $D=t^4y$.  All the terms involving $D$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption} are then bounded above by
\[
       t^8\bigl(-17y+K_6\sqrt y+K_7y^{1/4}\bigr)=O(t^8),
\]
because the continuous expression in parentheses tends to $-\infty$
as $y\to\infty$.  Finally,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5\}
        =C_5t^6,
 \qquad b=\beta_5t.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:quadratic-optimum}
\end{equation}
Rescaling by $\delta^8$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:21:eq:main-upper}.  The error is
$O(\delta^8t^8)=O(u^8)$ with an absolute constant, not merely
an unspecified density-dependent error.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp phase-dependent coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, choose a largest
conjugate pair.  If $b>0$ and the phases are as in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:angles}, then, with absolute $c,C>0$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
   +C_5\frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi}\,\delta^2u^6
   +Cu^8\quad(u\le c\delta).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope}
\end{equation}
For $b=0$, the same assertion holds with the $u^6$ coefficient zero.
For each prescribed pair of phases, the coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope} is attained asymptotically by weights on
$\Z/5\Z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
As before, the case $F\le0$ is immediate.  In the case $F>0$,
localization applies.  The elementary inequality
$(x-y)_+^2\ge x^2-2xy$ for $x,y\ge0$ turns
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap} into
\[
 \eta\ge\frac32D+2^{1/4}(1+\cos^2\phi)b^2
                    -O(t^4+bD).
\]
The selected quintic term is $2\rho^4b\cos\theta$.
Replacing $2\rho^4$ by $S_0$ here introduces an absolute error
$O((\eta+D)b)=O(t^3)$, regardless of the sign of the cosine;
after multiplication by $t^5$ this is $O(t^8)$.
The extra $O(bD)t^4$ is absorbed against the negative tail term
because $b=O(t)$.  The other tail terms are treated exactly as
in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption}.

The remaining one-variable optimization is
\[
 \sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\,2^{1/4}(1+\cos^2\phi)b^2t^4
                    +4\sqrt2\,b\cos\theta\,t^5\}
 =C_5\frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi}t^6.
\]
The maximizing scale is
\begin{equation}
        b=\beta_5t\,
              \frac{(\cos\theta)_+}{1+\cos^2\phi}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-b}
\end{equation}
For fixed phases with $\cos\theta>0$, the exact five-point
formulas in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:five-point-next}, with unnormalized
second amplitude
$\beta_5\delta^{-1}u^2(\cos\theta)_+/(1+\cos^2\phi)$,
give a matching coefficient and an $O_\delta(u^8)$ error.
The first amplitude is chosen to make the centered norm exactly $u$.
If $\cos\theta\le0$, take a positive second amplitude
$o(\delta^{-1}u^2)$ with the specified phase.  The coefficient is
then zero; for example $b=\delta^{-3}u^4$ gives an $O_\delta(u^8)$
error.  The case $b=0$ follows directly from the same absorption
argument with no selected quintic term.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Real Fourier coefficients lose a factor of two]
For a positive real dominant coefficient and a positive real second
coefficient, $\theta=\phi=0$.  The phase factor in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope} is $1/2$.  The full coefficient requires
$\theta=0$ and $\cos\phi=0$, which can be achieved by
$a_\xi=\rho e^{i\pi/10}$ and $a_{2\xi}=b e^{i\pi/5}$.
The extremizing physical-space function is still real: the negative
Fourier coefficients are the complex conjugates of the positive ones.
\end{remark}


\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.96\textwidth]{figures/21-characteristic-five-phase_envelope.pdf}
\caption{The exact phase factor in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}.
The marked point $\theta=0$, $\phi=\pi/2$ gives the full sharp
coefficient; positive real coefficients give the value $1/2$ at
$\theta=\phi=0$.  The factor vanishes when $\cos\theta\le0$.}
\label{gsr:cc:21:fig:phase}
\end{figure}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Near equality and the scale of rigidity\srctag{21}}]{Near equality and the scale of rigidity}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d6}
\srcnote{21}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:rigidity}

\begin{theorem}[Second-term rigidity]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity}
Fix $\delta>0$.  Suppose $G_j$ are nontrivial exponent-five groups,
$f_j$ are real and centered, $0<u_j=\|f_j\|_{U^3}\to0$, and
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f_j)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u_j^4
                         +C_5\delta^2u_j^6+o_\delta(u_j^6).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:near-equality}
\end{equation}
For any choice of a largest conjugate pair $\{\pm\xi_j\}$, write
$\widehat f_j(\xi_j)=\rho_j e^{i\alpha_j}$ and
$\widehat f_j(2\xi_j)=b_j e^{i\beta_j}$.  Then
\begin{align}
 b_j&\sim\beta_5\delta^{-1}u_j^2,
       &e^{i(2\alpha_j-\beta_j)}&\longrightarrow1,\notag\\
 e^{10i\alpha_j}&\longrightarrow-1,
       &\sum_{r\notin\{\pm\xi_j\}}|\widehat f_j(r)|^4
          &=o_\delta(u_j^6),\notag\\
 \rho_j^4&=\frac{u_j^4}{2\sqrt2}
             -\frac{C_5}{24}\delta^{-2}u_j^6+o_\delta(u_j^6).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:rigidity}
\end{align}
Consequently the remainder after removing the dominant pair is
$o_\delta(u_j^{3/2})$ in $U^2$.  This conclusion does not assert
an $o(u_j^2)$ remainder or an $L^2$ approximation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normalize $g_j=f_j/u_j$, $t_j=u_j/\delta$.  All variables in this
paragraph refer to $g_j$.  The localization lemma gives
$D=O(t^2)$ and $b=O(t)$.  Dividing the upper argument by $t^6$,
and retaining the phase and tail losses, gives
\[
 \frac F{t^6}\le-18\frac D{t^2}
          -12\,2^{1/4}\left(\frac bt\right)^2
          +4\sqrt2\frac bt\cos\theta+o(1).
\]
Here the sextic and septic errors are respectively $O(t)$ and
$O(t^{3/2})$ after division, so both tend to zero.  The quadratic
has unique maximum $C_5$ at $b/t=\beta_5$, $\cos\theta=1$.
Thus $D/t^2\to0$, $b/t\to\beta_5$, and $e^{i\theta}\to1$.

The phase envelope then forces $\cos\phi\to0$, since its factor
must tend to one.  As $\theta+\phi=5\alpha$, it follows that
$e^{10i\alpha}\to-1$.

The exact expansion gives
\[
 C_5=-12\lim\frac\eta{t^2}
             +4\sqrt2\beta_5.
\]
Since $4\sqrt2\beta_5=2C_5$, this yields
$\eta/t^2\to C_5/12$.  Finally,
$\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ gives the last line of
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:rigidity}.  Restore the powers of $u_j$ and $\delta$.
The Fourier identity for $U^2$ identifies the fourth power of the
remainder norm with the displayed tail mass.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{The same conclusions in source~23} (checked at the write). Source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:rigidity} writes $a_\xi=\rho e^{i\theta}$, $a_{2\xi}=be^{i\psi}$ (its $\theta,\psi$ are this theorem's $\alpha,\beta$) and $\kappa=2^{1/4}/6=\beta_5$. Its $e^{i(\psi-2\theta)}\to1$ is the second limit here; its $\cos(5\theta)\to0$ is equivalent to $e^{10i\alpha}\to-1$; and its last line $\rho^4=2^{-3/2}u^4-2^{-3/4}\kappa^2\delta^{-2}u^6+o(u^6)$ is the last line here, since $2^{-3/4}\kappa^2=2^{-1/4}/36=C_5/24$.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Why the remainder scale cannot be silently strengthened}

The forced second harmonic has amplitude of order $u^2$, while the
tail conclusion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity} is only
$o(u^{3/2})$ in $U^2$.  These statements are consistent.  A further
independent harmonic of amplitude $u^a$, with $3/2<a<2$, can have
fourth-power mass $o(u^6)$ while being larger than $u^2$.
Such a harmonic is invisible to extremality through order $u^6$.
To obtain sharper Fourier approximation one must control the
objective at the next order as well.

The indicator examples in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:indicators} give a stronger
obstruction to $L^2$ rigidity.  For them the centered $L^2$ norm
tends to $\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$, even though every fixed finite
collection of Fourier coefficients tends to zero.  Thus the
appropriate topology for the stated rigidity conclusion is essential.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact next coefficient on the five-point group\srctag{21}}]{The exact next coefficient on the five-point group}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d7}
\srcnote{21}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:five-point-next}

Let $G=\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, and use normalized averages.  For real
mean-zero $f:G\to\mathbb R$, put $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$ and
\[
 Q_3(W)=\mathbb E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}W(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
For fixed $0<\delta<1$, let $M_{\delta,5}(u)$ be the maximum of
$Q_3(W)$ over $W:G\to[0,1]$ with mean $\delta$ and
$\|W-\delta\|_{U^3}=u$.  The same conclusions hold with the boundedness
restriction omitted and with any fixed $\delta>0$.

\begin{theorem}[Third extremal term on $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}
As $u\downarrow0$,
\[
 M_{\delta,5}(u)
 =\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
   +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8
   +O_\delta(u^{10}).
\]
The assertion concerns this fixed five-point group.  It does not
identify the coefficient of $u^8$ when the dimension of an exponent-five
group is allowed to vary.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit and scope.} Source~23's Appendix~A (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:23:sec:dA}) computes the coefficient $20/9$ for one five-point family, which bounds the coefficient of the maximum from below; the theorem here proves that $20/9$ is the coefficient of the maximum on $\Z/5\Z$. The intake's independent maximization on $\Z/5\Z$ (50-digit arithmetic) gave normalized eighth-order residuals $2.32462$, $2.24655$, $2.22823$, $2.22372$ at $t=0.2,0.1,0.05,0.025$, converging to $20/9=2.2222\ldots$ with an $O(t^2)$ gap; that is evidence only. The universal coefficient, over groups of growing dimension, is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{An exact Fourier certificate with arbitrary phases}

Write
\[
 \widehat f(1)=\rho e^{i\alpha},\qquad
 \widehat f(2)=b e^{i\beta},\qquad
 \widehat f(-r)=\overline{\widehat f(r)},
\]
where $\rho,b\ge0$, and set
\[
 \theta=2\alpha-\beta,\qquad \phi=3\alpha+\beta,
 \qquad \psi=\phi-\theta.
\]
Interchanging the two conjugate frequency pairs, if necessary, makes
$\rho\ge b$.  For $a_r=\widehat W(r)$ define
\[
 T(s,t)=\sum_{r\in G}
    a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,\overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
\]
Fourier expansion and orthogonality give
$Q_3(W)=\sum_{s,t\in G}|T(s,t)|^2$.  Because $W$ is real,
substitution $r\mapsto-r-s-t$ shows that $T(s,t)$ is real; shifts of
$r$ and interchange of $s,t$ show that its value is unchanged under
independent sign changes of $s,t$ and their interchange.  The following
six representatives therefore exhaust all $25$ slots:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
 (s,t)&\text{multiplicity}&T(s,t)\\ \hline
 (0,0)&1&\delta^4+2\rho^4+2b^4\\
 (0,1)&4&2\delta^2\rho^2+2\rho^2b^2+b^4\\
 (0,2)&4&2\delta^2b^2+2\rho^2b^2+\rho^4\\
 (1,1)&4&\delta^2\rho^2+2\delta\rho^2b\cos\theta
                    +2\rho b^3\cos(2\theta-\phi)\\
 (2,2)&4&\delta^2b^2+2\delta\rho b^2\cos\psi
                    +2\rho^3b\cos\phi\\
 (1,2)&8&\rho^2b^2+2\delta\rho^2b\cos\theta
                    +2\delta\rho b^2\cos\psi.
\end{array}
\]
Each row is obtained by substituting the five possible values of $r$.
In particular, the exact centered norm is
\begin{align}
 N(\rho,b,\theta,\phi):=u^8
 &=8\rho^8+16(1+\cos^2\phi)\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4\notag\\
 &\quad+16\bigl(1+\cos^2(2\theta-\phi)\bigr)\rho^2b^6+8b^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:five-phase-norm}
\end{align}
Squaring the rows of the table gives the following complete formula:
\begin{align}
 Q_3(\delta+f)
 &=\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)\notag\\
 &\quad+16\delta^3\bigl(\rho^4b\cos\theta
                            +\rho b^4\cos\psi\bigr)\notag\\
 &\quad+24\delta^2\Bigl((3+\cos2\theta)\rho^4b^2
                    +(3+\cos2\psi)\rho^2b^4\notag\\
 &\hspace{40mm}+2\rho^3b^3
                         (\cos\phi+\cos(2\theta-\phi))\Bigr)\notag\\
 &\quad+16\delta\Bigl(\rho^4b^3
                         (3\cos\theta+\cos(2\phi-\theta))\notag\\
 &\hspace{36mm}+\rho^3b^4
                         (3\cos\psi+\cos(3\theta-\phi))\Bigr)
 +N(\rho,b,\theta,\phi).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:five-phase-Q}
\end{align}
Thus the amplitude penalty $16\rho^6b^2$ cannot be decreased by a
different phase choice.  It is minimized by $\cos\phi=0$, which is
compatible with maximizing the leading quintic contribution through
$\cos\theta=1$.

\subsection{Localization of every maximizer}

We first optimize without the interval restriction.  By homogeneity it
suffices to take $\delta=1$ and write $t=u/\delta$.
For a five-point function the norm sphere is compact, so a maximum
exists.  More explicitly, the nonnegative coefficients in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:five-phase-norm} and $\rho\ge b$ give
\[
 8\rho^8\le t^8\le128\rho^8.
\]
Consequently $\rho\asymp t$, uniformly in the phases, and
$\|f\|_\infty\le2(\rho+b)=O(t)$.  After rescaling back to fixed
$0<\delta<1$, the interval restriction $0\le\delta+f\le1$ is therefore
inactive for all sufficiently small $u$.

Put $S=2(\rho^4+b^4)$.  The exact norm gives
\[
 t^8-2S^2\ge16\rho^6b^2,
\]
and hence
\[
 6\sqrt2\,t^4-24(\rho^4+b^4)
 =\frac{6(t^8-2S^2)}{t^4/\sqrt2+S}
 \ge c t^2b^2
\]
for an absolute $c>0$.  Since $b\le\rho=O(t)$, all the quintic,
sextic, and septic terms in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:five-phase-Q} are bounded in
absolute value, respectively, by
$C t^4b$, $C t^4b^2$, and $C t^4b^3$.  In particular, for small $t$,
\[
 Q_3(1+f)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4
 \le -c' t^2b^2+C t^4b+t^8.
\]
The pure-pair example $b=0$ gives the value
$1+6\sqrt2\,t^4+t^8$.  A maximizing function must therefore have
$b\le C't^2$.  This is the needed compactness statement at the
secondary scale: write $b=kt^2$, with $k$ bounded independently of $t$.

\subsection{The leading phase optimization}

Set $q=2^{-3/4}$ and $\rho^2=t^2R$.  After dividing the exact norm by
$t^8$, its defining equation is
\begin{align*}
 1={}&8R^4+16(1+\cos^2\phi)R^3k^2t^2+48R^2k^4t^4\\
     &+16(1+\cos^2(2\theta-\phi))Rk^6t^6+8k^8t^8.
\end{align*}
At $t=0$, its positive solution is $R=q$.  The derivative with respect
to $R$ is $32q^3>0$, so the implicit function theorem gives a real
analytic solution $R(t,k,\theta,\phi)$, uniformly on each bounded set
of $k$.  In fact it is analytic in $t^2$.

Subtract the constant and quartic terms from the objective and divide
by $t^6$.  The apparent singularity at $t=0$ is removable.  The resulting
real analytic function $H$ has the uniform expansion
\[
 H(t,k,\theta,\phi)
   =H_0(k,\theta,\phi)+t^2H_2(k,\theta,\phi)
                      +t^3H_3(k,\theta,\phi)+O(t^4),
\]
where
\[
 H_0=-24q(1+\cos^2\phi)k^2+16q^2k\cos\theta.
\]
For $k\ge0$, the maximum is
\[
 \max H_0=\frac{8q^3}{3}=\frac{2^{3/4}}3,
\]
and equality holds precisely at
\[
 k_0=q/3,\qquad \theta=0\pmod{2\pi},\qquad
 \phi=\pi/2\pmod\pi.
\]
Indeed, $H_0\le-24qk^2+16q^2k$, with equality forcing those phases
when $k>0$, and the remaining quadratic has its unique maximum at
$k_0$.  Compactness and uniform convergence imply that every maximizer
for sufficiently small $t$ lies near one of these two phase classes.
At either class the Hessian, in coordinates $(k,\theta,\phi)$, is
\[
 \operatorname{diag}\left(-48q,-\frac{16q^3}{3},
                                      -\frac{16q^3}{3}\right).
\]
It is negative definite.  Applying the implicit function theorem to
$\nabla H=0$ produces one analytic local maximum near each class;
these exhaust the global maxima.  Complex conjugation interchanges
the two classes and preserves the objective, so their values agree.
The map $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(\theta,\phi)$ has determinant $5$;
its finite collection of lifts merely produces the translates of
these same functions on the five-point group.

\subsection{Calculation of the coefficient \texorpdfstring{$20/9$}{20/9}}

At $\theta=0$, $\phi=\pi/2$, equation
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:five-phase-norm} becomes
\[
 t^8=8\rho^8+16\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4+16\rho^2b^6+8b^8.
\]
Let $x=t^2$, $b=kx$, and write $\rho^2=qxX(z)$, where $z=k^2x/q$.
Then
\[
 X^4+2zX^3+6z^2X^2+2z^3X+z^4=1,
 \qquad X(0)=1.
\]
Successive coefficient comparison gives
\[
 X(z)=1-\frac12z-\frac98z^2+\frac34z^3+O(z^4),
\]
and therefore
\[
 \rho^4=q^2t^4-qk^2t^6-2k^4t^8+O(t^{10}).
\]
The exact objective at these phases simplifies to
\[
 Q_3(1+f)=1+24(\rho^4+b^4)+16\rho^4b
        +96\rho^4b^2+48\rho^2b^4+32\rho^4b^3+t^8.
\]
It follows that
\begin{align*}
 H_0(k,0,\pi/2)&=-24qk^2+16q^2k,\\
 H_2(k,0,\pi/2)&=1-24k^4-16qk^3+96q^2k^2.
\end{align*}
At $k_0=q/3$, using $q^4=1/8$, we obtain
\[
 H_2(k_0,0,\pi/2)
 =1-\frac1{27}-\frac2{27}+\frac43=\frac{20}{9}.
\]

It remains to justify the claimed $O(t^{10})$ remainder, rather than
merely $o(t^8)$.  The analytic maximizing coordinates differ from their
$t=0$ limits by $O(t^2)$ because $H$ has no term of order $t$ and the
Hessian of $H_0$ is invertible.  Substitution changes $H_0$ by $O(t^4)$
and changes $t^2H_2$ by $O(t^4)$.  The only possible contribution of
order $t^3$ in $H$ is
\[
 H_3(k,\theta,\phi)
 =16\sqrt q\,k^4\cos(\phi-\theta)
  +48q^{3/2}k^3\bigl(\cos(2\theta-\phi)+\cos\phi\bigr).
\]
It vanishes at both limiting phase classes.  Thus its contribution at
the moving maximizers is $O(t^5)$, and in particular $O(t^4)$.
Consequently
\[
 \max H=\frac{2^{3/4}}3+\frac{20}{9}t^2+O(t^4).
\]
Multiplying by $t^6$, restoring the constant and quartic terms, and
rescaling by $\delta^8$ proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}.

\paragraph{What the optimizing phases do.}
The limiting phase choice is sufficient to calculate the terms through
$u^8$, but it need not remain exactly optimal for positive $u$.
The $t^3H_3$ perturbation can move the phases.  The theorem therefore
uses the analytic optimizing branch, and does not assume exact phase
stationarity of the displayed elementary model away from $t=0$.

\paragraph{Reproducible certificate.}
The accompanying Python program
\nolinkurl{verify_order5.py} independently enumerates the $5^4$ solutions
of the Fourier cube constraints, records their monomials, and checks
the six-slot formula against direct averages over $5^4$ physical cubes.
It also checks the rational series coefficients and the evaluation
$20/9$.  These finite computations verify identities; the maximization
and the asymptotic remainder follow from the argument above.

\subsection{Sharpness on every exponent-five group}

\begin{corollary}[Pullback of the extremizing model]
\label{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}
Let $G$ be any fixed nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five
and $0<\delta<1$.  There are $[0,1]$ weights $W_u$ on $G$, with
mean $\delta$ and centered norm exactly $u$, for all sufficiently
small $u>0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(W_u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+C_5\delta^2u^6
                       +\frac{20}{9}u^8+O_\delta(u^{10}).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:pullback-lower}
\end{equation}
Consequently the uniform coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main} is
optimal on each such fixed group.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose a nonzero linear functional $\pi:G\to\F_5$.  It is surjective,
and the image of a uniform element of $G$ is uniform on $\F_5$.
For any weight $V$ on $\F_5$, the pullback $V\circ\pi$ has the same
mean, centered $U^3$ norm, and normalized cube count as $V$, since
the four cube parameters push forward independently and uniformly.
Pull back the five-point maximizers from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}.
\end{proof}

For the coefficients through $u^8$, an elementary explicit model
already suffices.  Set
\begin{equation}
 b=\beta_5\delta^{-1}u^2,\qquad
 a_1=\rho e^{i\pi/10},\qquad a_2=b e^{i\pi/5},
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:elementary-model}
\end{equation}
with conjugate coefficients at $-1,-2$, and choose the unique
positive $\rho$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 8\rho^8+16\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4+16\rho^2b^6+8b^8=u^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:elementary-norm}
\end{equation}
Existence and uniqueness for small $u$ follow from strict monotonicity
in $\rho$ and from $8b^8<u^8$.  In physical space this is
\[
 W_u(x)=\delta+2\rho\cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{5}+\frac\pi{10}\right)
              +2b\cos\left(\frac{4\pi x}{5}+\frac\pi5\right).
\]
The coefficients tend to zero, so $W_u\in[0,1]$ when $u$ is small.
The fixed choice of the limiting amplitude and phases has the same
$20/9$ coefficient, although its terms beyond $u^8$ need not be
globally optimal.  Figure~\ref{gsr:cc:21:fig:convergence} illustrates the
approach to the two sharp coefficients using the exact formulas.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/21-characteristic-five-coefficient_convergence.pdf}
\caption{The exact elementary model at $\delta=0.4$, evaluated with
high-precision arithmetic.  The horizontal axis is $t=u/\delta$.
Left: the normalized sixth-order correction tends to $C_5$.
Right: after subtracting that correction as well, the normalized
eighth-order residual tends to $20/9$.  The plot evaluates a proven
formula; it is not used as evidence for the general upper bound.}
\label{gsr:cc:21:fig:convergence}
\end{figure}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Indicator sharpness and its limitations\srctag{21}}]{Indicator sharpness and its limitations}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d8}
\srcnote{21}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:indicators}

Weights are convenient because the Fourier parameters vary
continuously.  The sharp coefficients also have consequences for
actual sets.  A fixed five-point group has only finitely many sets,
so a nontrivial small-norm limit at a prescribed positive density
requires the group to grow.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp indicator families]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:indicator}
For every $0<\delta<1$, there are dimensions $n_j\to\infty$ and
sets $A_j\subset\F_5^{n_j}$ with densities $\delta_j\to\delta$
and centered norms $v_j=\|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_{U^3}\to0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(1_{A_j})=\delta_j^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta_j^4v_j^4
           +C_5\delta_j^2v_j^6+\frac{20}{9}v_j^8+o(v_j^8).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:indicator-sharpness}
\end{equation}
Thus $C_5$ remains optimal for indicator sets in growing exponent-five
groups, and $20/9$ is a lower bound for any universal eighth-order
extremal coefficient in that setting.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $u_j\downarrow0$ and lift the elementary model
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:elementary-model} to $G_j=\F_5^{n_j}$ by its first
coordinate.  Denote the lifted weight by $W_j$.  Its mean is $\delta$,
its centered norm is $u_j$, and its cube count has expansion
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:pullback-lower} through $u_j^8$, independently of $n_j$.

Include each point $x\in G_j$ independently with probability $W_j(x)$.
Let $X_x$ be its indicator.  We approximate three statistics:
the density, $Q_3(X)$, and $Q_3(X-\delta)$.
If the eight vertices of a cube are distinct, independence makes the
expectation of its product equal to the corresponding weighted
product.  For any two distinct vertices, the equation that they
coincide is a nontrivial linear equation in the sidelengths and holds
with probability $|G_j|^{-1}$.  Hence at most $28/|G_j|$ of all
normalized cubes have a repeated vertex.  Since all relevant factors
have absolute value at most one, the expectation error in either
cube statistic is at most $56/|G_j|$.

Changing one inclusion variable affects at most $8/|G_j|$ of either
normalized cube polynomial, by a union bound over the vertex at
which that point occurs.  A bounded-difference variance estimate,
or the elementary Efron--Stein inequality, gives variance
$O(|G_j|^{-1})$.  The density has variance at most
$1/(4|G_j|)$.  Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound therefore
show that, for sufficiently large $n_j$, some realization
simultaneously approximates all three target statistics to an
arbitrarily prescribed positive accuracy.

Choose the accuracy to be $o(u_j^{12})$, for example a sufficiently
small multiple of $u_j^{14}$.  Recentring $X$ from $\delta$ to its
actual density $\delta_j$ changes a cube product by at most
$8|\delta_j-\delta|$, by telescoping.  Thus
\[
 v_j^8=u_j^8+o(u_j^{12}),\qquad
 \delta_j-\delta=o(u_j^{12}),\qquad
 Q_3(1_{A_j})-Q_3(W_j)=o(u_j^{12}).
\]
It follows that $v_j/u_j\to1$ and
$v_j^4-u_j^4=o(u_j^8)$; the corresponding changes in the sixth- and
eighth-order terms are also $o(u_j^8)$.  Substitution proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:indicator-sharpness}.  The dimensions can be chosen
strictly increasing at each step.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} Source~23's Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:23:prop:indicator} realizes the coefficients through order $u^6$ by indicator sets in the same way; the theorem here goes through $u^8$. Both are lower examples, not upper bounds.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A strengthened set version of Lemma 3.10]
\label{gsr:cc:21:cor:alpha}
Let $A\subset G$, where $G$ is a nontrivial finite abelian group
of exponent five, let $N=|G|$ and $\delta=|A|/N>0$, and suppose
\[
            \|1_A-\delta\|_{U^3}^8\le\alpha.
\]
For absolute $c,C>0$, if $\alpha^{1/8}\le c\delta$, then
\begin{equation}
 \#\{\text{parameterized three-cubes in }A\}
 \le N^4\left(\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4\alpha^{1/2}
                    +C_5\delta^2\alpha^{3/4}+C\alpha\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:alpha-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main} at the actual centered norm and then
increase that norm to its budget $\alpha^{1/8}$.  All displayed
powers have positive coefficients, so this substitution preserves
the upper bound.  Multiply the normalized count by $N^4$.
\end{proof}

In this setting the triangle-inequality estimate corresponding to
Gowers's Lemma~3.10 is
$N^4(\delta+\alpha^{1/8})^8$.
The first error in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:alpha-bound} is order $\alpha^{1/2}$,
and its next sharp coefficient occurs at $\alpha^{3/4}$.
The characteristic-five restriction is essential to this particular
secondary statement.  It is not a replacement for the prime-cyclic
bound at arbitrary primes.

\subsection{Failure of stronger \texorpdfstring{$L^2$}{L2} rigidity}

For the indicator examples,
\[
 \|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_2^2
       =\delta_j(1-\delta_j)\longrightarrow\delta(1-\delta)>0.
\]
On the other hand each Fourier coefficient is $O(v_j)$, by
$\|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_{U^2}^4\le v_j^4/\sqrt2$.
If $P_j$ projects onto at most a fixed number $m$ of frequencies,
Parseval gives $\|P_j(1_{A_j}-\delta_j)\|_2^2=O(mv_j^2)\to0$.
The orthogonal remainder therefore has $L^2$ norm tending to
$\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$.  Even the strong asymptotic equality
in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:indicator-sharpness} does not force a small
$L^2$ remainder after removing finitely many harmonics.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A quantitative projection consequence of cube Cauchy--Schwarz\srctag{21}}]{A quantitative projection consequence of cube Cauchy--Schwarz}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d9}
\srcnote{21}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:projection}

The proof of the sharp coefficient used the stronger explicit
sixth- and seventh-degree formulas.  For related problems where such
formulas are unavailable, a general norm argument still provides a
uniform way to pass from near equality to approximation on a quotient.
The following is an elementary consequence of classical norm
geometry; its inclusion is methodological, not a priority claim.

\begin{proposition}[Loss under subgroup averaging controls the remainder]
\label{gsr:cc:21:prop:projection}
Let $G$ be any finite abelian group, $d\ge2$, $p=2^d$, and
\[
 P_H f(x)=\E_{h\in H}f(x+h)
\]
for a subgroup $H\le G$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \|f-P_Hf\|_{U^d}
 \le2\left(\|f\|_{U^d}^{p}-\|P_Hf\|_{U^d}^{p}\right)^{1/p}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:projection}
\end{equation}
In particular, equality of the two norms holds if and only if
$f=P_Hf$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Cube expansion and Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz yield, with
$a=\|f\|_{U^d}$ and $b=\|g\|_{U^d}$,
\[
 \|f+g\|_{U^d}^{p}+\|f-g\|_{U^d}^{p}
 \le2\sum_{j\ {\rm even}}\binom pj a^{p-j}b^j.
\]
Use weighted AM--GM on each monomial and the identities
\[
 \sum_{j\ {\rm even}}j\binom pj
 =\sum_{j\ {\rm even}}(p-j)\binom pj=p2^{p-2}
\]
to obtain Clarkson's inequality
\begin{equation}
 \left\|\frac{f+g}{2}\right\|_{U^d}^{p}
 +\left\|\frac{f-g}{2}\right\|_{U^d}^{p}
 \le\frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^{p}+\|g\|_{U^d}^{p}}2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:clarkson}
\end{equation}
Subgroup averaging is contractive by translation invariance and the
triangle inequality.  Apply \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:clarkson} to $f$ and its
translate $T_hf$ for $h\in H$.  Since
$P_H((f+T_hf)/2)=P_Hf$, the first summand on the left is at least
$\|P_Hf\|_{U^d}^p$.  Hence
\[
 \|f-T_hf\|_{U^d}
 \le2\left(\|f\|_{U^d}^{p}-\|P_Hf\|_{U^d}^{p}\right)^{1/p}.
\]
Average $f-T_hf$ over $h\in H$ and use the triangle inequality.
The final equivalence follows because $U^d$ is a norm for $d\ge2$.
\end{proof}

For $d=3$ and $H=\ker\xi$, $P_H$ retains exactly the frequencies in
$\langle\xi\rangle$.  Thus near saturation of its norm implies
approximation by a five-point quotient in $U^3$, uniformly over the
ambient dimension.  The proposition alone does not establish that a
global maximizer of $Q_3(\delta+f)$ lies on that quotient: projection
also changes the centered norm, and restoring the norm by rescaling
changes the different-degree terms unequally.  This is precisely an
obstacle in the higher-dimensional eighth-order question.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp secondary three-cube asymptotics in characteristic five\srctag{23}}]{Sharp secondary three-cube asymptotics in characteristic five}\label{gsr:cc:23:sec:d7}
\srcnote{23}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:23:five:section}

The earlier project report \emph{Sharp Extremal Refinements in Gowers's
Szemer\'edi Framework} proved that exponent five changes the first secondary
power from $u^{16/3}$ to $u^6$ \cite{prior23extremal}. Its explicit example had coefficient
$2^{3/4}/3$, but optimality of this coefficient was left open.  We determine
that coefficient, uniformly in the dimension, and obtain an $O(u^8)$
remainder.  These are local extremal statements about cube counts, with no
claim of an improved global quantitative Szemer\'edi theorem.

For a real function $W$ on a finite abelian group $G$, write
\[
 Q(W)=\mathbb E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3\in G}
       \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^3} W(x+v\cdot h)
       =\|W\|_{U^3}^8.
\]
All averages and Fourier transforms are normalized; sums on the dual are
unnormalized.  Repeated vertices and zero directions are included.

For comparison with Gowers's Lemma~3.10, his degree-two uniformity
parameter is $\alpha=u^8$.  His triangle-inequality bound has normalized
form $(\delta+u)^8$ \cite{gowers}.  The sharper leading term
$6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$ and the order-five lower example were established
in the earlier project reports \cite{repo23research,prior23extremal}.
The result below determines the previously unresolved secondary constant.

\begin{theorem}[The exact characteristic-five coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:23:five:main}
There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that the following holds for every
nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five.  If $\delta>0$, $f:G\to
\mathbb R$ has mean zero, and $u=\|f\|_{U^3}\le c\delta$, then
\[
 Q(\delta+f)\le \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u^6+Cu^8.
 \tag{F1}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:bound}
\]
No pointwise bound on $f$ is required, and $c,C$ are independent of the group
and its dimension.  For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, on every fixed nontrivial
group $G$ of exponent five, the supremum over weights $W:G\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\mathbb EW=\delta$ and $\|W-\delta\|_{U^3}\le u$ obeys
\[
 M_{\delta,G}(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u^6+O(u^8)
       \qquad(u\downarrow0).
 \tag{F2}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:sup}
\]
The same expansion holds when the supremum also ranges over all such groups.
The range of sufficiently small $u$ in the lower construction may depend on
$\delta$, because the weights must lie in $[0,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route.} This is source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, proved independently by the same mechanism (a positive cubic statistic for the incomplete cubes, the quadratic cost of the second harmonic); source~21 has sharper intermediate constants, the phase envelope and the next coefficient on $\Z/5\Z$ (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:charfive}). It answers source~14's Question~1 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:exponentfive}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Ordered cube counts in uniform subsets]
\label{gsr:cc:23:five:sets-bound}
There are absolute $c,C>0$ such that, if $A\subset G=\F_5^n$ has density
$\delta>0$ and $\|1_A-\delta\|_{U^3}^8\le\alpha$ with
$\alpha^{1/8}\le c\delta$, its number of ordered three-cubes is at most
\[
 |G|^4\left(\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4\alpha^{1/2}
 +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2\alpha^{3/4}+C\alpha\right).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main} at the actual centered norm and use
monotonicity of the displayed nonnegative terms.  Normalization of the
four independent cube parameters supplies the factor $|G|^4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact terms of degree six and a useful degree-seven bound}

Let $a_r=\widehat f(r)$, so $a_0=0$ and $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$.  Put
\[
 \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\qquad S=\sum_r\lambda_r^2=\|f\|_{U^2}^4,
 \qquad
 T(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                    \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
\]
Fourier inversion and orthogonality give
\[
 u^8=\sum_{s,t}|T(s,t)|^2.
 \tag{F3}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:T}
\]
One can see this identity directly by expanding all eight physical-space
factors into characters.  The surviving frequencies satisfy the four
equations saying that the coefficient of $x,h_1,h_2,h_3$ is zero.
After multiplying the frequency at vertex $v$ by $(-1)^{|v|}$, their
solutions are exactly affine cubes $r+s v_1+t v_2+z v_3$ in the dual
group.  This follows either by solving the four equations or by Boolean
finite differences.  Since $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$, the surviving product
is the usual conjugated dual cube product.  Summing over the last
direction $z$ pairs two translated square products, giving
$\sum_{s,t}|T(s,t)|^2$ with no missing normalization factor.
Define the following homogeneous forms:
\begin{align*}
 B_5&=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^{3}a_r,\\
 A_6&=\sum_{s,t}\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_{s+t},\\
 B_6&=\sum_{s,t}a_t^2\lambda_{s+t}a_s\overline{a_{s+2t}},\\
 C_6&=\sum_{s,t}a_s^2a_t^2\overline{a_{s+t}}^{2}.
\end{align*}
These are real: for instance, simultaneous negation of all frequency
variables conjugates the summands.  There is a real homogeneous form $V_7$
of degree seven for which
\[
 Q(\delta+f)=\delta^8+12\delta^4S+8\delta^3B_5
       +\delta^2(12A_6+12B_6+4C_6)+8\delta V_7+u^8.
 \tag{F4}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:centered}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 |B_6|,|C_6|\le A_6,
 \qquad |V_7|\le u^4\sqrt{A_6}.
 \tag{F5}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:67-bounds}
\]

Here are details of the finite cube calculation in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:centered}.
Terms with one, two, or three selected vertices vanish by centering.  Of the
$70$ four-vertex supports, twelve are parallelograms and contribute $S$;
the other supports have independent forms.  Of the $56$ five-vertex
supports, eight have no dependent four-subset.  These are the cube-symmetric
copies of $\{000,100,010,001,111\}$ and contribute $B_5$; every other
five-vertex support has a Fourier constraint forcing a selected coefficient
to be $a_0$.  All nonzero minors needed here are units in characteristic
five.  More explicitly, each of the twelve parallelograms has four
extensions to a five-set.  No five-set contains two different
parallelograms: their affine planes would share three cube vertices,
whereas two distinct planes meet in a line and a line contains at most
two Boolean vertices.  These $48$ extensions have an independent fifth
form, whose centered factor averages to zero.  The other eight supports
are the stated symmetric copies.  A six-vertex support is classified by the Hamming distance of the
two omitted vertices.  Distances one, two, and three occur $12,12,4$ times.
For the representatives omitting respectively
\[
 \{000,100\},\qquad\{000,110\},\qquad\{000,111\},
\]
the Fourier constraints have solutions, in the lexicographic order of the
remaining vertices,
\[
 (s+t,-s,-t,-s-t,s,t),\quad
 (t,s+t,-s-2t,-s-t,s,t),\quad
 (t,s,-s-t,-s-t,s,t).
\]
Their products are exactly the summands defining $A_6,B_6,C_6$.  Cube
symmetries preserve normalized averages by invertible changes of the cube
parameters.  The eight seven-vertex supports are also symmetric.

The bound for $C_6$ follows by taking absolute values.  For $B_6$, put
$r=s+t$ and apply Cauchy--Schwarz:
\begin{align*}
 |B_6|&\le\sum_{r,t}\lambda_r\lambda_t
                    |a_{r-t}|\,|a_{r+t}|\\
 &\le\left(\sum_{r,t}\lambda_r\lambda_t\lambda_{r-t}\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_{r,t}\lambda_r\lambda_t\lambda_{r+t}\right)^{1/2}
       =A_6.
\end{align*}
For the last equality use $\lambda_{-t}=\lambda_t$.

For the septic bound, let $P(s,t)$ be the coefficient of $\delta$ when the
Fourier coefficient $a_0=0$ in $T(s,t)$ is replaced by $\delta$.  It is the
sum of four cubic expressions, one from each possible zero position in the
four factors.  Each expression has squared $\ell^2(s,t)$ norm $A_6$;
for example, the first is
$\overline{a_s}\,\overline{a_t}a_{s+t}$.  The others are obtained by
invertible changes of $(s,t)$ and conjugation.  Consequently
$\|P\|_2\le4\sqrt{A_6}$.  The coefficient of $\delta$ in
$\sum_{s,t}|T_{\delta+f}(s,t)|^2$ is
$2\operatorname{Re}\langle T,P\rangle=8V_7$.  Equation
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:T} and Cauchy--Schwarz prove the septic bound.

\subsection{A Fourier concentration penalty specific to order five}

Choose a largest conjugate pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$, and write
\[
 \rho=|a_\xi|,\qquad b=|a_{2\xi}|,\qquad
 D=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4,
 \qquad S=2\rho^4+D.
\]
Since every nonzero character has order five, the doubled pair is distinct
from the largest pair, and $2b^4\le D$.  Define
\[
 E=\sum_{r+s=t+w}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w
   =\|\lambda*\lambda\|_2^2,
 \qquad M=\sum_r|a_r|^8.
\]
The slots $s=0$ or $t=0$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:T} contribute exactly $2E-S^2$.
In the nonnegative energy sum retain the three families
\[
 (r=t,\ s=w),\qquad(r=w,\ s=t),\qquad(s=-r,\ w=-t).
\]
Each has weight $S^2$, each pairwise intersection has weight $M$, and their
triple intersection has zero weight, since it forces $2r=0$ and $a_0=0$.
Thus $E\ge3S^2-3M$.  Conjugate pairing gives $M\le S^2/2$, so
\[
 u^8\ge5S^2-6M\ge2S^2.
 \tag{F6}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:basic}
\]
Maximality of $\rho$ also gives $M\le\rho^4S$ and hence
\[
 u^8\ge(2+3D/S)S^2.
 \tag{F7}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:localize}
\]

Order five supplies eight additional energy quadruples.  Start with
$(\xi,\xi,-\xi,-2\xi)$ and apply interchange of the two sides,
interchange of the unequal entries on a side, and simultaneous negation.
These are eight distinct solutions of $r+s=t+w$, since $5\xi=0$.
They belong to none of the three preceding families, and each has weight
$\rho^6b^2$.  The tail eighth-power mass is at most $D^2/2$, so retaining
both the new quadruples and the concentration defect proves
\[
 \boxed{\quad u^8\ge2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2.\quad}
 \tag{F8}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:combined-penalty}
\]
Indeed, the axes are at least
$5S^2-6(2\rho^8+D^2/2)+16\rho^6b^2
 =2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2$.

There is also a useful dimension-free estimate for the sextic quantity:
\[
 A_6\le3\sqrt E\sqrt D,
 \qquad E\le\frac{u^8+S^2}{2}\le\frac34u^8.
 \tag{F9}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:A-small}
\]
To prove the first inequality, set $q_r=\lambda_r$ outside
$\{\xi,-\xi\}$ and zero on that pair.  No three members of
$\{\xi,-\xi\}$ sum to zero, because $\xi$ has order five.
Every nonzero term of $A_6$ therefore uses at least one tail index.
The union bound, evenness of $\lambda$, and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 A_6\le3\langle q,\lambda*\lambda\rangle
     \le3\|q\|_2\|\lambda*\lambda\|_2=3\sqrt D\sqrt E.
\]
The second inequality follows from the axes contribution and
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:basic}.  This step is crucial: small fourth-power Fourier
tail mass need not imply small $L^2$ mass, but it does control these
particular incomplete-cube terms.

\subsection{Uniform optimization and proof of the upper bound}

The zero function is immediate.  Otherwise write $g=f/u$, $t=u/\delta$,
and use all Fourier letters in this subsection for $g$, so $\|g\|_{U^3}=1$.
Put
\[
 S_0=1/\sqrt2,\quad\eta=S_0-S\ge0,\quad
 F=Q(1+tg)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4.
\]
We may assume $0<t\le1$ and $F>0$; otherwise the assertion is immediate.
The ordinary cube Cauchy--Schwarz bounds on the $28$ sextic and eight
septic terms give
\[
 F=-12\eta t^4+8t^5B_5+R,
 \qquad |R|\le37t^6.
 \tag{F10}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:first-local}
\]
Since $|B_5|\le\rho S<1$, first $\eta=O(t)$.  For small absolute $t$,
$S\ge S_0/2$, and \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:localize} gives $D\le8\eta/3$.
Consequently $\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ is bounded away from zero.
Equation \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:combined-penalty} gives $b^2=O(\eta)$.

If $a_\xi=\rho e^{i\theta}$, the two selected terms of $B_5$ are
\[
 2\rho^4\operatorname{Re}(a_{2\xi}e^{-2i\theta}).
\]
The remaining terms have total absolute value at most $\rho D$.
Thus $|B_5|=O(\sqrt\eta+\eta)$.  Inserting this in
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:first-local}, absorbing the $O(t\eta)$ term, and solving the
quadratic inequality in $\sqrt\eta$ yields
\[
 \eta=O(t^2),\qquad D=O(t^2),\qquad b=O(t).
 \tag{F11}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:local-scale}
\]
All constants here are absolute.

Let $A_0=2^{-3/2}$.  Since
$\rho^4=A_0-(\eta+D)/2$, expanding
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:combined-penalty} using \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:local-scale} gives
\[
 \eta\ge\frac32D+2^{1/4}b^2-O(t^4).
 \tag{F12}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:eta-sharp}
\]
For clarity, $12\rho^4D=3\sqrt2D+O(t^4)$,
$16\rho^6b^2=2^{7/4}b^2+O(t^4)$, and
$1-2S^2=2\sqrt2\eta-2\eta^2$; division by $2\sqrt2$ gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:eta-sharp}.

Also $B_5\le S_0b+D$.  By \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:A-small}, $A_6\le3\sqrt D$.
Using the exact expansion \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:centered} and the sharper
incomplete-cube bounds \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:67-bounds} now gives
\begin{align*}
 F\le{}&-18Dt^4-12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5+8Dt^5\\
       &+84t^6\sqrt D+8\sqrt3\,t^7D^{1/4}+O(t^8).
\end{align*}
For $t\le1$, the two terms linear in $D$ are at most $-10Dt^4$.
Completing the square in $b$ yields
\[
 -12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5
 \le\frac{2^{3/4}}3t^6,
 \quad b=\kappa t\text{ at equality},
 \qquad\kappa=\frac{2^{1/4}}6=\frac{2^{5/4}}{12}.
\]
Finally, on putting $y=D^{1/4}/t$, the remaining terms involving $D$ are
\[
 t^8\bigl(-10y^4+84y^2+8\sqrt3\,y\bigr)=O(t^8),
\]
because this polynomial is bounded above on $y\ge0$.  Thus
$F\le(2^{3/4}/3)t^6+O(t^8)$ with absolute constants.  Multiplication by
$\delta^8$ proves \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:bound}.

\subsection{An exact five-point model}

On $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, set
\[
 a_0=0,\qquad a_1=\rho e^{i\pi/10},\qquad
 a_2=b e^{i\pi/5},\qquad a_{-j}=\overline{a_j}.
\]
The resulting function $f$ is real and centered.  Direct use of
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:T} gives the exact identities
\begin{align*}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8
   &=8\rho^8+16\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4+16\rho^2b^6+8b^8,\\
 Q(\delta+f)
   &=\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)+16\delta^3\rho^4b
      +96\delta^2\rho^4b^2+48\delta^2\rho^2b^4
      +32\delta\rho^4b^3+\|f\|_{U^3}^8.
 \tag{F13}\label{gsr:cc:23:five:model}
\end{align*}
A compact certificate is the following table for $T_{\delta+f}(s,t)$.
Sign changes in either coordinate and interchange of the coordinates
give the stated multiplicities.
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|l}
 (s,t)&\text{multiplicity}&T_{\delta+f}(s,t)\\\hline
 (0,0)&1&\delta^4+2\rho^4+2b^4\\
 (0,1)&4&2\delta^2\rho^2+2\rho^2b^2+b^4\\
 (0,2)&4&2\delta^2b^2+2\rho^2b^2+\rho^4\\
 (1,1)&4&\delta^2\rho^2+2\delta\rho^2b\\
 (2,2)&4&\delta^2b^2\\
 (1,2)&8&\rho^2b^2+2\delta\rho^2b
\end{array}
\]
The multiplicities sum to $25$.  Each entry is a sum over five bases $r$;
the potentially additional terms cancel since $\cos(5\pi/10)=0$.
Squaring and summing proves \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:model}.

Choose $b=\kappa u^2/\delta$ and the unique positive $\rho$ making the
first expression in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:model} equal to $u^8$.  Such a $\rho$
exists for sufficiently small $u/\delta$, since the expression is strictly
increasing in $\rho$ and $8b^8<u^8$.  With $t=u/\delta$,
\[
 \rho^4=u^4\left(2^{-3/2}-2^{-3/4}\kappa^2t^2+O(t^4)\right).
\]
Substitution gives
\[
 Q(\delta+f)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u^6+O(u^8).
\]
The weights lie in $[0,1]$ when $u$ is sufficiently small depending on
$\delta$, because $|f|\le2\rho+2b\to0$.  Every nontrivial exponent-five
group has a surjective character quotient onto $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$;
pullback along that quotient preserves normalized cube averages, means,
and uniformity norms.  This proves the lower bound on each fixed group.
For a norm budget, the upper bound applies at the actual norm, and the
positive terms in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:bound} are increasing in that norm.
This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}.

\subsection{Phase selection for families attaining the secondary term}

\begin{theorem}[Necessary Fourier geometry]
\label{gsr:cc:23:five:rigidity}
Fix $\delta>0$.  Suppose $f_j$ are real centered functions on finite groups
of exponent five, $u_j=\|f_j\|_{U^3}\downarrow0$, and
\[
 Q(\delta+f_j)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u_j^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u_j^6+o_\delta(u_j^6).
\]
Choose a largest pair and write
$a_{j,\xi_j}=\rho_j e^{i\theta_j}$ and
$a_{j,2\xi_j}=b_j e^{i\psi_j}$; the latter is nonzero for large $j$.
Then
\begin{align*}
 b_j&\sim\kappa\delta^{-1}u_j^2,\\
 e^{i(\psi_j-2\theta_j)}&\longrightarrow1,
       \qquad\cos(5\theta_j)\longrightarrow0,\\
 \sum_{r\notin\{\xi_j,-\xi_j\}}|a_{j,r}|^4
       &=o_\delta(u_j^6),\\
 \rho_j^4&=2^{-3/2}u_j^4
       -2^{-3/4}\kappa^2\delta^{-2}u_j^6+o_\delta(u_j^6).
\end{align*}
These are necessary conditions, not a claimed sufficient characterization
of all extremizing families.  No $L^2$ approximation is asserted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Work in the normalized variables of the upper proof and set
$\phi=\psi-2\theta$.  Its estimates, retaining the actual phase, give
\[
 \frac{F}{t^6}\le
 -18\frac D{t^2}-12\,2^{1/4}\left(\frac bt\right)^2
 +4\sqrt2\,\frac bt\cos\phi+o(1).
\]
Here $D=O(t^2)$, $b=O(t)$, the sextic error divided by $t^6$ is $O(t)$,
and the septic error is $o(1)$.  The displayed expression has unique
maximum $2^{3/4}/3$ in the variables $b/t\ge0$, $D/t^2\ge0$ and
$\cos\phi\le1$, attained when $b/t=\kappa$, $D/t^2=0$ and
$\cos\phi=1$.  It follows that these three limits hold.  The exact
centered expansion then gives
$\eta/t^2\to2^{1/4}\kappa^2$ and the claimed expansion of $\rho^4$.

To detect the phase of the largest coefficient, also retain the four
off-axis slots $(s,t)=(\pm2\xi,\pm2\xi)$.  They have the same modulus.
The contribution to $T(2\xi,2\xi)$ from $r\in\langle\xi\rangle$ is
exactly $2\rho^3b\cos(3\theta+\psi)$.  All remaining terms stay outside
$\langle\xi\rangle$ in all four positions, so their sum has absolute
value at most
$D_{\rm out}=\sum_{r\notin\langle\xi\rangle}|a_r|^4\le D$
by H\"older.  Since $D=o(t^2)$ and $b\sim\kappa t$, the four slots supply
\[
 16\rho^6b^2\cos^2(3\theta+\psi)+o(t^2)
\]
in addition to the axes lower bound.  Applying the already established
limits in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:combined-penalty} forces
$\cos(3\theta+\psi)\to0$.  Since
$e^{i(\psi-2\theta)}\to1$, this is equivalent to $\cos(5\theta)\to0$.
Rescaling proves every stated conclusion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sharpness for subsets in growing dimension}

\begin{proposition}[Indicator realization]\label{gsr:cc:23:prop:indicator}
For every $0<\delta<1$, there are dimensions $n_j\to\infty$ and subsets
$A_j\subset\mathbb F_5^{n_j}$, with densities $\delta_j\to\delta$ and
$v_j=\|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_{U^3}\downarrow0$, such that
\[
 \frac{Q(1_{A_j})-\delta_j^8-6\sqrt2\,\delta_j^4v_j^4}
      {\delta_j^2v_j^6}\longrightarrow\frac{2^{3/4}}3.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Take the five-point model at parameters $u_j$ decreasing geometrically and
pull it back to $\mathbb F_5^n$ using the first coordinate.  Include each
point independently with its prescribed weight.  With $N=5^n$, at most
$28/N$ of normalized cube parameter tuples have two coincident vertices:
each equality of two distinct cube forms holds with probability $1/N$.
On all other tuples, independence makes the expected indicator product
equal the weighted product.  The same holds for products centered at the
fixed mean $\delta$.  Both expectation errors are therefore $O(1/N)$.

Changing one inclusion decision changes either cube polynomial by at most
$8/N$, because each of the eight vertex forms has uniform fibers.
Their variances are $O(1/N)$ by the bounded-difference variance estimate;
the density variance is at most $1/(4N)$.  Choosing $n$ sufficiently large
gives a realization in which the density, the indicator cube count, and
the cube count centered at $\delta$ all approximate their weighted values
to any prescribed error.  Recentring at the realized density costs at most
eight times the density error, by telescoping the bounded products.

Choose all these errors $o(u_j^{10})$.  Then
$v_j^8=u_j^8+o(u_j^{10})$, hence
$v_j^4=u_j^4+o(u_j^6)$ and $v_j/u_j\to1$.
The model expansion transfers to the displayed ratio.  The geometric
choice of $u_j$ makes the actual $v_j$ strictly decrease after finitely many
terms are discarded.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A closer expansion of the five-point example\srctag{23}}]{A closer expansion of the five-point example}\label{gsr:cc:23:sec:dA}
\srcnote{23}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:cc:23:app:tertiary}

This appendix records a lower-model computation useful for the second
research question.  It does not identify the global tertiary optimum.
Use the model of \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:model}, with
$\kappa=2^{1/4}/6$, $t=u/\delta$, and $b=\kappa u^2/\delta$.
Let $A=2^{-3/2}$.  Solving the norm equation to two further orders gives
\[
 \frac{\rho^4}{u^4}
 =A-A^{1/2}\kappa^2t^2-2\kappa^4t^4+O(t^6).
\]
To verify this, substitute $A+a t^2+c t^4$ into the first equation in
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:model}, divide by $u^8$, and compare coefficients.
The constant coefficient is $8A^2=1$; the next two equations are
\[
 16Aa+16A^{3/2}\kappa^2=0,
\]
\[
 8a^2+16Ac+24A^{1/2}a\kappa^2+48A\kappa^4=0.
\]
They give $a=-A^{1/2}\kappa^2$ and $c=-2\kappa^4$.
The positive root is analytic in $t^2$ near zero, since the derivative
of the constant norm equation with respect to $\rho^4/u^4$ is
$16A\ne0$, so the expansion has the indicated remainder.

Substitution into the weighted-count formula gives the coefficient of
$u^8$ as
\[
 -24\kappa^4-16A^{1/2}\kappa^3+96A\kappa^2+1
 =-\frac1{27}-\frac2{27}+\frac43+1=\frac{20}{9}.
\]
Consequently this particular family satisfies
\begin{equation}
 Q(\delta+f)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
 +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8
 +O(u^{10}/\delta^2).
 \label{gsr:cc:23:eq:model-tertiary}
\end{equation}
It follows that a global tertiary coefficient, if it exists in this
normalization, must be at least $20/9$.  The uniform upper argument in
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:section} bounds that coefficient but does not equate
it with the model value.
